q: A team manages servers by SSHing into each machine and running setup commands by hand. After an outage, nobody can reconstruct exactly what was configured on the failed server. Which statement best describes the Infrastructure as Code practice that would have prevented this?
options: Infrastructure defined declaratively in version-controlled, machine-readable files that are provisioned automatically
A shared wiki page documenting every manual step the team performs on each server
A backup script that snapshots each server's disk nightly
Hiring a dedicated engineer to run all setup commands from a single laptop
explain: IaC means infrastructure lives as declarative, version-controlled code — so every server is reproducible and every change is a reviewable commit. A wiki (B) documents but does not enforce; snapshots (C) preserve a mess without explaining it; centralizing manual work (D) keeps the same unrepeatable process. Only A makes the environment reconstructable.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: An engineer writes a shell script that creates a VPC, then a subnet, then a security group, executing each AWS CLI call in order. A colleague proposes replacing it with Terraform. What is the fundamental difference between the two approaches?
options: The shell script is declarative and Terraform is imperative
The shell script describes ordered steps to execute, while Terraform describes the desired end state and determines the steps itself
Terraform runs shell scripts faster than bash does
There is no difference; both are Infrastructure as Code
explain: The shell script is imperative — it lists steps in order and knows nothing about the desired end state. Terraform is declarative — you declare what you want and it computes the how, including ordering from the dependency graph. A reverses the terms. C is nonsense. D is wrong: a hand-run script with no state, no plan, and no versioning of intent is not IaC practice.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company runs `terraform apply` twice in a row with no configuration changes. The second run reports `0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy`. Which IaC advantage does this demonstrate?
options: Elasticity
Idempotency — the same configuration applied repeatedly converges on the same result
High availability
Immutable infrastructure
explain: Idempotency is exactly this: repeated applies of the same configuration produce no changes after the first converges. Elasticity (A) is about scaling capacity; high availability (C) is about uptime design; immutability (D) is about replacing rather than modifying — related, but the observed behavior is idempotency.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A startup runs production on AWS, analytics on GCP, and DNS through Cloudflare. The platform team is tired of maintaining three different native toolchains (CloudFormation, Deployment Manager, and API scripts). Which Terraform characteristic directly solves their problem?
options: Terraform provisions infrastructure faster than any native tool
Terraform's provider-agnostic workflow: one language, one CLI, and one plan/apply loop across all providers
Terraform is free, while native tools charge per deployment
Terraform automatically converts CloudFormation templates into working HCL
explain: Terraform's strategic pitch — and a 004 objective — is the provider-agnostic, multi-cloud workflow: one HCL language and one workflow across hundreds of providers. A is an unprovable speed claim the exam never makes. C is false (native tools are generally free; clouds charge for resources). D is false; Terraform does not translate CloudFormation.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: After a security incident, an auditor asks: `Who changed the production firewall rules last month, when, and was it approved?` The team manages firewalls in Terraform with every change merged through pull requests. Which IaC advantage answers the auditor?
options: Automation and speed — changes deploy in minutes
Version control — every change is a timestamped, peer-reviewed, reversible commit
Cost control — `terraform plan` shows changes before they happen
Consistency — every environment looks identical
explain: Version-controlled infrastructure gives a complete audit trail: who, when, what, and the review record. Speed (A) and cost visibility (C) are real IaC advantages but don't answer an audit question. Consistency (D) is about environments matching, not about change history.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team manages AWS infrastructure with Terraform and also needs to manage GitHub repositories, Datadog monitors, and PagerDuty schedules. What does this illustrate about Terraform?
options: Terraform only works with cloud compute resources
Terraform is service-agnostic: providers exist for any API-backed resource, not just clouds
Terraform requires a separate binary for non-cloud providers
GitHub and Datadog must be managed with the `null` provider
explain: Terraform is service-agnostic — the provider ecosystem covers SaaS APIs like GitHub, Datadog, and PagerDuty alongside clouds. That's a 004 objective (1c). A is false. C is false; providers are plugins of the same CLI. D is wrong; the null provider is for throwaway test resources, not real integrations.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company keeps expensive GPU instances running in a dev environment `just in case`, because tearing them down manually takes a full day to rebuild. How does IaC change this cost picture?
options: IaC makes cloud providers discount idle instances
IaC lets the team destroy the environment when idle and recreate it identically in minutes with `terraform apply`
IaC automatically pauses billing on unused instances
IaC moves the workloads to cheaper regions automatically
explain: Because the environment is code, destroying it is safe — it can be recreated identically on demand. That turns always-on dev infrastructure into an on/off cost switch. A, C, and D describe billing magic Terraform does not perform; the savings come from confident teardown and fast recreation.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A CTO asks why the team should adopt IaC instead of continuing with well-documented manual procedures. Which answer captures the core value proposition the 004 exam expects?
options: IaC eliminates the need for cloud provider accounts
IaC makes infrastructure consistent, reviewable, versioned, and automatically deployable — the configuration becomes executable documentation
IaC guarantees zero downtime during every deployment
IaC is required by compliance frameworks before any cloud use
explain: The exam's IaC advantages: consistency/idempotency, automation, version control, collaboration via review, and configuration-as-documentation. A is false (you still need provider accounts). C overpromises — IaC enables safer deploys but guarantees nothing. D invents a compliance mandate.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A configuration needs the AWS provider and the `random` provider. Where are these requirements declared, and what does each declaration include?
options: In `provider` blocks, listing only the provider name
In the `terraform` block under `required_providers`, with a source address and a version constraint for each
In `terraform.tfvars`, as variable assignments
Nowhere — Terraform detects which providers a configuration needs at apply time
explain: required_providers inside the terraform block declares each provider's source address (e.g. hashicorp/aws) and version constraint. A confuses provider configuration blocks (settings like region) with provider requirements. C is for variable values. D is false — init must know what to download before plan can run.

q: You clone a Terraform repository and run `terraform init`. Which of the following does init do? (Select the best answer.)
options: It creates all infrastructure defined in the configuration
It downloads provider plugins into `.terraform/`, downloads modules, configures the backend, and writes the dependency lock file
It validates the configuration syntax without contacting any APIs
It formats all `.tf` files to canonical HCL style
explain: init prepares the working directory: provider plugins into .terraform/, child modules into .terraform/modules/, backend setup, and the lock file. Creating infrastructure (A) is apply's job. Validation without APIs (C) is validate. Formatting (D) is fmt.

q: After `terraform init`, a file named `.terraform.lock.hcl` appears. A teammate suggests adding it to `.gitignore`. What is the correct response?
options: Agree — it contains secrets and must never be committed
Agree — it is regenerated identically on every machine, so committing it is redundant
Disagree — it records the exact provider versions and checksums selected, and committing it keeps every teammate and CI run on identical providers
Disagree — Terraform refuses to run unless the lock file is committed first
explain: The lock file pins exact provider versions and hashes; committing it is how teams get reproducible runs. A is wrong — it holds versions and checksums, not secrets (state holds secrets). B is wrong — without it, each init may select different versions within constraints. D is false; Terraform runs fine without a committed lock file, just less reproducibly.

q: A team wants to pick up the newest provider versions allowed by their version constraints. Which command does this, and what else changes as a result?
options: `terraform init -upgrade`, which selects the newest allowed provider versions and rewrites the lock file
`terraform apply -upgrade`, which upgrades providers during the apply
`terraform providers upgrade`, which edits `required_providers` automatically
Delete `.terraform/` and run `terraform plan`; plan upgrades providers by default
explain: init -upgrade re-resolves providers to the newest versions within constraints and rewrites the lock file. There is no apply -upgrade (B) or providers upgrade command (C). D is wrong — a plain plan reuses the locked versions; only -upgrade re-resolves.

q: A module declares `version = "~> 1.4"` for a provider. Which provider versions satisfy this constraint?
options: 1.4.0 only
Any version >= 1.4, including 3.x
explain: EXAM TRAP: the pessimistic operator `~>` allows only the rightmost specified component to increment. With two components specified (`~> 1.4`), the minor version may rise but the major is locked: >= 1.4, < 2.0. (With three components, `~> 1.4.0` would mean >= 1.4.0, < 1.5.0.) A describes `= 1.4.0`. D describes `>= 1.4`.

q: Terraform's architecture is described as plugin-based. What does this mean in practice?
options: The Terraform core binary contains all provider logic; plugins are optional UI themes
All infrastructure logic ships as separate provider plugins downloaded at init, keeping the core binary small and provider-agnostic
Each `.tf` file is compiled into a plugin at plan time
Provider plugins must be written in HCL
explain: Terraform core is a small engine; every provider is a separate plugin binary fetched during init. That is why init is required before plan, and why one CLI manages hundreds of providers. A inverts the design. C confuses configuration with compiled code. D is false — providers are typically Go binaries.

q: In `required_providers`, the AWS provider is listed with `source = "hashicorp/aws"`. What does this source address identify?
options: The GitHub repository where the provider's documentation lives
The provider's address on the Terraform registry: namespace `hashicorp`, type `aws` (defaulting to registry.terraform.io)
The AWS region the provider will manage
The local filesystem path to a provider binary
explain: Source addresses are registry coordinates: [hostname/]namespace/type. `hashicorp/aws` means the official AWS provider in the hashicorp namespace on the default registry. A confuses source with docs. C is the region argument in a provider block. D would be a dev_overrides path, not a source address.

q: A configuration declares two `provider "aws"` blocks — one for us-east-1 and one aliased `west` for us-west-2. A resource block has no `provider` meta-argument. Which provider configuration will Terraform use for that resource?
options: The apply fails — every resource must declare an explicit provider
The unaliased (default) provider configuration, us-east-1
Terraform picks whichever provider block was declared first
The aliased `west` provider, because aliases take precedence
explain: Resources without an explicit provider meta-argument use the default (unaliased) configuration of that provider type. A is false — the default exists precisely so most resources need no declaration. C and D invent selection rules; the rule is simply default-vs-aliased.

q: Why does `terraform plan` need the state file even when the configuration alone describes everything to be built?
options: It doesn't — plan works identically with no state file present
The state file caches provider binaries so plan runs faster
Plan diffs the desired configuration against the state (the record of what already exists) to decide what to create, update, or destroy
The state file stores the plan output for later approval
explain: State is Terraform's memory of reality: plan compares desired config against recorded state to compute the diff. With no state (first run), everything is new — hence all `+` creates. B confuses state with .terraform/. D confuses state with saved plan files (-out).

q: A team configures the AWS provider with hardcoded `access_key` and `secret_key` arguments in `provider "aws"`. What is the exam-correct best practice, and why?
options: Hardcoding is fine as long as the file is committed to a private repository
Pass credentials via environment variables or shared config files instead — never commit secrets to version-controlled configuration
Credentials must always be passed with `-var` on the command line
The AWS provider does not accept credentials; it uses IAM roles only
explain: Provider credentials belong in environment variables, shared credentials files, or workload identity — never in committed configuration. A is the classic exam trap: private repos still leak, get cloned, and get breached. C is too narrow (one of several valid methods). D is false; the provider accepts multiple auth methods.

q: One Terraform configuration manages an AWS S3 bucket and also generates a random password with the `random` provider. How does Terraform handle the two providers?
options: It cannot — a configuration may only use one provider type
Each resource block is handled by the provider matching its resource type prefix (`aws_*` vs `random_*`); both providers are declared in `required_providers`
The random provider must be wrapped in a module; the root module may only use one provider
Terraform merges both providers into a single plugin at init
explain: A configuration routinely uses many providers (objective 2c): each resource's type prefix selects its provider, and all are declared in required_providers and downloaded at init. A is false — multi-provider configs are normal. C invents a module restriction. D misunderstands the plugin architecture.

q: A new engineer asks for the standard Terraform workflow in order. Which sequence is correct?
options: Apply -> Plan -> Write
Write -> Plan -> Apply (with init first in a new working directory)
Validate -> Destroy -> Init
Fmt -> Import -> Push
explain: The core loop is Write -> Plan -> Apply, and a fresh working directory needs `terraform init` before anything else. A reverses the loop. C and D string together unrelated commands — destroy tears everything down and is not part of the normal loop.

q: A CI pipeline needs a fast check that a pull request's Terraform configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent. The check must not require cloud credentials and must not contact any cloud APIs. Which command fits?
options: terraform plan, because plans are always credential-free
terraform validate — it checks syntax and consistency using provider schemas, with no API calls
terraform apply -refresh-only
terraform fmt -check
explain: validate is the credential-free correctness gate: it checks block types, attribute names, and references without touching APIs. A is wrong — plan refreshes state via APIs by default. C contacts APIs to refresh. D only checks formatting, not correctness.

q: Before computing its diff, `terraform plan` first reaches out to providers to read the current values of managed resources. What is this step called, and why does it matter?
options: Reconciliation — it deletes resources that are no longer in the configuration
Refresh — it syncs state with real-world values so the plan is computed against reality, which is also how drift gets detected
Rebase — it rewrites the state file to match the configuration
Locking — it prevents other engineers from running plan concurrently
explain: Plan's first phase is refresh: read live values into state, then diff. That is why plan detects drift — reality changed, so the diff shows corrections. A describes destroy behavior. C invents a term. D describes state locking, a separate backend feature.

q: In a `terraform plan` output, a resource is marked with `~` (tilde). What will Terraform do to this resource?
options: Create it from scratch
Update it in place, without destroying and recreating it
Destroy it and then recreate it
Remove it from state but leave the real object running
explain: `~` means in-place update: the change can be applied without replacement (e.g., changing tags). `+` is create, `-/+` is destroy-then-recreate, and removal from state without destruction is `terraform state rm` — none of which is `~`.

q: A plan output shows `<=` next to a `data "aws_ami" "ubuntu"` block. What does this symbol mean?
options: The data source will be destroyed
The data source will be read during the plan/apply
The data source has a syntax error
The data source is being imported into state as a managed resource
explain: `<=` marks a read: data sources are fetched, not managed. They are never destroyed (A) or imported as managed resources (D). C is wrong — a syntax error would fail validate long before plan.

q: A bank's policy requires every production infrastructure change to be reviewed as a plan before anything is applied, with a guarantee that apply executes exactly what was reviewed. Which workflow satisfies this?
options: `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, review the file, then `terraform apply tfplan`
`terraform apply -auto-approve`, then review the logs afterward
`terraform validate`, then `terraform apply` immediately
`terraform plan -refresh-only`, then `terraform destroy`
explain: A saved plan file decouples review from execution: `apply tfplan` runs the identical artifact that was reviewed, skipping the prompt. B skips review entirely — the opposite of the policy. C never previews changes. D is incoherent: refresh-only proposes nothing, and destroy tears everything down.

q: An engineer runs `terraform apply -auto-approve` from their laptop during a production incident `to go faster`. What is the exam-correct view of this?
options: Best practice — incidents justify skipping confirmations
Acceptable only in automation (CI/CD) where the plan was already reviewed; by hand it skips the last safety check and is treated as a red flag
Required — apply will not run in production without it
`-auto-approve` only works with `terraform destroy`, not apply
explain: -auto-approve is for automation pipelines where review happened earlier (e.g., on the saved plan). Interactively it removes the final human confirmation — the exam treats that as dangerous. A glorifies skipping safety. C is false. D is false; the flag works on both apply and destroy.

q: An engineer runs `terraform destroy` in a directory whose state tracks 12 resources. The AWS account also contains 5 manually created EC2 instances. What will be destroyed?
options: All 17 instances — destroy removes everything in the account
Only the 12 state-tracked resources; the 5 manually created instances are untouched because destroy only acts on what Terraform manages
Nothing — destroy requires a `-target` for each resource
Only resources whose configuration files still exist in the directory
explain: EXAM TRAP: destroy acts on state, not on the account. Anything Terraform does not track in state is invisible to it — manually created infrastructure survives. (Bringing such resources under management is what import is for.) A overstates destroy's reach. C invents a requirement. D confuses config presence with state tracking.

q: A CI pipeline should fail a pull request if any `.tf` file is not in canonical format, without modifying the files. Which command implements this gate?
options: terraform fmt -check — exits non-zero when files need formatting, changing nothing
terraform validate -check
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
terraform fmt -write=false
explain: `fmt -check` is the CI formatting gate: it reports unformatted files via its exit code and rewrites nothing. There is no validate -check (B). C is a real flag but tests for plan diffs, not formatting. D is not a real flag combination.

q: A teammate says: `Just run terraform fmt — it will fix the broken variable reference in main.tf.` What is wrong with this advice?
options: Nothing — fmt fixes both formatting and broken references
fmt only rewrites formatting (indentation, alignment); it never changes what the configuration does or fixes logic errors — that is validate's job to catch
fmt cannot run on files with errors; it deletes them instead
fmt only works on `.tfvars` files, not `.tf` files
explain: The classic fmt-vs-validate trap: fmt is cosmetic only; validate checks correctness. A attributes magic to fmt. C is false — fmt happily reformats files that have logic errors. D reverses the file types.

q: Someone edited a production security group directly in the AWS console. You suspect drift but want to see exactly what changed in the real world before deciding whether to revert it or update the configuration. Which command shows you the drift without proposing any configuration changes?
options: terraform plan -refresh-only — syncs state to reality and reports drift, proposing no changes
terraform apply -auto-approve
terraform destroy -target=aws_security_group.web
terraform state push
explain: Refresh-only mode updates state to match reality and shows what drifted, without proposing config changes — the safe first step in a drift investigation. B would blindly apply. C destroys the resource. D uploads a state file, which is dangerous and unrelated.

q: After running `terraform plan -refresh-only` and confirming the drift is legitimate (an approved out-of-band change), what is the correct next step to make Terraform's record match reality permanently?
options: Nothing — refresh-only already updated the state file, so Terraform now agrees with reality
Run `terraform apply -refresh-only` to write the refreshed values into state
Run `terraform destroy` and re-apply
Delete the state file so the next plan starts clean
explain: Subtle but tested: `plan -refresh-only` only previews the refresh; `apply -refresh-only` actually writes the synced state. A confuses the preview with the write. C is wildly destructive. D discards all tracking — the opposite of fixing drift.

q: You run `terraform apply` without arguments. What happens before any infrastructure changes?
options: Terraform applies immediately with no preview
Terraform generates a plan, displays it, and prompts for confirmation — you must type `yes` to proceed
Terraform runs `destroy` first to ensure a clean slate
Terraform requires a saved plan file or it exits with an error
explain: A bare apply generates a fresh plan, shows it, and waits for interactive `yes`. A describes -auto-approve. C is false. D is false — saved plan files are optional (though recommended in production).

q: You clone a Terraform repository, skip init, and run `terraform plan`. What happens?
options: Plan runs using providers cached from a previous project
Plan fails — providers and modules are not installed and the backend is not configured until init runs
Plan succeeds but skips the refresh phase
Plan automatically runs init for you and continues
explain: Without init there are no provider plugins, no modules, and no backend — plan cannot run and errors out. A is wrong; providers are per-working-directory in .terraform/. C is wrong; there is no degraded plan mode. D is wrong — Terraform never auto-inits (that would hide backend and version decisions).

q: Like apply, `terraform destroy` prompts for confirmation. An engineer wants to script nightly teardown of a dev environment. Which is the correct automation approach?
options: Pipe `yes` into the command with `yes | terraform destroy`
Use `terraform destroy -auto-approve` in the scheduled job, after the pipeline has already reviewed what will be destroyed
Run `terraform plan -destroy` and exit — the plan alone tears down the environment
`-auto-approve` is not supported on destroy; nightly teardown must be manual
explain: -auto-approve is the designed automation path for both apply and destroy, used inside pipelines where review happened earlier. A is a hack the exam would not bless. C is wrong — plan -destroy only previews destruction. D is false; the flag works on destroy.

q: A configuration references a provider that was just added to `required_providers`. `terraform validate` now fails with `Missing or incomplete provider configuration`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The configuration has a syntax error
init has not been re-run since the provider was added, so provider schemas are unavailable to validate
validate cannot be used with more than one provider
The provider's credentials are missing
explain: validate needs provider schemas, which only exist after init downloads the provider. Adding a provider without re-running init is the classic cause. A is possible but the error message points at the provider, not syntax. C is false. D is wrong — validate never needs credentials.

q: A repository has Terraform configurations in the root directory and in `./modules/*` subdirectories. Which command formats every `.tf` file in the whole tree?
options: terraform fmt (run in the root — it always recurses)
terraform fmt -recursive
terraform fmt -all
terraform validate -recursive
explain: Plain `fmt` formats only the current directory; `-recursive` walks subdirectories. A is the trap — root-only is the default. C and D are not real flag combinations.

q: A plan summary reads: `Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.` What does this tell the reviewer?
options: Two resources will be created, one will be updated in place, and nothing will be deleted
Two resources will be destroyed and one created
The plan failed — these numbers should always be zero
Two data sources will be read and one state file rewritten
explain: The summary is literal: 2 creates (+), 1 in-place update (~), 0 deletions. B inverts the meaning. C is wrong — non-zero plans are the normal reason you run plan. D confuses the summary with data-source reads (<=).

q: HashiCorp documentation describes the Terraform workflow as `Write, Plan, Create`. A practice question asks for the core Terraform workflow and offers `Write -> Plan -> Apply` as a choice. How should you interpret this?
options: It is a different workflow — choose another answer
`Create` and `Apply` describe the same final phase; the phrasing is equivalent
`Write, Plan, Create` refers to the 003 exam only and is retired
The correct workflow has four phases, so any three-phase answer is wrong
explain: HashiCorp uses `Write -> Plan -> Create` and `Write -> Plan -> Apply` interchangeably — Create is what apply does. The exam tests the concept (author config, preview the diff, execute it), not the exact verb. A, C, and D over-literalize the wording.

q: A team needs to launch instances in a VPC that was created years ago by another department and is not in any Terraform configuration. How should the configuration reference that VPC's ID?
options: With a `resource "aws_vpc"` block — Terraform will adopt the existing VPC automatically
With a `data` block (data source) that reads the existing VPC — Terraform reads it without managing it
By hardcoding the VPC ID as a string literal everywhere
It cannot be referenced; Terraform only works with infrastructure it created
explain: Data sources read existing infrastructure Terraform does not manage — exactly the case for a pre-existing VPC. A is wrong: a resource block would make Terraform try to create (or fight over) the VPC. C works but is brittle and untestable. D is false; data sources exist precisely for this.

q: A data source references an attribute of a resource that Terraform itself manages (e.g., the ID of an `aws_instance` created in the same configuration). When is that data source read?
options: Always during plan, before any resources are created
Its read is deferred until apply, because the value it needs does not exist yet
Data sources can never reference managed resources — the configuration is invalid
It is read once at init time and cached
explain: Data sources are read during plan when possible, but if they depend on a not-yet-created resource, the read must wait until apply when the value exists. A ignores the ordering problem. C is false — this pattern is legal and common. D invents init-time caching.

q: An EIP resource references `aws_instance.web.id`. Why does Terraform create the instance before the EIP, even though nothing in the configuration states an order?
options: Resources are always created in alphabetical order by type
The reference creates an implicit dependency — Terraform builds a dependency graph from references and orders operations automatically
The EIP resource has an invisible `depends_on` added by the provider
It is coincidence; Terraform creates resources in random order
explain: Cross-resource references create implicit dependencies; Terraform topologically sorts the resource graph so dependencies are created first. A invents alphabetical ordering. C is wrong — depends_on is explicit and written by you. D denies the deterministic graph ordering.

q: A provisioner on an `aws_instance` needs a DNS record to exist first, but nothing in the configuration references the DNS record from the instance. How do you guarantee the ordering?
options: Rename the resources so alphabetical order works out
Add an explicit `depends_on = [aws_route53_record.web]` to the instance — depends_on covers orderings that references cannot express
Add a `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` block
Ordering cannot be controlled; provisioners always run first
explain: depends_on is the explicit dependency mechanism for orderings invisible to the reference graph (provisioners, external side effects). A is nonsense. C controls replacement behavior, not ordering. D is false — depends_on exists exactly for this.

q: A variable `instance_type` has `default = "t3.micro"`. It is also set in `terraform.tfvars` to `t3.small`, and the engineer runs `terraform apply -var="instance_type=t3.large"`. Which value wins?
options: t3.micro — defaults always win
t3.small — tfvars files override the command line
t3.large — `-var` flags have the highest precedence
The apply fails — setting a variable three ways is an error
explain: EXAM TRAP — the precedence ladder: environment variables < terraform.tfvars < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file < -var. The command line always wins. A and B invert the ladder. D is false; multiple sources are normal and resolve by precedence.

q: An engineer wants to set the variable `region` from a shell environment variable without touching any files or command flags. Which environment variable name will Terraform pick up automatically?
options: TERRAFORM_region
TF_VAR_region
TF_region
REGION_TF_VAR
explain: The convention is `TF_VAR_<name>` — Terraform automatically maps TF_VAR_region to variable "region". The other names are invented; only the TF_VAR_ prefix is recognized.

q: A file named `prod.auto.tfvars` sits in the working directory. When are its variable values loaded?
options: Only when passed explicitly with `-var-file=prod.auto.tfvars`
Automatically, on every plan and apply — `*.auto.tfvars` files load without flags, after `terraform.tfvars`
Only during `terraform init`
Never — `.auto.tfvars` is not a recognized extension
explain: `*.auto.tfvars` (and `*.auto.tfvars.json`) are auto-loaded in lexical order, sitting above terraform.tfvars in precedence. A describes -var-file behavior. C is wrong — values load at plan/apply. D denies a real, heavily used feature.

q: A configuration uses `count = 3` to create three servers: `aws_instance.web[0]` through `[2]`. The team removes the middle element from the list driving the count. What happens to the remaining servers?
options: Nothing — the other two are untouched
Indexes shift: the old `[2]` becomes `[1]`, forcing Terraform to destroy and recreate instances because their addresses changed
Terraform keeps the original indexes automatically
Count-based resources cannot be reduced; you must taint them first
explain: EXAM TRAP: count addresses by position, so removing from the middle renumbers everything after it — Terraform sees address changes as destroy/recreate. This is exactly why `for_each` (keyed by identity) is preferred for sets of meaningful instances. A ignores the renumbering. C and D invent protections that do not exist.

q: An engineer writes `for_each = var.availability_zones` where the variable is a list of strings. Terraform errors out. What is the fix, and why?
options: Wrap it with `toset()`: `for_each` accepts maps and sets of strings, not lists — lists have no stable keys
Change it to `count = length(var.availability_zones)` — for_each cannot iterate variables
Add `depends_on` to the resource
Lists work fine; the error must be from something else
explain: for_each needs keys: it accepts maps or sets of strings. A list must be converted with toset() first. B dodges the question by switching to count (losing keyed identity). C is irrelevant. D denies a real, frequently tested error.

q: A database resource must never experience downtime during replacement, so the new instance must be fully created before the old one is destroyed. Which lifecycle rule implements this?
options: `prevent_destroy = true`
`create_before_destroy = true`
`ignore_changes = all`
`replace_triggered_by = [aws_instance.db]`
explain: create_before_destroy inverts the replacement order: create the replacement first, then destroy the old. A (prevent_destroy) would block the replacement entirely. C ignores drift on attributes. D forces replacement when something else changes — the opposite need.

q: A production database must never be destroyed by any Terraform run, even if someone removes its block from the configuration. Which safeguard enforces this?
options: `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` — any plan that would destroy the resource fails with an error
`lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }`
Marking the resource `sensitive = true`
Storing the state file in a private S3 bucket
explain: prevent_destroy is the safety rail: plans proposing destruction fail loudly instead of executing. B changes replacement ordering, not permission. C only redacts CLI output. D protects state access but does not stop a legitimate apply from destroying.

q: An external tagging tool manages the `tags` on instances, and every `terraform plan` wants to revert its changes. How do you make Terraform leave the tags alone?
options: `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags] }` — Terraform stops tracking drift on those attributes
Remove the `tags` argument from the configuration entirely
`lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }`
Run every plan with `-refresh=false`
explain: ignore_changes tells Terraform to accept external modifications to listed attributes instead of reverting them. B does not help — Terraform would still manage tags as empty. C blocks destruction, unrelated to attribute drift. D disables refresh globally, hiding all drift — dangerous and wrong.

q: A team wants three layers of defense: (1) reject invalid variable values as early as possible, (2) fail a run if a resource's assumptions are violated around its create/update, (3) continuously warn after apply if infrastructure drifts out of policy without ever failing runs. Which trio implements this?
options: Input variable `validation` blocks, `precondition`/`postcondition` blocks, and `check` blocks
`check` blocks, `precondition` blocks, and variable `validation` blocks, in that order
Three `terraform validate` runs with different flags
`sensitive = true`, `prevent_destroy`, and `ignore_changes`
explain: EXAM TRAP — the 004 custom-conditions trio: validation rejects bad input early; pre/postconditions assert around actions and fail the run; check blocks assert continuously post-apply and only warn. B scrambles the mapping. C invents validate flags. D lists unrelated lifecycle/sensitivity features.

q: A `check` block asserting `aws_s3_bucket.logs` has versioning enabled starts failing after someone disables versioning in the console. What happens on the next `terraform plan`?
options: The plan fails with an error and cannot proceed
Terraform emits a warning but the plan and apply continue normally — check blocks never fail runs
Terraform automatically re-enables versioning
The check block is deleted from the configuration
explain: Check blocks are non-blocking health assertions: failures warn, never fail. That distinguishes them from preconditions/postconditions, which do fail runs. A describes precondition behavior. C and D invent automatic remediation.

q: A variable `ami_id` must reject any value that does not start with `ami-`. Where does this rule belong?
options: In a `validation` block inside the variable declaration, with a `condition` and an `error_message`
In a `precondition` on each resource using the variable
In the `terraform` block under `required_version`
In a `check` block at the root
explain: Variable validation blocks reject bad input at the earliest moment — before plan even evaluates resources. B works but is the wrong layer (preconditions guard resource actions, not input). C constrains Terraform CLI versions. D warns post-apply instead of rejecting early.

q: A database password is marked `sensitive = true` in its variable and output. It no longer appears in CLI output. A teammate claims the password is now encrypted in the state file. Is this correct?
options: Yes — sensitive values are encrypted at rest in state
No — `sensitive = true` only redacts CLI output; the value still sits in the state file in plaintext
Yes, but only when using the S3 backend
No — sensitive values are never written to state at all
explain: EXAM TRAP: sensitive is display-only. State still contains the plaintext value — real protection means encryption at rest, access control, Vault, or ephemeral values. A is the exact misconception the exam hunts. C invents backend-specific encryption. D describes ephemeral values, not sensitive.

q: A compliance rule states: `Database credentials must never be persisted in the Terraform state file, even in encrypted form.` Which Terraform feature satisfies this?
options: Marking the variable `sensitive = true`
Using `ephemeral` resource blocks or write-only attributes — the values are used during apply but never written to state
Storing the state file in a private Git repository
Using `terraform state push` after every apply
explain: Ephemeral values (and write-only attributes) exist precisely for secrets that must not touch state — used at apply time, never persisted. A only hides CLI output. C is terrible practice (state in Git). D uploads state but does not remove secrets from it.

q: A security group needs ingress rules for ports 80, 443, and 8080, driven by a variable list that changes per environment. What is the DRY way to generate these repeated nested blocks?
options: Write three separate `ingress` blocks and comment out the ones not needed
A `dynamic` block with `for_each` over the port list, generating one `ingress` block per value
Use `count` on the security group resource
Nested blocks cannot be generated — each must be written literally
explain: Dynamic blocks generate repeated nested blocks from a collection — the purpose-built DRY mechanism. A is manual and error-prone. C creates multiple security groups, not multiple rules. D denies a core HCL feature.

q: A variable needs to hold a structured server spec: a name (string), a CPU count (number), and a list of tags. Which type fits, and how does it differ from a tuple?
options: `list(string)` — it holds mixed attribute types
`object({ name = string, cpus = number, tags = list(string) })` — an object types each attribute by name, while a tuple is a fixed-length sequence of positional types
`map(string)` — identical to an object in every way
`tuple([string])` — the only complex type allowed for variables
explain: object() gives each named attribute its own type — the workhorse for structured variables. A tuple is positional ([string, number]) with fixed length. A is wrong (list(string) holds only strings). C is wrong (maps have uniform value types). D is false.

q: A configuration looks up `var.instance_types["prod"]` but the key might not exist. Which function safely returns a fallback instead of erroring?
options: `lookup(var.instance_types, "prod", "t3.micro")` — returns the default when the key is absent
`element(var.instance_types, "prod")`
`coalesce(var.instance_types)`
Direct indexing is safe — missing keys return null automatically
explain: lookup(map, key, default) is the safe-access function with a fallback. element() is for list indexes. coalesce() returns the first non-empty of its arguments — wrong tool. D is false; missing keys error without lookup or try().

q: After `terraform apply`, an engineer wants to see the value of the `web_ip` output without re-running apply. Which command retrieves it, and where does the value come from?
options: `terraform output web_ip` — it reads the value from the state file
`terraform show web_ip` — it re-queries the cloud API
`terraform get web_ip` — it downloads the value from the registry
Outputs are only visible in the apply log and cannot be retrieved later
explain: `terraform output` reads saved output values from state — no re-apply, no API calls. B and C invent commands for this purpose. D is false; outputs persist in state precisely so they can be queried.

q: A team wants to reuse a community VPC module in their root configuration. Which block calls it, and what does the `source` argument look like for the public registry?
options: A `resource` block with `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"`
A `module "vpc"` block with `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"` — registry address format is `<namespace>/<name>/<provider>`
An `import` block with the registry URL
A `data` block with `source = "registry/vpc"`
explain: Child modules are called with module blocks; public registry sources use namespace/name/provider form. A confuses modules with resources. C is for importing existing infrastructure. D confuses modules with data sources.

q: A module block declares `source = "git::https://example.com/vpc.git"` and `version = "1.2.0"`. What will `terraform init` do?
options: Install version 1.2.0 of the module from Git
Fail — the `version` argument is only valid for registry sources; Git modules are pinned with `?ref=` instead
Ignore the version and install the latest commit
Convert the Git URL into a registry address automatically
explain: EXAM TRAP: version is registry-only. On Git sources it is invalid — pin with `source = "git::https://example.com/vpc.git?ref=v1.2.0"`. A assumes version works everywhere. C and D invent lenient behaviors; init errors on the invalid argument.

q: A team sources a module directly from GitHub and needs builds to always use the v2.1.0 tag, never floating to newer commits. How is this declared?
options: `source = "github.com/org/vpc"` with `version = "2.1.0"`
`source = "github.com/org/vpc?ref=v2.1.0"` — Git sources pin with the `ref` query parameter
`source = "github.com/org/vpc"` with `ref = "v2.1.0"` as a separate argument
GitHub sources always float; pinning is impossible
explain: Git-sourced modules pin via `?ref=` (tag, branch, or commit SHA) appended to the source URL. A uses version, which is registry-only and invalid here. C invents a separate ref argument. D is false — ref pinning is the standard mechanism.

q: A module is sourced from a local path: `source = "./modules/networking"`. Which statements are true about this module?
options: It supports the `version` argument for pinning releases
It is referenced by filesystem path, has no versioning, and is read directly — no download step needed
It must be published to a registry before init will accept it
Local modules cannot accept input variables
explain: Local-path modules are just directories on disk: no registry, no versions, no download. A is wrong — version is registry-only. C is false. D is false — local modules take inputs/outputs like any module.

q: A child module needs the value of the root module's `environment` variable. The child declares no input variable for it. What happens?
options: The child automatically inherits all root variables
The reference fails — variables are scoped to their module; the root must pass the value explicitly via a module block argument into a declared input variable
Terraform copies root variables into every child module at init
The child reads it from the state file
explain: EXAM TRAP: module variable scope is strict. A child sees only its own declared inputs, its locals, and its data sources. Data flows in through module block arguments and out through outputs — there is no inheritance (A), no auto-copying (C), and state is not a variable channel (D).

q: A child VPC module declares `output "vpc_id"`. The root module needs that ID for an instance's `subnet_id`. How does the root access it?
options: As `module.vpc.vpc_id` — child outputs are exposed on the module object in the calling configuration
As `vpc.vpc_id` directly, since outputs are global
As `data.module.vpc.vpc_id`
Outputs cannot cross module boundaries; the value must be hardcoded
explain: Module outputs are addressed `module.<name>.<output>` in the calling module — the standard data-out channel. B drops the required module. prefix. C invents a data. lookup. D denies the core module composition pattern.

q: After adding a new child module block, `terraform plan` errors that the module is not installed. Which command installs it, and where does it land?
options: `terraform get` — into `.terraform/modules/`
`terraform init` — child modules are downloaded into `.terraform/modules/`
`terraform apply` — modules install during the first apply
`terraform import` — modules are imported like resources
explain: init installs modules (as well as providers) into .terraform/modules/. A names a real but legacy command — modern Terraform installs modules via init. C is wrong; apply never installs. D confuses modules with resource import.

q: A registry module is pinned with `version = "~> 5.0"`. A new 5.9.0 release appears and the team wants it. Which command upgrades the installed module?
options: `terraform apply -upgrade`
`terraform init -upgrade` — re-resolves modules (and providers) to the newest allowed versions
Edit the lock file by hand to 5.9.0
`terraform module upgrade vpc`
explain: init -upgrade re-resolves both providers and modules within their constraints. A and D are not real commands. C is wrong — hand-editing the lock file bypasses checksum verification; the lock file is managed by init.

q: Documentation refers to the `root module`. What is it?
options: A special module published by HashiCorp that every configuration must call
The top-level configuration itself — the `.tf` files in the working directory where you run Terraform
The module with the highest version number in the dependency tree
The backend configuration block
explain: The root module is simply your working directory's configuration — every Terraform run has one, and it calls child modules. A invents a mandatory HashiCorp module. C confuses versioning with hierarchy. D confuses state storage with module structure.

q: A team wants fully reproducible builds: the same configuration must install the same module and provider versions on every machine, every time. Which two practices together achieve this?
options: Pinning module `version` constraints and committing the `.terraform.lock.hcl` file
Using only local-path modules and deleting `.terraform/` before each run
Running `terraform init -upgrade` before every apply
Storing modules in the same Git repo as the root configuration
explain: Reproducibility is version pins (constraints that bound what init may select) plus the committed lock file (the exact selections). B avoids the problem rather than solving it. C does the opposite — it actively re-resolves to newest. D helps availability but pins nothing.

q: A company publishes internal modules to its HCP Terraform private registry. What does a module source address for the private registry look like?
options: `app.terraform.io/my-org/vpc/aws` — the organization's hostname, org name, module name, and provider
`terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` — private modules use the same address as public ones
`github.com/my-org/vpc` — the private registry is just a GitHub alias
Private registry modules cannot be sourced; they must be copied locally
explain: Private registry addresses include the hostname and organization: app.terraform.io/<org>/<name>/<provider>. B is the public registry form. C is a Git source, a different mechanism. D is false — the private registry exists precisely for governed sharing.

q: Two engineers run `terraform apply` at the same time against a configuration using the default local backend. The state file becomes corrupted. What is the root cause?
options: The state file was too large for concurrent writes
The `local` backend provides no state locking — locking is a backend feature, and concurrent applies raced on the same file
Terraform core has a bug with parallel applies
One engineer forgot to run `terraform init`
explain: EXAM TRAP: locking is a backend feature, not a core feature. The local backend does not lock, so concurrent runs corrupt state. The fix is a remote backend with locking (HCP Terraform, S3, azurerm, etc.). A blames file size. C blames the core. D is unrelated to corruption.

q: A `terraform apply` was killed mid-run and now every command fails with `Error acquiring the state lock`. You have confirmed no Terraform process is running anywhere. What is the safe remediation?
options: Delete the state file and re-apply from scratch
`terraform force-unlock <lock-id>` — manually release the stuck lock, only because you verified no run is actually in progress
Run `terraform init -upgrade` to clear the lock
Wait 24 hours for the lock to expire on its own
explain: force-unlock releases a stale lock — safe only when you are certain nothing is running, since unlocking under a live run invites corruption. A destroys your state record. C does not touch locks. D invents an expiry; stuck locks persist until released.

options: Nothing — variables are the recommended way to parameterize backends
Backend blocks cannot contain variables or references — backends initialize before configuration is evaluated; use partial configuration with `-backend-config` flags instead
The `key` argument is not valid for the S3 backend
S3 backends require the `region` to be hardcoded
explain: EXAM TRAP: the backend block is evaluated before variables exist, so no variables or references are allowed inside it. The workaround is partial backend configuration via -backend-config files or flags. A states the exact misconception. C is false — key is required. D is false; region can come from -backend-config or env.

q: A team moves their state from local files to an S3 backend by updating the `backend` block. What must they run next, and what does it do?
options: `terraform apply` — it recreates all infrastructure in the new backend
`terraform init -migrate-state` — it copies the existing state to the new backend so nothing is recreated
`terraform state push` — it uploads the configuration files
Nothing — Terraform detects the backend change automatically on the next plan
explain: Changing backends requires init -migrate-state, which moves the state file to the new home; resources are adopted, not recreated. A would be catastrophic and wrong. C uploads state but does not reconfigure the backend. D is false — Terraform prompts for migration via init.

q: A configuration declares two backend blocks: `backend "s3"` for production state and `backend "gcs"` as a backup. What happens at init?
options: Terraform writes state to both backends for redundancy
Init fails — a configuration may have only one backend; state has a single home
The first backend is used and the second is silently ignored
Terraform merges both into a combined backend
explain: One configuration, one backend — state has exactly one home. A, C, and D invent multi-backend behaviors Terraform does not have. Redundancy comes from the backend's own durability (e.g., S3 versioning), not from two backends.

q: An engineer renames `aws_instance.web` to `aws_instance.frontend` in the configuration. Without any other change, `terraform plan` proposes to destroy the instance and create a new one. How do you rename it without recreation or downtime?
options: Add a `moved` block mapping `from = aws_instance.web` to `to = aws_instance.frontend` — Terraform updates the state address in place, keeping the same real object
Run `terraform state rm` on the old address first
Add `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }`
Renames are impossible without recreation
explain: A moved block tells Terraform the address changed but the object is identical — state is rewritten, zero destruction. B would make Terraform plan to create a brand-new instance. C changes replacement ordering, not addressing. D denies the exact feature built for refactoring.

q: A legacy database was brought under Terraform management for a migration, which is now complete. The team wants Terraform to stop managing it, but the database must keep running untouched. Which approach does this safely?
options: Delete the resource block — Terraform will leave the database alone
Add a `removed` block with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` — Terraform drops it from state without destroying the real object
Run `terraform destroy -target=aws_db_instance.legacy`
Run `terraform state push` to overwrite the state
explain: The removed block is the controlled decommission: with destroy = false, Terraform forgets the resource and the real database keeps running. A is the trap — deleting the block plans destruction. C destroys it outright. D uploads state and changes nothing about management.

q: An engineer runs `terraform state rm aws_instance.old` and a colleague runs `terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.old` in a different, identical setup. What is the difference in outcome?
options: Both destroy the EC2 instance
state rm removes the resource from state but leaves the real instance running; destroy deletes the real instance
state rm deletes the instance and destroy only removes it from state
There is no difference — the commands are aliases
explain: EXAM TRAP, tested constantly: `state rm` = forget (object lives on, unmanaged); `destroy` = delete the real infrastructure. A and C swap or merge the meanings. D is false — they are opposites in effect on the real world.

q: After a refactor, `terraform plan` wants to recreate a resource whose address changed in state but whose real-world object is fine. You prefer the CLI over a `moved` block. Which command fixes the state address?
options: `terraform state mv <old-address> <new-address>` — renames the resource in state without touching the real object
`terraform state rm` followed by `terraform import`
`terraform refresh`
`terraform fmt`
explain: `state mv` is the CLI equivalent of a moved block: it renames within state, so the next plan shows no changes. B is a clumsy two-step that risks recreation. C is deprecated in favor of refresh-only and does not rename. D formats files — unrelated.

q: An engineer tweaked an instance type directly in the cloud console. The next `terraform plan` shows `~` update to revert the instance type to the configured value. What is this phenomenon called, and what caused Terraform to notice?
options: State locking — caused by concurrent applies
Drift — the real infrastructure diverged from state/config, detected when plan refreshed live values
Taint — the resource was marked for recreation
Import — the console change was imported automatically
explain: Drift is out-of-band change; plan's refresh phase reads live values and the diff proposes reverting to config. A is about concurrency. C requires explicit tainting. D is backwards — import brings things under management deliberately, never automatically.

q: A teammate runs `terraform state pull > backup.tfstate` before a risky state operation. What did they capture, and what is the complementary command?
options: They downloaded the remote state to stdout; `terraform state push` uploads a state file (dangerous — it can overwrite remote state)
They backed up the configuration files; the complement is `terraform state restore`
They exported the plan file; the complement is `terraform apply`
They listed all resources; the complement is `terraform state show`
explain: `state pull` downloads remote state; `state push` uploads a local state file — powerful and dangerous since it can clobber the shared state. B invents a restore command. C confuses state with plans. D confuses pull with list.

q: A company has a manually created database (ID `db-0abc123`) that must come under Terraform management without any downtime or recreation. What is the modern, exam-preferred approach?
options: Write an `import` block (`to` + `id`) plus a matching resource block, then plan and apply — the import is configuration-driven, reviewable, and visible in the plan
Run `terraform destroy` first, then let Terraform recreate the database
Copy the database's configuration into a data source
Import is impossible for databases; only new resources can be managed
explain: The 004-era pattern is the configuration-driven import block: write it with a matching resource block, review the import in the plan, apply to adopt. B destroys production data. C only reads; it never manages. D is false — import works for any importable resource type.

q: An engineer runs `terraform import aws_instance.legacy i-0abcd1234` on the CLI and the import succeeds, but the next `terraform plan` proposes to change several attributes of the instance. Why?
options: The import failed silently
Import adopts the real object into state but does not generate configuration — the (possibly empty or mismatched) resource block differs from reality, so plan proposes reconciling the diff
CLI imports always recreate the resource on the next apply
The instance ID changed during import
explain: EXAM TRAP: import never writes configuration for you. It maps the real object into state; your resource block is your own declaration, and any mismatch shows up as a planned diff. That is why the workflow is import -> plan -> reconcile config -> apply. A is wrong (the import succeeded). C is false — import never recreates. D is nonsense.

q: A team debates `terraform import` (CLI) versus `import` blocks. What is the 004 exam's framing of the difference?
options: They are identical in every way
The CLI command is a one-shot imperative action; the `import` block is declarative, version-controlled, peer-reviewable, and shows up in `terraform plan` before anything happens
Import blocks are deprecated; the CLI is the modern approach
The CLI can import resources that import blocks cannot
explain: 004 prefers import blocks because they fit the IaC model: reviewed in PRs, stored in version control, and previewed in plans. The CLI still works but is imperative and invisible until run. A erases a real distinction. C reverses the deprecation direction. D is false — both import the same resource types.

q: After a successful import of a legacy server, what should you do immediately, and why?
options: Run `terraform destroy` to verify the import worked
Run `terraform plan` to see what Terraform wants to change to reconcile your resource block with the imported real object
Delete the state file to start fresh
Nothing — imports are always perfectly aligned with configuration
explain: Because import does not generate configuration, the immediate plan reveals the gap between your declared block and reality — reconcile it before it surprises you later. A destroys what you just adopted. C discards the adoption. D assumes a perfection imports do not provide.

q: An engineer wants a quick inventory of every resource address currently tracked in state. Which command lists them?
options: `terraform state list`
`terraform show -json`
`terraform providers`
`terraform output`
explain: `state list` prints every tracked resource address — the state inventory. B dumps full state as JSON (verbose, not an address list). C lists required providers. D shows output values, not resources.

q: A teammate asks: `What AMI is that web instance actually running according to Terraform's records?` Which command shows the full recorded attributes of one resource?
options: `terraform state show aws_instance.web`
`terraform state list aws_instance.web`
`terraform get aws_instance.web`
`terraform console aws_instance.web`
explain: `state show <address>` displays the recorded attributes of a single resource. B lists addresses (and takes no address argument). C and D are not the right tools — `terraform console` evaluates expressions interactively but is not the direct answer for inspecting recorded attributes.

q: A provider returns a cryptic error during apply. You need maximum diagnostic detail written to a file for a bug report. Which environment setup does this?
options: `TF_LOG=TRACE` with `TF_LOG_PATH=./terraform.log` — TRACE is the most verbose level and TF_LOG_PATH redirects logs to a file
`TF_DEBUG=1`
`terraform apply -verbose`
`TF_LOG=OFF` with `TF_LOG_PATH=./terraform.log`
explain: TF_LOG controls verbosity (TRACE > DEBUG > INFO > WARN > ERROR) and TF_LOG_PATH redirects from stderr to a file. B and C are not real settings. D sets logging OFF — the opposite of diagnostics. Remember to disable verbose logging afterward: TRACE logs are huge and can contain secrets.

q: Order these TF_LOG levels from most to least verbose: INFO, TRACE, ERROR, DEBUG.
options: TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, ERROR
ERROR, INFO, DEBUG, TRACE
INFO, DEBUG, TRACE, ERROR
DEBUG, TRACE, ERROR, INFO
explain: The verbosity ladder is TRACE (everything) > DEBUG > INFO > WARN > ERROR (only errors) > OFF. Memorizing the order matters when someone asks for `maximum detail` (TRACE) versus `errors only` (ERROR).

q: A new hire asks what an HCP Terraform workspace actually is. Which definition is correct?
options: A local directory containing `.tf` files
One managed unit: a Terraform configuration plus its state file, variables, and run history — with remote execution on HCP Terraform
A Git branch that HCP Terraform watches
A dashboard folder for billing reports
explain: An HCP workspace binds config + state + variables + run history into one managed unit with remote runs. A describes a CLI working directory (related but not a workspace). C confuses VCS integration with the workspace itself. D is billing, not infrastructure.

q: A developer opens a pull request against the infrastructure repository. Before anyone merges, HCP Terraform automatically shows what the change would do to infrastructure. What is this called?
options: A speculative plan — HCP Terraform runs plans on PRs so reviewers see infrastructure impact before merge
A Sentinel warning
A drift detection report
A state migration
explain: VCS-driven runs trigger speculative plans on pull requests: the plan is computed but nothing is applied — pure review signal. B is policy enforcement. C is scheduled drift health checks. D is moving state between backends.

q: An engineer runs `terraform login` on their laptop. What did this accomplish?
options: It stored cloud provider credentials (AWS keys) for Terraform to use
It authenticated the Terraform CLI to HCP Terraform, storing a token for API access
It logged into the AWS console in the browser
It initialized the backend for the current directory
explain: EXAM TRAP: `terraform login` authenticates the CLI to HCP Terraform (token in ~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json) — it has nothing to do with cloud provider credentials, which are a separate layer. A and C confuse the two auth layers. D is init's job.

q: A configuration needs its runs to execute in the organization's HCP Terraform `prod-network` workspace. Which block connects the configuration to it?
options: A `backend "s3"` block pointing at the workspace name
A `cloud` block with `organization = "my-org"` and `workspaces { name = "prod-network" }`
A `provider "hcp"` block with the workspace name
A `workspace "prod-network"` block at the root
explain: The cloud block (or equivalently backend "remote") links a configuration to an HCP Terraform organization and workspace. A points at S3, not HCP. C invents a provider-based link. D invents a block type.

q: An organization has 40 workspaces that all need the same AWS credentials and region variables. What is the DRY way to manage this in HCP Terraform?
options: Copy the variables into each workspace by hand
Variable sets — define the shared variables once and attach the set to all 40 workspaces (or their project)
Store them in `terraform.tfvars` in each workspace's repo
Variable sets only work for a single workspace, so this is impossible
explain: Variable sets are shared variable collections attached across workspaces or projects — define once, inherit everywhere. A is the manual anti-pattern. C works for CLI runs but misses HCP's native mechanism. D is false; multi-workspace attachment is the point.

q: A security team requires that no security group open to `0.0.0.0/0` can ever be applied, and that every resource carry a `cost-center` tag. Which HCP Terraform feature enforces these rules on every plan?
options: Drift detection
Policy enforcement with policy sets (OPA/Rego) — policies evaluate each plan and can warn or block the run
Speculative plans
Run triggers
explain: Policy-as-code (Sentinel/OPA policy sets) evaluates every plan against governance rules and can block violations. A detects drift after the fact. C previews changes but enforces nothing. D chains workspace runs — unrelated to policy.

q: Nobody has touched the `prod` workspace in weeks, but the dashboard flags it as `drifted`. What produced this flag?
options: Drift detection — HCP Terraform's scheduled health checks compare real infrastructure against state and flag divergence
A failed speculative plan
An expired workspace token
The workspace was automatically destroyed
explain: HCP Terraform runs scheduled drift detection: refresh the real world, compare to state, flag drifted workspaces in the UI. B is PR-related. C is auth. D is false — detection flags, never destroys.

q: A compliance audit flags long-lived static AWS access keys used by Terraform runs. Which HCP Terraform feature eliminates static keys entirely?
options: Variable sets with the keys marked sensitive
Dynamic provider credentials — short-lived, workload-identity-based credentials minted per run, so there is nothing to rotate or leak
Storing keys in the private module registry
Running all applies from one hardened laptop
explain: Dynamic credentials mint short-lived cloud credentials per run via workload identity — no static keys exist to leak. A still stores static keys (just hidden). C is for modules, not credentials. D centralizes risk instead of removing it.

q: The networking workspace manages the VPC; the application workspace needs to plan automatically whenever networking successfully applies. Which feature chains them?
options: Remote state sharing
Run triggers — one workspace's successful apply automatically queues a run in downstream workspaces
Workspace variables
The `depends_on` meta-argument across workspaces
explain: Run triggers chain workspaces: upstream apply -> downstream plan/apply. A lets workspaces read each other's outputs but triggers nothing. C shares values, not runs. D works within a configuration, not across HCP workspaces.

q: A platform team groups its dev, staging, and prod workspaces under a `payments-team` container with shared governance boundaries. What is this container in HCP Terraform?
options: A project — it organizes related workspaces with shared governance (variable sets, permissions) boundaries
A run trigger
A policy set
An organization — teams cannot subdivide an organization
explain: Projects group related workspaces and set governance boundaries: who can see and change which environments. B chains runs. C enforces policy. D is wrong — organizations absolutely subdivide into projects and teams.

q: With HCP Terraform remote operations, a developer runs `terraform plan` on their laptop. Where does the plan actually execute, and what is the security benefit?
options: On the laptop, as always — remote operations only affect `apply`
On HCP Terraform's runners — cloud credentials stay server-side, so developers never need sensitive keys on their machines
On the cloud provider's API servers directly
In the Git repository's CI system
explain: Remote operations move execution to HCP Terraform: plans and applies run there, credentials live server-side, laptops hold no secrets. A denies the feature. C misunderstands where Terraform runs. D describes VCS-driven triggers, not the execution location.

q: An operations team keeps servers healthy by SSHing in and installing patches in place, which has caused drift and unrepeatable states. They adopt Terraform and start rebuilding server images from versioned code for every change instead of modifying live machines. What is this practice called?
options: Immutable infrastructure — replace servers rather than modifying them, so every machine is rebuilt from known-good configuration
Mutable infrastructure — patch live servers faster with automation
Elastic provisioning — add more servers when load increases
Blue-green deployment — run two load balancers at once
explain: Immutable infrastructure means change happens by replacing, not by patching in place — every server is reproducible from code. B names the old practice they are leaving. C is about scaling capacity. D is a deployment strategy, not an infrastructure-change philosophy.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A retailer needs to go from 10 web servers to 200 for a one-day sale, then back to 10. With Terraform driving cloud APIs, what cloud characteristic makes this practical?
options: High availability
Elasticity — rapid, API-driven scale up and down on demand
Fault tolerance
Multi-tenancy
explain: Elasticity is the cloud's rapid scaling in both directions, and IaC makes it a code change rather than a procurement project. High availability (A) is about surviving failures; fault tolerance (C) about continuing through them; multi-tenancy (D) about shared infrastructure — none describes scaling.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: An engineer learning Terraform asks what the tool actually reconciles during a run. Which trio is correct?
options: Git history, CI logs, and billing reports
The provider API, the CLI version, and the lock file
The desired state (configuration), the known state (state file), and the actual state (real infrastructure)
Variables, outputs, and modules
explain: Every Terraform run reconciles three things: what you declared (configuration), what Terraform last recorded (state), and what actually exists (reality, via refresh). A lists observability artifacts, not the reconciliation model. B lists tooling components. D lists configuration building blocks.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company has a database server everyone is afraid to reboot because nobody knows exactly how it was configured — it was built by hand three years ago. In IaC terminology, what is this server, and what does IaC prescribe?
options: A canary server — keep it running as an early-warning system
Technical debt that Terraform cannot address
A bastion host — document its SSH keys and move on
A pet (snowflake) — hand-built, unique, and fragile; IaC replaces pets with reproducible, disposable infrastructure
explain: EXAM TRAP: 'pets vs cattle' — a pet is a unique hand-built server you nurse; IaC turns infrastructure into cattle: identical, replaceable, rebuilt from code. A misuses 'canary' (a deployment test group). B is defeatist and false. C mislabels the server type entirely.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A junior engineer needs to open a database port to the internet for debugging. The lead wants this change reviewed, discussed, and reversible like application code. How does managing infrastructure in Terraform deliver this?
options: Terraform automatically blocks all risky port changes
The change becomes a pull request against version-controlled configuration — reviewable, commentable, and revertible via Git history
Terraform requires two engineers to type `yes` at the apply prompt
The cloud provider emails the team about every change
explain: Version-controlled infrastructure turns every change into a code review: diffs, comments, approvals, and revertable history. A invents automatic blocking (that's policy-as-code, a separate feature). C invents a two-person prompt. D describes provider notifications, not IaC collaboration.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A new hire already knows Terraform from managing AWS. The company now adopts Azure for one workload. What does Terraform's provider-agnostic workflow mean for this hire?
options: They must learn an entirely new IaC tool for Azure
Terraform auto-translates AWS configurations into Azure ones
They reuse the same HCL language and write/plan/apply workflow; only the provider-specific resource arguments are new
Azure cannot be managed by Terraform
explain: Provider-agnostic means one language and one workflow across providers — the hire transfers their Terraform skill and learns only Azure's resource model. A denies the core value proposition. B invents auto-translation. D is false; the AzureRM provider is first-class.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A region-wide cloud outage destroys a company's primary environment. Their entire infrastructure is defined in Terraform. What is their fastest path back, and which IaC advantage is this?
options: Run the same configuration against a new region — reproducibility turns disaster recovery into a redeploy
Wait for the provider to restore the region; IaC cannot help with outages
Manually rebuild from screenshots of the cloud console
Restore from the state file backup alone, with no configuration
explain: Because the environment is code, recovery is `apply` against a new region — not archaeology. B surrenders the main IaC DR advantage. C is the manual nightmare IaC eliminates. D is wrong: state without configuration cannot recreate anything.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team debates whether Terraform replaces their Ansible playbooks. What is the exam-correct relationship between the two?
options: Terraform and Ansible are identical tools; pick either one
They are complementary: Terraform provisions infrastructure (creates servers, networks, DNS), while configuration management tools configure software on already-provisioned machines
Ansible can provision cloud infrastructure but Terraform cannot configure servers
Using both together violates HashiCorp licensing
explain: The classic division: Terraform = provisioning (the what exists), config management = configuration (what runs on it). They overlap at the edges but solve different problems. A erases the distinction. C inverts reality. D invents a licensing restriction.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A CI pipeline's `terraform apply` fails halfway through due to a network timeout. The engineer simply reruns the pipeline and it completes cleanly with no duplicates. Which property made the retry safe?
options: Elasticity
High availability
Eventual consistency of the CI cache
Declarative idempotency — Terraform converges toward the declared end state, so re-applying only finishes what is missing
explain: Because Terraform declares the end state, a retry computes what's still missing and finishes it — already-created resources are left alone. A is about scaling. B is about uptime. C invents a cache property; the safety comes from the declarative model, not caching.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: An engineer manually deletes a production subnet in the cloud console by clicking the wrong row, causing an outage. How would a Terraform-managed workflow have reduced this risk?
options: Every change would first appear as a reviewable `terraform plan` diff with an explicit confirmation before apply
Terraform would have hidden the subnet from the console
Terraform prevents all human access to the cloud console
The state file would have restored the subnet automatically
explain: The plan/apply gate forces every change through a visible diff and a confirmation — misclicks don't survive review. B and C invent console restrictions Terraform doesn't impose. D is wrong: state records reality; it doesn't self-heal without an apply.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team wants every pull request to get its own complete copy of the staging environment, torn down on merge. Which IaC characteristic makes this economical?
options: IaC makes cloud resources free
Manual provisioning is faster for temporary environments
Environments become reproducible code — spin up with apply, destroy on merge, paying only while they exist
Terraform caches environments locally so they cost nothing
explain: Ephemeral environments work because the environment is code: create on demand, destroy when done, and the cloud bill only covers the lifetime. A and D invent free resources. B is backwards — manual builds are exactly what makes per-PR environments impractical.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A manager claims that adopting Terraform means the team no longer needs to understand AWS networking concepts. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Nothing — Terraform abstracts away all cloud concepts
Terraform is an automation layer over provider APIs; you still need to understand the underlying resources (VPCs, subnets, IAM) to declare them correctly
Terraform only works if the team forgets the console entirely
Understanding AWS is only needed for the state backend
explain: EXAM TRAP: Terraform automates the API calls but doesn't teach you what to declare — a bad VPC design in HCL is still a bad VPC. A is the misconception the exam hunts. C is nonsense. D narrows cloud knowledge to backends only.
