domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A new engineer joins and, instead of asking around, reads the Terraform configuration to learn how production is wired together. Which IaC advantage is this?
options: Cost optimization
Automated testing
Secrets management
Executable documentation — the configuration is a living, accurate description of the infrastructure
explain: Configuration-as-documentation: unlike a wiki, the config can't go stale without the infrastructure itself changing. A, B, and C are real concerns but none describes learning architecture from code.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A configuration uses features from Terraform 1.6, but a teammate on 1.2 gets cryptic errors. How does the team enforce the minimum CLI version?
options: In `required_providers`
With `required_version = ">= 1.6"` in the `terraform` block — Terraform errors early on older CLIs
By committing the `.terraform` directory
With a `check` block
explain: required_version gates the CLI itself: older binaries fail fast with a clear message instead of cryptic errors. A constrains providers, not the CLI. C commits throwaway install artifacts. D asserts on infrastructure, not tooling.

q: A `required_providers` block sets `version = ">= 3.0, < 4.0"` for a provider. Which versions are allowed?
options: 3.0 only
Any 3.x plus 4.0
3.x releases — from 3.0 up to but not including 4.0
Any version above 3.0 with no upper bound
explain: Comma-separated constraints combine with AND: >= 3.0 AND < 4.0, i.e. the whole 3.x line. A describes `= 3.0`. B wrongly includes 4.0. D drops the upper bound the team deliberately set.

q: A bank's build servers have no internet access, but engineers still need provider plugins. Which provider installation method fits?
options: A filesystem or network mirror hosting provider packages internally — init installs from the mirror instead of the public registry
Vendoring providers into `.terraform/` and committing it to Git
`terraform init -offline`, which downloads from the registry anyway
Providers cannot be installed without internet access
explain: Mirrors are the documented air-gapped path: the CLI config points init at an internal mirror. B commits machine-specific binaries — brittle and wrong. C misunderstands -offline (it only uses what's cached). D denies a real enterprise feature.

q: A team's lock file only has checksums for linux_amd64, but developers run `init` on macOS and hit hash mismatches. Which command adds the missing platform hashes?
options: `terraform init -upgrade`
Delete the lock file on each machine
`terraform fmt -recursive`
`terraform providers lock -platform=darwin_arm64` — records checksums for additional platforms without changing versions
explain: `providers lock` adds per-platform hashes to the existing lock entries — the multi-OS team workflow. A re-resolves versions (unnecessary churn). B destroys reproducibility. C formats code, unrelated to hashes.

q: Every CI run re-downloads the same provider plugins, adding minutes to each pipeline. Which mechanism lets runs share one local copy?
options: Committing `.terraform/` to Git
The plugin cache directory (`TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR`) — init reuses cached provider packages across working directories
The `version` argument on module blocks
`terraform validate` pre-downloads providers for later runs
explain: The plugin cache lets many working directories (and CI runs on one machine) share downloaded providers instead of refetching. A commits binaries — wrong layer. C pins module versions, unrelated to downloads. D is false; validate doesn't install anything.

q: Module A requires `hashicorp/aws >= 4.0, < 5.0` and module B requires `>= 5.0, < 6.0`. What happens at `terraform init`?
options: Terraform installs both major versions side by side
Each module silently gets its own provider version
Init fails — one configuration resolves to a single provider version satisfying all constraints, and no version satisfies both ranges
The root module's constraint is ignored in favor of the child's
explain: EXAM TRAP: Terraform selects exactly one version per provider per configuration — the newest satisfying every constraint. Contradictory ranges make resolution impossible and init errors. A and B invent multi-version installs. D invents constraint priority rules.

q: A `required_providers` entry lists `source = "hashicorp/aws"` with no hostname. Where does Terraform download it from?
options: `registry.terraform.io` — the default registry hostname when none is specified
The AWS API endpoint
HashiCorp's GitHub releases page
It fails — a hostname is mandatory in every source address
explain: Source addresses default to registry.terraform.io when the hostname is omitted — `hashicorp/aws` is shorthand. B confuses the provider's API target with its distribution point. C is not how init resolves providers. D is false; the default exists precisely so most configs omit it.

q: A CI job only needs to install providers and validate syntax; it has no access to the state backend and must not touch it. Which init flag fits?
options: `terraform init -migrate-state`
`terraform init -backend=false` — skips backend configuration entirely
`terraform init -input=false`
`terraform plan -refresh-only`
explain: -backend=false tells init to skip backend setup — right for syntax-only CI stages with no state access. A migrates state (the opposite). C only disables prompts. D is a plan mode, not an init flag.

q: A configuration defines `provider "aws"` (us-east-1) and `provider "aws" { alias = "west" }` (us-west-2). How does a resource declare it belongs in us-west-2?
options: With `region = "us-west-2"` inside the resource block
With `alias = "west"` inside the resource block
It is automatic based on the resource's name
With the meta-argument `provider = aws.west` in the resource block
explain: The `provider` meta-argument selects a non-default (aliased) provider configuration: `provider = aws.west`. A confuses resource arguments with provider selection. B invents an alias argument on resources. C invents name-based routing.

q: A team refuses to put AWS keys in Terraform files. An engineer sets `AWS_PROFILE=prod` and runs Terraform with no credentials in the configuration, and authentication works. Why?
options: Providers fall back to their SDK's default credential chain (environment variables, shared config files, SSO) when no static credentials are configured
Terraform invents credentials from the profile name
`terraform init` generates IAM keys automatically
The state backend supplies provider credentials
explain: Provider authentication cascades: explicit config first, then the SDK's standard chain — env vars, shared credentials files, SSO, instance metadata. That's why zero credentials in HCL still works. B is nonsense. C invents key generation. D confuses backend auth with provider auth.

q: The root module allows `hashicorp/aws >= 5.0` and a child module pins `~> 5.7`. A new 5.9.0 provider is released. Which version does `terraform init` select?
options: 5.0.0 — the lowest allowed version
6.0.0 — the newest overall release
5.9.0 — the newest version satisfying every constraint in the configuration
Init fails on the conflicting constraints
explain: Init resolves one version: the newest that satisfies ALL constraints (`>= 5.0` and `~> 5.7`, i.e. >= 5.7, < 6.0) — that's 5.9.0. A picks the floor for no reason. B violates `~> 5.7`. D is wrong; the constraints are compatible, just bounded.

q: A CI pipeline hangs during `terraform init` waiting for keyboard input about backend settings. How should automation handle this?
options: Pipe `yes` into init
Run `terraform init -input=false` and supply all backend settings via `-backend-config` so nothing prompts
Delete the backend block in CI
`terraform init` never prompts; the hang must be a bug
explain: -input=false disables interactive prompts (init then errors instead of hanging), and -backend-config supplies the values non-interactively — the automation-safe pairing. A is a hack. C breaks the backend. D is false; init prompts for missing backend values by default.

q: A state file's metadata shows it was written by Terraform 1.9, but a teammate running 1.5 gets a version error. What do the `terraform version` command and the state metadata together tell you?
options: State files are forward-compatible with all older CLIs
The teammate must downgrade the state file by hand
`terraform version` only shows provider versions
Terraform records the writing CLI version in state and refuses older CLIs that cannot safely read the format — upgrade the CLI
explain: State carries the terraform_version that wrote it; older CLIs fail fast rather than misreading a newer format. `terraform version` confirms what you're running. A is false — forward compatibility isn't guaranteed. B invents manual downgrades. C is wrong; it shows CLI, provider, and platform versions.

q: Before applying, a reviewer wants to inspect the human-readable contents of the saved plan file `tfplan`. Which command does this?
options: `terraform show tfplan` — renders the saved plan in readable form
`terraform plan tfplan`
`terraform output tfplan`
`cat tfplan` (it is plain text)
explain: `terraform show` renders saved plan files (and state) as human-readable output — the review step before `apply tfplan`. B re-plans instead of reading. C reads output values, not plans. D fails: plan files are binary-encoded.

q: A pipeline runs `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -out=tfplan` and must apply only when the plan contains changes. How does it decide?
options: Exit 0 means changes, exit 2 means clean
Parse the stdout text for the word 'change'
Exit code 2 means changes are present, 0 means no changes, 1 means error
`-detailed-exitcode` only works with apply
explain: Detailed exit codes are the machine-readable plan signal: 0 = clean, 1 = error, 2 = diff present. A inverts 0 and 2. B is brittle text scraping. D is false — the flag is designed for plan in CI.

q: A bank requires the same review rigor for teardowns as for builds: a destroy must be reviewed as a plan file before execution. Which commands implement this?
options: `terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.plan`, review it, then `terraform apply destroy.plan`
`terraform destroy -auto-approve` and review the logs afterward
`terraform apply -destroy` with no plan file
`terraform plan -out=destroy.plan` (without `-destroy`)
explain: `plan -destroy -out` captures the teardown as a reviewable artifact, and `apply` executes exactly that artifact — the destroy equivalent of the build review workflow. B skips review. C applies without a saved review. D plans a build, not a destroy.

q: An engineer runs `terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web` to 'just fix one server' in a configuration where other resources depend on it. What is the exam-correct caution about `-target`?
options: `-target` is the recommended daily workflow
`-target` applies the whole configuration anyway
`-target` only works with destroy
`-target` creates a partial apply that can leave dependencies uncreated and state inconsistent — use it for exceptions, not routine work
explain: EXAM TRAP: -target skips the dependency graph's normal completeness, so routine use drifts state away from configuration. It's a surgical exception tool, never the daily driver. A glorifies it. B and C misstate what it does.

q: An engineer wants to verify that `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 3)` returns `10.0.3.0/24` before committing the configuration. Which tool evaluates the expression interactively without any cloud access?
options: `terraform plan` with a dummy resource
`terraform console` — an interactive REPL for HCL expressions against the current state
`terraform validate`
`terraform fmt`
explain: `terraform console` is the expression playground: test functions and references live, no apply needed. A wastes a plan cycle. C checks correctness but doesn't evaluate values. D only reformats.

q: A team is designing pull-request checks for Terraform code. Which ordering of gates is correct and cheapest-first?
options: `fmt -check`, then `init`, then `validate`, then `plan` (speculative) — style, then install, then correctness, then the diff
`apply`, then `plan`, then `validate`
`validate` before `init`
`plan` before `fmt -check`
explain: Order gates by cost: formatting (instant), init (downloads), validate (correctness, no APIs), plan (the expensive diff). B applies before reviewing — backwards. C fails: validate needs provider schemas from init. D runs the expensive step before the cheap one.

q: A configuration manages thousands of resources and the plan's refresh phase takes 20 minutes. The pipeline refreshed state five minutes ago in an earlier step. How can the apply step skip re-reading everything, and what is the risk?
options: `terraform apply -refresh-only`
Delete the state file to skip refresh
`terraform apply -refresh=false` — skips the refresh, trading speed against the risk of planning from stale state
`terraform plan` never refreshes anyway
explain: -refresh=false skips the API read phase — legitimate when a fresh refresh just happened, risky otherwise because drift goes unseen. A refreshes only (no changes applied). B destroys tracking. D is false; plan refreshes by default.

q: A security audit asks for a list of every provider (and version constraint) a configuration requires, without running a plan. Which command reports the provider dependency tree?
options: `terraform state list`
`terraform output`
`terraform version`
`terraform providers` — shows required providers and which modules need them
explain: `terraform providers` prints the provider requirements tree across the module hierarchy — the audit answer. A lists state resources. B shows outputs. C shows CLI/provider versions installed, not requirements.

q: A pull request sets a variable default to a string where the type constraint requires a number. The CI job runs `terraform init` then `terraform validate` with no cloud credentials. What happens?
options: Validate passes — type errors need a plan to surface
Validate fails with a type-mismatch error — it checks declarations and expressions using provider schemas, no API calls needed
Validate skips variable checking entirely
The job must run apply to catch this
explain: Validate is a static correctness check: types, references, and block structure are verified against provider schemas without credentials. A and D wrongly require a plan/apply for a static error. C is false; variables are squarely in validate's scope.

q: A team copies a configuration to bootstrap a brand-new environment and points it at a fresh, empty state backend. They must NOT migrate the old environment's state. Which init flag reconfigures the backend without offering migration?
options: `terraform init -reconfigure` — discards prior backend settings and starts clean against the new backend
`terraform init -migrate-state`
`terraform apply -refresh-only`
`terraform workspace new`
explain: -reconfigure rewrites backend config and ignores the saved backend state — for intentionally abandoning the old state location. B is the opposite: it migrates state to the new backend. C and D don't reconfigure backends.

q: An engineer runs `terraform plan -var-file=base.tfvars -var-file=prod.tfvars`. Both files set `instance_count`. Which value wins?
options: `base.tfvars` — the first file wins
The apply fails on duplicate definitions
Later `-var-file` flags override earlier ones — `prod.tfvars` wins
The variable's default always wins over files
explain: EXAM TRAP: within the same precedence tier, later sources win — the last -var-file on the command line overrides earlier ones. A inverts the order. B is false; overriding is normal. D inverts the ladder (defaults lose to any file).

q: A nightly job must alert when production drifts from configuration, without changing anything. Which command pair implements the check?
options: `terraform apply -auto-approve` and grep the logs
`terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode` — exit 2 means drift was detected, and nothing is modified
`terraform destroy -target` in check mode
`terraform fmt -check`
explain: Refresh-only mode surfaces drift as a plan diff, and -detailed-exitcode turns it into an alertable signal (2 = changes) — fully read-only. A would apply changes. C destroys. D checks formatting, not infrastructure.

q: An architect wants a visual map of resource dependencies in a large configuration to review ordering before a big refactor. Which command produces the dependency graph?
options: `terraform show -graph`
`terraform plan -visual`
`terraform output -dot`
`terraform graph` — emits the resource dependency graph in DOT format for rendering
explain: `terraform graph` outputs the dependency graph in DOT format (pipe to Graphviz to render). The other three are invented flag combinations — the exam loves offering plausible-but-fake CLI flags.

q: An engineer defines a `locals` block computing `name_prefix = "${var.env}-app"` and then tries to override it with `-var='name_prefix=demo'`. What happens?
options: It fails — locals are internal to the configuration and cannot be set from outside; only input variables accept `-var`, files, or environment values
The local is overridden by the `-var` flag
Locals and variables are interchangeable
Terraform prompts for the local's value interactively
explain: EXAM TRAP: locals are computed constants internal to a module — there is no external interface to set them. Input variables are the only values callers can supply. B, C, and D all treat locals as settable inputs, which they are not.

q: Three instances were created with `count = 3`. An output needs the list of all their IDs. Which expression collects them?
options: `aws_instance.web.id`
`[for i in aws_instance.web : i]`
`aws_instance.web[*].id` — the splat expression returns one ID per instance
`element(aws_instance.web, 0)`
explain: The splat `[*]` projects an attribute across every instance of a multi-instance resource — the idiomatic collector. A fails (no single id exists). B returns whole objects, not IDs. D returns only the first element.

q: A bastion host should exist only in production. The configuration uses `count = var.env == "prod" ? 1 : 0` on the instance. What does this express, and what happens in dev?
options: The ternary operator is invalid in resource blocks
A conditional resource: prod gets one bastion, dev gets zero — `count = 0` creates nothing
Dev gets one bastion too, because count cannot be zero
Terraform errors because count must be a literal number
explain: The count-ternary is the standard conditional-resource idiom: 1 creates it, 0 skips it. A is false — expressions are fully allowed. C misreads the ternary. D is false; count accepts any number expression.

q: A variable holds a list of server objects, each with a `name`. A `for_each` needs a map keyed by server name. Which expression converts the list?
options: `toset(var.servers)`
`var.servers[*].name`
`[for s in var.servers : s.name]`
`{ for s in var.servers : s.name => s }` — builds a map of name to object
explain: The object form of a for expression (`{ key => value }`) builds the keyed map for_each needs. A makes a set of objects (no string keys). B extracts names only. C builds a list of names — still not a map.

q: A team needs a resource that runs a `local-exec` script whenever a rendered config file's content changes, without managing any real infrastructure. What is the modern resource for this?
options: `terraform_data` with a `triggers_replace` argument — the supported successor to `null_resource`
`null_resource` — still the recommended approach
A `data` block with a provisioner attached
The `terraform console` resource
explain: `terraform_data` replaced `null_resource` as the trigger-driven placeholder resource; changing `triggers_replace` forces re-execution. B names the deprecated predecessor. C is invalid — data sources can't host provisioners. D invents a resource.

q: An instance's startup script is rendered from a template file. When the file changes, the team wants the instance replaced (not just updated) so the new script actually runs. Which lifecycle argument does this?
options: `create_before_destroy`
`ignore_changes`
`replace_triggered_by` — forces replacement when the referenced value changes
`prevent_destroy`
explain: replace_triggered_by ties a resource's replacement to another value: when the trigger changes, this resource is replaced. A only reorders replacement. B would suppress the change. D blocks replacement — the opposite.

q: A database volume must never be smaller than 100 GB or the database will fail to start. Where should this guard live so a bad value fails before anything is created?
options: In a `check` block — it will fail the apply
In a `precondition` block on the volume resource — violations fail the plan/apply before the resource is created
In the variable's `description`
In `terraform.tfvars` as a comment
explain: Preconditions assert before the action: a violated precondition fails the run before the resource is touched. A is wrong — check blocks only warn, never fail. C documents but enforces nothing. D is a comment, not a guard.

q: A data source looks up the latest approved AMI. Policy requires the AMI be built within the last 90 days. Which construct fails the run if the data source returns a stale AMI?
options: A `validation` block on the data source
A `postcondition` block on the data source — it asserts on the read result and fails the run when violated
A `precondition` block on the data source
`terraform fmt -check`
explain: Postconditions assert after the read: they see the data source's result and fail the run if the assertion is false. Validation blocks only exist on variables. Preconditions assert before the action (can't see the result yet). D checks formatting.

q: An output block returns `aws_db_instance.main.password` but does NOT set `sensitive = true`. What happens to the output value in CLI display?
options: It displays in plaintext — sensitivity requires the explicit flag
The apply fails on the missing flag
The password is removed from the state file
Terraform automatically treats it as sensitive because the referenced value is sensitive, redacting it from CLI output
explain: EXAM TRAP: sensitivity propagates — referencing a sensitive value makes the output sensitive automatically, with Terraform noting the redaction. A assumes sensitivity is purely manual. C invents a failure. D confuses display redaction with state storage (the value is still in state).

q: A variable is typed `list(object({ cidr = string, az = string }))`. A caller passes a list of plain strings. What happens?
options: Terraform coerces the strings into objects automatically
The plan succeeds with null attributes
Terraform raises a type error — the value does not match the declared object structure
The objects are created with empty-string attributes
explain: Type constraints are enforced at the boundary: a list of strings is not a list of objects, so Terraform errors before planning. A overstates coercion (Terraform converts number-to-string, not string-to-object). B and D invent silent null-filling.

q: A module's object variable has an attribute most callers never set. How can the type declaration give it a default so callers may omit it?
options: With `optional(string, "default")` in the object type constraint — omitted attributes fall back to the default
It is impossible — all object attributes are required
With `nullable = false`
By removing the attribute from the type entirely
explain: The `optional()` type modifier (with an optional default) lets object attributes be omitted — the modern way to build flexible module interfaces. B denies the feature. C controls nullability, not optionality. D removes the attribute for everyone.

q: A VPC uses `10.0.0.0/16` and each availability zone needs its own `/24` subnet. Which function call yields `10.0.1.0/24` for the second AZ (index 1)?
options: `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 1)` — 8 new bits carve /24s; index 1 picks the second
explain: cidrsubnet(prefix, newbits, netnum): 8 new bits turns /16 into /24s, and netnum 1 selects 10.0.1.0/24. A swaps the arguments. B returns a host address, not a subnet. C string-builds the CIDR — fragile and not the exam's function.

q: An instance's `user_data` script needs the database endpoint and environment name injected at deploy time. What is the cleanest way to render it?
options: `templatefile("${path.module}/init.sh", { db_endpoint = ..., env = ... })` — renders an external template with variables
Hardcode the values directly in the script
A `remote-exec` provisioner that SSHes in to edit the file afterward
Store the script in the state file
explain: templatefile() renders a template with a variables map — the DRY way to inject values into scripts and configs. B bakes per-environment values into code. C adds SSH moving parts for something rendering solves. D misuses state as a script store.

q: A team wants to publish their `vpc` module for AWS to the public registry. Which repository naming and versioning convention does the registry require?
options: Any repo name works; versions come from `version` arguments in calling configurations
A GitHub repo named `terraform-aws-vpc`, with Git tags like `v1.0.0` marking releases
The module must be uploaded as a zip through the registry web UI
Registry modules are versioned by branch names only
explain: The public registry convention is strict: `terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>` repos, and version tags (`v1.0.0`) become registry versions. A ignores the naming contract. C invents a manual upload flow. D is false — tags, not branches, define versions.

q: A company stores versioned module archives in a private S3 bucket (no registry, no Git). How can a module block source them?
options: It cannot — S3 is not a module source
Only by unzipping the archive into the working directory first
`source = "s3::https://s3.amazonaws.com/bucket/vpc.zip"` — Terraform's module installer supports generic getter addresses including S3 and GCS
Only with `version = "1.0.0"` added to the block
explain: Module sources use go-getter addresses: `s3::`, `gcs::`, `git::`, `hg::`, and plain HTTP(S) all work — no registry required. A denies a documented source type. B is manual toil the installer automates. D confuses versioning (registry-only) with sourcing.

q: A module block uses `for_each = toset(["dev", "staging", "prod"])`. How does the root configuration reference the prod VPC's `vpc_id` output?
options: `module.vpc.vpc_id["prod"]`
`module.vpc[0].vpc_id`
Outputs cannot be read from for_each modules
`module.vpc["prod"].vpc_id` — each module instance is keyed like a resource
explain: for_each on a module block creates keyed instances addressed `module.<name>[<key>]` — outputs hang off the instance. A indexes the output instead of the module. B uses count-style numeric indexing. C denies the standard composition pattern.

q: A monitoring module has no input from the application module, but it must only be applied after the application exists. How is this ordering expressed?
options: `depends_on = [module.app]` in the monitoring module block — orders the whole module
It is impossible; modules cannot depend on each other
Rename the modules so alphabetical order works out
Add a `provider` meta-argument to the monitoring block
explain: Module blocks accept depends_on, ordering the entire module after another — for orderings no data reference can express. B denies a real meta-argument. C is the alphabetical-order myth. D selects providers, not ordering.

q: A child module manages resources in us-west-2, but the root's default AWS provider is us-east-1. The child declares `configuration_aliases = [aws.west]`. How does the root wire the aliased provider in?
options: The child automatically inherits all root provider aliases
With `providers = { aws.west = aws.west }` in the module block — explicitly passing the aliased configuration
By setting `region = "us-west-2"` in the module block
Child modules cannot use aliased providers
explain: EXAM TRAP: providers never flow into modules implicitly — the module block's `providers` map explicitly passes configurations, matched against the child's `configuration_aliases`. A assumes inheritance that doesn't exist. C puts a provider argument in the wrong block. D is false.

q: A team wants a registry module to accept any 5.x release but never jump to 6.0. Which version constraint expresses this?
options: `version = "5"`
`version = ">= 5.0"`
`version = "~> 5.0"` — allows 5.x while excluding 6.0
`version = "= 5"`
explain: The pessimistic operator with two components locks the major version: >= 5.0, < 6.0. A is not valid constraint syntax. B allows 6.0+. D pins to exactly 5 (and is odd syntax for it).

q: A 200-engineer org shares Terraform modules via Git URLs today, but nobody can discover available modules or tell which version is current. Which problem does moving to the private registry solve?
options: Git is too slow for module downloads
Nothing — the registry is just a Git alias
The registry executes modules faster than Git checkouts
The private registry adds searchable discovery, version browsing, and enforced versioning — governance that raw Git URLs lack
explain: The private registry is a governance layer: discoverability, version history, and access control over the same modules. A invents a speed problem. B erases the distinction. C invents execution differences — the registry only distributes code.

q: A root module calls a `networking` module and a `compute` module. Compute needs the subnet IDs that networking creates. What is the correct wiring?
options: Networking declares output `subnet_ids`; the compute module block passes `subnet_ids = module.networking.subnet_ids` into its input variable
Compute reads networking's state file directly
Both modules share input variables automatically
Hardcode the subnet IDs inside the compute module
explain: Module composition is outputs-to-inputs: the producer exposes outputs, the root wires them into the consumer's inputs. B couples stacks to state files (that's terraform_remote_state's job, between configurations). C assumes variable inheritance that doesn't exist. D bakes environment specifics into reusable code.

q: A module block sets `count = 3` to stamp out three identical environments. How is the second environment's `bucket_name` output addressed?
options: `module.env.bucket_name[1]`
`module.env[1].bucket_name` — the whole module instance is indexed
`module.env[1].bucket_name[1]`
Count is not allowed on module blocks
explain: Count on a module indexes the module instances: `module.env[1]`, then the output. A indexes the output value instead. C double-indexes. D is false — count and for_each both work on module blocks.

q: After `terraform init`, where does Terraform record exactly which module versions and source addresses were installed?
options: In the state file
In `.terraform.lock.hcl`
In `.terraform/modules/modules.json` — the module installation manifest
Nowhere; modules are re-resolved on every run
explain: The modules manifest records installed sources and versions — distinct from the provider lock file (B), which only covers providers. A is wrong; state tracks resources, not module installs. D is false; init's installs persist in .terraform/.

q: A team changes a module block's `source` from a Git URL to the public registry address and runs `terraform plan`. What happens?
options: Plan transparently uses the new source
The old Git module keeps being used silently
Terraform edits the state file to match automatically
Plan fails — modules install at init; the team must run `terraform init` to reinstall from the new source
explain: Modules are installed artifacts: changing the source requires re-running init before plan can proceed. A assumes plan installs (it never does). B is wrong — Terraform detects the mismatch and errors. C invents state surgery.

q: An engineer writes `source = "github.com/org/${var.repo}"` in a module block to pick the repo per environment. What happens at init?
options: Init fails — the `source` argument must be a literal string; variables and interpolation are not allowed because modules install before variables are evaluated
It works — source supports interpolation
The variable is read from tfvars during init
Only locals are allowed in source, not variables
explain: EXAM TRAP: module installation happens before variable evaluation, so `source` must be static — per-environment modules are selected with separate blocks or count/for_each, not interpolation. B, C, and D all assume variables exist at install time, which they don't.

q: An engineer runs `terraform workspace new staging` and expects an HCP Terraform workspace to appear in the dashboard. What actually happened, and what is the exam-critical distinction?
options: An HCP Terraform workspace was created remotely
A CLI workspace was created — it only switches the state namespace within the current backend; it is unrelated to HCP Terraform workspaces, which are server-side managed units
The command created both a CLI and an HCP workspace
The command is deprecated and does nothing
explain: EXAM TRAP: CLI workspaces (state isolation via backend key prefixes) and HCP Terraform workspaces (managed config+state+variables+runs) share a name and nothing else. A confuses the two. C merges them. D is false — CLI workspaces are current.

q: A security review asks what the state file contains. Which description is accurate?
options: Only resource IDs — no attribute values
Encrypted secrets and hashed resource data
Full resource attributes (including secrets in plaintext), outputs, and metadata like serial and lineage — which is why state access must be tightly controlled
Only the configuration text, for diffing
explain: State is a complete attribute record — secrets included, unencrypted by Terraform itself — plus outputs and bookkeeping metadata. That's why state backends need encryption at rest and strict access control. A understates it. B invents encryption. D confuses state with configuration.

q: A team configures the S3 backend and wants concurrent applies to be safe. What provides state locking for the S3 backend?
options: Nothing — S3 cannot lock, so concurrent applies are always unsafe
The `local` backend's lock file, shared over the network
Terraform core locks every backend automatically
A DynamoDB table referenced in the backend configuration — locking is a backend feature, not automatic
explain: Locking is a backend feature: the S3 backend uses a DynamoDB table for the lock (the classic documented setup). A denies the mechanism. B mixes backends. C is the core-vs-backend trap — core never locks by itself.

q: Each engineer uses a personal state bucket, so the bucket name cannot be committed. The backend block omits `bucket`, and engineers run `terraform init -backend-config="bucket=my-bucket"`. What is this pattern?
options: Partial backend configuration — static settings live in code, while sensitive or per-user values are supplied at init time
Backend variables — fully supported inside the backend block
A deprecated `-backend-config` flag
Impossible — backends cannot be split across code and flags
explain: Partial configuration is the documented workaround for the no-variables-in-backends rule: code holds the static parts, -backend-config supplies the rest. B states the exact misconception (variables are forbidden in backends). C is false. D denies a real pattern.

q: Two separate configurations manage networking and applications. The application stack needs the VPC ID from the networking stack's state. Which mechanism reads it?
options: A `module` block pointing at the networking directory
The `terraform_remote_state` data source — reads outputs from another configuration's state via its backend
A `terraform import` of the VPC into the application state
Copy-pasting the ID into a variable each time it changes
explain: terraform_remote_state is the cross-stack reader: it pulls another configuration's outputs through its backend. A only works within one configuration. C would duplicate management of the VPC. D is manual toil that rots.

q: An `aws_instance.web` is refactored into a child module as `module.compute.aws_instance.web`. The real instance must not be recreated. Which command updates the state address?
options: `terraform state rm` followed by re-apply
`terraform import` of the instance
`terraform state mv aws_instance.web module.compute.aws_instance.web` — renames the address in state, keeping the real object
`terraform apply -replace`
explain: `state mv` renames within state — the CLI equivalent of a moved block for refactors. A would plan a fresh create. B re-adopts what's already tracked. D forces the recreation you're trying to avoid.

q: An engineer runs `terraform state rm aws_instance.web` to 'clean up', leaving the resource block in place. What does the next `terraform plan` propose?
options: Nothing — the resource is forgotten forever
To destroy the real instance
To update the instance in place
To create a new instance — the block still declares it but state no longer tracks one, so Terraform plans a fresh create while the old instance keeps running unmanaged
explain: EXAM TRAP: state rm only forgets — the configuration still declares the resource, so plan sees 'declared but untracked' and proposes creation, leaving you with two instances. A assumes forgetting deletes. B is what destroy does. C needs a tracked resource to update.

q: Remote state was corrupted by a failed push. The team has yesterday's `terraform state pull` backup file. How do they restore it?
options: `terraform state push backup.tfstate` — uploads the backup as the current remote state (after verifying no runs are in flight)
`terraform apply backup.tfstate`
`terraform init -migrate-state`
Manually edit the state object in the S3 console
explain: `state push` is the restore path: it uploads a local state file as the remote current state — powerful, so verify no runs are active first. B misuses apply. C migrates between backends, not restores. D invites JSON corruption by hand.

q: A legacy configuration uses `backend "remote"` to connect to HCP Terraform, while new docs show a `cloud` block. What is the relationship?
options: They are unrelated features
Both connect a configuration to HCP Terraform workspaces; the `cloud` block is the newer, preferred syntax for the same integration
The `cloud` block is for public cloud providers like AWS
`backend "remote"` was removed from Terraform
explain: Both wire a configuration to HCP Terraform (remote state + remote operations); `cloud` is the modern syntax. A denies the overlap. C confuses HCP's cloud block with cloud providers. D is false — backend "remote" still works.

q: Compliance requires the state file be encrypted at rest. Terraform itself does not encrypt state. How is this satisfied with the S3 backend?
options: Mark all resources `sensitive = true`
It cannot be satisfied — Terraform state is always plaintext on disk
Enable server-side encryption on the bucket (and restrict access) — encryption is the backend/storage layer's job
Commit the state to a private Git repository
explain: Terraform delegates encryption to the storage layer: S3 server-side encryption plus tight IAM satisfies 'encrypted at rest.' A only redacts CLI display. B gives up on a solved problem. D is an anti-pattern — state in Git leaks and conflicts.

q: A CI pipeline manages dev/staging/prod via CLI workspaces and needs to select one without interactive commands. Which environment variable does Terraform read for the workspace name?
options: `TF_VAR_workspace`
`WORKSPACE`
`TF_BACKEND_workspace`
`TF_WORKSPACE` — selects the CLI workspace non-interactively
explain: `TF_WORKSPACE` is the automation hook for CLI workspace selection. A would set an input variable named workspace. B and C are invented names — only the TF_WORKSPACE prefix is recognized.

q: An old runbook instructs engineers to run `terraform refresh` before every plan to sync state. What is the modern guidance?
options: The standalone `refresh` command is deprecated — plan and apply refresh by default; use `plan -refresh-only` / `apply -refresh-only` when you explicitly want a refresh-only operation
`terraform refresh` is still the recommended pre-plan step
Refresh was removed from plan; only the standalone command refreshes
Run `terraform init` instead to refresh state
explain: The standalone refresh command is deprecated: every plan/apply already refreshes, and -refresh-only covers the explicit-sync use case. B follows a retired runbook. C inverts reality. D confuses init with state sync.

q: An instance's local disk is corrupted beyond repair. The team wants Terraform to destroy and recreate exactly that instance on the next apply. Which flag does this?
options: `terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web`
`terraform apply -replace="aws_instance.web"` — forces replacement of the addressed resource
`terraform taint aws_instance.web`
`terraform state rm aws_instance.web`
explain: -replace marks the resource for destroy-and-recreate on the next apply — the modern, plan-visible way to force replacement. A only narrows scope; it doesn't force replacement. C names the deprecated command. D forgets the resource instead of replacing it.

q: A 2020 blog post recommends `terraform taint` to force resource recreation. What is the 004-era guidance?
options: `taint` is still the primary method
`taint` never existed as a command
`taint`/`untaint` are deprecated — use `terraform apply -replace="<address>"` instead
Use `terraform destroy -target` instead of tainting
explain: EXAM TRAP: taint was deprecated in favor of -replace, which shows the replacement in the plan before it happens. A follows outdated advice. B denies history. D destroys without recreating — not a replacement.

q: A team uses `local-exec` provisioners to run a dozen deployment scripts after every apply. What is HashiCorp's stance, and what is the risk?
options: Provisioners are the recommended deployment tool
Provisioners run before resources are created, which is ideal for bootstrapping
Provisioners are fully tracked in the state file

Provisioners are a last resort — they run outside Terraform's model, their side effects are not fully captured in state, and cleaner patterns (user_data, config management, immutable images) usually fit better
explain: HashiCorp documents provisioners as a last resort: they're imperative scripts bolted onto a declarative tool, invisible to plan and only partially reflected in state. A inverts the guidance. B is false — they run after creation. C overstates what state records.

q: A `remote-exec` provisioner must run commands on a newly created EC2 instance over SSH. What must the resource declare for this to work?
options: A `connection` block with `type = "ssh"`, host, user, and credentials — provisioners need explicit connection details
Nothing — Terraform SSHes into new instances automatically
A `provider "ssh"` block
The instance's password hardcoded in a variable
explain: remote-exec needs a connection block describing how to reach the machine — Terraform can't guess SSH details. B assumes magic connectivity. C invents a provider. D hardcodes secrets instead of configuring a connection.

q: When an instance is destroyed, the team wants a script to deregister it from an external monitoring service. Which provisioner configuration runs only during destruction?
options: `when = create`
`when = destroy` on the provisioner — it executes only when the resource is being destroyed
`on_failure = continue`
Provisioners cannot run on destroy
explain: `when = destroy` flips the provisioner to teardown time — the cleanup hook. A is the default (runs on create). C controls failure tolerance, not timing. D denies the documented destroy-time provisioner.

q: A `local-exec` provisioner sends a Slack notification after apply. If Slack is down, the apply should still succeed. How is the provisioner made non-blocking?
options: Remove the provisioner entirely
`when = destroy`
`on_failure = continue` — provisioner failure is tolerated and the apply continues
`terraform apply -auto-approve`
explain: on_failure = continue downgrades a provisioner failure from fatal to warning — right for non-critical side effects. A throws away the notification. B changes timing, not failure handling. D skips confirmation, unrelated to provisioner errors.

q: A `local-exec` provisioner on an `aws_instance` needs the instance's own private IP to register it in DNS. How does it reference the IP?
options: Via `var.private_ip`
Via `aws_instance.web.private_ip` — direct self-reference is allowed
It cannot — provisioners cannot see resource attributes
Via `self.private_ip` — the `self` object refers to the resource the provisioner is attached to
explain: Inside a provisioner, `self` refers to the enclosing resource — and it's the only way to reference it, since naming the resource directly would create a dependency cycle. A assumes a variable exists. B would be circular. C denies the self mechanism.

q: A provisioning script must re-run whenever the AMI ID in the configuration changes, even though no infrastructure needs replacing. Which pattern triggers this?
options: A `terraform_data` resource with `triggers_replace = { ami = var.ami_id }` — changing the trigger value forces the resource (and its provisioners) to re-run
A `check` block on the AMI variable
`ignore_changes = [ami_id]`
`terraform apply -refresh-only`
explain: triggers_replace turns an input change into a replacement event, re-running provisioners without touching real infrastructure. B only warns post-apply. C would suppress the change. D syncs state without applying anything.

q: The AWS provider releases 6.0.0 with breaking changes. The team's constraint is `~> 5.0`. What is the safe upgrade path?
options: Run `terraform init -upgrade` — 6.0 will install automatically
Widen the constraint deliberately, read the provider's changelog/upgrading guide, then `init -upgrade` and review the plan carefully — major versions can change resource behavior
Delete the lock file and apply immediately
Major versions never break anything, so upgrade freely
explain: Major versions may break: the safe path is deliberate — read the upgrade guide, widen the constraint on purpose, re-resolve, and scrutinize the plan. A is wrong: `~> 5.0` blocks 6.0 by design. C discards reproducibility. D ignores semver reality.

q: An apply fails halfway through creating a database, and the resource is marked tainted in state. What does the next `terraform apply` do with it?
options: Skips the tainted resource and continues with the rest
Errors — tainted resources must be manually untainted first
Replaces the tainted resource (destroy and recreate) and continues converging toward the configuration
Deletes the entire state file and starts over
explain: Tainted means 'known bad': the next apply replaces it automatically as part of converging on the declared state. A would leave a broken resource. B invents a manual step (untaint exists but isn't required). D is catastrophic overkill.

q: A provider crashes with a panic during apply, and support asks for the most detailed log possible. Which setup produces it, and what caution applies?
options: `TF_LOG=ERROR` — least detail is safest for bug reports
`terraform apply -verbose`
`TF_DEBUG=1`
`TF_LOG=TRACE` with `TF_LOG_PATH` to a file — maximum detail; scrub secrets from the log before sharing and disable verbose logging afterward
explain: TRACE is the most verbose level and TF_LOG_PATH captures it to a file — but TRACE logs can contain secrets, so scrub before sharing and turn logging off after. A gives the least detail. B and C are not real settings.

q: A policy tool needs to analyze a saved plan file programmatically. Which command renders the plan as machine-readable JSON?
options: `terraform show -json tfplan` — converts the saved plan to JSON for tooling
`terraform plan -json`
`terraform output -json tfplan`
`cat tfplan | grep json`
explain: `show -json` is the machine-readable bridge: plan files, state, and configs become JSON for policy and automation tools. B invents a plan flag. C reads outputs, not plans. D treats a binary plan file as greppable text.

q: A workspace manages infrastructure in a private datacenter with no inbound internet access. Which HCP Terraform execution mode fits, and why?
options: Remote — HCP runners can reach any private network
Agent — self-hosted agents poll HCP Terraform outbound and execute runs inside the private network, so no inbound firewall rules are needed
Local — developers apply from their laptops
Execution modes only matter for VCS-driven runs
explain: Agents invert the connection: they poll HCP Terraform outbound, then run Terraform where the targets live — the private-network execution model. A is wrong: HCP runners can't reach private networks. C pushes credentials to laptops. D is false; modes apply to all runs.

q: Developers need to provision standard database instances without writing Terraform. Which HCP Terraform feature serves versioned modules through a form-based UI?
options: Run triggers
The private registry alone
No-code provisioning — approved modules become clickable, variable-driven deployments for non-Terraform users
Speculative plans
explain: No-code provisioning publishes modules as UI-driven templates: pick inputs in a form, HCP Terraform runs the module. A chains workspace runs. B distributes modules but provides no deployment UI. D previews PRs — unrelated.

q: FinOps requires every infrastructure change to show its estimated monthly cost impact before apply, with the option to block expensive runs. Which HCP Terraform feature provides this?
options: Drift detection
Variable sets
`terraform plan` always shows costs natively
Cost estimation — HCP Terraform estimates resource cost deltas on runs, and policies can gate applies on the estimate
explain: Cost estimation computes the cost delta of each run before apply, and policy-as-code can block over-budget changes. A flags drift after the fact. B shares variables. C is false — the CLI has no cost data; it's an HCP Terraform feature.

q: A `check` block asserts that all load balancers use TLS 1.2+. The team wants this evaluated continuously after apply, not just during runs. Which HCP Terraform capability does this?
options: Health assessments with continuous validation — check blocks are re-evaluated on a schedule and failures surface in the UI
Speculative plans
Run triggers
Check blocks only evaluate during runs, so this is impossible
explain: Continuous validation re-runs check-block assertions on a schedule post-apply — drift in compliance surfaces without a new run. B previews PRs. C chains workspaces. D denies the exact feature built for this.

q: An infrastructure monorepo holds Terraform in `infra/` plus application code. The team wants HCP Terraform runs only when `infra/` changes, on the `main` branch. Where is this configured?
options: In the provider blocks
In the workspace's VCS settings — working directory, branch, and trigger patterns (with speculative plans on PRs)
In `terraform.tfvars`
Trigger patterns are not supported by HCP Terraform
explain: VCS workspace settings control the integration: which repo/branch, which working directory, and which path patterns trigger runs. A configures providers. C sets variable values. D denies a core VCS-workflow feature.

q: A workspace variable must hold a list of CIDR blocks. In the HCP Terraform UI, what must be set for `["10.0.0.0/16"]` to be interpreted as a list rather than a literal string?
options: Mark the variable sensitive
Nothing — all values are parsed as HCL automatically
The variable category must be Terraform (not Environment), and the HCL checkbox enabled so the value is parsed as an HCL expression
Lists are not allowed as workspace variables
explain: Workspace variables are strings by default; the HCL checkbox parses the value as an expression — and it only applies to the Terraform category (Environment variables are always strings). A hides the value. B is false. D denies complex variable values.

q: A variable set attached to a project defines `region = "us-east-1"`, but one workspace sets `region = "eu-west-1"` directly. Which value does that workspace use?
options: `us-east-1` — variable sets always win
The run fails on the conflicting definitions
The two values are merged
`eu-west-1` — workspace-level variables take precedence over variable set values
explain: EXAM TRAP: precedence runs workspace > variable set — the workspace's own value wins, letting sets provide defaults. A inverts the hierarchy. B invents a conflict error. C invents merging of scalar values.

q: Contractors should be able to run plans for review but must never apply. How is this enforced in HCP Terraform?
options: Team permissions with granular workspace access — grant plan-only rights without apply rights
It cannot be enforced; anyone who can plan can apply
Remove the contractors from the organization entirely
Set the workspace to local execution mode
explain: HCP Terraform's RBAC separates plan from apply at the team/workspace level — least privilege for reviewers. B denies the permission model. C is overkill. D changes where runs execute, not who can approve them.

q: A run's plan proposes opening port 22 to the world, violating a policy set. At which stage is the run stopped?
options: During the plan — the plan never completes
After planning, at the policy check stage — the plan is evaluated against policy sets before cost estimation and apply, and violations can block the run
Only after apply — policies are detective, not preventive
Policy sets only evaluate speculative plans, never real runs
explain: Policy-as-code is preventive: the plan completes, then the policy check evaluates it and hard/mandatory violations block the run before apply. A is wrong — the plan must exist to be evaluated. C describes drift detection, not policy. D inverts the enforcement scope.

q: A CI system needs HCP Terraform API access limited to a single team's workspaces. Which token type fits?
options: A user token — tied to an individual's identity
An organization token — full org-wide access
A team token — scoped to the team's workspaces, suitable for automation without tying access to an individual
There is only one token type for all API access
explain: Team tokens scope API access to a team's workspaces — the automation-safe choice. User tokens (A) tie access to a person. Organization tokens (B) are far too broad. D denies the token hierarchy.

q: A run is currently applying in a workspace when a second engineer triggers another apply. What happens?
options: Both applies run concurrently against the same state
The second apply silently overwrites the first
State corruption is expected and must be repaired afterward
HCP Terraform locks the workspace for the duration of a run — the second run queues until the lock releases
explain: HCP Terraform serializes runs per workspace with a lock — the same protection remote backends give the CLI, managed server-side. A, B, and C describe the corruption scenario that locking exists to prevent.

q: Platform engineering wants every team to consume the same hardened, reviewed modules and the same compliance policies. Which HCP Terraform combination delivers this?
options: The private module registry plus organization-level policy sets — shared modules with versioning, enforced policies on every workspace run
Emailing module zip files to each team
A shared GitHub repo with no versioning or access control
Each team writing and maintaining its own policies
explain: The governance pair: the private registry distributes approved, versioned modules, and org-level policy sets enforce compliance on every run. B, C, and D are the ungoverned anti-patterns this combination replaces.

q: A company's staging environment was built by hand from a runbook and production was built by a different engineer from memory. A release works in staging but breaks in production, and the team spends two days discovering the two environments were never identical. Which IaC advantage would have prevented this class of failure?
options: Environment parity — the same version-controlled configuration provisions every environment, so staging and production cannot silently diverge
Faster hardware — IaC provisions servers with higher clock speeds
Automatic bug fixing — Terraform rewrites application code to match environments
Free cloud resources — IaC eliminates infrastructure spend
explain: The failure is environment drift between hand-built environments; IaC makes each environment an instantiation of the same code, so parity is structural rather than aspirational. B invents hardware effects. C confuses infrastructure provisioning with application debugging. D invents free resources.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: An apply opens the wrong ports on a production firewall and the on-call engineer needs it undone immediately. The change was merged as a pull request an hour ago. What is the fastest IaC-native recovery?
options: Rebuild the firewall rules from memory in the console
Revert the commit in version control and re-apply — the previous known-good state is one revert away
Delete the state file so Terraform forgets the change
Wait for the next scheduled apply to fix it automatically
explain: Because every change is a commit, recovery is git revert plus apply — minutes, with the full history as the audit trail. A returns to the manual process that caused the incident. C discards Terraform's memory without changing reality. D invents self-healing; Terraform only converges on apply.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A SaaS company must run its full stack in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-2 with identical configuration. Doing it by hand tripled the misconfiguration incidents. How does IaC address this?
options: Terraform automatically translates us-east-1 resources into the other regions' equivalents
Cloud providers give discounts for multi-region IaC deployments
One version-controlled configuration is applied per region, so all three are built from the same declared intent
IaC removes the need for regional isolation entirely
explain: IaC scales consistency: the same code, applied with per-region inputs, produces identical stacks everywhere. A invents auto-translation of regional services. B invents IaC discounts. D misunderstands why regions exist.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Developers wait up to two weeks for the ops team to manually provision databases from ticket requests. After the platform team publishes a reviewed database module, developers provision their own databases in minutes via pull requests. Which IaC advantage is this?
options: IaC removes the need for database backups
IaC makes databases run faster
IaC eliminates the need for code review
Self-service provisioning — standardized, reviewed modules turn a manual ticket queue into a minutes-long pull request
explain: Modules package organizational knowledge into safe, reusable building blocks, letting consumers provision without deep expertise or waiting on a queue. A confuses provisioning with backup strategy. B invents performance effects. C inverts reality — the pull request IS the review.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Three teams name their S3 buckets three different ways, breaking the company's cost-allocation reports. The platform team wants every bucket to follow one naming convention going forward. How does Terraform enforce this structurally?
options: A shared module that constructs bucket names from required inputs — teams get correctly named buckets by construction, not by policy document
Terraform renames existing buckets automatically
IaC deletes non-compliant buckets without warning
A wiki page describing the naming convention
explain: Modules encode standards in code: consumers pass inputs and the module produces compliant resources, making the convention the default path. B is false — Terraform never renames out from under you. C invents destructive enforcement. D is documentation without enforcement — the pre-IaC approach.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: FinOps wants to review the cost impact of a proposed architecture change before anything is built. The change is a Terraform pull request. What does the IaC workflow give them?
options: The exact future cloud bill, guaranteed
A plan showing every resource that will be created, changed, or destroyed — the concrete inventory behind the cost impact, reviewable before spend happens
Automatic selection of the cheapest possible resources
Nothing — cost can only be assessed after apply
explain: The plan is a pre-execution bill of materials: reviewers see exactly what will exist before any money is spent. A overpromises — the plan shows resources, not a guaranteed invoice. C invents automatic cost optimization. D ignores the entire point of the plan phase.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A platform team wants application developers to provision their own infrastructure without learning every cloud service's API. Which IaC pattern delivers this safely?
options: Giving every developer root credentials and the cloud console
Writing longer runbooks for each service
Publishing opinionated, reviewed modules with a small set of inputs — developers consume safe abstractions while the platform team owns the complexity
Banning developers from provisioning anything
explain: Modules are the abstraction layer: the platform team encodes best practices once, and consumers get safe defaults through a narrow interface. A is the ungoverned anti-pattern. B scales documentation, not safety. D blocks productivity instead of enabling it safely.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: The wiki says the database is a db.m5.large, the console shows db.m5.xlarge, and last quarter's ticket says db.m5.2xlarge. Nobody knows which is authoritative. What does managing the database in Terraform change?
options: Terraform deletes the wiki automatically
The console becomes the source of truth instead
Tickets become legally binding
The version-controlled configuration becomes the single declared source of truth — the wiki, console, and tickets stop competing
explain: IaC collapses competing records into one authoritative declaration; drift from it is detectable and correctable. A invents wiki deletion. B keeps the console authoritative, which is the current problem. C elevates tickets, another competing source.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team proposes using Terraform to build their application binaries, run their test suite, and deploy code to servers on every commit. What is the exam-correct response about Terraform's role?
options: Terraform manages infrastructure lifecycle (provision, update, destroy); building and deploying application code is outside its scope — that belongs to CI/CD and deployment tooling
Terraform is a complete CI/CD replacement
Application deployment is Terraform's primary use case
Terraform cannot create servers, only deploy code
explain: The exam draws a clean line: Terraform provisions and manages infrastructure; artifact builds and code deploys are separate concerns handled by CI/CD. B and C erase the line. D inverts Terraform's actual purpose.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team must test a risky database migration against a full copy of production, including network topology. Building that copy by hand takes a week. How does IaC change the economics of this test?
options: It doesn't — test environments must be built by hand for accuracy
The production configuration is applied to an isolated environment, tested, then destroyed — a faithful copy costs only its lifetime, not a week of labor
Terraform tests migrations automatically with no copy needed
Migrations no longer need testing once IaC is adopted
explain: Because environments are code, a production-faithful copy is an apply away and teardown is a destroy away — testing expensive scenarios becomes cheap and routine. A defends the manual status quo. C invents automatic migration testing. D confuses easier testing with unnecessary testing.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A change ticket proposes 'updating the network configuration' with no further detail. The same change expressed as a Terraform pull request shows a plan touching 2 subnets. Which IaC advantage does this illustrate?
options: IaC makes network changes unnecessary
Terraform applies changes without review
Change transparency — the plan makes the blast radius explicit and reviewable before anything executes
IaC guarantees the change is safe
explain: The plan turns a vague change description into an exact, reviewable diff — reviewers approve the actual impact, not a description of it. A is nonsense. B inverts the workflow (review precedes apply). D overpromises; the plan shows impact, it doesn't certify safety.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: One senior engineer knows the 47 manual steps to rebuild the payments environment; everyone else is afraid to touch it. She announces she's leaving in a month. Which IaC property directly addresses this risk?
options: Terraform automatically documents engineers' knowledge by watching them work
IaC makes the payments environment too simple to need documentation
The engineer can be replaced by a larger team
Codified knowledge — the rebuild procedure becomes version-controlled code anyone can read, review, and execute
explain: IaC converts tribal knowledge into executable, reviewable artifacts — the runbook is the code, and it can't quit. A invents automatic knowledge capture. B confuses codification with simplification. C throws people at a knowledge problem.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Two engineers open the cloud console at the same time and both modify the same security group; the second save silently overwrites the first. How does the Terraform workflow prevent this class of conflict?
options: Changes flow through version control — concurrent edits become merge conflicts resolved in code, and applies are serialized through state locking
Terraform lets both engineers edit the console simultaneously without issues
Terraform disables the cloud console for everyone
Conflicts are impossible once IaC is adopted
explain: Version control turns silent overwrites into explicit merge conflicts, and state locking serializes applies — collaboration becomes structured. B keeps the broken console workflow. C invents console prohibition. D overpromises; IaC manages conflicts, it doesn't abolish them.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A new hire commits the entire working directory — including `.terraform/` and `terraform.tfstate` — to the team's Git repository. The repo balloons and a teammate's apply corrupts shared state. Which files belong in version control?
options: Commit `.tf` files, `.tfvars` files, and `.terraform.lock.hcl`; never commit `.terraform/` (reinstallable provider binaries and modules) or `*.tfstate` (live state with secrets)
Commit everything including `.terraform/` for reproducibility
Commit only the state file — it contains everything
Commit `.terraform/` but never the `.tf` files
explain: Version control holds intent (config, variables, lock file); machine-specific installs and live state stay out — state in Git leaks secrets and corrupts under concurrency. B bloats the repo with binaries. C commits secrets and invites corruption. D inverts what matters.

q: A security team asks how Terraform ensures a downloaded provider binary wasn't tampered with in transit. What is the mechanism?
options: Terraform trusts any binary the registry serves
The dependency lock file records cryptographic checksums for each provider; init verifies downloads against them, and the registry signs its provider packages
Providers are never verified — verification is the user's job
The state file stores provider checksums
explain: Integrity is cryptographic: lock-file checksums plus registry signatures mean a tampered binary fails verification at install time. A describes blind trust, the opposite of the design. C denies the built-in mechanism. D puts checksums in the wrong artifact.

q: A provider block hardcodes `region = "us-east-1"` while the shell exports `AWS_REGION=eu-west-1`. Which region does the provider use?
options: eu-west-1 — environment variables always win
The apply fails on the conflict
us-east-1 — explicit arguments in the provider block take precedence over environment variables
Terraform picks one at random
explain: The credential/config cascade puts explicit provider-block arguments above environment variables — static config wins when both are set. A inverts the precedence. B invents a conflict error; the cascade resolves it deterministically. D invents randomness.

q: A configuration uses `aws` resources but contains no `provider "aws"` block at all. `AWS_REGION` and credentials are exported. What happens at plan time?
options: Plan fails — every provider needs an explicit block
Terraform uses the credentials to pick a region automatically
Init downloads the provider but plan cannot proceed
It works — Terraform creates an implicit empty (default) provider configuration, filled in by the SDK's credential and region chain
explain: Provider blocks are optional when defaults suffice: Terraform synthesizes an empty default configuration and the provider's standard chain supplies credentials and region. A invents a mandatory-block rule. B invents region inference. C invents a plan-time blockage.

q: An engineer places a `resource` block inside the `terraform { }` block, reasoning that 'everything goes in terraform'. What is wrong?
options: The `terraform` block holds only Terraform-level settings — `backend`, `required_providers`, `required_version`, `cloud`, and similar; resources, providers, variables, and outputs live at the top level
Nothing — resources belong inside the terraform block
Resources go inside `required_providers`
The terraform block is deprecated
explain: The terraform block configures Terraform's own behavior; infrastructure and input declarations are top-level blocks. B states the exact misconception. C confuses provider requirements with resources. D is false — the block is current and required for backend/version settings.

q: A CI job vendors modules into the working directory and must not reach the network during init, but providers still need installing. Which init invocation fits?
options: `terraform init -backend=false`
`terraform init -get=false` — skips module installation while still installing providers and configuring the backend
`terraform init -upgrade`
Delete the module blocks before init
explain: -get=false disables only the module installer — right when modules are vendored but providers still come from the registry. A skips the backend instead. C re-resolves everything, the opposite of hermetic. D mutilates the configuration.

q: A bank runs an internal provider mirror and needs every engineer and CI job to use it instead of the public registry. Where is this configured?
options: In each `.tf` file's `required_providers` block
In the state file
In the CLI configuration file (`~/.terraformrc` / `terraform.rc`) via a `provider_installation` block — it controls installation behavior, not configuration
In `terraform.tfvars`
explain: Mirrors are a CLI installation concern, configured in the CLI config file — .tf files declare what is needed, the CLI config controls where it comes from. A puts installation policy in configuration. B and D use artifacts that never control installs.

q: A company publishes an internal provider to its private registry at `registry.example.com`. What does a valid `source` address for it look like?
options: `source = "example"` — hostnames are not allowed
`source = "https://registry.example.com/acme/widget"` — source takes a URL
Private registries cannot be referenced; the provider must be vendored
`source = "registry.example.com/acme/widget"` — the hostname slot accepts any registry, defaulting to registry.terraform.io only when omitted
explain: Source addresses are hostname/namespace/type; any registry hostname works, with the public registry merely the default. A denies custom hosts. B uses URL form, which source doesn't accept. C denies a core enterprise feature.

q: A configuration uses twelve providers and the team wants to upgrade only the AWS provider to its newest allowed version. Which approach is correct?
options: There is no selective upgrade flag — widen the AWS constraint if needed and run `terraform init -upgrade`, which re-resolves all providers (unchanged constraints keep the others pinned by the lock file)
`terraform init -upgrade=hashicorp/aws`
`terraform providers upgrade aws`
Edit `.terraform.lock.hcl` by hand
explain: Init's upgrade is all-or-nothing by design; unchanged constraints plus the lock file keep other providers stable while AWS re-resolves. B and C invent selective flags. D hand-edits a managed file, bypassing checksum verification.

q: A team pins `required_version = ">= 1.9"` and assumes their provider versions are now also locked to 1.9+. After init, the AWS provider installs 6.x. What did they misunderstand?
options: `required_version` also constrains providers — this is a bug
Nothing — `required_version` constrains only the Terraform CLI; provider versions are governed separately by `required_providers` version constraints
Provider versions always match the CLI version
The lock file overrides `required_version`
explain: Two separate version domains: required_version gates the CLI binary, required_providers gates each provider — pinning one never pins the other. A states the misconception as fact. C invents version coupling. D inverts the lock file's role.

q: A fresh clone has no `.terraform.lock.hcl` (it was never committed). The constraints allow AWS provider 5.x. What does `terraform init` do?
options: It fails — the lock file is mandatory
It installs the oldest allowed version for stability
It selects the newest version satisfying the constraints, writes the lock file with checksums, and every later init reuses those locked versions
It prompts the engineer to pick a version
explain: Init resolves constraints to the newest allowed version on first run and records the choice — the lock file is created, not required, and makes later runs deterministic. A invents a mandatory-file rule. B picks the wrong end of the range. D invents interactive version picking.

q: A configuration contains two `provider "aws"` blocks — one with `region = "us-east-1"`, one with `region = "eu-west-1"` — and neither declares an `alias`. What happens at init/validate?
options: Terraform merges them into one multi-region provider
The second block silently overrides the first
Resources round-robin between the two
It fails — two default (unaliased) configurations for the same provider conflict; the second must declare an `alias`
explain: There can be only one default provider configuration; a second needs an alias to coexist. A invents merging. B invents silent override. C invents round-robining.

q: The backend needs `bucket`, `key`, and `region`, but the team keeps them in a per-environment file instead of CLI flags. How does init consume `backend-prod.hcl`?
options: With `-var-file=backend-prod.hcl`
With `terraform init -backend-config=backend-prod.hcl` — the file supplies partial backend configuration at init time
By importing it from the `terraform` block
Backend config files are not supported
explain: -backend-config accepts files or key=value pairs to complete a partial backend block — the file-based variant of the flag pattern. A uses the variable-values flag, which backends can't read. C invents block-level importing. D denies the documented mechanism.

q: An engineer runs `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, a teammate edits a variable default, then the engineer runs `terraform apply tfplan`. What happens?
options: Apply fails — the saved plan is bound to the configuration that produced it; any config change invalidates the plan and it must be regenerated
Apply silently uses the new variable value with the old plan
Terraform merges the old plan with the new configuration
The plan file updates itself automatically
explain: Saved plans are checksummed against their configuration — Terraform refuses to apply a stale plan rather than execute something unreviewed. B and C invent silent merging of reviewed and unreviewed inputs. D invents self-updating plans.

q: A plan shows `-/+` next to `aws_instance.web` with the note `# forces replacement`. What will apply do to this instance?
options: Update it in place
Destroy it and create a new one — `-/+` marks replacement, and the note names the attribute forcing it
Only read its current values
Skip it and continue with the rest
explain: `-/+` is the replacement symbol: delete-then-create (or create-then-delete with create_before_destroy), and the `# forces replacement` note identifies the triggering change. A is the `~` symbol's meaning. C is the `<=` data-source read. D ignores a planned action.

q: At the apply confirmation prompt, an engineer types `y` and presses Enter. What happens?
options: Apply proceeds — `y` is accepted as shorthand
Terraform asks for the password
Apply aborts — only the exact string `yes` confirms; anything else cancels
Terraform retries the prompt three times
explain: The confirmation gate requires the literal word `yes` — a deliberate friction against accidental confirmation. A assumes shell-style shorthand. B invents a password step. D invents retries.

q: An apply creates 4 of 10 resources then fails on the fifth due to a quota error. The engineer fixes the quota. What is the state of the infrastructure, and what does the next apply do?
options: Terraform rolled back the 4 created resources automatically
The state file was discarded and everything must be recreated
The 4 resources were deleted by the provider
Nothing is rolled back — the 4 resources remain and are recorded in state; the next apply creates only the remaining 6
explain: Terraform has no transactional rollback: partial applies leave created resources tracked in state, and the next run converges from there. A assumes database-style transactions. B invents state disposal. C invents provider cleanup.

q: A deployment pipeline needs the database endpoint output as a variable for the next job step. Which command gives the pipeline a machine-readable value?
options: `terraform output -json db_endpoint` — JSON output is designed for scripting and automation
`terraform show db_endpoint`
Reading the value from the plan file with grep
`terraform console -json`
explain: output -json renders values for machines — the automation interface for outputs. B renders human-readable state/plan, not scriptable output values. C greps a binary plan file. D invents a console flag.

q: A CI pipeline runs `terraform plan` and hangs waiting for keyboard input because a required variable has no default and no value was supplied. How should the pipeline handle this?
options: Pipe `yes` into plan
Run `terraform plan -input=false` — Terraform errors immediately instead of prompting, and the pipeline supplies all values via `-var`, `-var-file`, or `TF_VAR_`
