Remove the variable from the configuration
Plans never prompt; the hang is a bug
explain: -input=false converts interactive prompts into fast failures — the automation contract — while values arrive through non-interactive channels. A answers prompts blindly. C deletes needed inputs. D denies that plan prompts for missing variables.

q: An engineer passes a database password with `terraform plan -var="db_password=s3cr3t"`. A teammate flags a security issue with this exact invocation. What is it, and what is the fix?
options: The password is too short — use a longer one
Command-line flags cannot carry sensitive values at all
The secret lands in shell history and process listings — pass it via `TF_VAR_db_password` (environment) or a var file instead
The `-var` value is written to the state file unredacted
explain: The risk is exposure on the command line (history, ps output) — environment variables or files keep secrets out of the invocation itself. A misses the point. B overstates; -var works, it's just visible. D is true of state generally but isn't the issue with this invocation.

q: An engineer runs `terraform plan` and gets `Error acquiring the state lock`. A teammate's apply is visibly running in CI. What is the correct response?
options: Run `terraform force-unlock` immediately to clear it
Delete the lock from the backend console
Restart the Terraform daemon
Wait for the in-flight apply to finish — the lock is doing its job; force-unlock is only for stale locks with no live process
explain: A held lock during a live run is protection, not a bug — the plan queues behind it. Force-unlocking a running apply invites state corruption. A and B break the lock under a live writer. C invents a daemon.

q: Before committing, an engineer wants to see exactly what `terraform fmt` would change, without modifying any files. Which invocation does this?
options: `terraform fmt -diff` — prints the formatting diff without writing changes
`terraform fmt -check`
`terraform validate -diff`
`terraform plan -diff`
explain: -diff previews the rewrite; -check only reports whether files need formatting via its exit code. B answers a different need (CI gating). C and D invent flags on other commands.

q: A plan shows `~ instance_type` changing in place on one resource, but for `aws_db_instance.main` the plan shows `-/+` with `# forces replacement` next to a storage change. What does the note signify?
options: The database will be updated in place
Terraform is suggesting the change be reverted
That attribute change cannot be applied in place, so Terraform must destroy and recreate the resource — the note names the forcing attribute
The plan failed and must be regenerated
explain: Some attributes are immutable in the provider API; changing them forces replacement, and Terraform annotates exactly which change forces it. A misreads `-/+`. B invents advisory semantics. D misreads a normal plan annotation.

q: A reviewer approved the saved plan file `tfplan`. The release engineer runs `terraform apply tfplan`. Does Terraform compute a fresh plan before applying?
options: Yes — apply always re-plans
Only if the `-refresh` flag is passed
It prompts for confirmation and then re-plans
No — applying a saved plan file skips planning and executes the approved artifact exactly
explain: That's the entire point of the saved-plan workflow: the reviewed artifact executes verbatim, with no fresh diff that could differ from what was approved. A defeats the workflow's guarantee. B invents a flag. C invents a prompt (a plan file argument implies the earlier approval).

q: A pipeline's `terraform plan` reports `No changes` but the engineer just merged a pull request raising `instance_count` from 2 to 4. The pipeline command is `terraform plan -out=tfplan` with no other flags. What is the most likely cause?
options: Terraform caches plans across runs
The pipeline didn't pass `-var-file=prod.tfvars` (or the equivalent `-var`), so plan evaluated the variable's default instead of the intended value
Plan cannot detect variable changes
The state file was deleted
explain: The classic pipeline bug: the value lives in a file or flag the command didn't include, so the default (2) evaluated to no changes. A invents plan caching. C denies variable-driven diffs. D would propose creates, not 'no changes'.

q: A CI job runs `terraform apply -auto-approve` with no saved plan file. A reviewer approved the pull request an hour earlier. What safety property is lost compared to the plan-file workflow?
options: None — approving the PR is equivalent
The apply runs slower
The guarantee that apply executes exactly what was reviewed — without a saved plan, apply re-plans at execution time and can act on changes merged after the review
Auto-approve requires a plan file
explain: The saved plan binds review to execution; a fresh plan at apply time can include anything merged since the review. A equates code review with plan review — they cover different things. B invents a speed difference. D invents a requirement.

q: A resource uses `for_each = var.subnets` where the variable is a map of AZ name to CIDR. Inside the resource, the team needs each instance tagged with its AZ name and its CIDR. Which references provide them?
options: `each.key` gives the AZ name and `each.value` gives the CIDR — `each` exposes the current element's key and value
`each.index` and `each.id`
`count.index` works the same under for_each
Keys are unavailable inside for_each resources
explain: for_each exposes `each.key`/`each.value`; with a map, the key is the map key and the value the map value. B invents attributes. C mixes the count and for_each addressing models. D denies the core iteration mechanism.

q: Instances are created with `for_each = var.servers` (a map). An output needs the list of all instance IDs. `aws_instance.web[*].id` errors. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Splat expressions are deprecated
Use `values(aws_instance.web)[*].id` — splat works on lists/tuples, and for_each produces a map, so `values()` converts it to a list first
for_each resources have no IDs
Use `aws_instance.web.id` directly
explain: Splat needs a sequence; for_each instances are a map keyed by the for_each keys, so values() bridges the two. A is false. C is nonsense. D addresses a single instance that doesn't exist.

q: A module input `subnet_id` must always receive a real value — an explicit `null` from a caller should fail fast. Which declaration enforces this?
options: `sensitive = true`
A `validation` block checking `var.subnet_id != ""`
`nullable = false` in the variable block — rejects explicit null assignments at the boundary
Omitting the `default`
explain: nullable = false makes null an invalid input — the direct guard. A redacts display. B checks empty strings, not null. D makes the variable required but still accepts an explicit null.

q: A configuration reads `var.policy.statements[0].effect`, but some callers pass a policy object without `statements`. Which function returns a fallback instead of erroring?
options: `lookup(var.policy, "statements", [])` — handles nested paths
`coalesce(var.policy.statements[0].effect)`
Direct indexing never errors
`try(var.policy.statements[0].effect, "Allow")` — evaluates the expression and returns the fallback if any part fails
explain: try() is the safe-navigation function: it returns the first expression that doesn't error. A only handles top-level map keys. B still evaluates the failing path first. C is false — missing attributes error.

q: Every resource needs `Owner` and `Project` tags, plus optional per-resource extra tags from `var.extra_tags`. Which expression builds the final tag map?
options: `merge({ Owner = "platform", Project = "billing" }, var.extra_tags)` — later maps override earlier ones on key conflicts
`concat({ Owner = "platform" }, var.extra_tags)`
`join(",", var.extra_tags)`
Tags cannot be combined programmatically

q: An IAM policy document is assembled from variables and must be passed as a JSON string to the `policy` argument. Which function renders it?

q: A child module renders `templatefile("${path.module}/init.sh", ...)` and works. The team changes it to `path.root` and the module breaks when called from a different directory. Why?

q: A dynamic block generates ingress rules: `dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.ports ... }`. Inside `content`, the team wants a clearer name than `ingress.value`. How?

q: A `terraform_data` resource sets `input = var.ami_id` and a provisioner reads `self.input`. The AMI changes but the provisioner does NOT re-run. The team switches to `triggers_replace = { ami = var.ami_id }` and it re-runs. Why the difference?

q: A module passes a sensitive database password into a `local-exec` provisioner whose `command` needs the plaintext value, but Terraform errors that a sensitive value can't be used there. Which function unwraps it, and what is the caution?

q: A registry module `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` bundles a submodule for VPC endpoints. How does a configuration call just the endpoints submodule?

`source = "git::https://example.com/infra.git//modules/network"` — the double-slash selects the subdirectory after checkout
With a `path = "modules/network"` argument

q: A team deletes an entire `module "legacy"` block from the configuration and runs plan. What does the plan propose?

q: A legacy VPC must be imported, but it was created by the `network` child module's `aws_vpc.main` resource. What does the import block's `to` address look like?

`to = network.aws_vpc.main`

q: An entire `module "legacy"` must stop being managed, but its 30 resources must keep running. Which block does this declaratively?

q: A module block uses `count = var.create_vpc ? 1 : 0`. Elsewhere, the configuration references `module.vpc[0].vpc_id` unconditionally. When `create_vpc` is false, what happens?

q: A child module's resources use `provider = aws.west`, but the child module declares no `configuration_aliases`. The root passes `providers = { aws.west = aws.west }`. What happens?

q: A module block pins `version = "~> 2.0"`. Version 2.7.0 is released and the team runs plain `terraform init` (no flags). Which version is installed?

q: Two engineers push state to the same backend nearly simultaneously. The second push is rejected with a serial mismatch error. What is the `serial` in state?

options: Workspace notifications — event-based alerts (run success/failure, drift) delivered to Slack, email, or webhooks
A `local-exec` provisioner posting to Slack
Polling the API every minute
Notifications only exist for VCS events
explain: Notifications are the native event bus: run outcomes and drift delivered where the team lives. B bolts alerting onto resources. C is polling toil. D understates the event catalog.

q: After an unauthorized variable change in a production workspace, auditors ask who made the change and when. Where is this recorded?
options: In the state file
In the organization's audit logs — HCP Terraform records who changed what and when across workspaces, variables, and settings
In the provider's CloudTrail only
Nowhere — variable changes aren't tracked
explain: Audit logs are the compliance trail for control-plane actions: variable edits, permission changes, runs. A records infrastructure, not who edited variables. C covers the cloud, not HCP. D denies the trail.

q: A variable set holding `region` is attached to the `payments` project. A new workspace is created inside that project. Does it receive `region`?
options: No — variable sets must be attached per workspace
Only if the workspace name matches
Yes — project-scoped variable sets are inherited by all workspaces in the project, including ones created later
Variable sets can't attach to projects
explain: Project scope is inherited: member workspaces — current and future — receive the set's variables (workspace-level values still take precedence). A denies project attachment. B invents name matching. D denies the scope.

q: Workspace B needs to read workspace A's outputs via `terraform_remote_state`. The runs fail with an authorization error. What setting in workspace A controls this?
options: The `cloud` block in workspace B
Nothing — remote state is always world-readable
The organization must be public
Remote state sharing — workspace A must explicitly allow other workspaces to read its state
explain: HCP Terraform gates cross-workspace state reads: the source workspace enables remote state sharing (globally or per-consumer). A configures B's own connection, not A's permission. B and C invent open access.

q: An engineer opens a security group to 0.0.0.0/0 directly in the cloud console on Monday. The team only runs Terraform during Friday deploys. When will Terraform revert the change?
options: Immediately — Terraform agents continuously enforce the configuration
At the next plan/apply — Terraform only reconciles desired vs actual when it runs; nothing watches between runs
Never — Terraform ignores console changes permanently once made
At the next terraform init, which re-syncs all infrastructure
explain: Terraform is not an agent: it reconciles only during plan/apply, so Monday's console change persists until Friday's refresh detects it. A describes agent-based tools (Chef/Puppet), the exact misconception the exam hunts. C is wrong — refresh does detect drift at the next run. D is wrong; init installs providers and never touches infrastructure.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A Friday 5 PM deploy opens the wrong ports and breaks the checkout service. The change was merged as a single commit. What is the fastest IaC-native recovery?
options: git revert the commit and re-apply — infrastructure rolls back to the last known-good declared state in minutes
Manually close the ports in the console, then update the code to match later
Run terraform destroy and rebuild the entire environment from scratch
Restore last night's state file backup over the current one
explain: Version-controlled infrastructure makes rollback a revert plus apply — the same mechanism as application code. B reintroduces the manual drift IaC eliminates. C is needlessly destructive for a one-commit error. D is wrong: restoring an old state file doesn't change real infrastructure, it only corrupts Terraform's tracking of it.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team migrating from sequential shell scripts worries that creating 60 instances with Terraform will take 60 times as long as creating one. What actually happens at apply time?
options: Terraform creates resources strictly one at a time, in file order
Terraform is slower because it writes the state file after every single resource
Terraform builds a dependency graph and creates independent resources in parallel (10 at a time by default)
Parallelism only works with count, not with separate resource blocks
explain: The dependency graph lets Terraform create independent resources concurrently — a core speed advantage over sequential scripts, tunable with -parallelism. A denies the graph ordering entirely. B invents a state-write bottleneck. D is false; parallelism applies to all independent resources regardless of how they're declared.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: After every production incident the team hears 'but it worked in dev'. Dev was clicked together in the console; prod was built from Terraform months later by a different engineer. Which IaC practice kills this class of incident?
options: Giving developers production console access so they can visually compare environments
Writing longer, more detailed runbooks for the dev environment
Running terraform apply more frequently against production
Defining dev and prod from the same version-controlled configuration, differing only in variable values
explain: Same code plus different inputs equals parity: environment differences become explicit variables instead of archaeology. A worsens the problem by spreading console access. B documents drift instead of removing it. C applies the same divergent configuration more often — frequency doesn't fix divergence.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company replaces an agent-based configuration tool with Terraform. An engineer asks what now runs on the servers to keep Terraform's configuration enforced. What is the correct answer?
options: The Terraform agent, installed on every managed machine
Nothing runs on the machines — Terraform is agentless and acts through provider APIs only when you run it
A lightweight state-sync daemon that Terraform installs automatically
The provider plugin, which stays resident on each server
explain: Terraform has no agents: the CLI talks to provider APIs at run time, and provider plugins are local CLI-side binaries, not server daemons. A and C describe Chef/Puppet-style architectures — the exact confusion the exam tests. D mistakes the CLI's plugin for something deployed to targets.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A manager declares that adopting IaC means infrastructure misconfigurations are now impossible. What is the exam-correct correction?
options: He is right — code cannot contain errors the way manual clicks can
Misconfigurations become impossible, but only when the team uses modules
IaC doesn't eliminate human error; it moves mistakes into reviewable code where plan diffs, tests, and approvals can catch them before apply
Human error is eliminated for cloud resources, though SaaS resources are still risky
explain: Errors move from console clicks to code — still human, but now gated by review and the plan/apply checkpoint. A states the fantasy the exam hunts. B invents module magic. D invents a cloud-versus-SaaS split that doesn't exist.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team wants quarterly disaster-recovery drills without the chaos of rebuilding from runbooks while executives watch. How does IaC change the drill?
options: The drill becomes 'apply the same configuration to a fresh account and verify' — recovery is rehearsed as a routine redeploy
Drills become unnecessary because IaC prevents all outages
The team must still rebuild manually; Terraform only documents the drill steps
State file backups replace the need for drills entirely
explain: Reproducibility turns disaster recovery from archaeology into a repeatable apply — drills test the real recovery path. B overpromises; IaC doesn't prevent outages, it changes recovery. C denies the core DR advantage. D confuses state backups (bookkeeping) with recovery capability.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Security mandates every server be rebuilt from the latest patched image weekly, with no SSH patching allowed. How does the team implement this with Terraform?
options: They can't — Terraform cannot replace running servers
SSH in weekly and patch, then run terraform refresh to sync state
Manually rebuild the AMIs and click-replace each instance in the console
Update the AMI variable and apply — Terraform replaces the instances from the new image, implementing immutable infrastructure
explain: Immutable change means new image plus replacement, never in-place patching — exactly the weekly-rebuild mandate. A denies Terraform's replacement capability. B violates the no-SSH rule (and refresh only syncs state, it changes nothing). C is the manual process IaC exists to replace.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A three-person team manages infrastructure through the console with a shared admin login. They're hiring to thirty engineers. Why does the exam consider IaC the answer to this growth?
options: Terraform lets thirty people share one admin login more efficiently
Console workflows don't scale — code brings per-change identity, peer review, and non-overlapping work via version control
Terraform automatically trains new hires on the infrastructure
Cloud consoles technically limit accounts to three concurrent users
explain: IaC scales collaboration: Git history, pull-request review, and per-engineer accountability replace one shared login and its race conditions. A preserves the shared-login anti-pattern. C invents training. D invents a console limit.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Two engineers keep overwriting each other's console changes to the same load balancer. The team moves the load balancer into Terraform. Which mechanisms prevent the overwrite problem?
options: Terraform hides the load balancer from the cloud console
Nothing — Terraform has the same overwrite problem as the console
Version control serializes proposals through pull requests, and state locking serializes applies
Terraform emails both engineers for approval before each apply
explain: Git workflow plus state locking removes silent overwrites: proposals merge in order, applies run one at a time. A invents console hiding. B denies the fix the question asks for. D invents an email approval gate.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team promotes releases dev → staging → prod. Today each stage is configured by hand from tickets. What does the IaC promotion model look like?
options: The same configuration and module versions progress through stages with stage-specific variable files; promotion is a variable change, not a rebuild
Each stage gets its own hand-written configuration for maximum control
Production is configured by copying the staging state file
Promotion requires terraform destroy in the lower environment first
explain: Promotion becomes data, not new authoring: identical code, stage-specific inputs. B keeps the manual model IaC replaces. C copies bookkeeping instead of provisioning. D invents a destroy requirement between stages.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of Infrastructure as Code?
options: Changes are peer-reviewed before they affect infrastructure
Environments can be reproduced exactly from version-controlled code
The full history of infrastructure changes is auditable
Infrastructure automatically costs less because Terraform negotiates cloud pricing
explain: D is the planted fiction — Terraform negotiates nothing; savings come from confident teardown and fast recreation, not discounts. A, B, and C are the canonical IaC advantages the exam expects you to recognize.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A developer prototypes an architecture in a personal AWS account with Terraform over a weekend. Monday the team wants it in production. What makes this handoff clean?
options: Nothing — prototypes must always be rebuilt by hand for production use
The prototype IS the production design: the same configuration applies against the production backend and variables
The state file is copied to production and apply is skipped
Terraform converts the prototype into CloudFormation for the production account
explain: Code portability: same configuration, new backend and variables, equals production — the prototype graduates instead of being rewritten. A denies reuse. C skips the actual provisioning. D invents a CloudFormation conversion that doesn't exist.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: An engineer changes the S3 backend's key from prod/terraform.tfstate to prod/v2/terraform.tfstate and runs terraform init. What does init do?
options: Silently starts using the new empty key, abandoning the old state
Errors — backend keys can never be changed once set
Detects the backend configuration change and asks whether to migrate the existing state to the new location
Deletes the old state file automatically and starts fresh
explain: Init detects backend changes and offers migration — the safe default that keeps tracked infrastructure bound. A would orphan everything Terraform manages. B is false; key changes are routine. D is wrong; init never deletes state unprompted.

q: A new repository's .gitignore must cover Terraform working files. Which set is correct?
options: Ignore .terraform/, *.tfstate, *.tfstate.backup, and plan files — but COMMIT .terraform.lock.hcl
Ignore .terraform.lock.hcl and commit the .terraform/ directory
Commit everything including state files, for complete history
Ignore *.tf files and commit only the state file
explain: The canonical split: install artifacts, state, and plan files stay out of Git; the lock file is committed so every machine resolves identical providers. B inverts the lock/.terraform handling. C commits secrets-bearing state. D ignores the actual configuration.

q: A CI pipeline must verify the runner's Terraform version satisfies required_version, and it needs the version in machine-readable form. Which command provides it?
options: terraform providers -json
terraform show -json
Grepping the state file for the CLI version
terraform version -json — emits CLI, platform, and provider versions as JSON
explain: version -json is the scriptable version check for automation gates. A lists provider requirements, not versions. B renders state or plan data. C scrapes an internal format instead of using the supported command.

q: A provider developer needs Terraform to use their locally built provider binary instead of the registry download, without changing the configuration. Where is this configured?
options: In required_providers with source = 'local'
In the CLI configuration file's dev_overrides block — local development binaries bypass version checks and the lock file
By committing the binary into .terraform/ and pushing it
With terraform init -local-providers
explain: dev_overrides is the documented local-development escape hatch. A invents a source value. C commits machine-specific binaries. D invents a flag.

q: A configuration declares source = 'kreuzwerker/docker' in required_providers. What does 'kreuzwerker' identify?
options: The Docker Hub organization owning the container images
A HashiCorp partner tier required for support
The registry namespace (the publisher) — community providers live outside the hashicorp namespace on the public registry
The GitHub branch the provider is installed from
explain: Namespace equals publisher; community providers publish under their own namespace on registry.terraform.io. A confuses the provider namespace with Docker Hub. B invents support tiers. D confuses source addresses with git refs.

q: Version 2.0.0 of a provider has a known bug, but the team wants any other 2.x release. Which constraint expresses this?
options: version = '!= 2.0.0, ~> 2.0' — excludes exactly 2.0.0 while allowing the rest of the 2.x line
version = '! 2.0.0'
version = 'except 2.0.0'
Excluding a single version is impossible; the team must pin = 2.0.1
explain: The != operator excludes one version and composes with other constraints via comma (AND). B and C invent syntax. D denies the exclusion operator and forces an exact pin the team doesn't want.

q: A data source must read an AMI from us-west-2 while the default AWS provider is us-east-1 (an alias aws.west exists). How is the data source directed at us-west-2?
options: Data sources always use the default provider; this is impossible
With region = 'us-west-2' inside the data block
With alias = 'west' inside the data block
With the meta-argument provider = aws.west — data blocks accept provider selection just like resources
explain: The provider meta-argument works on data sources too — provider selection isn't resource-only. A is false. B puts a provider-level setting in the wrong block. C invents an alias argument on data blocks.

q: An engineer writes provider 'aws' { alias = var.region_alias } hoping to select the alias per workspace. What happens?
options: It works — aliases accept variables like any other argument
It fails — alias must be a static string because provider configurations resolve before variables are evaluated
It works only with terraform.workspace, not with variables
The alias is silently ignored and the default provider is used
explain: Provider configuration (including alias) resolves before variables exist, so only static strings are allowed. A and C assume variables are available at that phase — they aren't. D invents a silent fallback; Terraform errors instead.

q: A documentation tool needs the full attribute schema of every resource in the AWS provider — required vs optional, types, descriptions. Which command emits it?
options: terraform providers — the human-readable requirements tree
terraform show -json — renders state data
terraform providers schema -json — dumps every provider's resource, data source, and function schemas as JSON
terraform console with a describe() function
explain: providers schema -json is the schema-dump command that tooling consumes. A shows which providers are required, not their schemas. B renders state or plan data. D invents a console function.

q: The lock file pins hashicorp/aws 5.9.0. A teammate tightens the constraint to < 5.0 and runs terraform init. What happens?
options: Init errors — the locked version violates the new constraint; terraform init -upgrade re-resolves within the new bound
Init silently downgrades to the newest 4.x
Init ignores the lock file whenever constraints change
The new constraint is ignored because the lock file always wins
explain: A lock/constraint conflict fails loudly instead of silently resolving — then -upgrade re-resolves inside the new bound. B invents a silent downgrade. C misstates the lock's role. D inverts the relationship; constraints always bound resolution.

q: Two unrelated configurations (networking and apps) both configure the S3 backend with key = 'terraform.tfstate'. What is the consequence?
options: Nothing — Terraform namespaces state per configuration automatically
Init fails on the duplicate key
The second apply safely merges both configurations' resources
Both configurations read and write the SAME state file — resources collide and each team's runs corrupt the other's tracking
explain: The backend key IS the state's identity; sharing it merges two configurations' tracking into one file — a classic corruption. A invents automatic namespacing. B is false; init can't detect the collision. C mistakes corruption for safe merging.

q: Every plan in CI must run with -no-color and -input=false, but engineers keep forgetting the flags. How can the pipeline inject them without editing every command line?
options: In the required_version argument
With TF_CLI_ARGS_plan='-no-color -input=false' — the CLI prepends these arguments to every terraform plan invocation
In the backend block
Flags cannot be injected; every command must spell them out
explain: TF_CLI_ARGS_<command> injects arguments per command — the documented automation mechanism. A constrains CLI versions. C configures state storage. D denies a real feature.

q: A CI step vendors modules into the working directory from an internal mirror and must install modules WITHOUT touching providers or the backend. Which command performs only the module installation?
options: terraform init -backend=false — still installs providers
terraform providers install
terraform get — installs/updates modules only, skipping provider installation and backend setup
terraform fmt -recursive
explain: get is the modules-only installer — the narrow tool for vendored-module workflows. A still installs providers. B invents a command. D formats code and installs nothing.

q: A monorepo keeps environments in envs/dev, envs/staging, and envs/prod. A script must run plan in each without cd-ing around (which breaks relative paths in the wrapper). Which invocation works?
options: terraform -chdir=envs/prod plan — the global flag sets the working directory for that run
terraform plan -dir=envs/prod
terraform plan envs/prod — a positional path argument
Copy the .terraform directory into each env directory first
explain: -chdir is the global working-directory flag, designed for exactly this scripting pattern. B invents a flag. C invents a positional argument (plan takes no path). D is toil for something one flag solves.

q: A plan shows bucket = '(known after apply)' for an aws_s3_bucket created in the same configuration. What does this mean?
options: The value is a syntax error that Terraform cannot evaluate
The value is computed by the provider during apply (e.g., a generated name) and cannot be known until then
The plan failed to refresh, so the value is missing
The attribute will be empty in the real infrastructure
explain: '(known after apply)' marks provider-computed values — normal for generated IDs and names, not an error. A misreads the renderer as a failure. C confuses it with a refresh problem. D is wrong; unknown does not mean empty.

q: A plan line reads ~ instance_type = 't3.micro' -> 't3.small'. What is the reviewer seeing?
options: A syntax error in the diff renderer
The resource will be destroyed and recreated
Two different resources being compared side by side
An in-place update changing the value from t3.micro (current) to t3.small (new)
explain: old -> new is the in-place change notation, and ~ confirms update without replacement. A misreads normal renderer output. B would display -/+. C misreads a single resource's diff as a comparison.

q: A deploy script needs the database endpoint output as a bare string, but terraform output db_endpoint wraps it in quotes. Which flag strips the quoting?
options: terraform output -quotes=false
terraform output -plain
terraform output -raw — prints a single string output with no quoting or formatting
terraform show -raw db_endpoint
explain: -raw is the scripting flag for consuming one string output cleanly. A and B invent flags. D invents a command form.

q: An engineer clones a configuration and runs terraform output db_endpoint before the first apply. What happens?
options: Terraform warns that no state exists — outputs are read from state, and there is nothing to read yet
It evaluates the configuration and prints the planned value
It silently returns null
It triggers an apply automatically to produce the value
explain: Outputs come from state; with no state there is nothing to show, so Terraform warns. B confuses output with plan evaluation. C is wrong — it warns rather than returning silent null. D is wrong; output never applies.

q: CI logs are flooded with the same deprecation warning repeated for all 200 instances of a resource. Which flag collapses the duplicates?
options: terraform plan -warnings=once
terraform plan -compact-warnings — shows each distinct warning once, with a repetition count
TF_LOG=ERROR
terraform validate -quiet
explain: -compact-warnings dedupes repeated warnings for automation logs. A invents a flag. C changes log verbosity, not warning rendering. D is a different command that doesn't plan at all.

q: CI runs terraform plan -input=false. A required variable has no default and no value was supplied. What happens?
options: Plan hangs waiting for keyboard input anyway
Plan substitutes an empty string and continues
Plan silently skips the variable
Plan fails immediately with an error naming the missing variable — -input=false turns the prompt into a fast failure
explain: That fast failure is the point of -input=false in automation: no hanging, just a clear error. A is what happens WITHOUT the flag. B and C invent silent defaults that don't exist.

q: A CMDB sync job needs a machine-readable inventory of everything in the state file — addresses, types, and attribute values. Which command feeds it?
options: terraform state list — addresses only, in human-readable form
terraform output -json — outputs only
terraform show -json — renders the full state as JSON for tooling
cat terraform.tfstate — the supported machine interface
explain: show -json is the stable machine interface to state; the raw state file is an internal format. A gives addresses without attributes. B gives outputs only. D scrapes internals instead of the supported command.

q: A CI gate must parse validation failures programmatically to annotate pull requests. Which invocation emits machine-readable diagnostics?
options: terraform validate -json — diagnostics as JSON with severity, summary, and source ranges
terraform validate -text — the default output is already JSON
terraform plan -json
Validation output cannot be machine-parsed
explain: validate -json is the PR-annotation feed. B invents a flag (the default is human-readable text). C is wrong — plan has no -json flag. D denies a real feature.

q: A pull-request job runs terraform init then terraform validate with no cloud credentials, and passes. The next step, terraform plan, fails with an authentication error. Why?
options: The configuration must be invalid
Validate is credential-free, but plan's refresh phase calls provider APIs — plan genuinely needs credentials
Init deleted the credentials from the environment
Plan always requires -auto-approve before it will authenticate
explain: The credential boundary sits between validate (static, offline) and plan (API calls during refresh). A is ruled out — validate already proved correctness. C invents credential deletion. D confuses approval with authentication.

q: A script runs terraform fmt on a directory and checks the exit code to detect unformatted files. It always sees exit 0, even when files were rewritten. What is the correct detection command?
options: terraform fmt -verbose
Grep the stdout for the word 'formatted'
terraform fmt always exits 3 when it changes files
Use terraform fmt -check — plain fmt exits 0 after rewriting; -check exits non-zero (3) when files need formatting
explain: fmt's job is to fix and succeed; -check is the detector with its meaningful exit code. A invents a flag. B scrapes output instead of using exit codes. C inverts the actual exit codes.

q: A pipeline reviewed the saved plan file tfplan and must now apply it in a non-interactive job. Which command is correct?
options: terraform apply -auto-approve — without the plan file, which re-plans and skips the review
cat tfplan | terraform apply
terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan — executes the reviewed plan file without prompting
-auto-approve cannot be combined with a plan file argument
explain: The flags compose: the plan file preserves exactly-what-was-reviewed, and -auto-approve skips the prompt. A re-plans, breaking the review guarantee. B pipes a binary file to stdin. D denies a valid, common combination.

q: A pipeline archives plan logs, but ANSI color codes render as garbage like [0m in the log viewer. Which flag produces clean logs?
options: terraform plan -no-color — disables ANSI color codes in output
TF_LOG=ERROR
-compact-warnings
Pipe the output through terraform fmt
explain: -no-color is the log-hygiene flag for archived output. B changes diagnostic log verbosity. C dedupes repeated warnings. D formats configuration code, not command output.

q: A data source returns a list that must contain exactly one subnet; the configuration needs its ID as a string. Which function converts the single-element list?
options: element(list, 0) — which also errors when the length is wrong
tostring(list)
list[0] with a comment asserting the length
one(list) — returns the single element, and errors if the list has zero or more than one element
explain: one() both extracts and asserts exactly-one — the intent-expressive choice the exam favors. A extracts but never validates the count. B cannot stringify a list. C is manual toil with no enforcement.

q: A module accepts var.ami_id, falling back to a data-source AMI, then to a hardcoded default — the first non-empty value should win. Which expression implements this?
options: var.ami_id || data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id || 'ami-default'
lookup(var.ami_id, data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id)
try(var.ami_id, data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id, 'ami-default')
coalesce(var.ami_id, data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id, 'ami-default') — returns the first argument that isn't null or empty
explain: coalesce() is the first-non-empty selector. A invents || operators that HCL doesn't have. B misuses lookup, which is a map function. C is wrong: try() catches evaluation errors, it doesn't skip empty values.

q: Two modules each output a list of subnet IDs; a resource needs one flat list of all IDs. Which function merges them?
options: flatten([module.a.subnet_ids, module.b.subnet_ids]) — collapses nested lists into a single list
merge(module.a.subnet_ids, module.b.subnet_ids)
concat() applied to the two maps
toset() of the two lists
explain: flatten() collapses a list of lists — exactly this shape. B is wrong; merge() is for maps. C is confused about the input types. D is invalid: toset of lists doesn't flatten anything.

q: A user_data script needs one firewall line per port in var.ports. Which template syntax iterates inside a string?
options: '${for p in var.ports : p}'
A dynamic block nested inside the string
'%{ for p in var.ports }allow ${p} %{ endfor }' — template directives iterate within strings
Strings cannot contain loops; use one resource per port
explain: %{ for } / %{ endfor } are the string-template iteration directives. A invents for-expression syntax inside strings. B is wrong; dynamic blocks generate nested blocks, not string content. D denies template directives entirely.

q: An IAM policy needs a multi-line JSON document inline in the configuration. Which HCL construct holds it readably?
options: A single quoted string with escape sequences
A heredoc (<<EOT ... EOT) — multi-line literal strings without escape noise
A data source block
Concatenating one-line strings with the + operator
explain: Heredocs are the multi-line string construct — readable JSON without escaping. A works but is unreadable. C is the wrong tool for inline content. D is toil for what a heredoc does natively.

q: A local value derives a connection string from a sensitive password variable, and the derived string appears in plan output. How is it redacted?
options: It can't be — only variables and outputs accept sensitivity
Delete the local value
Mark the entire configuration as sensitive
Wrap it with sensitive() — marks any derived value sensitive so CLI output redacts it
explain: sensitive() propagates sensitivity to derived values — the function exists for exactly this. A denies the function. B and C are absurd overreactions to a display concern.

q: A module output is sensitive because it references a sensitive value, but one derived field (a username) is safe to display and needed by scripts. How is it exposed?
options: nonsensitive() on that field — explicitly lifts redaction where the author judges it safe
Remove sensitive from the original password variable
Sensitive outputs can never be partially exposed
terraform output -force
explain: nonsensitive() is the deliberate declassification escape hatch for safe fields. B would expose the actual secret. C denies the function. D invents a flag.

q: var.servers is a map of objects, each with an 'enabled' bool. Only enabled servers should get instances, keyed by name. Which for_each expression does this?
options: for_each = var.servers — creates the disabled ones too
for_each = toset([for s in var.servers : s if s.enabled])
for_each = { for name, s in var.servers : name => s if s.enabled } — filters the map before iteration
count = length(var.servers)
explain: The if clause in a for expression filters — the idiomatic conditional for_each. A ignores the flag. B builds a set of objects, losing the string keys for_each needs. D switches to count, losing keyed identity.

q: Three instances from count = 3 need distinct Name tags web-0, web-1, and web-2. Which expression produces them?
options: 'web-${each.key}' — the for_each iterator
'web-${count.index}' — count.index is the per-instance position
'web-${count}' — the total count
Names cannot differ between count instances
explain: count.index distinguishes instances; each.* doesn't exist under count. A confuses count with for_each. C gives all three the identical name. D denies a basic feature.

q: A resource uses for_each = var.subnets (a map of AZ name to CIDR). Inside the block, how are the current key and value referenced?
options: var.subnets.key and var.subnets.value
count.key and count.value
self.key and self.value
each.key (the AZ name) and each.value (the CIDR) — the per-instance iterator object
explain: each.key/each.value is the for_each iterator. A references the whole map, not the current element. B confuses count with for_each. C is wrong; self exists only in provisioner and connection blocks.

q: A team sets tags = { DeployedAt = timestamp() } on every resource. Every plan — with zero configuration changes — proposes updates to all resources. Why?
options: timestamp() returns the current time on every evaluation, so the value differs each run — a perpetual diff; only use it where constant re-evaluation is intended
Tags always cause perpetual diffs regardless of value
The state file is corrupted
Terraform has a bug with time functions
explain: EXAM TRAP: timestamp() (and uuid()) re-evaluate on every plan — embedding them in config guarantees endless diffs. B is false; stable tags are quiet. C and D blame the tool for a configuration error.

q: aws_instance.web exists as a single resource. The team adds count = 3, making it aws_instance.web[0] through [2]. How do they keep the existing server bound to index 0 instead of recreating everything?
options: Nothing — Terraform figures out the rebinding automatically
terraform import the server three times, once per index
A moved block: moved { from = aws_instance.web to = aws_instance.web[0] } — rebinds the existing state entry to the new address
Delete the state file and re-apply from scratch
explain: moved blocks rebind addresses declaratively in config — the in-code alternative to CLI state mv for refactors. A is wrong; Terraform sees an address change as replacement. B misuses import for an already-tracked resource. D destroys all tracking.

q: A large IAM policy lives in policy.json. The aws_iam_policy resource needs its JSON as a string argument. Which expression loads it?
options: templatefile('policy.json') with an empty variables map
file('${path.module}/policy.json') — reads the file contents as a string; jsondecode() additionally parses it when the structure must be traversed
A data source for local files
Hardcode the JSON directly into the resource block
explain: file() reads static content; jsondecode() parses it when traversal is needed. A misuses templatefile, which is for templates with variables. C invents a data source. D bakes content into code instead of keeping it in its own file.

q: A module block sets source = 'git::https://github.com/org/vpc.git?ref=v2.0.0' and version = '1.5.0'. Which version is installed?
options: The version argument is ignored for non-registry sources — ref=v2.0.0 selects the code; version only applies to registry sources
1.5.0 — the version argument overrides the git ref
Init fails on the conflicting version selectors
Terraform installs the newer of the two selections
explain: EXAM TRAP: version is registry-only; git sources are versioned via ref. B inverts the precedence. C invents a conflict error — the argument is silently ignored. D invents version merging.

q: A module lives in a self-hosted GitLab instance, not GitHub. Which source form addresses it?
options: source = 'gitlab.example.com/org/vpc' — the GitHub shorthand generalizes to any host
Only the public registry supports non-GitHub Git hosts
source = 'https://gitlab.example.com/org/vpc.git' without any prefix
source = 'git::https://gitlab.example.com/org/vpc.git' — the git:: prefix forces Git protocol handling for arbitrary hosts
explain: The :: prefix selects the getter: git:: clones, while a bare HTTPS URL would be treated as a generic archive download. A misapplies the GitHub shorthand. B is false. C would attempt an archive download, not a clone.

q: The organization 'acme' publishes a private VPC module for AWS. Which source address is correct?
options: source = 'acme/vpc'
source = 'app.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws' — hostname/namespace/name/provider, the same shape as public with the private hostname
source = 'terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws'
Private modules can only be sourced from Git, never a registry address
explain: Private registry addresses mirror the public form with the TFC hostname. A omits the hostname and provider segments. C uses the wrong hostname. D denies the private registry's purpose.

q: A child module declares no configuration_aliases and uses plain aws_* resources. The root module block passes no providers map. Which provider configuration do the child's resources use?
options: None — the apply fails with missing provider configuration
The child must declare its own provider blocks to work at all
The root's default (unaliased) AWS provider configuration is inherited implicitly — only aliased configurations require the explicit providers map
A provider configuration is chosen at random
explain: The counterpart to the alias rule: default provider configurations flow into child modules implicitly; the explicit providers map exists only for aliases. A invents a failure. B forces redundant provider blocks. D invents randomness.

q: A registry module is pinned version = '~> 2.0'. Version 2.4.0 is released. The team runs terraform init and plan — the old 2.1.0 is still installed. Why, and what upgrades it?
options: Init never upgrades already-installed modules by default (the manifest pins them); terraform init -upgrade re-resolves to the newest allowed version
The ~> 2.0 constraint blocks 2.4.0
Modules upgrade automatically on every plan
The version argument must be edited to '= 2.4.0'
explain: Installed modules are sticky like providers; -upgrade re-resolves within constraints. B misreads ~> 2.0, which allows 2.4.0. C is false. D forces an exact pin the team doesn't need.

q: The root module calls module 'app', which itself calls a registry module 'db'. After terraform init, which modules are installed?
options: Only module app — nested calls require a separate init inside the child directory
Only module db
Neither — nested module calls are not allowed
Both — init recursively installs the entire module tree
explain: Init walks the full module tree; nesting is normal composition, not a special case. A invents per-module init runs. C denies nested modules entirely.

q: A child module declares configuration_aliases = [aws.west] for its us-west-2 resources. The root wants those resources in eu-west-1 instead, using its own aws.eu alias. How?
options: It can't — the child's alias names are permanently tied to regions
providers = { aws.west = aws.eu } — the map keys are the child's declared aliases; the values are any root provider configuration
Edit the child's source code to change the alias
Rename the root's alias from eu to west
explain: The providers map remaps by alias name: key is the child's declared alias, value is the root's configuration — names are just labels, not regions. A confuses alias names with regions. C edits shared code for a local need. D renames instead of remapping.

q: Two teams each own a Terraform configuration with its own state. Team B needs Team A's VPC ID, which Team A already exposes as an output. What is the correct integration?
options: Convert both configurations into modules of one giant configuration
Hardcode the VPC ID in Team B's variable defaults
A terraform_remote_state data source (or HCP remote state sharing) — module outputs compose within one configuration; separate configurations integrate via remote state reads
Copy Team A's state file into Team B's working directory
explain: Modules compose inside one configuration; separate configurations with separate states integrate through remote state reads. A merges ownership boundaries unnecessarily. B bakes in brittleness. D copies bookkeeping instead of reading it.

q: A team publishes its first shared module. Reviewers expect the conventional file layout. Which is it?
options: main.tf (resources), variables.tf (inputs), outputs.tf (outputs), plus a README.md — the community convention every registry module follows
A single module.tf containing everything
Files named after the cloud provider being managed
Terraform accepts only one .tf file per module
explain: The conventional split is the documented standard that tooling, registries, and humans expect. B works technically but breaks convention. C invents naming rules. D is false; a module is a directory of .tf files.

q: A module block uses for_each over regions AND needs an aliased provider passed in. Which block is valid?
options: for_each and providers cannot be combined on one module block
providers = { aws = aws[each.key] } — selecting the provider dynamically per instance
The provider alias must be interpolated per instance
module 'x' { for_each = var.regions, source = '...', providers = { aws.alt = aws.west } } — for_each and a static providers map compose normally
explain: The two meta-arguments are orthogonal: for_each multiplies instances while the providers map stays static. A denies the combination. B and C attempt dynamic provider selection, which Terraform forbids.

q: The root module sets required_version = '>= 1.5' and a child module sets required_version = '~> 1.9'. Which CLI versions satisfy the configuration?
options: Any version >= 1.5
>= 1.9, < 2.0 — constraints from all modules combine, and the effective bound is their intersection
Any version >= 1.5 except the 1.9.x line
Child module constraints are ignored for the CLI version
explain: Like provider constraints, required_version merges across the module tree — the intersection wins. A ignores the child. C invents an exclusion. D denies the merging behavior.

q: A child module outputs db_password = aws_db_instance.main.password. The root re-exports it as output 'db_password' with no sensitive flag. What appears in CLI output?
options: The plaintext password — the root output lacks the sensitive flag
The apply fails on the missing flag
Redacted output — sensitivity propagates through module outputs automatically, exactly like resource outputs
The value is deleted from the state file
explain: Sensitivity is a property of the value, not the block — it flows through module boundaries untouched. A assumes flags are purely manual. B invents a failure. D confuses display redaction with state storage.

q: An engineer runs terraform state mv aws_instance.web aws_instance.frontend, then watches the cloud console expecting the instance to be renamed or recreated. What actually happens?
options: Nothing in the cloud — state mv only rebinds Terraform's bookkeeping; the real instance is untouched
The instance is renamed in the cloud provider
The instance is destroyed and recreated under the new name
The command fails — renames must be done in the console
explain: State subcommands edit the map, never the territory — no API calls rename or replace anything. B and C attribute infrastructure effects to a bookkeeping command. D denies the command's purpose.

q: A team uses CLI workspaces for dev/staging/prod in one S3 bucket, assuming developers with dev state access cannot see prod state. What is wrong with this assumption?
options: Nothing — workspaces are hard access boundaries
Workspaces are a naming convenience, not a security boundary — anyone with backend access can read every workspace's state
S3 automatically encrypts each workspace's state with a different key
Prod state is automatically stored in a separate AWS account
explain: EXAM TRAP: workspace separation is not access isolation — true isolation needs separate backends or accounts. A states the misconception. C and D invent automatic protections that don't exist.

q: With the local backend, an engineer runs terraform workspace new staging. Where is the staging state file written?
options: staging.terraform.tfstate in the working directory
It is kept in memory only until the next apply
.terraform/staging.tfstate
terraform.tfstate.d/staging/terraform.tfstate — each CLI workspace gets its own directory under terraform.tfstate.d
explain: The terraform.tfstate.d/<name>/ layout is the documented local convention for workspace states. A and C invent filenames. B denies persistence.

q: An engineer runs terraform state pull, hand-edits resource IDs in the JSON to 'fix' a mismatch, and pushes it back. What is the exam-correct view of this?
options: Recommended — the fastest fix for any state mismatch
Safe as long as the JSON remains syntactically valid
Dangerous — hand-edited state can desync serial/lineage checks and silently corrupt tracking; use state mv, state rm, or import instead
Push will refuse any hand-edited file, so no harm is possible
explain: Hand surgery bypasses the safety of the state subcommands — valid JSON does not mean correct tracking. A glorifies the riskiest path. B underestimates the risk. D is wrong; push accepts the file, which is exactly the danger.

q: Every state file contains a 'serial' number that increments on each write. What is its purpose?
options: A concurrency guard — backends reject writes carrying a stale serial, preventing lost updates from concurrent runs
A version counter tracking the Terraform CLI release
The count of resources tracked in the state
A billing meter for HCP Terraform usage
explain: Serial is the optimistic-locking token behind state locking. B confuses it with the CLI version (stored separately as terraform_version). C is derived, not stored. D invents billing.

q: A team moves a small project OFF the S3 backend back to local state by deleting the backend block. On the next terraform init, what happens?
options: Init silently starts a fresh, empty local state
Init detects the backend removal and offers to copy the remote state back to local
The S3 state object is deleted automatically
Init fails — backends can never be removed once configured
explain: Init handles migration in both directions with the same prompt — remote to local included. A would orphan tracked infrastructure. C is wrong; init never deletes remote state unprompted. D is false.

q: The state bucket lives in a dedicated security account. Engineers' IAM users have no direct bucket access but can assume a role that does. How does the S3 backend authenticate?
options: It can't — the backend requires static keys in the configuration
Engineers must copy the state file manually before each run
The backend automatically inherits the AWS provider's credentials
With an assume_role block in the backend configuration — the backend assumes the role before reading or writing state
explain: Backends carry their own auth chain, including assume_role — independent of provider credentials. A forces static keys. B is manual toil. C confuses backend auth with provider auth; they are separate chains.

q: A company standard requires CLI workspace state keys like acme/prod/terraform.tfstate instead of the default env:/prod/ prefix layout. Which backend argument customizes this?
options: key_prefix
workspace_dir
workspace_key_prefix — overrides the env:/ prefix used for non-default workspace states
State key layouts cannot be customized
explain: workspace_key_prefix is the documented customization for workspace state keys. A invents an argument. B is the local-backend equivalent, not the S3 one. D denies a real feature.

q: A script must record which CLI workspace the current run is operating in. Which command prints just the workspace name?
options: terraform workspace show — prints the current workspace name
terraform workspace list — prints all workspaces with an asterisk
terraform state list
Grepping the backend block for the workspace name
explain: workspace show is the direct answer. B lists everything and forces parsing. C lists resource addresses, not the workspace. D scrapes configuration for runtime state.

q: An engineer runs terraform workspace delete default to clean up unused workspaces. What happens?
options: The default workspace is deleted along with its state
It fails — the default workspace can never be deleted
All workspaces are deleted
The backend configuration is deleted instead
explain: The default workspace is permanent; Terraform refuses to delete it. A assumes deletability. C and D invent mass destruction from a guarded command.

q: Two configurations share one S3 backend; networking uses CLI workspaces (dev/staging/prod). The app configuration needs networking's PROD outputs while running in its own prod workspace. How does terraform_remote_state address the right state?
options: It can't — terraform_remote_state only reads the default workspace
Hardcode the full S3 key including env:/prod/ in the backend config
workspace = 'prod' is not a valid argument on the data source
With workspace = 'prod' in the terraform_remote_state block — it selects which CLI workspace's state to read
explain: The workspace argument targets a specific workspace's state key. A denies the argument. B hardcodes the key layout, which is brittle. C denies a documented feature.

q: A state file contains a 'lineage' UUID that never changes across applies. An engineer copies prod's state file over staging's to 'clone' the environment. What does lineage reveal, and why is the copy dangerous?
options: Lineage is the resource count; the copy is safe
Lineage changes on every apply, so nothing is revealed
Lineage is the state's unique identity — the copy makes two environments share one identity, so Terraform cannot tell them apart and concurrent writes corrupt both
Lineage is cosmetic metadata that Terraform ignores
explain: Lineage IDs a state lineage (serial changes per write; lineage never does) — duplicating it merges two environments' identities, the deep reason state files must never be copied. A misdefines it. B is false. D denies its role in init's safety checks.

q: A local-exec provisioner bootstraps an instance. The engineer tweaks an unrelated variable and re-applies; the provisioner does not re-run. Is this a bug?
options: Yes — provisioners run on every apply by design
No — provisioners run only when their resource is created (or replaced); re-runs require triggers_replace
Yes — unless on_failure = 'continue' is set on the provisioner
Provisioners never run at all without -auto-approve
explain: Create-time semantics are by design, not a bug — the exam tests whether you know provisioners are one-shot per resource lifecycle. A states the misconception. C confuses failure handling with scheduling. D invents an approval link.

q: A local-exec provisioner runs a deploy script needing API_TOKEN and REGION, which must not appear in the command string. How are they passed to the script?
options: Interpolated directly into the command string — the only channel available
As Terraform input variables literally named API_TOKEN and REGION
With the environment argument — environment = { API_TOKEN = var.token, REGION = 'us-east-1' } passes them as process environment variables
Provisioners cannot receive environment variables
explain: The environment map is the clean channel — it keeps secrets out of the command string (and thus out of logs and state). A leaks secrets into recorded output. B confuses Terraform variables with process env. D denies the argument.

q: A local-exec provisioner runs on an engineer's Windows laptop and fails because the command is PowerShell, not cmd. How is the interpreter set?
options: interpreter = ['PowerShell', '-Command'] — overrides the default shell used to run the command
It can't be — local-exec only runs on Linux
Rename the command to end with a .ps1 extension
Set working_dir to the PowerShell install directory
explain: interpreter selects the shell explicitly — the documented cross-platform answer. B denies Windows support. C is wrong; the extension doesn't change the executing shell. D changes the working directory, not the interpreter.

q: A remote-exec script needs a config file present on the new instance before its commands run. Which provisioner uploads it?
options: local-exec running scp in its command string
remote-exec with an inline heredoc faking the file
The file must be baked into the AMI — provisioners cannot upload files
The file provisioner — copies files and directories to the remote machine over the connection
explain: file is the upload provisioner; remote-exec runs commands, local-exec runs locally. A shells out manually for what a provisioner does natively. B fakes uploads. C denies a core provisioner.

q: A remote-exec provisioner fails intermittently on large instances that boot slowly — SSH isn't ready when Terraform dials in. Which connection argument helps?
options: retries = 100
timeout = '10m' — extends how long Terraform waits for the connection to become available
on_failure = 'continue'
A larger private_key value
explain: timeout governs how long Terraform waits for connection establishment — the slow-boot answer. A invents a retries argument. C masks the failure instead of waiting through the boot. D is nonsense.

q: Two resources each have when = destroy provisioners deregistering them from a monitoring service; the database depends on the app. During terraform destroy, in what order do the destroy provisioners run?
options: Alphabetical by resource address
In the same order the resources were created
Reverse dependency order — dependents' destroy provisioners run before the dependencies they rely on are destroyed
Simultaneously, with no ordering
explain: Destroy inverts the dependency graph — dependents tear down first, so their cleanup runs while dependencies still exist. A invents alphabetical ordering. B keeps creation order, which is the wrong direction for teardown. D denies the deterministic ordering.

q: After a successful apply using import blocks, the legacy infrastructure is tracked in state. Should the import blocks stay in the configuration forever?
options: No — they are one-shot: once the resource is in state the block can be removed; leaving it is harmless but unnecessary
Yes — removing them deletes the resources from state
Yes — otherwise every plan re-imports the infrastructure
They must be converted into removed blocks immediately
explain: Import blocks only act when the target isn't yet in state; post-apply they're inert, so removal is safe cleanup. B confuses block removal with state rm. C invents re-importing. D invents a mandatory conversion.

q: A configuration contains both resource 'aws_instance' 'old' { ... } and removed { from = aws_instance.old }. What happens on plan?
options: The instance is destroyed as the removed block requests
The removed block is silently ignored
The instance is imported into state
Terraform errors — removed declares the address must NOT be in configuration, so having both is contradictory
explain: removed asserts 'this address is gone from config' — a live resource block at the same address contradicts it, and Terraform fails loudly. A is wrong; destroy-via-removed needs no resource block. B is wrong; contradictions error, never silently pass. C is the opposite operation.

q: A routine plan prints a section headed 'Objects have changed outside of Terraform' listing a security group rule added in the console. The plan then proposes no changes to it. What does this mean?
options: Terraform will delete the rule on apply
Refresh detected the out-of-band change and updated state, but the configuration produces no diff for it — so no action is proposed
The plan is corrupted and must be discarded
The state file was deleted and this is a recovery notice
explain: The section reports refresh findings; no proposed change means there's nothing to reconcile — an informational notice, not an error. A assumes deletion. C and D catastrophize routine drift reporting.

q: Support asks for a full TRACE log of a failing apply, but the console buffer truncated the output. How is the complete log captured to a file?
options: terraform apply | tee log.txt — the only way to capture output
TF_LOG=TRACE alone, which writes to a file by default
TF_LOG=TRACE TF_LOG_PATH=./trace.log — TF_LOG_PATH persists the log stream to a file instead of stderr
Logs cannot be saved; re-run and screenshot the terminal
explain: TF_LOG_PATH is the persistence knob; without it, logs go to stderr and can be truncated. A works partially but misses the designed mechanism. B is wrong — TF_LOG alone still writes to stderr. D gives up.

q: In an automated pipeline, why is terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web preferred over the legacy terraform taint workflow?
options: Taint is faster and safer in pipelines
There is no operational difference between them
-replace works without a state file
taint mutates state BEFORE apply — if the pipeline aborts mid-way, the resource is left tainted; -replace plans the replacement inside a single apply with no advance state edit
explain: -replace keeps the replacement inside the plan/apply transaction; taint's pre-mutation can strand state if automation dies between commands — the real reason taint was retired. A inverts the safety case. B denies the operational difference. C is false.

q: An apply fails and the engineer shares the TRACE log with support. A database password variable was marked sensitive. What appears in the log?
options: The value is redacted — Terraform masks sensitive values in console output AND logs
The plaintext password — log output bypasses redaction
The apply refuses to write logs when sensitive values exist
Only the first and last characters are shown
explain: Redaction covers logs as well as console output — that's what makes sharing TRACE logs safe. B is the dangerous misconception the exam hunts. C invents a refusal. D invents partial masking.

q: A configuration contains both a cloud block and a backend 's3' block. What happens on terraform init?
options: Both are used — state goes to S3 while runs execute remotely
Init errors — a configuration can declare exactly one backend; cloud and backend are mutually exclusive
The backend block is silently ignored
The cloud block is silently ignored
explain: One state backend per configuration — the two blocks declare competing backends, so init fails instead of guessing. A imagines merging. C and D invent silent precedence rules.

q: A workspace uses HCP Terraform for state and variables, but compliance requires plans and applies to execute on the company's own hardened runners, not on HashiCorp's infrastructure. Which execution mode fits?
options: Remote — runs execute on HashiCorp-managed infrastructure
Agent — for private datacenters with no inbound internet access
Local — operations run on the operator's machine or runner while state, variables, and run history stay in HCP Terraform
Execution modes cannot be mixed; every workspace must use remote
explain: Local mode splits the planes: execution happens locally, management stays in HCP Terraform. A runs on HashiCorp's infra — the rejected option. B targets isolated networks, a different need. D denies per-workspace execution modes.

q: The network workspace's apply must automatically queue a plan in the app workspace, since the apps consume the VPC outputs. Which HCP Terraform feature chains them?
options: Run triggers — the app workspace triggers on the network workspace's successful applies
A human must manually queue the app workspace's run each time
terraform_remote_state with polling enabled
Workspaces cannot be chained together
explain: Run triggers are the workspace-chaining feature — downstream runs queue automatically. B is the manual toil triggers eliminate. C is wrong; remote_state reads data but triggers nothing. D denies the feature.

q: A workspace needs AWS credentials for the provider and a Terraform input variable instance_type. How are they entered in HCP Terraform?
options: Both as Terraform variables
Both as environment variables
Credentials hardcoded in the configuration, instance_type as a variable
Credentials as environment variables (e.g., AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID), instance_type as a Terraform variable — the category determines how the value is exposed to runs
explain: Providers read credentials from the environment; Terraform inputs arrive as HCP 'Terraform' variables — the category is the mechanism. A is wrong; TF_VAR-style values don't authenticate providers. B wouldn't map instance_type to the input variable. C commits secrets.

q: A variable set attached to the project defines region = 'us-east-1'. One workspace in the project sets region = 'eu-west-1' directly on itself. Which value do that workspace's runs use?
options: us-east-1 — variable sets always win over workspace values
eu-west-1 — workspace-specific values override variable set values
The run fails on the conflicting definitions
A value is chosen at random per run
explain: The more specific scope wins: workspace values beat variable set values. A inverts the precedence. C and D invent failure and randomness where a clean override rule exists.

q: One configuration is shared across 30 microservice workspaces tagged team:payments. How does the cloud block select all of them instead of naming a single workspace?
options: workspaces { names = ['*'] } — glob syntax
A separate cloud block per workspace is required
cloud { organization = 'acme' workspaces { tags = ['team:payments'] } } — tags select the workspace set; name selects one
Tags cannot be used; every workspace must be listed individually
explain: The tags selector is the multi-workspace form; name is the single-workspace form. A invents glob syntax. B denies the tags selector. D denies a documented feature.

q: A run is queued in HCP Terraform. Which stage order does it follow?
options: Plan → cost estimation → policy check → apply — each stage gates the next
Apply → plan → policy check
Policy check → plan → apply
Cost estimation → apply → plan
explain: The documented pipeline: plan first, then the cost and policy gates, then apply. B, C, and D scramble an order the exam expects you to know cold.

q: A CI job must authenticate the Terraform CLI to HCP Terraform non-interactively, without running terraform login. Which mechanism works?
options: Hardcode the API token in the cloud block
terraform login -auto-approve
API tokens cannot be used non-interactively
The TF_TOKEN_app_terraform_io environment variable — the CLI reads API tokens from credential environment variables
explain: The documented non-interactive auth path for automation. A commits a secret. B invents a flag for an interactive command. C denies automation entirely.

q: A personal automation script needs HCP Terraform API access acting as the engineer — with their permissions, not a team's. Which token type fits?
options: Organization token — full admin access owned by no individual
User API token — acts with the individual user's permissions
Team token — acts with the team's permissions
The browser session cookie from terraform login
explain: User tokens are personal automation with personal permissions. A is org-wide admin — overprivileged for the need. C acts as the team, not the individual. D invents a cookie mechanism.

q: A VCS-driven workspace's runs fail at init while cloning modules from a private GitHub repo. The VCS OAuth connection works fine for the configuration repo. What is missing?
options: Nothing — the OAuth connection automatically covers all private repos
The module repos must be made public
An SSH key added to the workspace or organization for the module repos — module fetching authenticates independently of the workspace's VCS connection
terraform init must be run locally before each remote run
explain: Module sources authenticate independently of the VCS workspace connection — SSH keys fill the gap. A assumes transitive auth that doesn't exist. B weakens security unnecessarily. D misunderstands remote execution.

q: A policy set is connected to a VCS repository. The security team merges a new Sentinel rule to the repo's main branch. What happens?
options: HCP Terraform picks up the new policy on subsequent runs — VCS-backed policy sets track the branch
Nothing — policy sets are snapshots frozen at creation time
Every workspace using the set must be recreated
The policy must be pasted into the UI again after each merge
explain: VCS backing means continuous sync — merges flow into future runs automatically. B describes one-time manual upload. C and D invent toil that the VCS connection eliminates.

q: A company runs Terraform Enterprise self-hosted at tfe.example.com. Which backend configuration connects the CLI to it?
options: backend 's3' pointed at the TFE address
The cloud block, which only works with HCP Terraform
backend 'http' with the TFE address
terraform { backend 'remote' { hostname = 'tfe.example.com' organization = 'acme' workspaces { name = 'prod' } } } — the remote backend targets any TFE-compatible hostname
explain: The remote backend's hostname argument points at self-hosted Terraform Enterprise. A uses the wrong backend type. B is false; the remote backend (and cloud block) both support TFE hostnames. C uses the generic HTTP backend, the wrong protocol.

q: A plan reports `Objects have changed outside of Terraform`: an engineer resized the production database in the cloud console without approval. The team wants the approved configuration to win. What happens on the next `terraform apply`?
options: Terraform reverts the database to the configured size — apply reconciles real infrastructure back to the declared desired state
Terraform adopts the console change into the configuration automatically
The apply fails until someone fixes the size in the console first
Terraform deletes the database because it is no longer tracked
explain: Apply is reconciliation toward the declared state, so unauthorized drift gets reverted to what the code says. B is wrong — Terraform never edits your .tf files. C invents a failure; apply proceeds normally. D confuses drift with removal from the configuration.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A junior engineer asks why the team runs `terraform plan` on every pull request even though nothing is deployed from CI. Which statement best captures the value?
options: It deploys to a staging account for testing
It is a dry run — it shows exactly what would change, catching mistakes before any real infrastructure is touched
It is only useful for estimating cost
It replaces code review of the .tf files
explain: Plan is a safe preview: reviewers see adds, changes, and destroys with zero side effects. A is wrong — plan touches nothing. C is too narrow; cost is one benefit among many. D is wrong — the plan complements code review, it does not replace reading the code.

q: A company is expanding from a single AWS region to three and wants every region built identically without tripling its maintenance burden. Which Terraform approach delivers this?
options: Copy the configuration directory three times and hand-edit the region in each copy
Maintain three separate hand-built environments and sync them monthly
Keep one configuration parameterized by region, with a separate state per region — the same code deploys everywhere
Build one region in Terraform and clone it with console snapshots

q: A production web server starts behaving erratically. The team practices immutable infrastructure with Terraform. What is the correct response?

Take a snapshot and keep the sick server running for study
Reboot it and hope the problem clears
Replace it — destroy and recreate the server from the versioned configuration so the fleet stays known-good

q: A bad firewall rule reached production last Tuesday. The team manages firewalls in Terraform under version control. What is the fastest way to identify exactly which change introduced it?
