Ask every engineer what they remember doing last Tuesday
Re-read the entire current configuration top to bottom
Disable version control so the history stops growing

q: A security team wants misconfigurations (public S3 buckets, open security groups) caught before infrastructure is created, not after. Which IaC practice delivers this?

Scanning the Terraform code in CI — policy checks run against the planned changes before anything is applied
Waiting for the provider to reject bad values at apply time
IaC cannot be security-scanned; only running infrastructure can
explain: Because infrastructure is code, policy-as-code scans evaluate every change pre-apply — shift-left security. A is slow and sampled. C catches only API-invalid values, not policy violations. D is false; static analysis of .tf files is standard practice.

q: A developer commits AWS access keys directly in a `provider` block, arguing the repository is private so it is safe. What is the exam-correct objection?
options: Private repositories are always breached, so nothing is safe
Terraform does not support private repositories
Git history is forever — keys leak through clones, forks, logs, and PRs; secrets belong in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in versioned code
Keys in code are fine as long as they are base64-encoded

q: A team pays for a full staging environment 24/7 but only uses it during work hours. How does IaC change the economics?
options: It doesn't — cloud costs are fixed
Engineers must manually delete resources every evening
Buy smaller instances and accept the performance hit
Schedule `terraform destroy` each evening and `terraform apply` each morning — the environment becomes code that is rebuilt on demand instead of rented idle

q: A configuration declares a database, an app server, and a DNS record pointing at the server. The engineer never wrote any ordering instructions, yet Terraform creates them in the right sequence. Why?

Resources are created in alphabetical order by name
Resources are created in the order the blocks appear in the files
Terraform prompts the engineer to approve the order at plan time

domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A manager claims that because the team adopted Terraform, they no longer need to test infrastructure changes. What is the exam-correct correction?
options: The manager is right — Terraform changes are always safe
IaC moves testing earlier — plan review and non-production applies — but it does not remove the need to test
Testing is only needed for application code, never infrastructure
Terraform applies should always go straight to production to save time

domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Dev and prod keep diverging: dev was clicked together in the console, prod was built from Terraform months ago. How does the IaC model fix environment parity going forward?

Rebuild prod by hand to match dev
Manage both from the same configuration with per-environment variable files — the code is identical, only the inputs differ
Give up on parity; environments are naturally different

q: An auditor asks for evidence that production firewall changes go through review and approval. The team manages infrastructure with Terraform on a VCS-backed workflow. What serves as the evidence?

A spreadsheet where engineers log their changes
Verbal confirmation from the team lead
The version-control history plus the reviewed plan on each pull request — every change is proposed, reviewed, and recorded

q: A team rotates database credentials quarterly: an engineer logs into the cloud console and types in new passwords by hand. With the database now managed by Terraform, how does rotation improve?
options: Change the credential variable value and apply — rotation becomes a reviewed, repeatable, auditable change like any other
Credentials never need rotating once Terraform manages them
Terraform rotates credentials automatically on a schedule
Keep rotating in the console; Terraform only manages servers

q: An engineer finds `provider::aws::arn_parse("arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/jdoe")` in a configuration. No module defines it and it is not in the core HCL documentation. What implements this function?
options: The AWS provider plugin — provider-defined functions live under the `provider::` namespace (Terraform 1.8+)
Terraform core's built-in functions
A child module
An external data source
explain: Provider-defined functions are implemented by provider plugins and addressed as provider::<source>::<name>. B is wrong — core functions have no provider:: prefix. C and D cannot define namespaced functions.

q: A child module contains its own `provider "aws" { region = "eu-west-1" }` block. What happens when the configuration is initialized and planned?
options: It works — child modules configure their own providers
The child's provider silently overrides the root's
Terraform errors — provider configuration blocks belong only in the root module; children declare `configuration_aliases` and receive providers through the `providers` meta-argument
The block is silently ignored
explain: Only the root module may contain provider configurations — this keeps provider wiring explicit and reviewable. A and B describe behavior Terraform forbids. D is wrong; it errors rather than ignoring.

q: Before installing anything, an engineer wants a quick list of every provider a configuration requires. Which command does this?
options: `terraform init`
`terraform plan`
`terraform version`
`terraform providers`
explain: terraform providers lists the providers required by the configuration without installing them. A installs. B needs credentials and state access. C shows the CLI version, not requirements.

q: A `provider "aws"` block sets `region = "us-east-1"` statically, but the shell has `AWS_REGION=eu-west-1` exported. Which region does the provider use?
options: us-east-1 — explicit provider arguments take precedence over environment variables
eu-west-1 — environment variables always win
Terraform errors on the conflict
The provider's compiled-in default
explain: Static provider configuration beats environment variables in the precedence chain. B reverses it. C is wrong — no conflict error exists. D only applies when neither is set.

q: A `required_providers` entry declares the `docker` provider with no `source` argument, intending the community `kreuzwerker/docker` provider. What happens at `terraform init`?
options: Terraform auto-detects the community provider
Init fails — with no source, Terraform assumes the `hashicorp/docker` address, which doesn't exist; community providers need an explicit source
Terraform installs the newest docker provider from any namespace
Terraform prompts the engineer to pick a namespace
explain: The default source namespace is hashicorp — omitting source for a community provider addresses a nonexistent provider. A and C invent auto-detection. D is wrong; init fails instead of prompting.

q: During `terraform plan`, something must call the AWS API to refresh the current state of every managed resource. Which component makes those API calls?
options: Terraform core
The configured backend
The AWS provider plugin — providers own all communication with their APIs; core manages the plan and state
HCP Terraform
explain: Plugin architecture: providers translate Terraform operations into API calls; core never talks to clouds directly. A inverts the split. B stores state. D is the SaaS platform, not the API client.

q: An engineer writes `provider "aws" { version = "~> 5.0" }` to pin the provider version. What happens?
options: It works — this is the standard way to pin providers
The version argument is silently ignored
It pins the version but only for data sources
Terraform errors — provider version constraints belong in `required_providers`, not in provider configuration blocks
explain: Provider blocks accept configuration (region, credentials, aliases) — never version constraints, which live in required_providers. A describes the wrong location. B is wrong; it's an error, not silent. C invents a distinction.

q: The lock file records `hashicorp/aws` 5.9.0. The constraints allow any 5.x, and 5.10.0 was just released. A teammate runs plain `terraform init`. Which version is installed?
options: 5.9.0 — the lock file's recorded selection wins on a plain init; only `init -upgrade` moves to newer allowed versions
5.10.0 — init always takes the newest allowed
Init errors because a newer version exists
Init prompts to choose between them
explain: The lock file exists to make installs deterministic — plain init honors it. B describes -upgrade behavior. C and D invent failures; init is non-interactive here.

q: A bank's build network has no internet access, but an internet-connected workstation must prepare a local directory of provider plugins for it. Which command populates that directory?
options: `terraform init` on the workstation
Copying the workstation's `.terraform` directory by hand
Manually downloading zips from the registry website
`terraform providers mirror` — downloads packages for all required providers into a filesystem mirror layout
explain: providers mirror exists to build a local mirror from a connected machine. A installs into one working directory, not a mirror layout. B copies installed plugins but not the mirror structure. C is manual toil the command automates.

q: A CI system cannot easily pass CLI flags to Terraform, but every run must be fully non-interactive. Which environment variable disables all input prompts?
options: `TF_VAR_input`
`TF_LOG`
`TF_INPUT=0` — the environment equivalent of `-input=false`
`TF_DATA_DIR`
explain: TF_INPUT=0 disables prompts exactly like -input=false. A sets a variable literally named input. B controls logging. D relocates the data directory.

q: A configuration has two `terraform {}` blocks: one sets `required_version`, the other configures the backend. What happens?
options: Terraform errors — only one terraform block is allowed
They are merged — multiple terraform blocks are allowed and their settings combine
The second block silently replaces the first
Only the first block is read; the second is ignored
explain: Terraform merges multiple terraform blocks, so settings can be split across files. A states the common misconception. C and D invent override/ignore semantics.

q: A configuration sets `required_version = "~> 1.9"` in the terraform block. One engineer runs CLI 1.12, another tries CLI 2.0. What happens?
options: Both versions work
CLI 1.12 works; CLI 2.0 is rejected — `~> 1.9` allows 1.x at 1.9+, but not 2.0
CLI 2.0 works; CLI 1.12 is rejected
Both are rejected
explain: The pessimistic operator ~> 1.9 means >= 1.9, < 2.0 — minor/patch flexibility without major jumps. A ignores the upper bound. C inverts it. D is wrong; 1.12 satisfies the range.

q: Two configurations on the same machine need different AWS provider versions. How does Terraform keep them from interfering?
options: It can't — one machine gets one provider version
Each working directory installs its own plugins under its own `.terraform` directory, so versions are isolated per configuration
By using provider aliases
By running each in a container
explain: Plugin installs are per-working-directory (.terraform/), so configurations are version-independent. A is false. C selects configurations, not versions. D is unnecessary for this.

q: The team schedules a full teardown of the dev environment for Friday night and wants to review the complete list of doomed resources beforehand, without deleting anything yet. Which command does this?
options: `terraform destroy -dry-run`
`terraform apply -destroy`
`terraform plan -destroy` — computes the destroy plan with no changes executed
`terraform show -destroy`
explain: plan -destroy renders the full destroy diff safely. A is not a real flag. B would actually destroy after prompting. D is not a real command.

q: A provider's API rate-limits aggressively, and creating 50 resources in parallel keeps failing. How can the team serialize resource operations?
options: Add `-target` for each resource
Chain `depends_on` through all 50 resources
`-refresh=false`
`terraform apply -parallelism=1` — caps concurrent operations (default is 10)
explain: -parallelism directly limits concurrent operations for rate-limited APIs. A is manual toil. B fakes dependencies that don't exist. C skips refresh, which is unrelated to concurrency.

q: An engineer runs `terraform apply` twice in a row with no configuration changes. Does the second run contact the cloud provider at all?
options: Yes — refresh still runs before the (empty) diff, and the state file may be updated with refreshed values
No — Terraform detects nothing changed and skips all provider calls
No — the second apply is rejected as redundant
Only if `-refresh=true` is passed explicitly

q: Overlapping CI runs occasionally collide on the state lock, and the pipeline fails immediately instead of waiting. How can a run wait up to five minutes for the lock?
options: `terraform force-unlock` before every run
`-lock-timeout=5m` — waits for the lock instead of failing fast
`-parallelism=1`
Disabling state locking in the backend
explain: -lock-timeout retries lock acquisition for the given duration. A is dangerous — it steals locks from live runs. C limits resource concurrency, not lock waits. D removes safety entirely.

q: Inside `terraform console`, an engineer evaluates `aws_instance.web.ami` for an instance created last week. Where does the returned value come from?
options: The resource block's arguments in the configuration
A live query to the cloud API
The state file — console evaluates expressions against recorded state
The input variables
explain: Console resolves managed-resource references from state, which is why initialized state is required. A gives configured, not actual, values. B is wrong — console doesn't call APIs for this. D only covers variables.

q: A deployment pipeline needs every output value in machine-readable form for the next job step. Which command provides this?

Querying each output individually with `-raw`
Parsing `terraform.tfstate` by hand
`terraform output -json` — renders all outputs as JSON

q: A pipeline runs `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode`. The command exits with code 2. What does this mean?
options: Success — the plan contains changes (0 = no changes, 1 = error, 2 = changes present)
The plan failed with an error
The plan succeeded with no changes
The plan produced only warnings
explain: detailed-exitcode encodes the diff in the exit status: 2 means a non-empty plan. B is exit 1. C is exit 0. D is not an exit-code category.

q: An approved hotfix was applied in the cloud console. The team wants the state file reconciled with reality without changing any infrastructure. Which command does this?

`terraform apply -refresh-only` — refreshes state to match real infrastructure and saves it, changing nothing
`terraform state push`
`terraform taint` on the changed resources

q: A teammate claims `terraform show` displays what the configuration declares. Is this accurate?
options: Yes — show renders the .tf files
It queries the cloud provider live
No — show reads the state file (or a plan file), displaying recorded reality, not declared intent
It reads the input variables

q: `instance_count` is set four ways: `default = 1`, `terraform.tfvars` sets 2, `prod.auto.tfvars` sets 3, and the CLI passes `-var=instance_count=4`. Which value wins?
options: 1 — defaults always win
2 — terraform.tfvars beats everything
3 — .auto.tfvars files beat the CLI
4 — CLI `-var` flags beat all variable files, which beat defaults
explain: Precedence: -var flags, then -var-file flags (later files win), then *.auto.tfvars, then terraform.tfvars, then defaults. A, B, and C each pick a lower-precedence source.

q: `terraform graph` prints a wall of text. How does the team turn it into a viewable diagram?
options: Pipe the DOT-format output through Graphviz (`dot -Tpng`) — graph emits DOT, not images
Pass `-format=png` to terraform graph
Open the text in `terraform console`
Graph output is already an image; rename it .png
explain: graph emits the DOT graph language; an external renderer like Graphviz draws it. B is not a real flag. C and D misunderstand the text output.

q: A fully automated pipeline must guarantee `terraform apply` never prompts for input or confirmation. Which combination is correct?
options: `-auto-approve` alone
`-input=false` together with `-auto-approve` (or a saved plan file) — no variable prompts and no confirmation prompt
`-no-color`
Piping `yes` into the command
explain: -auto-approve skips confirmation but missing variables can still prompt; -input=false closes that hole. A alone can still hang on input. C only strips color. D is fragile shell hackery.

q: Release policy requires the plan file to be built a day before the change window. Overnight, an unrelated hotfix changes real infrastructure. At the window, the engineer applies the day-old plan file. What happens?
options: The saved plan applies cleanly, ignoring the hotfix
Terraform merges the hotfix into the saved plan
Apply errors — the saved plan was computed against older state, so Terraform refuses and requires a fresh plan
Terraform silently skips the refresh step
explain: Saved plans are bound to the state they were computed from; apply detects the mismatch rather than applying a stale diff. A would clobber the hotfix blindly. B invents merging. D is false — the check is the point.

q: A resource sets both `create_before_destroy = true` and `prevent_destroy = true`. The provider forces a replacement. What happens on apply?
options: Terraform creates the replacement, then fails to destroy the original
Both lifecycle rules are honored without conflict
Terraform updates the resource in place instead
Terraform errors — `prevent_destroy` forbids the destroy that the replacement requires, so the two settings are incompatible here
explain: Replacement inherently destroys the original; prevent_destroy vetoes that destroy, making the plan impossible. A describes a partial outcome Terraform won't attempt. B ignores the contradiction. C is wrong — the provider still forces replacement.

q: An external tool manages the `Environment` tag on instances, but Terraform should still manage all other tags. How is this expressed?
options: `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags["Environment"]] }` — ignores that single tag key while managing the rest
`lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags] }` — the only way to ignore tags
It can't be done — ignore_changes is all-or-nothing per resource
Remove the tags argument entirely
explain: ignore_changes accepts attribute element addresses like tags["Environment"] for surgical ignores. B would also ignore Terraform-managed tags. C is false. D surrenders all tag management.

q: A `dynamic "ingress"` block iterates `var.extra_rules`, but the variable defaults to `null` and the block errors on null. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Wrap the resource in `count`
`for_each = coalesce(var.extra_rules, [])` — null becomes an empty list, so zero blocks are generated
Set the default to an empty string
Dynamic blocks cannot handle null; remove the variable
explain: coalesce substitutes an empty collection for null, cleanly generating nothing. A is the wrong tool. C makes the type error worse. D gives up instead of handling null.

q: A launch template's `user_data` must always render successfully — if the rendered script is empty, the run should fail before instances launch. Which construct enforces this on the resource itself?
options: A `validation` block on a variable
A `check` block
A `postcondition` in the resource's `lifecycle` block — it evaluates after that resource is applied and fails the run when false
A `precondition` on an unrelated data source
explain: Resource postconditions validate the resource's own attributes after apply and fail the run — exactly this gate. A validates inputs, not rendered results. B only warns and isn't a run gate. D checks the wrong object.

q: A variable `environment` must only accept `dev`, `staging`, or `prod`. Which validation rule enforces this?
options: `type = string` — the type system restricts values
A `precondition` on the resource
Documenting the allowed values in a comment
`validation { condition = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment) }` — fails plan early on anything else
explain: contains() against an allow-list is the standard enum-style validation, evaluated before resources are planned. A allows any string. B validates resources, not inputs. C doesn't enforce.

q: A refactor moves `aws_instance.web` into a child module as `module.compute.aws_instance.web`. The team wants this recorded in version control rather than run as a CLI command. Which block does it?
options: `moved { from = aws_instance.web to = module.compute.aws_instance.web }` — the declarative, reviewable equivalent of `state mv`
An `import` block
`terraform state mv` — blocks can't do this
Nothing — recreating is the only declarative path
explain: moved blocks rebind any address change, including into modules, as code. B is for unmanaged infrastructure. C is wrong; moved is the in-code alternative. D wastes the running instance.

q: An engineer writes `validation { condition = var.min_size < var.max_size }` inside the `min_size` variable block. What happens?
options: It works — cross-variable validation is supported
Terraform errors — a variable's validation may only refer to that variable itself, never to other variables
It warns but still applies
The condition is checked only during destroy
explain: Validation scope is deliberately limited to the variable being declared, so values can be checked before the full configuration is evaluated. A states the forbidden behavior. C and D invent leniency.

q: A module declares `variable "server" { type = object({ name = string, size = optional(number, 4) }) }`. A caller passes only `{ name = "web" }`. What is `var.server.size`?
options: An error — all object attributes are required
`null`
`4` — `optional()` supplies the declared default when the caller omits the attribute
explain: optional(type, default) makes the attribute omittable with a fallback — the modern way to do partial object defaults. A describes the old all-required behavior. B would be true without the default. D invents a zero value.

q: A validation rule must reject values that aren't valid CIDR strings, without producing a cryptic type error. Which function tests whether an expression evaluates successfully?
options: `try()`
`coalesce()`
`length()`
`can()` — returns true/false for whether the expression succeeds, e.g. `can(cidrhost(var.cidr, 0))`
explain: can() is the boolean probe for expression validity — ideal in validation conditions. A returns a fallback value instead of a boolean. B picks the first non-null. C measures length, not validity.

q: A resource block sets both `count = 2` and `for_each = var.servers`. What happens?
options: Terraform errors — `count` and `for_each` are mutually exclusive on one resource
`count` wins and `for_each` is ignored
Two instances per map element are created
`for_each` wins and `count` is ignored
explain: The two meta-arguments are explicitly incompatible — Terraform rejects the combination rather than guessing. B, C, and D invent precedence or multiplication rules.

q: A data source reads an S3 bucket that is created by a resource in the same configuration, but nothing references the bucket's attributes. The read intermittently fails because it runs too early. What fixes the ordering?
options: A provisioner on the bucket
`depends_on` on the data source — data sources honor it to delay their read until the dependency exists
`-target` on every apply
Changing the data source to a resource
explain: depends_on works in data blocks to sequence reads after creation. A is the wrong tool entirely. C is manual toil per run. D misunderstands data sources.

q: A team adds both a `postcondition` on a resource and a `check` block asserting the same thing. The assertion starts failing. How do the two failures differ?
options: Both block the apply
Both only warn
The failed `postcondition` fails the run; the failed `check` block reports a warning/status but does not block the apply
The `check` block fails the run; the postcondition only warns
explain: Postconditions are hard gates on the run; check blocks are continuous assertions that surface status without blocking. A, B, and D swap or conflate the two semantics.

q: A team keeps its service catalog in `catalog.yaml`. A local value needs it as a structured value. Which expression loads it?
options: `file("catalog.yaml")` alone — returns a string, not structure
`jsondecode(file("catalog.yaml"))`
`templatefile("catalog.yaml", {})`
`yamldecode(file("catalog.yaml"))` — parses YAML into HCL values
explain: yamldecode is the YAML counterpart of jsondecode. A returns raw text. B fails on YAML syntax. C renders templates instead of parsing.

q: A team pushes new module code to the GitHub repo backing their public registry module, but the registry page shows no new version. What did they forget?
options: Registry versions are published by pushing a git tag (e.g. `v2.1.0`) — code pushes alone release nothing
The registry polls the default branch hourly; they must wait
They must bump the `version` argument in every caller
They must re-run `terraform init -upgrade`
explain: The registry mints versions from git tags, not commits — no tag, no release. B invents polling. C confuses caller pins with publishing. D affects installs, not releases.

q: A team wants `terraform init` to reinstall modules at the newest versions allowed by their constraints, instead of keeping the recorded ones. Which flag does this?
options: Plain `terraform init`
`terraform init -upgrade` — upgrades both modules and providers within the allowed constraints
`terraform init -get=false`
Deleting the configuration files
explain: -upgrade re-resolves modules and providers to the newest allowed. A honors the lock/manifest. C skips module install. D is destructive nonsense.

q: A module block uses `for_each = toset(["us-east-1", "eu-west-1"])` and outputs `vpc_id`. How does the root collect every region's VPC ID?
options: `module.vpc[*].vpc_id`
`module.vpc.vpc_id`
`values(module.vpc)[*].vpc_id` — for_each makes the module a map, so `values()` is needed before splatting
Outputs can't be collected from for_each modules
explain: for_each modules are maps keyed by instance key; values() converts to a list for the splat. A is the count syntax. B addresses a single module. D is false.

q: A private GitHub repository holds a versioned module, and the team authenticates with SSH keys rather than tokens in URLs. Which source address is correct?
options: `https://github.com/org/vpc` with a password in the URL
`github.com/org/vpc`
The public registry address
`git::ssh://git@github.com/org/vpc.git?ref=v2.0.0` — SSH transport with a pinned ref
explain: The git::ssh:// form uses SSH keys with no secrets in the URL, and ?ref= pins the version. A leaks credentials. B is not a valid source. C is for public modules.

q: A module is sourced from `./modules/vpc`. An engineer edits a file inside that directory. Must they re-run `terraform init` before planning?
options: No — local path modules are read fresh on every run; init is only needed when the module set changes
Yes — every edit requires re-init
Only with `-upgrade`
Only after deleting `.terraform`
explain: Local modules aren't versioned installs — Terraform reads them live. B, C, and D confuse local paths with registry/git modules that are installed snapshots.

q: A team wants a registry module pinned to exactly version 2.4.0 — never floating to 2.4.1. Which version argument does this?
options: Omitting the version argument
explain: A bare version (or =) pins exactly. A allows 2.x patches. C allows anything newer. D floats to newest allowed.

q: A child module declares `configuration_aliases = [aws.west]`. The root passes `providers = { aws.west = aws.eu_central }`. Which provider configuration do the child's resources use?
options: It errors — the names don't match
The root's `aws.west`
The root's `aws.eu_central` — the map binds the child's alias name to any root provider configuration
The child's own `aws.west`, which it defines itself
explain: The providers map is a binding: child alias name to root provider configuration, and the target need not share the name. A invents a name-matching rule. B ignores the explicit map. D is impossible — children can't define providers.

q: A child module outputs a sensitive `db_password`. The root module needs to expose it to the operator running the root. What must the root do?
options: Nothing — child outputs are automatically visible
Reference it and mark it `nonsensitive()`
Read it from the state file directly
Declare its own `output` referencing `module.db.db_password` — values only leave a module through declared outputs, and sensitivity propagates
explain: Module boundaries are explicit: outputs must be re-declared at each level, and sensitivity follows the value. A ignores encapsulation. B would unmask a secret. C bypasses the CLI.

q: A registry module's page shows usage examples the author never wrote in a separate docs site. Where did they come from?
options: The module's `README.md` — the registry renders it as the documentation front page
They are auto-generated from the code
The registry's web editor
Only the `examples/` directory is shown
explain: README.md is the registry docs front page — that's why publishing guides require one. B is false; examples aren't synthesized. C doesn't exist. D is shown separately, not as the main docs.

q: A CI job runs `terraform init -backend=false` because it has no backend credentials. Are child modules still installed?
options: No — skipping the backend skips everything
Yes — `-backend=false` skips only backend configuration; providers and modules still install
Only providers install
Init fails without a backend
explain: -backend=false is surgical: backend setup is skipped, everything else proceeds. A and C overstate the skip. D is false; init succeeds.

q: A team wants to temporarily disable the `vpc` module without deleting its block (they'll re-enable it next sprint). Which approach works?
options: Delete the block and re-create everything next sprint
`terraform state rm` on its resources
`count = 0` on the module block — zero instances, resources planned for destruction, block and wiring preserved
Set `version = ""`
explain: count = 0 is the reversible off-switch: resources are destroyed but the block and its wiring stay, so re-enabling is one edit. A loses the wiring. B forgets resources without destroying them, leaving orphans. D is invalid.

q: A configuration needs the well-known public VPC module for AWS from the Terraform Registry. Which source address is correct?
options: `hashicorp/vpc/aws`
`aws/vpc`
`registry.terraform.io/vpc/aws`
`terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` — namespace/name/provider
explain: Public registry modules are addressed namespace/name/provider. A uses the wrong namespace. B omits the namespace. C misplaces the hostname into the address.

q: A backend block contains `bucket = var.state_bucket`. What happens at `terraform init`?
options: It works — backends accept variables
Init errors — backend configuration does not support variables or interpolations; partial config comes from `-backend-config` flags or files
It warns and uses a default bucket
The variable is read from `terraform.tfvars`
explain: Backends initialize before variables exist, so interpolation is impossible by design — that's why partial backend config exists. A states the forbidden behavior. C and D invent leniency.

q: An engineer hand-creates 5 EC2 instances in the console. The Terraform configuration manages other resources but mentions none of these. What does the next `terraform plan` do about the 5 instances?
options: Adopts them into state
Proposes to destroy them
Ignores them — plan only considers resources declared in configuration and tracked in state
Fails with an untracked-resources error
explain: Terraform manages a declared set; unknown real-world objects are invisible to it — adoption requires import. A skips the import step. B would be dangerous overreach. D invents an error.

q: An engineer runs `terraform import aws_instance.legacy i-0abcd1234` but the configuration contains no `aws_instance.legacy` resource block. What happens?
options: Terraform creates the resource block automatically
The import succeeds and the next plan is clean
The import succeeds but the object is forgotten
The import fails — a matching resource block must exist before the CLI can import into it
explain: CLI import binds a real object to a declared address; with no block there is no address. A confuses CLI import with `-generate-config-out`. B and C invent success.

q: To import an `aws_s3_bucket`, what value does the import `id` take?
options: The bucket name — the import ID is provider-defined and varies per resource type
Always the ARN
Always a numeric ID
The resource's state address
explain: Each provider documents its own import ID format — for S3 buckets it's the name. B, C, and D assume a universal format that doesn't exist.

q: A team uses the S3 backend and wants state locking without operating a DynamoDB table. What is the current option?
options: Locking is impossible without DynamoDB
`use_lockfile = true` — S3-native state locking without a separate lock table
Switch to the local backend
Disable locking with `-lock=false` on every command
explain: The S3 backend supports native locking via use_lockfile. A is outdated. C loses remote state. D removes protection.

q: A state file is corrupted during a failed push. The workspace uses HCP Terraform's remote state. What recovery option exists that plain S3-plus-local-backup lacks?
options: None — recovery is identical
Re-running apply always rebuilds state
HCP Terraform retains a history of state versions, so an earlier known-good version can be restored
The state is stored in Git automatically
explain: Remote state in HCP keeps versioned history per workspace — a built-in rollback point. A ignores the platform feature. B is false; apply needs state. D is wrong; state isn't in Git.

q: A configuration adds only a `moved` block renaming a resource address. What does the plan show for that resource?
options: Destroy and create
An in-place update
An error — moved blocks require recreation
No resource changes — the state address is rebound and the real object is untouched
explain: moved is bookkeeping-only: Terraform updates its address mapping with zero API calls. A is what happens without the block. B and C misunderstand the mechanism.

q: Before a demo, an engineer deletes the entire `.terraform` directory to `clean up`. What is actually lost?
options: Nothing durable — installed providers, modules, and backend settings cache live there and `terraform init` restores them; state and configuration are untouched
The state file
The `.tf` configuration files
The production infrastructure
explain: .terraform is a disposable working cache — init rebuilds it from configuration and the lock file. B is wrong; state lives in terraform.tfstate or the backend. C is wrong; config files are separate. D is absurd; no API calls happen.

q: An engineer runs `terraform state rm aws_instance.old` and also deletes its resource block from the configuration. What does the next plan propose, and what happens to the real instance?
options: The plan proposes nothing and the real instance keeps running unmanaged — removing both the block and the state entry orphans the resource
The plan proposes to destroy the instance
The plan proposes to recreate the instance
Terraform errors on the missing state entry
explain: With no block and no state entry, Terraform doesn't know the object exists — the classic orphan, still running and still billed. B is wrong; destroy requires a tracked object. C is what happens when the block stays but the state entry is removed. D invents an error.

q: An engineer runs `terraform init -migrate-state` when switching backends. What happens to the state in the OLD backend?
options: It is deleted immediately
It is left untouched with no backup anywhere
The state is copied to the new backend, and the old state remains (a local backup is kept) — nothing is deleted automatically
It is merged with the new backend's state
explain: Migration copies; Terraform never deletes your old state for you — verify before cleaning up. A is the dangerous assumption. B ignores the backup. D invents merging.

q: A stale lock blocks all commands after a crashed apply, and the team has the lock ID from the error message. Which command releases it?
options: `terraform init -force`
Deleting the state file
`terraform workspace delete`
`terraform force-unlock <lock-id>` — after confirming no apply is actually running
explain: force-unlock with the lock ID is the documented recovery — but only when the holder is truly dead, since it can corrupt state otherwise. A is not a command. B destroys tracking. C is unrelated.

q: `terraform state show aws_db_instance.main` displays the password attribute. How does it appear?
options: Redacted — Terraform masks values marked sensitive in state output
In plaintext — state show reveals everything
As a hash of the real value
The command refuses to display sensitive resources
explain: Sensitive marking flows through to display: CLI output redacts it. B is the misconception the question tests. C invents hashing. D is false; it displays with redaction.

q: During maintenance, an engineer accidentally taints the wrong instance and no apply has run yet. How is the taint undone?
options: Run apply and let it recreate the instance
`terraform untaint aws_instance.web` — clears the tainted status from state before anything is replaced
`terraform state rm` on the instance
It can't be undone; the instance must be replaced
explain: untaint reverses the taint marking while it's still only a state flag. A pointlessly recreates a healthy instance. C would orphan it from management. D is false before apply.

q: A team moves from local runs to HCP Terraform remote execution. Their `local-exec` provisioner that called an on-premises deployment script starts failing. What is the most likely cause?
options: Provisioners are banned on HCP Terraform
The script has a syntax error
`local-exec` runs on the machine executing Terraform — now HCP's remote runner, which cannot reach the on-premises script
Remote execution deletes provisioner blocks
explain: local-exec is `local` to the Terraform process; remote runs move that process off the laptop. A is false. B wouldn't coincide with the migration. D invents deletion.

q: An engineer runs `terraform taint aws_instance.web` and then decides not to apply. Separately, another engineer runs `terraform plan -replace=aws_instance.web` and also doesn't apply. How do the two situations differ?
options: They are identical
The taint is discarded; the -replace persists
The -replace is written to state; the taint is not
The taint already modified the state (the resource is marked tainted until untainted); `-replace` only lives in the plan and vanishes if never applied
explain: taint is an immediate state mutation; -replace is a plan-time request. B and C swap the mechanics. A misses the core distinction the exam tests.

q: A `local-exec` provisioner fails and the block sets no `on_failure`. What is the resource's status afterward?
options: Marked tainted — the next apply will destroy and recreate it, re-running the provisioner
Left alone; the failure is only logged
Immediately destroyed
Removed from state
explain: Default on_failure=fail taints the resource, forcing replacement so the failed provisioning is retried cleanly. B describes on_failure=continue. C and D invent immediate destruction/removal.

q: A resource has a provisioner with `when = destroy` that deregisters it from a monitoring service. When does this provisioner run?
options: On every apply
Only when the resource is being destroyed — create-time provisioners never run during destroy and vice versa
Before the resource is created
It runs twice: at create and destroy
explain: when=destroy scopes execution to the destroy phase. A ignores the scoping. C inverts it. D doubles it.

q: The team upgrades the AWS provider from 5.x to 6.0 (major version). The plan shows several resources forced to replacement. What is the safest way to proceed?
options: Apply directly in production — provider upgrades are always safe
Delete the lock file and re-init
Review the full plan in a non-production environment first — major provider upgrades can change resource schemas and force replacements
Downgrade the configuration to avoid the plan
explain: Major provider versions may break schemas; the plan must be reviewed where replacement is survivable. A gambles production. B doesn't address schema changes. D avoids the upgrade instead of managing it.

q: A provider panics during apply and Terraform writes a `crash.log`. Where is this file written?
options: To `/tmp`
To the state backend
It is only printed to stderr, never saved
To the current working directory — collect it with the TRACE log for the provider's bug report
explain: crash.log lands in the working directory alongside the run. A invents a temp path. B confuses logs with state. C is false; the file is the point.

q: `terraform validate` passes cleanly, but `terraform apply` fails because an AMI ID doesn't exist in the region. Why didn't validate catch this?
options: Validate is static — it checks configuration consistency without calling any provider APIs, so it can't know the AMI is invalid
Validate has a bug
Validate needs `-json` to check AMI IDs
The configuration was never initialized
explain: Validate never touches the network; only plan/apply (which refresh and call APIs) can catch real-world invalid values. B blames the tool. C invents a flag. D would fail validate itself.

q: A legacy configuration uses `null_resource` with `triggers = { ami = var.ami_id }` to re-run a script when the AMI changes. What happens when `var.ami_id` changes?
options: Nothing — triggers are informational
The null_resource is replaced, re-running its provisioners — the legacy pattern `terraform_data` with `triggers_replace` now replaces
The AMI is updated in place
Terraform errors — null_resource is removed
explain: Changed triggers force replacement of the placeholder, re-running provisioners — exactly the pattern terraform_data modernizes (built-in, no null provider needed). A ignores triggers. C is wrong; null_resource manages nothing. D is false; it's legacy, not removed.

q: A `when = destroy` provisioner deregisters a server from an external inventory, and the deregistration API is flaky. The team sets `on_failure = continue` on it. What happens if it fails during `terraform destroy`?
options: The destroy fails and the resource is tainted
Terraform retries until it succeeds
Destroy continues — the failure is logged as a warning instead of failing the run
The provisioner is skipped entirely
explain: on_failure=continue downgrades the failure to a warning so teardown isn't blocked by a non-critical hook. A describes the default fail behavior. B invents retries. D is wrong; it still runs.

q: After a console hotfix changed a database's instance class, `terraform output db_class` still shows the old value. Why?
options: Outputs query the cloud provider live and it is caching
The output block is misconfigured
A re-apply is required to update outputs
Outputs are read from state — a refresh (next plan/apply or refresh-only) updates them; the output was stale, not wrong
explain: Outputs render recorded state, so out-of-band changes leave them stale until refresh. A is false; outputs never call APIs. B invents misconfiguration. C overstates — refresh suffices.

q: An apply fails with `provider produced inconsistent result after apply`. The configuration is unchanged from last week's successful run. What does this error most likely indicate?
options: A provider bug — the provider's read-after-write disagrees with its own plan; capture TRACE logs and crash.log for a provider bug report
A syntax error in the configuration
State file corruption
Normal drift
explain: Inconsistent-result-after-apply is the signature of a provider-side bug, not config. B would fail validate/plan. C presents differently (serial/parse errors). D appears in the drift section, not as an error.

q: A team adds a third-party security scanner as an HCP Terraform run task. They want it to evaluate the planned changes after the plan finishes but before anyone can apply. Which run task stage is this?
options: Pre-plan
Post-apply
Post-plan — runs after plan completion, gating the apply decision
Pre-apply only
explain: Post-plan is the stage between plan and apply — the scanner sees the full diff before the apply decision. A runs before planning. B is after the fact. D is a different, narrower hook.

q: A Sentinel policy set is enforced as soft-mandatory and flags a run. Who can let the run proceed?
options: No one — the run is dead
Anyone on the team
Only organization owners
Users with override permission can approve through a soft-mandatory failure; hard-mandatory failures cannot be overridden by anyone
explain: Soft-mandatory is overridable with permission; hard-mandatory is absolute; advisory only warns. A confuses soft with hard. B ignores the permission requirement. C over-restricts.

q: A workspace defines `region` as both a Terraform variable and an environment variable. Is this a conflict?
options: No — Terraform variables and environment variables are separate namespaces in HCP Terraform; both can exist
Yes — Terraform errors on the duplicate name
Yes — the environment variable silently overwrites the Terraform one
Only one of them can be marked sensitive
explain: The two categories are distinct inputs (TF_VAR_* vs env), so identical names coexist. B invents an error. C invents shadowing across namespaces. D invents a restriction.

q: A platform team wants HCP Terraform organizations, workspaces, variables, and policies themselves defined in Terraform code. Which provider does this?
options: `hashicorp/aws`
The `tfe` provider — it manages HCP Terraform/TFE resources as code
The `terraform` provider
No provider exists; only the UI and raw API work
explain: The tfe provider is the as-code interface to the platform itself. A manages AWS. C doesn't exist. D ignores the provider.

q: Workspace A exposes outputs that every current and future workspace in the organization should be able to read via `terraform_remote_state`. Which setting enables this?
options: Listing each workspace by name
Making workspace A's state public
Global remote state sharing on workspace A — shares with all workspaces, present and future
Copying the outputs into a variable set
explain: Global sharing covers all workspaces including future ones; specific-sharing needs per-workspace grants. A doesn't scale to future workspaces. B isn't a thing — state is never public. D duplicates data instead of sharing.

q: A developer with access to a no-code HCP Terraform workspace wants to edit its `main.tf` to add a resource. What happens?
options: The edit is allowed — no-code is just a UI theme
They can fork the module from the workspace
The CLI can push code changes to it
Not possible — no-code workspaces expose only the versioned module's input variables; the module source itself is read-only to consumers
explain: No-code provisions from registry modules with variables as the only inputs — that's the guardrail. A, B, and C invent edit paths that don't exist.

q: During a production incident, the platform team wants to freeze all runs in the `prod` workspace without deleting anything. What is the cleanest mechanism?
options: Lock the workspace — locked workspaces queue (not start) new runs until unlocked
Delete the workspace and recreate it later
Disconnect the VCS repository
Stop the HCP Terraform agents
explain: Workspace locking is the built-in freeze: runs queue safely. B destroys state tracking. C breaks the pipeline. D affects agent pools org-wide.

q: A VCS-driven workspace has a change merged to its tracked branch. Does HCP Terraform apply it automatically?
options: Always — merges auto-apply
Only if the workspace has auto-apply enabled; otherwise the run waits for manual confirmation
Never — VCS workspaces are plan-only
Only for CLI-driven workspaces
explain: Auto-apply is a per-workspace setting; without it, runs pause for approval after plan. A ignores the setting. C is false — VCS workspaces apply fine. D inverts the workflow types.

q: An organization enables dynamic provider credentials for AWS. How does a run authenticate to AWS?
options: With long-lived access keys stored in workspace variables
With an IAM user's password in the provider block
HCP Terraform mints short-lived OIDC tokens per run — no static secrets are stored anywhere
Over SSH to the AWS console
explain: Dynamic credentials use workload identity federation: per-run OIDC, zero stored secrets. A and B are the static patterns this replaces. D is nonsense.

q: A script needs HCP Terraform API access to manage teams and organization-level settings across the whole organization. Which token type fits?
options: A team token
A user token
A workspace token
An organization token — scoped to organization-level management
explain: Organization tokens cover org-level resources; team tokens are team-scoped. A is too narrow. B acts as the user. C doesn't exist as an API token type.

q: An engineer saves an AWS secret key as a sensitive workspace variable in HCP Terraform, then tries to view the value in the UI the next day. What happens?
options: The value is shown in plaintext to workspace admins
It cannot be displayed — sensitive variables are write-only; the value can only be overwritten, never read back
The value is emailed to the organization owners
It is shown after re-authenticating
explain: Sensitive variables are write-only by design, so a UI or API breach can't exfiltrate them. A defeats the purpose. C invents an email flow. D invents a reveal flow.

q: An organization wants all newly created workspaces to default to agent execution mode. Where is this default set?
options: It can't be defaulted — every workspace must be set individually
Organization settings — the default execution mode applies to new workspaces
The `cloud` block in each configuration
A `TF_VAR` environment variable
explain: Org settings define the default execution mode for new workspaces. A ignores the setting. C selects workspaces, not modes. D sets variables, not platform defaults.

q: A company runs dev, staging, and production on AWS. Each environment was clicked together in the console and they keep diverging — a setting fixed in staging never makes it to prod. The platform team rewrites all three environments in Terraform using one shared configuration with per-environment variable files. Which IaC advantage does this design deliver?
options: Environment parity — the same versioned code builds every stage, so differences are explicit variable values instead of accidental drift
Faster instance boot times in production
Automatic failover between environments
Elimination of all variable files
explain: One shared configuration parameterized per environment means every stage is built from identical logic; the only differences are declared variable values, which kills the 'works in staging, breaks in prod' class of incidents. B invents a performance gain. C confuses environments with availability zones — Terraform doesn't fail over between them. D is backwards: variable files are the mechanism that makes the single configuration work.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team's runbook says the app servers boot in order: database, then API, then workers. The runbook hasn't been updated in a year, but the Terraform configuration — applied weekly — encodes the real dependency order. A new on-call engineer asks which document to trust during an outage. What is the exam-correct answer?
options: The runbook — written documents outrank code
The Terraform configuration — because it is executed regularly, it cannot drift from reality the way an unapplied document can
Neither — both are equally unreliable
The cloud console — it shows the current state
explain: Configuration that is continuously applied is executable documentation: any lie in it gets exposed by the next plan. A stale runbook (A) describes what someone once believed. C is defeatist and false — executed code is verifiable. D shows current state but explains nothing about intended order or relationships.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Developers wait days for ops to provision databases from tickets. The platform team publishes a Terraform module for databases with policy checks that reject unencrypted storage and oversized instances, then lets developers call the module themselves. Which combination of practices makes this safe?
options: Giving every developer admin credentials so tickets are unnecessary
Removing all database options so developers cannot make choices
Self-service provisioning through reviewed modules plus policy-as-code guardrails that enforce the rules automatically
Requiring ops approval on every apply, keeping the ticket queue
explain: Reusable modules package the blessed architecture and policy checks enforce the non-negotiables at plan time, so developers move fast inside a safe envelope. A destroys the security boundary. B confuses guardrails with removing all flexibility — modules still parameterize. D keeps the bottleneck the platform was built to remove.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: An engineer accidentally deletes the production resource group containing 40 resources. The entire environment is defined in Terraform and the state backend is intact. What is the fastest recovery, and why does it work?
options: Restore from the cloud provider's recycle bin, because Terraform cannot recreate deleted resources
Manually recreate each resource in the console, then import them one by one
Restore the state file from backup, which restores the actual infrastructure
Run `terraform apply` — Terraform compares state to reality, sees 40 missing resources, and recreates exactly what was deleted
explain: State still records the desired 40 resources, so the next apply detects the gap between state and reality and rebuilds precisely what vanished — no forensics needed. A is wrong; Terraform recreates anything the configuration declares. B is the slow manual path IaC exists to avoid. C confuses the map for the territory: restoring state without the resources just re-hides the deletion.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A startup's product launch needs a full environment — VPC, databases, queues, monitoring — in two weeks. The infra team estimates six weeks of ticket-driven manual provisioning. The CTO asks how Terraform changes the timeline. What is the honest answer?
options: The environment becomes code that can be reviewed, tested, and applied in minutes — the bottleneck shifts from manual labor to writing correct configuration once
Terraform provisions each resource faster than the cloud API allows
Terraform eliminates the need to design the architecture first
Timelines don't change; Terraform only helps after launch
explain: IaC converts weeks of sequential manual work into a reviewable artifact applied in minutes; the real work — designing it right — happens once, up front, in code. B is false; Terraform calls the same APIs at the same speed. C is backwards — IaC demands the design be explicit. D ignores that provisioning is exactly where IaC pays off first.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team's CI build agents accumulate polluted caches and stale toolchains, causing flaky builds. Reimaging them by hand takes a day each. The team defines the agent image and fleet in Terraform and rebuilds the whole fleet weekly from code. What principle is this?
options: High availability — more agents means fewer flakes
Immutable infrastructure — replace rather than repair, so every agent is a fresh, known-good build
Elasticity — scaling the fleet fixes cache pollution
Blue-green deployment of the CI system
explain: Treating agents as disposable and rebuilding from versioned code guarantees no machine carries forward yesterday's pollution. A is about surviving failures, not cleanliness. C scales capacity but polluted agents stay polluted. D is a release strategy, not a machine-lifecycle philosophy.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A security team must review 50 infrastructure changes a week. Reviewing console screenshots is hopeless. With Terraform, every change arrives as a pull request with a plan diff. Why does the exam consider this a security win?
options: Terraform automatically approves secure changes
Pull requests make the infrastructure encrypted
Every change is reviewable as a precise diff before anything exists — reviewers see exactly which ports, policies, and settings will result
Security teams no longer need to understand cloud services
explain: Plan diffs turn infrastructure review into code review: exact, complete, and pre-creation — the reviewer sees the future, not a screenshot of the past. A invents auto-approval (that's policy-as-code, still human-authored). B confuses review with encryption. D is the dangerous myth — IaC never replaces domain knowledge.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team adopts Terraform and assumes their architecture is now automatically well-designed. Which statement corrects this?
options: Terraform refuses to apply architectures that violate best practices
Only the premium edition of Terraform reviews architectures
Architecture quality is guaranteed once state is stored remotely
Terraform provisions what you declare — it cannot judge whether a single-AZ database or an open security group is a good idea
explain: IaC is an enforcement mechanism for your decisions, not a substitute for judgment — it will faithfully build a bad design at scale. A invents a review feature (policy-as-code can check rules you write, but ships with none). B invents a premium edition. C confuses state storage hygiene with design quality.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company's primary cloud provider suffers a prolonged multi-region outage. Their Terraform configurations use the provider-agnostic workflow with modules abstracting common patterns. What strategic option does this give them that console-built infrastructure would not?
options: The team can retarget the same workflow and patterns at a second provider's resources, rebuilding critical systems where capacity exists
Terraform automatically fails over to another cloud
The state file can be replayed directly into any provider's API
Nothing — Terraform configurations are locked to one provider forever
explain: Provider-specific resources still need rewriting, but the workflow, module structure, and operational knowledge transfer — the team isn't starting from zero with an unfamiliar toolchain. B invents automatic failover. C is false; state is provider-specific. D overstates — configurations aren't locked, though resources are provider-specific.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: FinOps cannot tell which team owns which resources, so showback reports are fiction. The platform team adds mandatory Owner and CostCenter tags via a shared Terraform module every team must use. Why does this work where console tagging failed?
options: Terraform tags are invisible to the cloud provider's billing system
Tags become part of the versioned, reviewed configuration — they are enforced at creation time on every resource, not applied as an afterthought
Modules automatically guess the correct cost center
Console tagging works fine; the problem was the billing system
explain: When tagging lives in the shared module, every resource is born tagged and every change is reviewed — compliance is structural, not aspirational. A is false; provider tags flow into cost allocation. C invents guessing. D denies the observed failure.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: After an outage caused by a firewall change, the incident review needs to know exactly what changed, when, who approved it, and what the previous value was. The firewall is managed in Terraform. Which capability answers all four questions from one place?
options: The Terraform state file — it records authors and approvals
The cloud provider's billing records
Git history on the configuration — the commit shows the diff, timestamp, author, reviewers, and the prior value is one revert away
Terraform's plan cache on the engineer's laptop
explain: Version control is the audit trail: diff, blame, timestamp, and review record in one system, with the old value recoverable via history. A is wrong — state records resource attributes, not who approved what. B shows spend, not changes. D invents a plan cache with none of these properties.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company's primary region suffers a total outage. One team's recovery plan is a 40-page runbook of console screenshots; a sister team runs `terraform apply` against their versioned configuration targeting the failover region and is serving traffic in 90 minutes. Which IaC advantage explains the difference?
options: Reproducibility — the environment is declarative, versioned code, so identical infrastructure can be rebuilt in any region from the repository instead of reconstructed from screenshots
Terraform prevents regional outages from happening
Multi-region failover happens automatically once Terraform is adopted
State backups eliminate the need for a recovery plan
explain: IaC makes environments reproducible artifacts: the same configuration rebuilds the same infrastructure anywhere, which is what turns disaster recovery from archaeology into an apply. B/C credit Terraform with preventing or automating the outage itself — it does neither. D confuses the state file (a mapping) with a recovery plan.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A regulated company requires its change advisory board to approve every production infrastructure change with evidence of exactly what will change. The team submits the Terraform plan output with each change request. Why does the board accept this as evidence?
options: The plan is a complete, computed preview of every addition, change, and destruction — generated from the actual configuration and current state, not a human estimate
The board accepts it because Terraform is a HashiCorp product
Plan output is legally binding on the cloud provider
The plan guarantees the change cannot fail
explain: A plan is derived, not described — Terraform computes the real diff against real state, so reviewers see precisely what will happen. B is an appeal to brand, not evidence. C invents legal force. D overpromises; plans can still fail at apply time.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: The root module requires `hashicorp/random >= 3.0` and a child module requires `hashicorp/random >= 3.2`. A teammate asks which constraint Terraform enforces. What is the answer?
options: Both — Terraform takes the intersection, so the effective requirement is `>= 3.2`
Only the root's — child module constraints are ignored
Only the child's — it overrides the root
Neither — the newest available version is always used
explain: Provider requirements from every module in the configuration combine; the effective constraint is the intersection of all declarations. B/C invent override rules that don't exist. D ignores the constraints entirely.

q: The lock file records provider version 5.9.0, but the registry has since yanked 5.9.0. A fresh `terraform init` fails trying to download it. What is the correct fix?
options: Edit the version number directly in `.terraform.lock.hcl`
Run `terraform init -upgrade` to re-resolve to the newest allowed version and rewrite the lock file
Delete the `required_providers` block so any version is allowed
Keep retrying init until the registry restores the version
explain: `-upgrade` re-resolves within the constraints and records a downloadable version. A is wrong — hand-editing breaks the recorded hashes and init will reject it. C removes the constraint but the lock file still pins the yanked version. D waits on something that won't happen; yanked means withdrawn.

q: A CI job runs `terraform init -lockfile=readonly`. During init, Terraform determines the lock file would need a new entry. What happens?
options: Init updates the lock file anyway; the flag is only a warning
Init skips provider installation entirely
Init fails with an error instead of updating the lock file — the pipeline surfaces the drift rather than silently changing pinned versions
The flag is invalid; init has no such option
explain: `-lockfile=readonly` makes lock-file changes a hard error, which is exactly what CI wants: reproducible builds, with version changes made deliberately by engineers. A inverts the flag's meaning. B confuses it with `-get=false`. D is false; the flag exists.

q: Every CI run re-downloads provider plugins. The team wants one shared plugin cache on each runner. Where is `plugin_cache_dir` configured?
options: In the `terraform` block of each configuration
In `terraform.tfvars`
As an argument to the `provider` block
In the Terraform CLI configuration file (`terraform.rc` / `.terraformrc`), selectable via the `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE` environment variable
explain: The plugin cache is a CLI-level concern, configured in the CLI config file — it applies across all configurations on the machine. A is wrong; the terraform block holds version and backend settings, not CLI behavior. B holds variable values. C configures provider behavior, not plugin storage.

q: A team keeps shared backend settings in `backend.hcl`, but each engineer passes their own state key via CLI: `terraform init -backend-config=backend.hcl -backend-config="key=alice.tfstate"`. Both sources set `key`. Which value wins, and why?
options: The CLI value wins — `-backend-config` sources merge in order and the last one takes precedence
The file value wins — files always beat CLI flags
Init fails — duplicate keys across sources are an error
Terraform prompts the engineer to choose
explain: Backend config sources merge with last-wins precedence, so a shared file plus per-run CLI overrides compose predictably. B reverses the precedence. C is false; merging is the designed behavior. D invents prompting.

q: A configuration pins `required_version = "= 1.9.0"`. The CI image is updated to Terraform 1.9.8. What happens on the next run?
options: It runs — patch versions are always compatible
It fails — `=` pins the exact version, so 1.9.8 does not satisfy `= 1.9.0`
Terraform auto-downgrades to 1.9.0
The pin is ignored in CI
explain: `=` is exact; even patch differences are rejected — that's the trade-off of exact pins. A confuses `=` with `~>`. C invents auto-downgrade. D is false.

q: A configuration uses `provider::aws::arn_parse(...)` but manages zero AWS resources — only the function. The engineer omits the AWS provider from `required_providers`, reasoning no resources means no provider. What happens at init?
options: It works — functions are built into the Terraform CLI
It works — Terraform downloads the provider on first function call
Init fails — provider-defined functions are dispatched to the provider plugin, so the provider must be declared and installed even with no resources
Init succeeds but the function returns null
explain: `provider::` functions execute inside the provider's plugin process, so Terraform must install that exact provider — declaration isn't optional just because no resources exist. A is wrong; only the handful of built-in functions ship with the CLI. B invents lazy downloading. D invents a silent null.

q: The AWS provider block sets no credentials. The shell exports `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, and `~/.aws/credentials` also has a `[default]` profile. Which credentials does Terraform use?
options: The shared credentials file — files always win over environment
It fails — exactly one source must be present
It merges both sets of keys together
The environment variables — the provider's credential chain prefers explicit static/env credentials over the shared credentials file
explain: The AWS provider follows the standard chain: explicit provider arguments first, then environment variables, then shared config/credentials files — so the exported variables win. A reverses the precedence. B is false; multiple sources are normal. C is nonsense — credentials aren't merged.

q: A configuration declares two AWS provider blocks, both with aliases (`us` and `eu`), and no unaliased default block. A resource sets no `provider` argument. What happens?
options: Terraform uses an implicit empty default provider configuration — the plan typically fails asking for a region, because the aliases are never selected automatically
Terraform picks the first aliased provider automatically
Terraform requires every resource to set an explicit provider argument
Init fails — a default provider block is mandatory
explain: Resources without a provider argument always bind to the default (unaliased) configuration, which Terraform synthesizes as empty when none is declared — aliased providers are opt-in only. B is the trap: aliases are never chosen implicitly. C is false; the default binding exists precisely so most resources need no argument. D is false; init succeeds.

q: An engineer widens a provider version constraint in `required_providers` and runs `terraform plan` without re-running init. What happens?
options: Plan automatically re-resolves providers and continues
The command fails and tells the engineer to run `terraform init` — the installed plugins and lock file no longer match the declared requirements
Plan uses the old locked version with a warning
Nothing — constraints are only checked at apply time
explain: Changing requirements invalidates the working directory's installed state; Terraform refuses to proceed rather than plan against the wrong provider build. A invents auto-re-resolution. C is wrong; Terraform errors instead of silently using stale plugins. D is false — the mismatch is caught before any plan.

q: A team runs `terraform init -upgrade` intending to update only providers. What else changes?
options: Nothing else — `-upgrade` affects providers only
The backend is reconfigured
Modules are also re-resolved to the newest versions allowed by their constraints — `-upgrade` applies to both providers and modules
Variable values are re-read
explain: `-upgrade` means 're-resolve everything selectable': newest allowed provider builds and newest allowed module versions, recorded in the lock file and module manifest. A is the common misconception the flag's docs explicitly contradict. B is wrong; backend config is untouched. D is unrelated — variables are read at plan/apply.

q: A locked-down corporate workstation reaches the internet only through a proxy. `terraform init` fails to reach the registry. Which mechanism lets Terraform use the proxy?
options: A `proxy` argument in the `terraform` block
The `TF_PROXY` environment variable
`proxy = true` in the provider block
Standard `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` / `NO_PROXY` environment variables — Terraform's HTTP client honors them
explain: Terraform uses Go's standard HTTP client, which respects the conventional proxy environment variables — no Terraform-specific setting exists. A/B/C invent settings Terraform doesn't have.

q: After init, an engineer inspects `.terraform/providers/` and finds versioned subdirectories per platform. A teammate asks whether these should be committed so nobody re-downloads. What is the correct response?
options: Yes — committing them is the only way to pin provider versions
No — `.terraform/` is a local working directory (plugins, modules, backend selection); it is gitignored and rebuilt by init, with the lock file providing reproducibility
Yes, but only the linux_amd64 subdirectory
No — providers are downloaded fresh on every plan regardless
explain: The working directory is disposable by design; the lock file pins versions and hashes so every init reproduces the same plugins. A is wrong — pinning is the lock file's job. C is arbitrary. D is false; init reuses installed providers.

q: A CI script runs plain `terraform plan` and checks the exit code to decide whether changes exist. The plan proposes 12 new resources, but the script sees exit code 0 and reports 'no changes'. What is wrong?
options: Without `-detailed-exitcode`, plan exits 0 whether or not changes exist — the script must use `-detailed-exitcode`, where 2 means changes are present
Plan is broken — any proposed change should exit non-zero
The script must parse stderr instead
Exit code 0 means the 12 resources already exist
explain: By default plan signals only success (0) or failure (1); distinguishing 'no changes' from 'changes' requires `-detailed-exitcode`'s three-way contract (0/1/2). B misunderstands the default contract. C is wrong; the signal isn't in stderr. D misreads the output — the plan clearly proposed additions.

q: An engineer builds `tfplan` with Terraform 1.9, then a colleague tries `terraform apply tfplan` with CLI 1.8. What happens?
options: It applies fine — plan files are version-independent
Apply refuses — the plan file records the Terraform version that created it, and an older CLI will not apply a newer plan
Terraform 1.8 silently upgrades itself to 1.9
The plan is converted automatically with a warning
explain: Plan files embed the creator's version because provider schemas and plan semantics can differ across releases; applying with an older CLI is rejected to prevent misinterpretation. A ignores the recorded version. C invents self-upgrading. D invents conversion.

q: A team runs `terraform apply -refresh=false` to skip the slow refresh phase on a huge configuration. The apply then makes a wrong decision about a resource someone changed in the console. What is the exam-correct lesson?
options: `-refresh=false` also skips the plan phase
Refresh is never needed because state is always current
Skipping refresh means Terraform decides from stale state — legitimate for speed on stable configs, but dangerous when reality may have moved
The flag is invalid on apply; it only works with plan
explain: Refresh exists to reconcile state with reality before deciding; disabling it trades accuracy for speed — fine when nothing changes out-of-band, hazardous otherwise. A is false; plan still runs. B denies drift's existence. D is false; the flag is valid on both.

q: A nightly cron runs `terraform plan -refresh-only -out=drift.tfplan` to detect console changes. During the maintenance window, the on-call engineer reviews the drift report and runs `terraform apply drift.tfplan`. What does the apply change?
options: It reconciles the drift by modifying the real infrastructure back to the configured state
It discards the saved plan and runs a fresh refresh
It fails — refresh-only plans are report-only and cannot be applied
It updates the state file to match reality; no infrastructure is created, changed, or destroyed
explain: A refresh-only plan's sole action is reconciling state with reality — applying it writes the refreshed state and touches nothing else. A describes a normal config apply, which fixes drift by changing infrastructure; refresh never modifies infrastructure. B is wrong; apply executes the saved plan, it doesn't re-plan. C is false; refresh-only plans are applicable.

q: An engineer runs `terraform apply`, reviews the plan showing `2 to add`, and types `yes`. While typing, a teammate merges a commit adding a third resource. Does this apply create the third resource?
options: No — the apply executes the plan computed before the prompt; the merged change needs its own plan and apply
Yes — apply always uses the latest configuration
Yes, but only if the merge finishes before `yes` is typed
The apply fails with a merge-conflict error
explain: The confirmation approves a specific computed plan; Terraform doesn't silently re-plan when you type yes. B is the misconception. C invents timing rules. D invents merge conflicts in Terraform.

q: An engineer runs `terraform destroy -target=aws_db_instance.main`. Three app servers reference the database endpoint. What happens?
options: Only the database is destroyed; the app servers keep working
Terraform refuses — destroying a resource that other managed resources depend on would orphan them, so the targeted destroy errors
The database and all three app servers are destroyed
The database is destroyed and the app servers are automatically reconfigured
explain: Dependencies are a safety net even for targeted operations — Terraform won't orphan dependents. A ignores the dependency graph. C is wrong; `-target` limits scope, it doesn't cascade. D invents automatic reconfiguration.

q: An engineer runs `terraform plan -var='tags={Name="web"}'` and gets a parsing error. The same map works in a .tfvars file. What is the most likely cause?
options: `-var` cannot accept maps at all; only .tfvars files can
The variable must be declared `type = string`
Shell quoting mangled the HCL — the inner quotes were consumed by the shell before Terraform saw them, so the fix is quoting that survives the shell
Terraform does not support the `=` sign in `-var` arguments
explain: `-var` values are parsed as HCL, but the shell processes quoting first — a classic layering bug, fixed with single-quote wrapping or careful escaping. A is false; `-var` accepts any HCL value. B is wrong; the type is map. D is false; `-var=name=value` is the documented form.

q: A plan output shows `password = (sensitive value)` for a database resource. A reviewer asks to see the actual value to verify it. What is the correct response?
options: Re-run plan with `-show-sensitive` to reveal it
The value is empty; sensitive means unset
Remove `sensitive = true` temporarily to check, then re-add it
The value is intentionally redacted everywhere in CLI output because the variable or provider schema marks it sensitive — verify it at the source, not in the plan
explain: Sensitivity is a display contract: Terraform hides the value in all human-readable output to keep it out of logs and screens. A invents a flag that doesn't exist. B confuses redaction with emptiness. C is the risky workaround the feature exists to prevent — and it would leak into shell history.

q: A script runs `terraform output -json` to feed values to a deployment tool. One output is marked sensitive. What does the JSON contain, and what is the implication?
options: The raw sensitive value in plaintext — `-json` bypasses CLI redaction, so the pipeline must treat that output as a secret
The string `"(sensitive value)"` — redaction applies to JSON too
Sensitive outputs are omitted from `-json` entirely
The command fails unless the output is marked non-sensitive
explain: Redaction is a UI courtesy, not encryption — machine-readable output carries real values, which is why piping `output -json` into logs is a classic secret leak. B is the dangerous assumption. C is false; they're included. D invents a failure.
