q: An engineer runs `terraform plan -target=aws_instance.web -out=web.tfplan`, reviews it, then runs plain `terraform apply` (without the file) and approves. What gets applied?
options: Only aws_instance.web — the target persists for the session
Everything the configuration declares — the `-target` limit applied only to that plan invocation; a fresh apply without arguments plans and applies all resources
Nothing — apply requires the plan file
Only aws_instance.web and its dependencies
explain: Targeting is per-command, not sticky — the second command computed a brand-new full plan. Engineers get burned assuming the earlier `-target` carries over. A invents session persistence. C is false; apply without a file is normal. D describes what the targeted plan contained, not what the fresh apply did.

q: A compliance policy requires every production apply (local backend) to archive the pre-apply state snapshot as `/archives/state-20261018-0900.tfstate` instead of the default `terraform.tfstate.backup` beside the working directory. How does the release engineer satisfy this?
options: Pass `-backup=/archives/state-20261018-0900.tfstate` on the apply command — `-backup` overrides where the pre-apply snapshot is written
Pass `-state=/archives/state-20261018-0900.tfstate` so the apply writes its snapshot there
Move `terraform.tfstate` into /archives before each apply
Set the archive path in the `terraform` block's `backup` argument
explain: `-backup` sets the destination of the pre-apply state snapshot; the default is `terraform.tfstate.backup` next to the state. B is the classic trap — `-state` selects which state file the command USES, not where it backs up. C would break the run by hiding the active state. D invents a terraform-block argument that doesn't exist.

q: A team reviews `tfplan`, then the release engineer runs `terraform apply` without naming the file and types yes. A teammate says the reviewed plan is what got applied. Is that correct?
options: Yes — apply automatically finds the most recent plan file
Yes — the review locks the plan into the state
No — apply fails unless a plan file is named
No — without the filename, apply computes a fresh plan at that moment; the reviewed tfplan file was never used
explain: The saved plan only governs the run when passed explicitly (`terraform apply tfplan`); otherwise Terraform re-plans, and anything changed since the review is included. A invents auto-discovery. B invents review-locking. C is false; fileless apply is standard.

q: A team changes the backend block from `backend "s3"` to `backend "azurerm"` and runs plain `terraform init`. What happens?
options: Init silently switches backends and copies the state
Init succeeds; the backend change takes effect on the next plan
Init errors — changing the backend type requires `-reconfigure` (discard the old backend link) or `-migrate-state` (copy state to the new backend)
The s3 backend continues to be used with a warning
explain: Terraform refuses to guess what should happen to existing state when the backend type changes — the engineer must explicitly choose reconfigure or migrate. A invents silent migration. B is false; init handles backend setup, not plan. D is wrong; the mismatch is a hard error.

q: A configuration sets `for_each = toset(aws_instance.web[*].id)` to create one monitor per instance. `terraform plan` fails. What is the fundamental problem?
options: for_each keys must be known during plan, but instance IDs don't exist until apply — Terraform cannot build the resource graph from unknown keys
`toset()` cannot be used with `for_each`
Splat expressions are not allowed in `for_each`
Monitors must use count instead
explain: `for_each` determines how many instances exist and their addresses, which must be settled before planning — keys derived from not-yet-created resources are unknowable. B is false; `toset` is the standard list-to-set conversion. C is wrong; the splat is fine, the timing isn't. D misses the point — count has the identical known-at-plan requirement.

q: A variable `servers` is a map of server configs, and each config includes a `password` attribute marked sensitive. The configuration sets `for_each = var.servers`. `terraform plan` fails. What is the rule?
options: `for_each` over a map containing sensitive values is fine; the error must be elsewhere

Sensitive values cannot be used in `for_each` — instance keys become part of resource addresses shown in every plan, where they cannot be redacted, so Terraform rejects them; iterate over non-sensitive keys instead
Mark the whole resource block `sensitive = true` instead
Switch to `count` — sensitive values are allowed there
explain: Instance addresses appear in all plan and state output; sensitive data in `for_each` keys could not be hidden, so Terraform refuses it outright. A denies the documented limitation. C is wrong — resources take no `sensitive` meta-argument. D doesn't help; the sensitive values still flow into the configuration.

q: A data source may return zero or one subnet. The configuration uses `one(data.aws_subnets.selected.ids)`. When the data source returns no subnets, what does the expression produce?
options: An error — `one()` requires exactly one element
An empty string
`null` — `one()` returns null for an empty list, the single element for a one-element list, and errors on two or more
The expression is skipped
explain: `one()` is the safe unwrapper: null for empty, the element for one, error for many — no conditional needed. A is wrong; emptiness is explicitly allowed. B confuses null with empty string. D invents skipping.

q: A module computes `coalesce(var.ami_id, data.aws_ami.selected.id, "")`. All three arguments are null or empty. What happens?
options: It returns an empty string silently
It returns null silently
It returns the last argument regardless
An error — `coalesce()` requires at least one non-null, non-empty-string argument and fails when everything is empty
explain: `coalesce()` picks the first usable value; with none available it errors rather than silently propagating emptiness downstream. A/B describe silent behavior the function deliberately avoids. C misreads the contract — the last argument is only returned if it's non-empty.

q: An expression reads `try(var.policy.statements[0].effect, var.policy.default_effect, "Allow")`. `var.policy` has no `statements` key but does have `default_effect = "Deny"`. What is the result?
options: "Deny" — `try()` evaluates arguments in order and returns the first one that doesn't produce an error
"Allow" — `try()` skips to the last argument on any failure
An error — the first argument failed
null — `try()` gives up after the first failure
explain: `try()` is ordered fallback: first success wins, so the valid `default_effect` is returned without ever reaching the literal. B wrongly jumps to the end. C/D deny `try()`'s entire purpose — swallowing the error and continuing.

q: A variable `db_name` must match the pattern `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,30}$`. Which validation condition enforces this without a cryptic type error on mismatch?
options: `condition = regex("^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,30}$", var.db_name) != ""`
`condition = can(regex("^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,30}$", var.db_name))` — `can()` converts the regex match failure into a clean false
`condition = var.db_name == "^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,30}$"`
Validation blocks cannot use functions
explain: `regex()` returns the matched string but ERRORS on no match, so wrapping it in `can()` turns 'doesn't match' into false — the idiomatic pattern. A errors before the comparison can run. C compares against the literal pattern text. D is false; functions are the point of conditions.

q: A configuration builds tags with `merge(var.default_tags, var.extra_tags)`. Both maps define `Environment`. Which value wins?
options: `var.default_tags` — earlier arguments win
Terraform errors on conflicting keys
`var.extra_tags` — in `merge()`, later arguments override earlier ones on key conflicts
The keys are combined into a list
explain: `merge()` is last-wins, which is why the convention is defaults first, overrides last. A reverses the precedence. B is false; conflicts are resolved, not rejected. D invents list-combining.

q: A variable holds a list of ports that may contain duplicates: `[80, 443, 80]`. The configuration needs one firewall rule per distinct port with stable addresses. Which `for_each` expression is correct?
options: `for_each = var.ports` — duplicates are handled automatically
`for_each = tolist(toset(var.ports))`
`count = length(var.ports)` with duplicate filtering
`for_each = toset(var.ports)` — the set deduplicates and keys each instance by its own value
explain: `toset()` both satisfies `for_each`'s type requirement and collapses duplicates, with each port as its own stable key. A fails twice: lists are rejected and duplicates would double-create. B converts back to a list, reintroducing the type error. C invents a filtering function (and count gives shifting indexes).

q: A configuration must output one health-check URL per hostname in `var.hostnames`: `https://web-01.example.com/health`, `https://web-02.example.com/health`, and so on. Which expression builds the URL list?
options: `formatlist("https://%s.example.com/health", var.hostnames)`
`format("https://%s.example.com/health", var.hostnames)`
`join("https://%s.example.com/health", var.hostnames)`
`"https://${var.hostnames}/health"`
explain: `formatlist()` applies the format string to EACH element of the list, returning a list — built for exactly this. B is wrong; `format()` takes scalar arguments, not a list. C misuses `join()`, which concatenates with a separator. D interpolates the whole list's HCL representation, not per-host URLs.

q: An output must render the AZ list `["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]` as the single string `"us-east-1a, us-east-1b"`. Which function does this?
options: `split(", ", var.azs)`
`join(", ", var.azs)`
`concat(var.azs)`
String interpolation `"${var.azs}"`
explain: `join()` flattens a list of strings with a separator — the standard list-to-string rendering. A does the reverse (string to list). C merges lists into a list, not a string. D renders the HCL tuple syntax, not a clean string.

q: A configuration reads `lookup(var.instance_types, "prod")` with no default argument, and the map has no `prod` key. What happens?
options: It returns null silently
It returns an empty string
`lookup()` without a default fails on a missing key — only the three-argument form returns a fallback, so this is an error
It returns the first value in the map
explain: Two-argument `lookup()` treats a missing key as an error — the default argument is what makes absence survivable. A/B/D invent silent fallbacks that don't exist.

q: A data source looks up an AMI by a variable `ami_id`. The team wants the run to fail fast with a clear message if `ami_id` is empty, before the provider API is even called. Which construct does this?
options: A `postcondition` on the data source
A `check` block referencing the data source
Variable validation on `ami_id` inside the data source block
A `precondition` block on the data source — it evaluates before the read and fails the run with its error message
explain: Preconditions guard the action itself — evaluated before the data source is read, so a bad input fails fast without an API call. A is wrong; postconditions evaluate AFTER the read. B is wrong; checks run after apply and only warn. C is invalid syntax — validation blocks live on variables, not data sources.

q: A team manages DNS records for services that come and go by name: `api`, `web`, `worker`. Today they use `count` over a list, and removing `web` renumbers `worker`'s address, forcing needless churn. What is the exam-correct fix and principle?
options: Keep count but sort the list alphabetically
Use count with a larger number to leave gaps
`for_each` has the same renumbering problem
Use `for_each` over a set of names — instances keyed by a meaningful identifier keep stable addresses when siblings are added or removed; count is for identical, ordered replicas
explain: `for_each` addresses instances by key, so removing one name leaves the others untouched — count's index addresses are inherently positional. A doesn't help; any removal still shifts positions. B wastes addresses and still shifts. C is false; key-based addressing is exactly what solves it.

q: A module block sets `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"` with no `version` argument. What does `terraform init` install, and what happens on later inits?
options: The newest available version — and it stays pinned to that version in the module manifest until `init -upgrade` re-resolves
Init fails — version is mandatory for registry modules
The newest version on every init, floating freely
The oldest published version
explain: No constraint means 'latest at install time', recorded in `.terraform/modules/modules.json`; subsequent inits reuse the recorded version for reproducibility. B is false; version is recommended, not required. C is wrong — the manifest pins it. D is backwards.

q: A vendor publishes a Terraform module as a plain `.zip` file at `https://example.com/modules/vpc.zip` — no registry, no Git. How can a module block consume it?
options: It can't — Terraform only installs from registries and Git
`source = "https://example.com/modules/vpc.zip"` — Terraform supports generic HTTP(S) URLs serving module archives
Download and unzip it manually into the configuration
`source = "http::https://example.com/modules/vpc.zip"`
explain: The generic HTTP source downloads and unpacks archives directly — registries and VCS are conveniences, not requirements. A ignores the documented generic downloaders. C works but forfeits versioned, repeatable installs. D mangles the syntax; plain `https://` suffices.

q: A configuration sets `for_each = module.network.subnet_ids` where `subnet_ids` is a list output computed from created resources. `terraform plan` fails. Why?
options: Module outputs cannot be used in `for_each` at all
The output must be converted with `tostring()` first
`for_each` keys must be known at plan time, but module outputs from not-yet-applied resources are unknown — Terraform cannot determine the instance set
`for_each` over modules requires count instead
explain: The known-at-plan rule applies to module outputs too: if the values depend on resources being created, the instance keys are unknowable. A is too broad — outputs known at plan (e.g., from data sources or variables) work fine. B is nonsense. D confuses the meta-arguments.

q: A module block for monitoring sets `depends_on = [module.app]`. The monitoring module needs the app's endpoint URL. Does `depends_on` provide it?
options: Yes — `depends_on` implicitly passes all outputs as inputs
Yes, but only for string outputs
No — modules cannot depend on other modules at all
No — `depends_on` only orders operations; data still flows through input variables fed by `module.app`'s outputs
explain: `depends_on` is pure ordering — it says 'after', never 'here is the value'; the endpoint still needs an explicit input wired to `module.app.endpoint`. A invents implicit data flow. B invents a string-only rule. C is false; module `depends_on` is valid.

q: On the public registry, the team sees modules under `hashicorp/`, `terraform-aws-modules/`, and individual usernames. What do these namespaces signal?
options: Provenance tiers — `hashicorp/` is official, partner namespaces like `terraform-aws-modules/` are vetted collaborators, and usernames are community-published with no HashiCorp endorsement
All namespaces are officially maintained by HashiCorp
The namespace determines the module's price
Usernames indicate deprecated modules
explain: The namespace is the trust signal: official, partner, and community tiers tell you who stands behind the code before you run it with your credentials. B erases the distinction the registry exists to provide. C invents pricing. D invents deprecation semantics.

q: A team renames `module "old_vpc"` to `module "vpc"`. Without any other change, plan wants to destroy and recreate 30 resources. How do they record the rename in version control?
options: Run `terraform state mv` once per resource
Add `moved { from = module.old_vpc to = module.vpc }` — the moved block rebinds every resource address under the module without recreation
Rename and accept the recreation; renames always recreate
Use `terraform import` for each of the 30 resources
explain: A single moved block with module addresses rebinds the whole subtree — that's what moved blocks are for. A works but is 30 manual commands outside version control. C is the costly misconception moved blocks exist to prevent. D is far more work for the same result.

q: The root module declares the AWS provider with `source = "hashicorp/aws"`. A child module declares `source = "example.com/custom/aws"` for its own aws provider requirement. What happens at init?
options: The child's source wins for its own resources
Terraform installs both and namespaces them
Init fails — every module in a configuration must agree on a single source address per provider; conflicting sources are an error
The root's source is silently used everywhere
explain: Provider identity includes its source — two sources means two different providers claiming the same name, which Terraform rejects rather than guess. A/B invent per-module provider resolution. D is wrong; there's no silent winner.

q: A child module creates firewall rules with `for_each = var.services` (a map of service name to port). The root needs a map of service name to rule ID. Which output value produces it?
options: `value = [for r in aws_security_group_rule.svc : r.id]`
`value = values(aws_security_group_rule.svc)[*].id`
`value = aws_security_group_rule.svc`
`value = { for name, r in aws_security_group_rule.svc : name => r.id }`
explain: `for_each` resources form a map keyed by service name, so a for-expression rebuilds the name-to-ID map the root needs. A produces a list, losing the service keys. B also yields a list of IDs without keys. C exposes whole resource objects instead of the ID map.

q: A child module at `modules/app` calls a nested module with `source = "../shared/vpc"`. Relative to what is `../shared/vpc` resolved?
options: The module containing the block (`modules/app`) — local sources are always relative to the calling module, never to the shell's working directory
The shell's current working directory
The root module directory
The `.terraform/modules` cache directory
explain: Local module sources resolve against the module that declares them, so nested modules stay portable regardless of where Terraform is invoked. B is the classic mistake — cwd is irrelevant. C is wrong for nested calls. D is the install target, not the resolution base.

q: A team stores versioned module archives in Google Cloud Storage. Which source address form downloads a module from GCS?
options: `source = "https://storage.googleapis.com/BUCKET/modules/vpc.zip"` with no prefix
`source = "gcs::https://www.googleapis.com/storage/v1/BUCKET/modules/vpc.zip"` — the `gcs::` prefix selects the GCS downloader
GCS is not a supported module source
`source = "bucket::BUCKET/modules/vpc.zip"`
explain: Terraform's go-getter style addresses use a double-colon prefix to select the storage backend — `gcs::` for Google Cloud Storage, `s3::` for S3. A omits the required prefix. C is false; GCS is documented. D invents a prefix.

q: A CI job needs to install providers and configure the backend but must NOT install child modules (they're vendored by an earlier step). Which init invocation does this?
options: `terraform init -backend=false`
`terraform init -upgrade=false`
`terraform init -get=false` — skips downloading and installing modules
There is no way to skip module installation
explain: `-get=false` disables module downloading and installation, for workflows that vendor modules themselves. A is wrong — `-backend=false` skips backend config but still installs modules. B is not the flag for this. D is false; `-get=false` exists for exactly this.

q: A child module declares no `provider` blocks and no `required_providers` entry, yet its `aws_instance` resources are created successfully in the root's configured region. A new engineer asks what provider configuration the child's resources used. What is the answer?
options: They implicitly inherit the root module's default provider configurations — no wiring is needed when the child declares none of its own
Terraform prompts for provider credentials at init
They use hardcoded provider defaults compiled into the AWS provider
The child silently skips creating resources that lack a provider block
explain: Provider configurations are inherited from the root by default — a child that declares nothing simply uses the root's default configurations. Explicit wiring (the `providers` map, `configuration_aliases`) is only needed for non-default setups like aliased providers. B invents prompting. C invents compiled-in defaults. D is false; the resources are created normally.

q: An engineer needs to move `aws_instance.web` from the current state file into a different state file at `legacy.tfstate`. Which command does this?
options: `terraform state mv -state-out=legacy.tfstate aws_instance.web aws_instance.web`
`terraform state mv aws_instance.web legacy.tfstate`
Copy the resource block into the other configuration and run apply
`terraform import` in the other configuration
explain: `-state-out` redirects the destination of `state mv` to another state file — the standard cross-state move. B misplaces the path as a resource address. C would recreate the resource. D re-imports from the cloud rather than moving the binding.

q: A configuration manages instances with `for_each = toset(["a", "b"])`. An engineer must import an existing server into the `"a"` instance via the CLI. Which command is correct?
options: `terraform import aws_instance.web i-0abcd1234`
`terraform import 'aws_instance.web["a"]' i-0abcd1234` — the quoted address targets the specific instance
`terraform import aws_instance.web[0] i-0abcd1234`
CLI import cannot target for_each instances
explain: `for_each` instances are addressed by key, so the import target includes `["a"]` — quoted for the shell. A addresses the whole collection, which isn't a valid instance. C uses a count-style index that doesn't exist. D is false; any instance address is importable.

q: A team configures the S3 backend with DynamoDB state locking. They create the lock table with a partition key named `id`. Applies fail to acquire the lock. What is wrong?
options: DynamoDB tables need a sort key as well
The table name must match the bucket name
The partition key must be named `LockID` (string) — the backend looks up lock records by that exact key name
DynamoDB locking requires the table in the same region as the instances
explain: The S3 backend's DynamoDB locking has a hard-coded contract: partition key `LockID` of type string. A is wrong; no sort key is used. B invents a naming rule. D is wrong; the table must be in the backend's region, but that's not the failure here.

q: An S3 backend sets `key = "app/terraform.tfstate"` and the team uses CLI workspaces dev and prod. Where is the DEFAULT workspace's state stored?
options: At `env:/default/app/terraform.tfstate`
The default workspace cannot be used with the S3 backend
At `app/terraform.tfstate/default`
Exactly at `app/terraform.tfstate` — only non-default workspaces get the `env:/<name>/` prefix
explain: The default workspace always uses the bare key; workspace separation prefixes only named workspaces. A wrongly prefixes default. B is false. C invents a suffix layout.

q: Workspace B reads workspace A via `terraform_remote_state`. An engineer tries `data.terraform_remote_state.vpc.aws_vpc.main.id` to reach a resource attribute directly. What happens?
options: An error — remote state exposes only the source workspace's OUTPUTS; resource attributes must be explicitly output first
It works — remote state exposes every resource
It returns null with a warning
It works if both workspaces share a backend
explain: The remote state data source surfaces the outputs map and nothing else — it's an explicit publishing boundary, not full state access. B ignores that boundary. C invents a silent null. D invents a sharing condition.

q: With the local backend, an engineer keeps per-developer state files and must apply using `dev-alice.tfstate` instead of the default `terraform.tfstate`. Which command does this?
options: `terraform apply -backup=dev-alice.tfstate`
`terraform apply -state=dev-alice.tfstate`
Rename the file to terraform.tfstate first — the path is fixed
`terraform workspace select dev-alice`
explain: `-state` overrides the state file path for the command — the local backend's escape hatch for parallel states. A sets the backup path, not the active state. C is unnecessary. D selects a workspace, which with the local backend still maps to fixed paths.

q: A configuration contains `import` blocks for 5 legacy servers with matching resource blocks. The engineer runs `terraform plan`. What does the plan summary show for the servers?
options: Nothing — imports only appear at apply time
`5 to add` — imports look like creations in the plan
`5 to import` — import blocks produce explicit import actions in the plan, previewable before anything is bound
An error — import blocks require `-target`
explain: Import blocks are first-class plan actions: Terraform previews each binding before apply, so surprises surface early. A is wrong; planning is the point. B confuses importing (adopting existing objects) with creating. D invents a flag requirement.

q: Workspace B needs workspace A's outputs, and both live in HCP Terraform. Which `terraform_remote_state` backend configuration reads A's state?
options: `backend = "s3"` with the HCP Terraform state bucket
`backend = "http"` pointing at the HCP Terraform UI
Remote state cannot read HCP Terraform workspaces
`backend = "remote"` with `organization` and `workspaces { name = "workspace-a" }` in config
explain: The remote backend is the native reader for HCP Terraform/Enterprise state, addressing workspaces by organization and name. A is wrong; HCP state isn't in your S3. B invents an HTTP approach. C is false — this is a core integration.

q: An engineer must import an `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment`, whose import ID is a composite like `role-name/policy-arn`. They guess the ID format and the import fails. What is the exam-correct lesson?
options: Import ID formats are defined per resource by the provider — always check the resource's documentation instead of guessing
All import IDs are the resource's name
Composite IDs are never valid for import
Import always uses the Terraform resource address as the ID
explain: Each provider documents the exact ID shape per resource (plain IDs, ARNs, composites) — guessing wastes cycles. B is true only for some resources. C is false; composites are common. D confuses the address (config-side) with the ID (provider-side).

q: A team switches a configuration from the S3 backend to Terraform Cloud and does NOT want the existing state copied — they'll import fresh. Which init flag does this?
options: `terraform init -migrate-state`
`terraform init -reconfigure` — switches backend configuration without migrating state
Plain `terraform init`
Delete the backend block and run apply
explain: `-reconfigure` rewrites the backend link and leaves existing state where it is; `-migrate-state` is the flag that copies state over. A does the opposite of what's wanted. C errors on a backend change. D never reconfigures the backend.

q: An engineer must stop managing one subnet created by a module: `module.vpc.aws_subnet.public[0]`. The resource block stays for the other subnets. Which command removes just that instance from state?
options: `terraform state rm module.vpc.aws_subnet.public`
`terraform destroy -target='module.vpc.aws_subnet.public[0]'`
`terraform state rm 'module.vpc.aws_subnet.public[0]'`
Delete the whole module block
explain: `state rm` accepts a full instance address including module path and index — quoted for the shell. A would remove all three subnets' bindings. B destroys the real subnet instead of unmanaging it. D destroys everything the module manages.

q: With the S3+DynamoDB backend, an apply fails with `ConditionalCheckFailedException` from DynamoDB during lock acquisition. Another apply is visibly running in CI. What does the error mean?
options: The DynamoDB table was deleted
The state file is corrupted
IAM permissions are missing on the S3 bucket
State lock contention — the lock record already exists because another run holds it; wait or confirm it's stale before force-unlocking
explain: The lock is a conditional write on the LockID item — a conditional-check failure means someone else already holds the lock, which is the mechanism working as designed. A/B/C describe different failures with different errors.

q: A database resource has `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }`. An engineer runs `terraform apply -replace=aws_db_instance.main`. In what order does the replacement happen?
options: The new database is created before the old one is destroyed — `-replace` forces the replacement, but lifecycle ordering still governs how it executes
The old database is destroyed first — `-replace` overrides `create_before_destroy`
Both are destroyed, then the new one is created
`-replace` is rejected on resources with `create_before_destroy`
explain: `-replace` only decides THAT a replacement happens; `create_before_destroy` still decides the ORDER — the safety property survives forced replacement. B inverts the guarantee. C describes destroy-before-create. D invents a rejection.

q: A team's runbook script handles tainted instances: it runs `terraform taint aws_instance.web`, applies (the instance is replaced), then unconditionally runs `terraform untaint aws_instance.web` as a cleanup step. The cleanup step fails. Why?
options: Untaint is deprecated and always errors
The script ran untaint before the apply finished
Taint marked the old state object, which the replacement destroyed — there is nothing left to untaint, so the command errors
The new instance inherited the taint and refuses to boot
explain: Taint marks a specific state object; the replacement destroys that object, so untaint has no target — the error is harmless but informative, and the unconditional cleanup step is the bug. A is false; `untaint` is a valid command. B invents a timing problem. D invents taint inheritance; replacements are born untainted.

q: An engineer runs `terraform taint data.aws_ami.ubuntu` hoping to force the AMI lookup to re-run. What happens?
options: The data source is marked tainted and re-read on the next apply
The data source is deleted from state
An error — only managed resources can be tainted; data sources are read fresh on every run by design
All resources using the AMI are tainted instead
explain: Taint is a managed-resource concept (it forces destroy/create); data sources have no lifecycle to force — they're re-read each run anyway. A applies resource semantics to data. B/D invent destructive side effects.

q: A compliance script must execute via a `local-exec` provisioner on EVERY `terraform apply`, even when nothing changed. Which pattern achieves this?
options: A plain provisioner on the resource — provisioners run on every apply
A `null_resource` with no triggers
Set `on_failure = continue` on the provisioner
A `terraform_data` resource with `triggers_replace = { run = timestamp() }` and the provisioner on it — the timestamp changes every run, forcing replacement and re-running the provisioner
explain: Provisioners run only when their resource is created or replaced; `terraform_data` with an always-changing trigger makes every apply a replacement. A is the misconception — unchanged resources don't re-run provisioners. B never re-runs without trigger changes. C only affects failure handling.

q: An engineer runs `terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web`, and the instance is replaced. They immediately run the exact same command again. What happens?
options: Nothing changes — the replacement already happened, so the second run finds a healthy resource and reports no changes
The instance is replaced a second time
Terraform errors — `-replace` can only be used once
The instance is tainted instead
explain: `-replace` is a one-shot instruction for that run, not a persistent mark (that's the taint-vs-replace distinction) — once replaced, there's nothing to replace. B describes taint-like persistence. C invents a usage limit. D confuses the two mechanisms.

q: The team's provider constraint is `~> 5.0` and they need AWS provider 6.0's new features. What is the safe upgrade path?
options: Edit the version in the lock file to 6.0.0 and apply
Widen the constraint to allow 6.x, run `terraform init -upgrade`, review the plan carefully for forced replacements, then apply
Run `terraform apply -upgrade` — providers upgrade during apply
Delete `.terraform/` and run plan — the newest provider is picked automatically
explain: Major versions can change resource schemas and force replacements, so the upgrade is: permit, re-resolve, scrutinize the plan, then apply. A breaks lock-file hashes. C invents an apply flag. D ignores the lock file, which still pins 5.x.

q: An instance must be replaced whenever the content of a rendered `user_data` script changes, but the script is computed in a `terraform_data` resource, not referenced by the instance. Which lifecycle argument wires this?
options: `depends_on = [terraform_data.bootstrap]`
`create_before_destroy = [terraform_data.bootstrap]`
`lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [terraform_data.bootstrap] }` — replacing the trigger resource forces replacement of the instance
Provisioners with `when = destroy`
explain: `replace_triggered_by` declares 'if that resource is replaced, replace me too' — the declarative way to cascade replacement. A only orders creation. B is a boolean, not a reference list. D runs cleanup scripts; it doesn't force replacement.

q: A configuration manages three instances with `count = 3`. Only `aws_instance.web[1]` is corrupted. The engineer runs `terraform apply -replace='aws_instance.web[1]'`. What does the apply do?
options: Replaces all three instances
Replaces `web[1]` and `web[2]`
Errors — `-replace` requires the unindexed resource address
Replaces only `aws_instance.web[1]`; the other two are untouched
explain: `-replace` accepts a full instance address, scoping the forced replacement to exactly that instance. A is the taint-everything misconception. B invents index-range behavior. C is false; indexed addresses are valid `-replace` targets.

q: A `create_before_destroy` replacement fails halfway: the new instance exists but the old one was never destroyed. What does the state contain, and what does the next apply do?
options: The old instance is recorded as a 'deposed' object — the next apply retries the replacement and cleans up the deposed instance
The state is corrupted and must be restored from backup
Both instances are now permanently managed as separate resources
Terraform automatically deletes the new instance
explain: Deposed objects are how Terraform tracks 'replaced but not yet destroyed' — the next run completes the sequence instead of leaving orphans. B overreacts; this is a designed state, not corruption. C is wrong; deposed objects aren't addressable resources. D invents rollback.

q: A team is refactoring legacy infrastructure into modules AND bringing unmanaged resources under Terraform at the same time. They write `import` blocks for the legacy IDs and `moved` blocks mapping old addresses to new module addresses. What does a single plan/apply accomplish?
options: An error — `import` and `moved` blocks cannot be combined
Both operations in one run — imports bind the real objects to the old addresses, and moved blocks rebind those addresses into the module structure, with no recreation
The resources are imported but then recreated in the modules
The `moved` blocks are ignored when `import` blocks are present
explain: The two features compose: import establishes state bindings, moved rewrites addresses — together they absorb legacy infrastructure directly into a refactored module layout. A invents an incompatibility. C defeats the purpose of both blocks. D invents precedence.

q: A `remote-exec` provisioner must reach an instance in a private subnet through a jump host. The connection block sets host, user, and private_key, but connections time out. What is missing?
options: A `local-exec` provisioner instead
The instance's public IP — private instances can't use provisioners
`bastion_host` (plus bastion credentials) — the connection block needs the jump host's address to tunnel through it
`when = destroy` on the provisioner
explain: Reaching private subnets requires an explicit bastion/jump configuration in the connection block — Terraform won't discover the jump host. A changes where the script runs, not how SSH routes. B is false; bastion tunneling is the documented pattern. D is unrelated to connectivity.

q: A database with `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` must actually be decommissioned — the protection has served its purpose. What is the correct sequence?
options: Run `terraform destroy -force` to override it
Delete the resource block — removal from configuration overrides `prevent_destroy`
Hand-delete the database in the console, then remove the block
Remove the `prevent_destroy` setting, apply so the state records the change, then destroy — the guard is configuration, so it is lifted in two deliberate steps
explain: `prevent_destroy` is just configuration — removing it and applying updates the guard, and only then can destroy proceed; the two-step sequence is the deliberate 'are you sure'. A invents a `-force` flag. B is wrong; removing the block still proposes destruction, which the guard blocks. C creates unmanaged drift.

q: A workspace sets its Terraform version to `latest`. A new Terraform release ships with a deprecation that affects the configuration. What is the risk?
options: The next run may execute on the new version unannounced — `latest` trades reproducibility for convenience, and version changes should be deliberate
There is no risk — HCP Terraform tests every configuration against new versions first
The workspace is locked to the version from its first run
`latest` only updates patch versions
explain: Pinning versions is how teams get reproducible runs; `latest` lets the platform move underneath you. B invents pre-testing. C describes pinning, the opposite. D invents a patch-only rule.

q: A configuration's `cloud` block selects workspaces by tags (`tags = ["app:payments"]`), and three workspaces match. An engineer runs `terraform plan` locally. How does Terraform choose which workspace to operate on?
options: It plans against all three workspaces at once
Via the `TF_WORKSPACE` environment variable — with tag selection, the operator must disambiguate which matching workspace to use
It picks the first alphabetically
Tag selection only works for applies, not plans
explain: Tags select a SET of workspaces; `TF_WORKSPACE` picks the one for this run — the documented disambiguation mechanism. A is wrong; one run targets one workspace. C invents alphabetical selection. D invents a plan/apply distinction.

q: Workspace B has a run trigger on workspace A. Workspace A completes a speculative plan for a pull request (no apply). Does workspace B get a triggered run?
options: Yes — any completed run triggers downstream workspaces
Yes, but only if the plan had changes
No — run triggers fire after successful APPLIES; plan-only runs don't propagate downstream
No — run triggers only work with CLI-driven runs
explain: Triggers chain completed infrastructure changes — a speculative plan changes nothing, so there's nothing downstream to react to. A ignores the apply requirement. B invents a changes condition. D invents a driver limitation.

q: FinOps wants cost visibility on pull requests before merge. A developer opens a PR against a VCS-driven workspace. Does the speculative plan include a cost estimate?
options: No — estimates only appear on applies
Only if the workspace is pinned to a specific version
Cost estimation requires a manual trigger per PR
Yes — cost estimation runs on speculative plans too, so reviewers see the projected cost impact before anything is applied
explain: Estimates are computed from the plan, and speculative plans are full plans — so cost review happens pre-merge, which is the whole point. A misses the PR use case. B invents a version condition. C invents manual triggering.

q: A team wants policy-as-code in HCP Terraform but has standardized on Open Policy Agent (Rego) instead of Sentinel. What are their options?
options: HCP Terraform supports both Sentinel and OPA policy sets — they can enforce Rego policies natively
Only Sentinel is supported; OPA requires a third-party run task
OPA policies must be rewritten as check blocks
Policy-as-code is not available in HCP Terraform
explain: HCP Terraform's policy framework includes both Sentinel and OPA engines — teams use the language they've standardized on. B is outdated; OPA is natively supported. C confuses config-level checks with platform policy sets. D is false.

q: An organization-level variable set defines `region = "us-east-1"`. A project-level variable set attached to the payments project defines `region = "eu-west-1"`. A workspace in the payments project sets nothing directly. Which value do its runs use?
options: "us-east-1" — organization scope always wins
"eu-west-1" — when variable sets overlap, the more specific scope (project) wins over the broader one (organization)
The run fails — conflicting variable sets are an error
The values are merged
explain: Variable-set precedence goes from most to least specific: workspace, then project, then organization — so the project's value overrides the org default. A reverses the precedence. C is false; overlap is resolved, not rejected. D invents merging of scalar values.

q: A CI job authenticates to the HCP Terraform API with a team token for the `payments-deploy` team. What can the token do?
options: Anything in the organization — team tokens are organization-scoped
Only read workspace state, never trigger runs
Whatever the `payments-deploy` team can do on its workspaces — the token carries the team's permissions, no more and no less
Act as the engineer who created the token
explain: Team tokens are permission-scoped to the team: they inherit exactly the team's access on the team's workspaces. A confuses team tokens with organization tokens. B invents a read-only limit. D describes a user token, not a team token.

q: A company runs Terraform Enterprise at `tfe.example.com`. An engineer connects the CLI using a `cloud` block, but a legacy configuration uses `backend "remote"` with a hostname argument. What is the relationship between the two?
options: They connect to different products and cannot be mixed in one organization
`backend "remote"` only works with Terraform Cloud, not Enterprise
The `cloud` block cannot set a custom hostname
Both connect to HCP Terraform/Enterprise — `backend "remote"` is the legacy spelling, the `cloud` block is the current one
explain: The remote backend was the original HCP Terraform integration; the cloud block is its modern replacement — both speak the same API. A invents product separation. B is false; hostname configures Enterprise. C is false; the cloud block supports custom hostnames for TFE.

q: A platform engineer installs the HCP Terraform agent binary on a hardened runner with no inbound network access. What credential does the agent use to register with HCP Terraform and pick up runs?
options: With agent tokens — tokens minted per agent pool that the agent presents to register and receive work
With the engineers' personal user tokens pasted into config files
Agents need no authentication on private networks
With the organization's AWS access keys
explain: Agent pools issue dedicated agent tokens — scoped credentials for the agent-to-platform channel, rotatable independently of humans. B misuses user tokens. C is false; authentication is always required. D confuses cloud credentials with platform auth.

q: A platform team publishes a no-code module for standard databases. A developer with workspace access but no Terraform experience needs a database. What is their workflow?
options: They must learn HCL — no-code still requires writing configuration
Pick the module version, fill in the declared input variables in the UI, and queue a run — no HCL editing, with the module's code fixed and reviewed
They edit main.tf directly in the workspace
No-code workspaces provision without any runs
explain: No-code workspaces turn approved modules into forms: version selection plus variable inputs, executed as normal runs with full plan/policy/cost stages. A defeats the feature's purpose. C is blocked — no-code workspaces don't expose editable configuration. D is false; runs still execute.

q: A module is listed in the organization's HCP Terraform private registry. An engineer on a different team wants to call it from their workspace. What sharing or permission step is required first?
options: Only workspaces in the same project
Only the workspace that published it
Every workspace in the organization — the private registry is organization-scoped and shared, with usage governed by workspace permissions
Any Terraform user on the internet
explain: The private registry is an org-level catalog — published once, consumable everywhere in the org ('private' means private to the org, not to a workspace). A invents project scoping. B defeats sharing. D confuses private with public.

q: An engineer writes a `cloud` block naming a workspace that doesn't exist yet in the organization, then runs `terraform init`. What happens?
options: Init fails — workspaces must be created in the UI first
Init succeeds but all commands fail until the workspace is created
Terraform uses the default workspace instead
Init creates the workspace — the cloud block's named workspace is provisioned on first init if missing
explain: First init with a cloud block provisions the named workspace automatically — infrastructure-as-code extends to the workspace itself. A is the old manual workflow. B invents a limbo state. C is wrong; no silent fallback.

q: An engineer with production access applies an urgent fix from their laptop with `terraform apply`, bypassing the CI pipeline. The fix works. A month later, nobody can explain why production differs from the main branch. Which IaC discipline was violated?
options: All infrastructure changes must flow through the version-controlled, automated pipeline — direct applies break the guarantee that the repository describes production
Engineers must never have production access under any circumstances
Terraform should be run only from laptops, never from CI
Urgent fixes must be made in the cloud console instead
explain: IaC's GitOps discipline makes the repository the single path to production: every change is committed, reviewed, and applied by automation, so the code always describes reality. B overstates — break-glass access can exist, but changes still go through code. C inverts the practice. D reintroduces untracked console changes, the exact problem IaC solves.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Three product teams each wrote their own S3 bucket configuration; one forgot encryption, another forgot versioning. The platform team publishes one reviewed `secure-bucket` module and requires its use. Which IaC advantage does this demonstrate?
options: Buckets become free when defined in modules
Reusability — best practices are encoded once in a shared module instead of reimplemented (and mis-implemented) by every team
Encryption becomes automatic for all Terraform resources
Teams no longer need to understand S3 at all
explain: Reusability is a core IaC advantage: the blessed pattern is written and reviewed once, then consumed everywhere, so every team inherits the guardrails. A is nonsense — modules don't change pricing. C is false; encryption must still be configured (here, inside the module). D is the dangerous myth — IaC never replaces domain knowledge.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company names its servers after Greek gods — `zeus` is hand-tuned and everyone fears rebooting it. After moving to Terraform, servers are numbered, identical, and replaced rather than repaired. What is this shift called?
options: Cattle to pets — servers need individual names to be manageable
Immutable deployment — servers can never be replaced once created
Pets to cattle — infrastructure becomes disposable and replaceable instead of unique and hand-tended
Horizontal scaling — adding more Greek gods
explain: Pets are unique, hand-tended machines; cattle are identical, disposable ones — IaC enables the cattle model because any machine can be rebuilt from code. A reverses the direction. B misdefines immutable infrastructure, which means replace-don't-patch, not never-replace. D confuses naming with scaling.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team's 'IaC' is a Jenkins job that runs ordered AWS CLI commands. After a network timeout mid-run, rerunning the job creates duplicate resources. What is the fundamental gap versus Terraform?
options: The scripts lack desired-state management — Terraform tracks state and converges toward it, so reruns are safe instead of blindly re-executing steps
Jenkins executes shell commands slower than Terraform does
AWS CLI commands cannot create real resources
There is no gap; the Jenkins job is equivalent IaC
explain: The missing piece is the state model: Terraform compares desired, known, and actual state and converges, making reruns idempotent. Imperative scripts just re-execute steps, so partial failures duplicate work. B is irrelevant. C is false. D denies the distinction the exam tests — automation alone is not IaC.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: An insurer asks for proof that every production database is encrypted. The team points to the Terraform configuration: all databases come from one reviewed module with encryption hardcoded, and plan output confirms it. Why does the auditor accept this over console screenshots?
options: Terraform encrypts all databases automatically
Screenshots are illegal as audit evidence
The insurer trusts HashiCorp as a brand
The configuration is the enforced source of truth — every database is created from the same reviewed code, so the control is structural rather than anecdotal
explain: Code that every database is built from is a structural control: the auditor verifies the rule once in the module instead of sampling screenshots. A is false — encryption must be configured (here, in the module). B overstates; screenshots are weak evidence, not illegal. C is an appeal to brand, not evidence.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team once had monthly 4-hour maintenance windows for manual infrastructure changes. With Terraform in CI, they now ship small infrastructure changes daily. What changed about risk?
options: Risk disappeared entirely — automation cannot fail
Daily changes are inherently riskier than monthly windows
Risk per change dropped — small, reviewable, automated changes are safer than rare big-bang manual windows, and each is revertible via version control
Maintenance windows are required by Terraform
explain: IaC enables continuous delivery of infrastructure: small batches are easier to review, test, and roll back than massive monthly changes. A overpromises — automation can still fail. B inverts the lesson. D invents a Terraform requirement.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Every new AWS account in the company must have CloudTrail enabled, a baseline IAM role, and mandatory tags. The platform team writes one Terraform configuration applied to each new account at creation. Which IaC advantage is this?
options: Terraform creates AWS accounts automatically
Standardized baselines — every account is born compliant because the same versioned code provisions the guardrails, instead of relying on engineers remembering them
Baselines are only possible with Terraform Cloud
New accounts don't need guardrails if engineers are careful
explain: IaC turns organizational policy into executable, versioned baselines — compliance becomes structural rather than a matter of memory. A is false; account creation itself is a separate step. C is false; any Terraform workflow can do this. D denies the observed failure mode that baselines exist to fix.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company hires contractors for a 3-month migration. Instead of granting them console admin, contractors open pull requests and the pipeline plans and applies. Which security property does IaC enable here?
options: Contractors cannot make mistakes if they use Terraform
Pull requests encrypt the infrastructure
The pipeline grants contractors admin automatically
Least privilege — contributors propose changes through reviewed code without standing administrative access to the cloud accounts
explain: Because infrastructure is code, contributors need only repository access; the automation holds the credentials and every change is reviewed. B is nonsense. A overpromises — reviewed code can still be wrong. C inverts the design; the pipeline avoids granting admin.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A regulation requires that the person who writes an infrastructure change cannot be the one who approves its application. How does a Terraform-based pipeline satisfy this?
options: The author opens the pull request; a different reviewer approves it, and only the approved pipeline applies — authorship and application are separated by design
Terraform automatically detects the author's identity and blocks them from applying
Two engineers must type `yes` at the same keyboard
Separation of duties is impossible with IaC
explain: The pipeline separates the roles structurally: authors propose, reviewers approve, automation applies — no single person both writes and ships a change. B invents identity-blocking. C is theater, not control. D is false; IaC pipelines are a textbook way to implement it.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A vendor sells a tool that drives the cloud console's web UI with scripted mouse clicks, marketed as 'IaC'. Why does the exam reject this claim?
options: Only HashiCorp products can be IaC
Mouse clicks are too slow to count as automation
IaC requires declarative, version-controlled desired state with a state model — scripted clicking is still imperative manipulation with no plan, diff, or convergence
The tool would qualify if it clicked faster
explain: IaC is defined by its substance — declarative desired state, version control, a state model, plan/diff, and convergence — not by the mere fact of automation. Scripted UI clicks have none of these. A is brand gatekeeping. B and D mistake speed for the defining property.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team manages two servers that haven't changed in a year and asks whether Terraform is overkill. What is the exam-correct response?
options: Terraform is only for infrastructure that changes daily
The advantages still apply — the servers become versioned, reviewable, reproducible, and auditable, even if changes are rare
Static infrastructure cannot be expressed in Terraform
They should delete the servers instead
explain: IaC's value isn't only change frequency — version control, auditability, disaster recovery, and executable documentation apply to static infrastructure too. A invents a frequency threshold. C is false; Terraform manages static resources fine. D is flippant, not an answer.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A production bug reproduces only in production. The team applies their Terraform configuration to an isolated account, reproduces the bug in 20 minutes, and destroys the clone afterward. Which IaC advantage made this possible?
options: Terraform debugs application code automatically
Production bugs should be debugged directly in production
Cloning production is free of charge
Cheap, faithful reproduction — environments are code, so a production-identical clone is an apply away and teardown is a destroy away
explain: Because environments are defined in code, a production-faithful clone costs minutes of compute instead of weeks of manual rebuild — debugging no longer risks production itself. A invents auto-debugging. B is the risky practice this avoids. C is false; clones are billable, just cheap and temporary.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Five years ago 4 engineers managed 200 resources by hand. Today the same 4 manage 3,000 resources with Terraform and report less toil. Which IaC advantage explains this?
options: Terraform manages infrastructure without any engineers
The 3,000 resources manage themselves
Operational leverage — automation and reuse let a fixed-size team manage an order of magnitude more infrastructure without linear headcount growth
Headcount always shrinks after adopting Terraform
explain: IaC multiplies each engineer's reach: modules, automation, and declarative management absorb scale that manual work cannot. A and B eliminate the engineers, which is false — judgment and design still matter. D overstates; the point is leverage, not layoffs.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Two projects on one workstation need different CLI settings: project Atlas wants a shared plugin cache, project Beacon must never use one. How can each project get its own CLI configuration?
options: Set `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE` per project to point at different CLI config files — the environment variable selects which `terraform.rc` Terraform reads
Add a `cli_config` block to each project's `terraform` block
Pass `--cli-config` to every Terraform command
CLI settings are machine-global and cannot differ per project
explain: `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE` overrides the CLI config file path per invocation, so each project can carry its own settings. B invents a `terraform`-block argument. C invents a CLI flag. D is false — the environment variable exists precisely for per-context configuration.

q: A team develops on Intel Macs, ARM Macs, and Linux CI. They want the committed lock file to carry provider hashes for all three platforms so nobody hits a checksum mismatch. Which command does this?
options: `terraform init -platform=all`
`terraform providers lock -platform=darwin_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64 -platform=linux_amd64` — records hashes for platforms beyond the current machine
Manually copy the `h1:` hashes between lock files
Delete the lock file so every platform resolves independently
explain: `terraform providers lock` fetches and records hashes for additional platforms, so one committed lock file serves every developer machine and CI. A invents an init flag. C breaks hash integrity — hashes must come from the registry. D destroys the reproducibility the lock file provides.

q: A configuration needs the AWS provider 5.x for its legacy resources and 6.x for new ones. An engineer asks whether one configuration can install both major versions. What is the answer?
options: Yes — declare both versions in `required_providers` and Terraform installs each
Yes — aliased provider blocks can each pin a different version
No — a configuration selects exactly one version per provider; all resources share it, which is why major upgrades are planned carefully
No — Terraform only supports one provider per configuration
explain: Provider version selection is per-configuration: one version of each provider serves every resource using it. A invents multi-version installs. B confuses aliases — they select configurations (regions, credentials), not versions. D overstates; many providers are fine, but each resolves to a single version.

q: A developer configures `dev_overrides` for `hashicorp/aws` pointing at a locally built binary, while the CLI config file also defines a `network_mirror` for the same provider. Which source does Terraform use?
options: The network mirror — mirrors always win
It fails — only one installation method may be configured
The public registry, ignoring both
The `dev_overrides` binary — development overrides take precedence over mirrors and the registry, and Terraform prints a warning that overrides are active
explain: `dev_overrides` is the highest-precedence installation method, designed for provider development, and Terraform warns that normal installation is bypassed. A reverses the precedence. B invents mutual exclusivity. C ignores both explicit configurations.

q: An engineer leaves the company. Their laptop's Terraform CLI holds an HCP Terraform API token from `terraform login`. What removes the stored credential?
options: `terraform logout` — deletes the stored API token for the configured hostname
Deleting the `.terraform` directory
Running `terraform login` again with an empty token
Tokens expire automatically when the laptop is closed
explain: `terraform logout` removes the credentials Terraform stored (in `credentials.tfrc.json`) for the hostname. B deletes working-directory data — plugins, modules — not credentials. C invents an empty-token flow. D invents expiry tied to the laptop lid.

q: A corporate TLS-inspecting proxy modifies provider downloads in transit; `terraform init` fails with a checksum mismatch against the lock file. What is the exam-correct response?
options: Delete the hashes from the lock file so init stops checking
Run `terraform init -upgrade` to skip verification
Fix the proxy (allowlist the registry) or use an internal provider mirror — the mismatch proves the bytes differ from the registry's, and bypassing verification defeats supply-chain security
Checksums are advisory; re-run init until it passes
explain: Lock-file hashes are tamper evidence: a mismatch means the downloaded bytes aren't what the registry published — the fix is at the proxy/mirror layer, never at the verification layer. A destroys the protection. B doesn't skip verification. D treats a security signal as noise.

q: A CI job runs `terraform init -upgrade -lockfile=readonly`. What happens?
options: Init upgrades providers and leaves the lock file untouched
Init fails — `-upgrade` must write new selections to the lock file, which `-lockfile=readonly` forbids
The flags cancel out and init behaves normally
Only modules upgrade; providers stay pinned
explain: The flags contradict: `-upgrade` re-resolves versions and must record them, while `-lockfile=readonly` makes any lock change a hard error. A ignores the readonly contract. C invents flag cancellation. D invents a providers/modules split that `-upgrade` doesn't have.

q: A CI system exports `TF_IN_AUTOMATION=true` for all Terraform runs. What changes about Terraform's behavior?
options: All prompts are answered `yes` automatically
Plans are skipped and apply runs directly
Nothing — the variable is ignored
Terraform adjusts its output for automation — it suppresses interactive suggestions like `run terraform apply next` hints, keeping logs machine-friendly
explain: `TF_IN_AUTOMATION` tells Terraform its output goes to logs, not a human — it drops next-step suggestions and similar interactive affordances. A confuses it with `-auto-approve`. B is a dangerous fiction. C is false; the variable is honored.

q: A fresh clone has no lock file. The configuration constrains the AWS provider to `>= 5.0`. Version 6.0.0 was just released. What does `terraform init` install?
options: The newest 5.x — init avoids new major versions automatically
5.0.0 — the minimum satisfying version
6.0.0 — with no lock file, init selects the newest version satisfying the constraint, and `>= 5.0` permits the new major
Init fails — major versions need explicit opt-in
explain: Constraints are the only gate: with no lock file, init picks the newest version the constraints allow, and `>= 5.0` includes 6.0.0. A invents major-version avoidance. B describes minimum-version selection, which isn't Terraform's behavior. D invents an opt-in that doesn't exist — which is exactly why upper bounds matter.

q: Two working directories on one build machine share a single `plugin_cache_dir`. One configuration needs AWS provider 5.x, the other needs 6.x. Will they conflict in the cache?
options: No — cached providers are stored per version, so multiple versions coexist in the same cache directory
Yes — the cache holds only one version per provider
Yes — the second init deletes the first version
Sharing a cache directory is not allowed
explain: The plugin cache is keyed by provider version — different configurations' versions coexist, which is the whole point of sharing it. B and C invent single-version limits. D is false; sharing the cache across working directories is its designed purpose.

q: An engineer exports `TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR=/opt/cache` expecting Terraform to use it as the provider plugin cache. What happens?
options: Terraform uses /opt/cache as the plugin cache
Init fails — the directory must exist first
Init errors — unknown `TF_` variables are rejected
Nothing uses it — no such environment variable exists; the plugin cache is configured only via `plugin_cache_dir` in the CLI config file
explain: This is the trap: there is no `TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` variable — the plugin cache lives in the CLI configuration file (`terraform.rc`), selectable per invocation via `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE`. A assumes the variable exists. B invents directory validation. C invents rejection of unknown variables.

q: A configuration manages only `terraform_data` resources and declares no providers. An engineer wonders what, if anything, `terraform init` installs. What is the answer?
options: Nothing — `terraform_data` needs no provider
The internal `terraform.io/builtin/terraform` provider — `terraform_data` is implemented by a built-in provider that init installs automatically
The `null` provider as a fallback
Init fails — every configuration must declare at least one provider
explain: `terraform_data` is backed by the internal `terraform.io/builtin/terraform` provider, which init installs like any other provider. A misses the implementation detail. C confuses it with `null_resource`'s provider. D is false — init succeeds and installs the built-in provider.

q: After a routine `terraform init -upgrade`, Friday's plan suddenly shows 40 forced replacements nobody expected. What changed, and what is the lesson?
options: The state file was corrupted by the upgrade
The `-upgrade` flag only affects modules, never providers
`-upgrade` re-resolved provider and module versions, and the new versions changed resource schemas — upgrades are deliberate acts, followed by careful plan review before apply
Upgrades are always safe; the plan output is a bug
explain: `-upgrade` changes pinned versions, and new versions can alter resource schemas or force replacements — the surprise replacements are the re-resolved versions at work, which is why upgrades are deliberate and paired with plan scrutiny. A invents state corruption. B contradicts the documented behavior (`-upgrade` covers both). D denies the risk the plan just demonstrated.

q: An engineer emails the `tfplan` file to an external reviewer for a second opinion. What is the exam-correct caution?
options: Plan files can contain sensitive values in plaintext — they must be shared only through secure channels, if at all
Plan files are encrypted by default
Plan files contain no real data, only diff summaries
Emailing plan files is required by compliance
explain: A saved plan embeds the attribute values it will set — including secrets — in plaintext, so it must be handled like a secret itself. B is false; no encryption is applied. C is false; plans carry full proposed values. D invents a compliance mandate.

q: A team runs every change with `-target` 'to keep applies small and safe'. What is the exam-correct caution?
options: `-target` is the recommended daily workflow
Routine targeting bypasses the dependency graph and leaves the configuration partially applied — it is for exceptional situations, not everyday use
`-target` cannot be used with apply
Targeted applies are always faster and safer than full applies
explain: Targeting is an escape hatch for exceptional cases (e.g., recovering one resource); routine use fragments the configuration's state and hides interactions between resources. A inverts the documented guidance. C is false. D overpromises — skipping the graph is what makes it risky.

q: Before Friday's scheduled teardown of the dev environment, the team wants to review exactly what a destroy would do — with no confirmation prompt and no actual destruction. Which command?
options: `terraform destroy -dry-run`
`terraform plan` with no flags
`terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.tfplan` — previews the full destroy as a reviewable saved plan
`terraform show -destroy`
explain: `-destroy` switches the plan into destroy mode, computing the complete teardown as a normal, reviewable plan file. A and D invent flags that don't exist. B plans the ordinary (non-destroy) diff, which shows nothing about teardown.

q: A repository keeps modules in subdirectories. An engineer runs `terraform fmt` in the root; only root files are reformatted. How are the subdirectories included?
options: `terraform fmt --all`
Run fmt separately in each directory — there is no recursive option
fmt always recurses, so the subdirectories must contain no `.tf` files
`terraform fmt -recursive` — formats the configuration files in subdirectories too
explain: `-recursive` extends formatting to subdirectories. A invents a flag. B denies the option that exists. C draws a false conclusion — fmt simply doesn't recurse by default.

q: An engineer exports `TF_VAR_instance_count=5` and also runs `terraform plan -var='instance_count=3'`. Which value does the plan use?
options: `3` — command-line `-var` arguments take precedence over `TF_VAR_` environment variables
`5` — environment variables always win
The run fails — conflicting sources are an error
The variable's default, ignoring both
explain: Variable precedence is strict: `-var` beats `TF_VAR_*`, which beats `.tfvars` files, which beat defaults. B reverses the top two. C is false — precedence resolves conflicts instead of erroring. D ignores both supplied values.

q: Two files sit in the working directory: `a.auto.tfvars` and `z.auto.tfvars`, both setting `region`. Which value wins?
options: `a.auto.tfvars` — earlier alphabetically wins
The run fails — duplicate definitions are an error
`z.auto.tfvars` — multiple `.auto.tfvars` files load in lexical filename order, with later files overriding earlier ones
Neither — `.auto.tfvars` files are ignored when more than one exists
explain: Terraform loads `.auto.tfvars` files in lexical order and merges them last-wins, so `z.auto.tfvars` overrides `a.auto.tfvars`. A reverses the order. B is false — merging is the designed behavior. D is false; all matching files load.

q: A team stores variable values in `terraform.tfvars.json` instead of `terraform.tfvars`. How does Terraform treat this file?
options: It is ignored — only HCL `.tfvars` files auto-load
It is loaded automatically like `terraform.tfvars`, with values expressed in JSON syntax
It must be passed explicitly with `-var-file`
JSON variable files are only for outputs
explain: `terraform.tfvars.json` is a first-class auto-loaded variable file — same precedence as `terraform.tfvars`, just JSON syntax. A denies it. C is unnecessary; explicit `-var-file` is only for non-default names. D invents an outputs-only restriction.

q: CI runs `terraform validate`. The configuration has a deprecation warning but no errors. What is the exit code?
options: 1 — any diagnostic fails validation
2 — warnings use the detailed exit code
Validation cannot produce warnings
0 — warnings don't fail validation; only errors produce a non-zero exit
explain: Validate's exit code reflects errors only — warnings and deprecation notices are informational. A conflates warnings with errors. B borrows exit code 2 from `plan -detailed-exitcode`, which is unrelated. C is false; validators do emit warnings.

q: A team wants `terraform plan` to skip refresh for speed, but the subsequent `terraform apply` to refresh normally. Is this possible?
options: No — refresh settings apply to the whole workflow
No — `-refresh=false` permanently disables refresh
Yes — flags are per-command: `terraform plan -refresh=false` skips refresh for that plan, while a later plain `terraform apply` refreshes as usual
Yes — but only with the remote backend
explain: CLI flags are per-invocation, not sticky — each command decides independently whether to refresh. A invents workflow-scoped settings. B invents permanence. D invents a backend condition that doesn't exist.

q: An engineer runs `terraform plan -destroy -target=aws_instance.web -out=web-destroy.tfplan`. What does the saved plan contain?
options: The destruction of `aws_instance.web` (and anything that must go with it) — `-destroy` and `-target` compose to scope a destroy preview
The destruction of every managed resource
A normal non-destroy plan limited to the instance
An error — `-destroy` and `-target` cannot be combined
explain: The flags compose: `-destroy` selects destroy mode and `-target` scopes it, producing a reviewable teardown plan for just that resource. B ignores `-target`. C ignores `-destroy`. D invents an incompatibility.

q: After `terraform plan`, an engineer checks whether the state file's serial number incremented. What will they find?
options: It incremented — every plan writes state
It incremented only if the plan had changes
It decremented to mark a read
It is unchanged — plan never writes state; only apply (and state commands) modify it
explain: Plan is read-only with respect to state: it refreshes into memory and computes a diff, but the state file (and its serial) only changes on apply or explicit state operations. A and B invent state writes. C is nonsense.

q: An output `db_password` is marked sensitive. An engineer runs `terraform output db_password`. What is displayed?
options: The plaintext password — outputs are always shown
`(sensitive value)` — CLI redaction applies to direct output queries too; the value stays hidden in human-readable display
An error — sensitive outputs cannot be queried
An empty string
explain: Sensitivity is a display contract across all human-readable CLI output — direct queries redact just like plans do. A ignores the marking. C invents a query failure. D confuses redaction with emptiness; the value exists, it's just hidden.

q: Release policy: the plan approved on Tuesday must be exactly what applies on Thursday. Which workflow guarantees this?
options: Re-run `terraform apply` on Thursday and trust it matches
Copy the plan output text into the change ticket
`terraform plan -out=release.tfplan` on Tuesday and `terraform apply release.tfplan` on Thursday — the apply executes the saved plan verbatim
Approve the pull request again on Thursday
explain: The saved plan file is the mechanism: apply executes exactly the approved plan instead of computing a new one. A re-plans, so Tuesday's review may not describe Thursday's reality. B preserves text, not an executable artifact. D re-reviews without pinning what gets applied.

q: A resource uses `for_each = var.servers` (a map). Inside one instance's provisioner, the engineer needs the private IP of the instance keyed `"db"`. Which reference works?
options: `aws_instance.web["db"].private_ip` — instances of a `for_each` resource are addressable by key from anywhere in the configuration
`aws_instance.web.db.private_ip` — keys use dot notation
`each.value["db"].private_ip` — `each` is visible outside the resource
Cross-instance references are impossible with `for_each`
explain: Key-based addresses are global: any instance of a `for_each` resource can be referenced by its key from anywhere. B invents dot-notation for keys. C misuses `each`, which exists only inside the resource or module block being expanded. D is false.

q: A `count = 3` web tier needs a single Elastic IP on the first server. Which argument attaches it?
options: `instance_id = aws_instance.web.id` — the collection has one ID
`instance_id = aws_instance.web[0].id` — index addresses select the first instance
`instance_id = each.value.id` — `each` works in any resource
`instance_id = aws_instance.web[count.index].id` — `count.index` is available everywhere
explain: Count instances are addressed by index, so `[0]` selects the first. A treats the multi-instance collection as a single resource. C misuses `each`, which only exists inside `for_each` blocks. D misuses `count.index`, which only exists inside the resource using `count`.

q: A variable declares `default = null` and `nullable = false`. What happens?
options: It works — null is always an acceptable default
The variable silently becomes required
Terraform raises an error — `nullable = false` forbids null, so a null default contradicts the declaration
Null is converted to an empty string
explain: `nullable = false` means the variable can never be null — declaring a null default contradicts that and Terraform rejects it. A ignores the `nullable` contract. B invents silent rewriting. D invents type coercion that doesn't happen.

q: A team must enforce `var.subnet_count <= length(var.azs)`. They try a `validation` block inside the `subnet_count` variable referencing `var.azs`. What is the exam-correct guidance?
options: It works — validation blocks can reference any variable
Move the validation into the `azs` variable instead
Validation blocks cannot use functions like `length`
Variable validation can only reference the variable being validated — cross-variable rules belong in `check` blocks or resource `precondition`/`postcondition` blocks
explain: Variable validation is deliberately scoped to the variable itself; it cannot see other variables. Cross-variable assertions move to `check` blocks (post-apply warnings) or preconditions/postconditions on resources and outputs. A denies the documented limitation. B doesn't fix the scoping rule. C is false — functions are fully allowed.

q: A `user_data` template must include an extra monitoring line only when `var.env == "prod"`. Which template syntax does this?
options: `%{ if var.env == "prod" }` … `%{ endif }` — template directives conditionally render sections
`${var.env == "prod" ? "line" : ""}` hidden inside a comment
Templates cannot contain conditionals — use two separate files
`#if prod` shell preprocessor directives
explain: String templates support `%{ if }` directives for conditional rendering — the idiomatic way to vary rendered output. B is a hack, not the directive. C is false; templates are built for this. D invents a shell preprocessor.

q: An SSM parameter stores JSON configuration. The configuration needs the `retention_days` field as a number. Which expression extracts it?
options: `data.aws_ssm_parameter.config.retention_days` — parameters expose JSON fields directly
`json(data.aws_ssm_parameter.config.value).retention_days` — the encoder parses JSON
`jsondecode(data.aws_ssm_parameter.config.value).retention_days` — `jsondecode` parses the JSON string into a value
