`yamldecode(data.aws_ssm_parameter.config.value).retention_days`

q: A subnet is `10.0.1.0/24`. The configuration needs the 5th usable host address as a string. Which function call produces it?
options: `cidrsubnet("10.0.1.0/24", 5, 0)` — this carves subnets, not hosts
`cidrhost("10.0.1.0/24", 5)` — returns the host address at the given index within the prefix
String concatenation: `"10.0.1." + 5`

q: A resource was created with `count` as `aws_instance.web[0]`. The team refactors to `for_each` with key `"a"`. How do they preserve the existing instance?
options: Delete and recreate — address changes always recreate
Only `terraform state mv` can do this — moved blocks can't change addressing schemes
Nothing — Terraform detects the rename automatically
`moved { from = aws_instance.web[0] to = aws_instance.web["a"] }` — moved blocks rebind across instance-addressing schemes

q: The team decommissions the `aws_s3_bucket.audit_logs` resource from Terraform but must preserve the log data for 7 years. Which `removed` block does this?
options: `removed { from = aws_s3_bucket.audit_logs }` — the default destroys the bucket
Delete the resource block and let the next apply destroy it

q: An engineer sets `lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [data.aws_ami.ubuntu] }` on an instance. What happens?

q: A `when = destroy` provisioner must deregister the instance from an external inventory using the instance's ID. Which reference provides it?
options: `aws_instance.web.id` — the standard reference works in destroy provisioners

q: A `local-exec` provisioner runs a script that must execute in the module's own directory (where its helper files live). Which argument sets this?
options: `cwd = path.module`
`working_dir = path.module` — the provisioner executes with the module directory as its working directory
`chdir = path.module`

q: A configuration reads a file with `file("${path.cwd}/policy.json")`. The team runs Terraform via `terraform -chdir=envs/prod`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing — `path.cwd` always equals the configuration directory
The run fails — `path.cwd` is deprecated
`path.cwd` is the directory where the CLI was invoked, not the configuration directory — with `-chdir`, the file lookup misses; `path.module` or `path.root` locate configuration files reliably

q: A team wants `terraform init` to upgrade modules to their newest allowed versions WITHOUT touching provider versions. Is there a modules-only upgrade flag?
options: No — `-upgrade` re-resolves both providers and modules together; there is no modules-only (or providers-only) upgrade mode

Yes — `terraform init -get-upgrade`
Modules upgrade automatically on every init

q: A CI lint job needs module code downloaded so it can parse configurations, but it must not configure backends or install providers. Which command fits?
options: `terraform init -get=false` — downloads nothing
`terraform get` — downloads and installs modules without the backend and provider steps of `init`
`terraform plan -get-only`

q: A standalone resource `aws_instance.web` must move into a for_each module instance: `module.pool.aws_instance.web["a"]`. Which moved block does this?
options: `moved { from = aws_instance.web to = module.pool }` — module addresses suffice
It can't be done — moved blocks don't cross module boundaries
`moved { from = aws_instance.web to = module.pool.aws_instance.web["a"] }` — full addresses on both sides, including the instance key

q: A team tags releases as `release-2.4.0` and wonders why the public registry shows no versions of their module. What is wrong?
options: The registry only accepts branches, not tags
Nothing — versions appear after 24 hours
Module versions must be even numbers
The registry publishes versions from Git tags matching semantic versioning (`1.2.0` or `v1.2.0`) — `release-2.4.0` is not recognized

q: A module block sets `source = "~/modules/vpc"`. What happens at init?
options: Init fails — `~` is not expanded; local sources must be relative paths (`./`, `../`) or absolute paths
Terraform expands `~` to the home directory
It works — `~` is the recommended shorthand
The module is downloaded from the registry instead

q: A module block uses `count = 3` and the team wants each of the three module instances to use a different aliased provider. Is this possible?
options: Yes — pass a list of providers to the `providers` map
Yes — `providers` accepts `each.value` for per-instance wiring
Yes — count instances automatically get `aws[0]`, `aws[1]`, `aws[2]`

q: The root calls module `app`, which calls module `db` (a grandchild). Neither declares providers. Which provider configurations do the grandchild's resources use?
options: None — grandchild modules must declare their own providers
The root's default provider configurations — inheritance flows down the whole module tree unless explicitly rebound
The `app` module's providers, which default to empty
Terraform prompts for credentials at init

q: A team vendors a registry module's code into `./modules/vpc` to customize it. What changes about version management?
options: Nothing — `version` keeps working with local paths
Terraform auto-updates the vendored copy
The `version` argument no longer applies — updates become manual file changes; the team owns the code now
The registry keeps updating the local copy

q: A for_each module instance `module.env["dev"]` must be renamed to `module.env["development"]` without recreation. Which moved block?
options: `moved { from = module.env["dev"] to = module.env["development"] }` — instance keys are part of the address and can be rebound
`moved { from = module.env to = module.env }`
Rename the key and accept recreation — keys can't be moved

q: Module block `a` pins the `vpc` module at version `2.0.0`; module block `b` pins it at `3.0.0`. Both are called in one configuration. What happens at init?
options: Init fails — all module blocks must agree on one version

Both blocks silently use 2.0.0

q: A module block manages networking. The whole module must be created only after `aws_instance.db` exists, but nothing in the module references the instance. Which module block argument does this?
options: `depends_on` cannot appear in module blocks
`depends_on = [aws_instance.db]` — module blocks accept `depends_on`, ordering all of the module's resources after the instance
`provider = aws_instance.db`

q: A registry module is pinned `version = ">= 1.0"` with no upper bound. A broken `99.0.0` is published. What does a fresh `terraform init` do?

q: Every command fails with `Error acquiring the state lock`. The team has the lock ID from the error message. How do they identify who holds the stale lock before force-unlocking?

Check CloudTrail for the lock event
Restart the Terraform process to clear it

q: A CI job passes `-lock=false` on every apply to 'avoid lock contention delays'. What is the exam-correct caution?
options: There is no downside — locking is optional overhead
Disabling the lock removes the safeguard against concurrent state writes — two applies can corrupt state; fix the contention instead of disabling the lock
`-lock=false` speeds up applies safely

q: Workspace B reads workspace A's outputs via `terraform_remote_state`. During planning, workspace A has never been applied, so it has no outputs yet. How can B's plan still succeed?
options: It can't — A must be applied first, no exceptions
Delete the data source until A is applied
Set `defaults` in the `terraform_remote_state` block — fallback values are used when the source state has no outputs yet

q: Compliance requires S3-stored state encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key (not the default S3 key). Which backend arguments do this?

State cannot use customer-managed keys
`kms_key_id` alone, without `encrypt`
`encrypt = true` plus `kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:..."` — `encrypt` enables server-side encryption and `kms_key_id` selects SSE-KMS with your key

q: With the local backend, an engineer accidentally deletes `terraform.tfstate` (no backup). The infrastructure still exists. What does the next `terraform plan` propose?

No changes — Terraform remembers the infrastructure independently
To destroy everything
An error — Terraform refuses to run without a state file

q: A team wants to rename the `staging` CLI workspace to `preprod`. Which workflow does this?
options: `terraform workspace rename staging preprod`

q: An S3 backend sets `key = "env:/prod/terraform.tfstate"` literally, expecting the prod workspace's state there. What actually happens?

The paths break — Terraform itself prepends `env:/<workspace>/` for non-default workspaces, so the literal `env:/` in the key double-prefixes and the default workspace writes to a mangled path

q: A team uses the GCS backend and asks what to configure for state locking, since there's no DynamoDB equivalent. What is the answer?

Nothing — the GCS backend provides native state locking; no separate lock resource is needed
Use `-lock=false` on every command

q: A team changes the S3 backend `key` from `app/v1.tfstate` to `app/v2.tfstate` and migrates. What happens to the object at the old key?

Terraform deletes it automatically

The old key keeps receiving writes

q: The state bucket lives in a security account. Engineers authenticate via SSO with short-lived credentials and an IAM profile named `prod-state`. How does the S3 backend use that profile?
options: Backends can't use profiles — credentials must be hardcoded
Set `profile = "prod-state"` in the backend block (or `AWS_PROFILE`) — the backend authenticates with that profile's credentials

q: An engineer runs `terraform state pull` to inspect state, believing the output is encrypted because the S3 backend uses SSE-KMS. What must they understand?

The output stays KMS-encrypted and unreadable

SSE-KMS encrypts values inside the JSON individually

q: A team wants a snapshot of the S3 state file before every apply, without manual `state pull` backups. Which bucket-level feature does this?
options: S3 Replication — copies state to another region per apply
`terraform apply -backup` — works with the S3 backend
DynamoDB point-in-time recovery on the lock table
S3 Versioning — every state write creates a new version, giving a complete history to roll back to
explain: Enabling versioning on the state bucket turns every state write into a retained version — automatic, complete snapshot history. A is cross-region DR, not per-apply history. B is local-backend-only; the S3 backend ignores it. C protects the lock table, not the state.

q: An engineer confuses two flags: `terraform plan -refresh-only` and `terraform apply -refresh=false`. What is the exam-critical distinction?
options: `-refresh-only` changes the plan's MODE (reconcile state with reality, touching no infrastructure); `-refresh=false` skips the refresh PHASE of a normal plan/apply — they do opposite things
They are synonyms
`-refresh-only` destroys infrastructure; `-refresh=false` is safe
Both flags are invalid on modern Terraform
explain: `-refresh-only` is a mode: the plan's only action is updating state to match reality. `-refresh=false` is a phase skip: a normal plan/apply that decides from potentially stale state. B conflates them. C inverts `-refresh-only`'s safety. D denies both documented flags.

q: An engineer runs `terraform taint aws_instance.web` but the address isn't in state (typo). What happens, and which flag changes this?
options: Terraform taints the closest matching resource
It errors — taint requires the address to exist in state; `-allow-missing` makes it succeed silently instead
It creates a tainted placeholder in state
Taint never validates addresses

q: A database replacement uses the default destroy-then-create order (no `create_before_destroy`). The apply destroys the old database, then the creation of the new one fails. What is the state of the world, and what is the recovery?

Terraform automatically restores the old database

explain: Without `create_before_destroy`, replacement is destroy-first — a failed create leaves nothing, and recovery is simply re-applying the configuration. q: A `removed` block successfully unmanaged a resource last week. The team leaves the block in the configuration. What happens on subsequent plans?
options: The resource is destroyed on the next apply
Plan errors — stale `removed` blocks are rejected
The resource is re-imported automatically
Nothing — once the address is gone from state, the block is inert and can be removed from the configuration

q: A configuration contains two moved blocks: `moved { from = aws_instance.a to = aws_instance.b }` and `moved { from = aws_instance.b to = aws_instance.c }`. State currently tracks `aws_instance.a`. What does plan propose?
options: It follows the chain — the resource is rebound from `a` through `b` to `c` with no recreation
An error — moved blocks cannot be chained
Recreation — only single-hop moves are honored
It applies only the first block, ending at `b`
explain: Terraform resolves moved-block chains: consecutive renames compose, so the original address rebinds all the way to the final one without recreation. B invents a chaining ban. C denies multi-hop resolution. D stops the chain arbitrarily.

q: An engineer renames a resource with `terraform state mv`; a reviewer asks why not a `moved` block. What is the substantive difference?
options: There is none — they are identical
`moved` blocks are slower
`state mv` is the only one that works with modules
`moved` blocks are version-controlled configuration — reviewed, repeatable for every teammate; `state mv` is an imperative local command that only fixes the runner's state

q: A team wants every resource in their `app` module protected from destruction, so they add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` to the module block. What happens?
options: All module resources are protected
Terraform errors — `lifecycle` is only valid in resource blocks, not module blocks; the setting must go on each resource (or in the child module's resources)
Only the first resource is protected
The module is never applied
explain: `lifecycle` is a resource-level meta-argument — placing it on a module block is a syntax error. Protection must be declared on the resources themselves. A assumes block-level inheritance. C invents partial application. D invents apply-skipping.

q: An engineer runs `terraform plan -target=aws_instance.web`. The plan also shows changes to the security group the instance references, which was NOT targeted. Why?
options: A bug — untargeted resources must never appear
The security group was implicitly targeted by name similarity
Targeting includes the target's dependencies — Terraform must plan anything the targeted resource depends on to produce a valid plan
The `-target` flag always plans the whole configuration
explain: Targeting scopes the plan but must include dependencies — a plan for the instance is meaningless without the security group it references. A cries bug at designed behavior. B invents name matching. D overstates; targeting does limit scope, dependencies aside.

q: A team sets `-parallelism=1` believing it will force resources to be created in configuration file order. What is wrong?
options: Ordering comes from the dependency graph, not parallelism — `-parallelism=1` only limits how many operations run concurrently; use references or `depends_on` for ordering
Nothing — `-parallelism=1` guarantees file order
`-parallelism` cannot be set below 10
File order always determines creation order

q: An instance has `create_before_destroy = true` and a `when = destroy` provisioner that removes its DNS record. The instance is replaced. When does the DNS removal run?

Never — destroy provisioners are skipped during replacements
On the new instance, after it boots
After the new instance is created, when the old instance is destroyed — the destroy provisioner runs against the old instance at its destruction, using its recorded state data

q: A `local-exec` provisioner must tag each deployment with the active CLI workspace name (dev/staging/prod). Which interpolation provides it?
options: `var.workspace` — Terraform provides this variable automatically
`${terraform.workspace}` — the built-in reference to the current workspace name
`env.WORKSPACE` — provisioners read shell environment directly in interpolation

q: An engineer runs `terraform apply -replace='module.app.aws_instance.web'` where the module declares the resource with `for_each`. What happens?
options: An error — `-replace` requires a single instance address
`-replace` marks the module for tainting instead
Every instance of `aws_instance.web` in the module is replaced — a collection address targets all its instances
Only the first instance is replaced

q: Compliance requires that plan operations run on the company's own machines (data residency), while state must stay centralized in HCP Terraform. Which execution mode fits, and what runs where?

Remote execution — everything runs in HCP Terraform regardless
State is downloaded to the laptop permanently
Local execution mode disables remote state

q: Workspace B (organization `acme`) sets a run trigger on workspace A in organization `partner`. What happens?
options: It works — triggers span organizations
It fails — run triggers connect workspaces within the same organization only
It works if both workspaces are public
Triggers are configured in the CLI, not the UI
explain: Run triggers are an intra-organization mechanism — cross-organization chaining isn't supported. A denies the boundary. C invents a public-workspace exception. D misplaces where triggers are configured.

q: A Sentinel policy must deny any `aws_instance` whose planned `instance_type` isn't in an approved list. Which Sentinel import exposes the planned resource attributes?
options: `tfconfig` — exposes the raw configuration
`tfstate` — exposes the prior state
`tfplan` — exposes the planned changes including proposed attribute values
`tfrun` — exposes resource attributes directly
explain: The `tfplan` import carries the planned new values — what the run intends to set — which is what the policy must inspect. A exposes configuration text, not planned values. B exposes the old state. D carries run metadata, not resource attributes.

q: A policy set is enforced as hard-mandatory and flags a run. A workspace admin asks to override it so the apply can proceed. What is the answer?

Only organization owners can override
Override it with a comment explaining the exception
No one can override — hard-mandatory policies cannot be bypassed; the configuration must be fixed

q: A Sentinel policy set must enforce on production workspaces only, not on dev workspaces. How is it scoped?
options: Attach the policy set to the production project (or specific workspaces) — policy sets scope to projects and workspaces, not just globally

Create a second organization for production
Sentinel cannot be scoped; use two separate policy files instead
explain: Policy sets are attached at organization, project, or workspace scope — production-only enforcement is a scoping choice, not a second organization. B describes only the global option. C is organizational overkill. D denies the documented scoping.

q: A dev workspace should apply automatically whenever its plan succeeds, with no human confirmation. Which workspace setting does this?
options: Remote execution mode
Auto-apply — successful plans proceed to apply without manual approval
Speculative plans
It isn't possible — applies always need confirmation
explain: Auto-apply removes the manual confirmation gate for workspaces where continuous delivery is safe (typically non-production). A controls where runs execute, not approval. C describes PR-time plans that never apply. D is false.

q: A SaaS provisions one workspace per customer: `customer-acme`, `customer-globex`, and 48 more. How does the `cloud` block select them by name pattern?
options: `workspaces { names = ["customer-*"] }` — wildcards are supported
It can't — each workspace needs its own configuration
Tags are the only selection method
`workspaces { prefix = "customer-" }` — prefix selection matches the name pattern, with `TF_WORKSPACE` choosing the active one
explain: The `cloud` block supports prefix-based workspace selection for exactly this fleet pattern; `TF_WORKSPACE` picks the active member per run. A invents wildcard support in `names`. B denies configuration reuse. C ignores the prefix mechanism.

q: A team debates run tasks vs notifications for a security scanner. What is the functional difference?
options: There is none — both only send messages
Notifications can block runs; tasks cannot
Run tasks return pass/fail and can block the run at their stage; notifications only inform humans after events
Run tasks only work with Sentinel
explain: Run tasks are gating integrations — their verdict can stop the run — while notifications are informational webhooks. A conflates them. B reverses the gating direction. D invents a Sentinel-only restriction.

q: An auditor asks for the state of the `prod` workspace as of last Tuesday. How does the team produce it?
options: HCP Terraform retains state versions from every run — download the version timestamped last Tuesday from the workspace's state history
States are overwritten — last Tuesday's is unrecoverable
Reconstruct it from the current plan
Ask HashiCorp support to restore it
explain: Every run snapshots a new state version, and HCP Terraform keeps the history — point-in-time state is downloadable from the UI or API. B denies the versioning. C invents reconstruction. D is unnecessary; it's self-service.

q: Workspace A enables remote state sharing limited to workspace B only. Workspace C configures `terraform_remote_state` against A. What happens?
options: It works — sharing can't be restricted
It works after a delay
Workspace C reads a cached copy
It fails authorization — A shares state exclusively with B, so C's reads are rejected
explain: Remote state sharing is an explicit allowlist — workspaces outside it get authorization failures on read. A denies the scoping feature. B and C invent workarounds that don't exist.

q: An engineer deletes the `prod` workspace in HCP Terraform without destroying first. What happens to the managed infrastructure?
options: It is destroyed automatically
It is orphaned — workspace deletion removes the state and configuration link, but the real resources keep running unmanaged until re-imported or destroyed out-of-band
It is transferred to the `default` workspace
Deletion is blocked until all resources are destroyed
explain: Deleting a workspace is not a destroy — the platform warns that infrastructure is left orphaned and running. A conflates deletion with destruction. C invents a transfer. D is false; HCP warns but permits deletion.

q: A CI job must run the same configuration against the `staging` and `prod` HCP Terraform organizations without editing files. Which mechanism selects the organization per run?
options: Two separate `cloud` blocks in the configuration
`TF_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION` (and `TF_WORKSPACE`) environment variables — they override the `cloud` block's organization per run
It can't be done — the organization is fixed in code
Re-running `terraform init` with a different backend
explain: The `TF_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION` and `TF_WORKSPACE` variables override the `cloud` block per invocation — the standard way to reuse one configuration across organizations. A is invalid (one `cloud` block only). C denies the override. D describes the backend flow, not the cloud integration.

q: A team provisions VMs with Terraform but installs and configures application software through long remote-exec provisioner scripts, and their builds are slow and flaky. Following IaC best practices, what should they change?
options: Move software installation and configuration out of Terraform — bake it into images with a tool like Packer or hand it to a configuration management tool, and treat provisioners as a last resort
Add more provisioner blocks so each software step is retried independently
Replace the provisioners with user_data scripts, which Terraform manages natively as infrastructure
Split the configuration into more workspaces so each provisioner runs in isolation
explain: Terraform's strength is provisioning infrastructure; software configuration belongs in images or config-management tools, and HashiCorp documents provisioners as a last resort because they are imperative, hard to debug, and run outside the plan/apply model. B doubles down on the anti-pattern. C just relocates the same imperative scripts (user_data is still configuration, not provisioning). D changes blast radius, not the layering problem.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A deployment pipeline runs terraform apply on every merge — even merges that only touch README files. The SRE worries each run will duplicate the infrastructure. Why is she wrong?
options: Every apply recreates all resources, so the pipeline will eventually hit cloud quota limits
The state lock taken by the first run permanently blocks all subsequent applies
Terraform caches the first plan and replays it forever, so nothing can ever change
Apply is idempotent — with no configuration change, Terraform finds reality already matching the desired state and the run is a safe no-op
explain: Idempotence is what makes apply safe to re-run: Terraform diffs desired vs actual state and acts only on differences, so a no-change run changes nothing. A describes non-idempotent behavior Terraform doesn't have. B confuses locking, which is held per-operation and released after. C invents plan caching — every run re-plans.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A contractor delivers a 400-line Bash script that creates a VPC, subnets, and route tables in a fixed order with sleep statements between steps. The platform team rewrites it in Terraform instead. What is the fundamental difference in approach?
options: Terraform scripts execute faster because they run steps in parallel
Terraform removes the need for cloud credentials
Declarative vs imperative — Terraform declares the desired end state and derives the ordering itself, while the script prescribes every step in sequence
Bash cannot call cloud APIs, so the script was shelling out to Terraform anyway
explain: The core IaC distinction: declarative configuration describes what should exist and lets Terraform build the dependency graph and ordering; imperative scripts dictate how, step by step, including brittle sleeps and manual ordering. A is a side benefit, not the fundamental difference. B is false — providers still need credentials. D is false — scripts call cloud CLIs/APIs directly all the time.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: On Friday a bad firewall rule change is applied to production. On Monday the team reverts the corresponding commit in git, runs terraform apply, and the old rules are restored. Why does this rollback work?
options: Terraform keeps automatic backups of previous infrastructure snapshots
The state file stores every historical configuration for rollback
Apply --rollback replays the previous state version
Versioned desired state — reverting the code restores the previous declared state, and apply reconciles reality back to it
explain: Because infrastructure is defined as versioned code, git revert restores the prior desired state and a normal apply converges reality to it — rollback is just another forward application of an older declaration. A is wrong — Terraform keeps no infra snapshots. B is wrong — state records the current known reality, not config history. C is wrong — there is no --rollback flag.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Staging works perfectly but production breaks on every deploy, because production was hand-built in the console two years ago and nobody knows its exact makeup. What does IaC prescribe as the durable fix?
options: Run terraform apply on production more frequently until it converges
Give production the same instance types as staging and the drift will resolve
Manage both environments from the same versioned code — one configuration parameterized per environment (workspaces, directories, or variable files) — so every environment is reproducible from code
Copy the staging state file over the production state file
explain: Environment parity through shared, parameterized code is the IaC answer to snowflake environments: the same declaration produces every environment, so staging actually predicts production. D is wrong — state files are environment-specific bindings, not portable definitions. A is wrong — apply can only converge toward what the config declares; it can't discover hand-built prod. B confuses one attribute with the whole environment definition.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A SOC 2 auditor asks for evidence that every production infrastructure change was peer-reviewed and previewed before it was made. The estate is managed with Terraform in version control. What does the team present?
options: The state file's serial numbers, which record reviewer identities
The pull request history showing plan output attached to each change, reviewer approvals, and the corresponding apply logs — the VCS plus plan workflow is the evidence trail
Screenshots of the cloud console taken before and after each change
The audit log that Terraform generates automatically on every run
explain: IaC in VCS makes changes attributable and reviewable by construction: commits, PR reviews, attached plans, and apply logs together prove what changed, who approved it, and what was previewed. A is wrong — state tracks resource bindings, not reviewers. C abandons the IaC workflow for manual evidence. D is wrong — Terraform generates no audit log; the VCS and run history provide it.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: During an incident, an on-call engineer resizes a database instance in the cloud console and forgets to update the Terraform code. A week later the scheduled apply downsizes it back, causing a second outage. What is the lesson?
options: Terraform should have ignored the console change since it wasn't in code
Apply only creates new resources, so the team should have used import first
Manual changes create drift, and the next apply reconciles managed attributes back to code — emergency changes must be codified in the configuration promptly
State locking would have prevented the console change
explain: Drift is the failure mode: Terraform owns the attributes it manages, so the next refresh+apply reverts out-of-band edits. The fix is process — codify emergency changes immediately. A inverts the model — Terraform's job is to enforce the declared state. B is wrong — apply updates and destroys too. D is wrong — state locks serialize Terraform runs; they can't block console actions.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team requires the output of terraform plan to be attached to every infrastructure pull request before merge. What value does this practice provide?
options: Plans apply faster when they have been attached to a pull request
A plan is required before the state file can be locked
Plan output in pull requests replaces the need to ever run apply
Change preview as code review — the plan shows the exact creates, updates, and destroys before anything is touched, so peers review infrastructure changes like code
explain: The plan is a safe, read-only preview of proposed changes, making infra changes reviewable in the same PR workflow as application code. A is nonsense — attachment doesn't affect speed. B confuses locking (which happens during plan/apply execution) with review. C is wrong — the plan proposes; only apply executes.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A new hire understands the company's entire network topology — VPCs, subnets, peering, gateways — in a single day just by reading the .tf files. What IaC property made this possible?
options: Configuration as living documentation — the code is a human-readable, current definition of the infrastructure, unlike tribal knowledge or stale wiki diagrams
Terraform auto-generates architecture diagrams from every configuration
Comments are mandatory in HCL, so every file explains itself
The state file serves as the official network documentation
explain: Because the code is the system of record, reading it reads the infrastructure — it can't go stale the way separate docs do. B is wrong — Terraform doesn't render diagrams natively. C is wrong — comments are optional, not mandatory. D is wrong — state is a JSON binding map for Terraform's use, not human documentation.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team believes Terraform only creates infrastructure, so they delete obsolete resources by hand in the console. What are they misunderstanding?
options: Terraform can only create resources during the very first apply
Terraform manages the full resource lifecycle — removing a resource block from configuration produces a destroy plan, so deletions should also go through code
Destroyed resources are automatically recreated on the next plan
Console deletions are the recommended way to decommission resources
explain: Terraform reconciles the whole lifecycle: create, update, replace, and destroy. Deleting a block declares 'this should not exist,' and apply carries it out — hand-deleting in the console just creates drift. A is wrong — creation happens on any apply. C inverts the model — Terraform recreates only what config declares. D contradicts the IaC workflow entirely.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company runs workloads on both AWS and Azure. Engineers learn one Terraform workflow instead of two cloud-specific toolchains. What makes this possible?
options: Terraform converts AWS resources into Azure equivalents automatically
A single universal provider manages every cloud
Providers abstract each cloud's API behind the same HCL language and the same init/plan/apply workflow
HCL syntax changes per cloud, but the CLI commands stay the same
explain: The provider model is the abstraction: each provider plugin translates the same declarative language and workflow into its cloud's native API calls. A is wrong — no cross-cloud conversion exists. B is wrong — each cloud has its own provider. D is wrong — HCL is consistent; only resource types and arguments differ per provider.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: An admin's script created 50 storage buckets last year. Now she must change the tagging on 10 of them and delete 5, but the script has no record of what it created. What does Terraform have that the script lacks?
options: Faster loops for bulk operations
Recorded state — the state file maps configuration addresses to real remote objects, so plans compute exact diffs instead of blindly re-executing steps
Direct API access that scripts cannot use
Automatic tagging policies
explain: State is the missing ledger: it binds each declared resource to its real-world ID, enabling Terraform to diff desired vs actual and act only on differences. Imperative scripts re-run steps blindly with no memory. A is incidental. C is false — scripts call the same APIs. D is a different feature (policy as code), not the differentiator here.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A startup destroys its entire development environment every night with a scheduled terraform destroy and recreates it each morning with terraform apply. What IaC characteristic makes this economical and safe?
options: Terraform negotiates lower cloud pricing for frequently recreated resources
State files consume the idle capacity, so destroying frees them
Environments are disposable and reproducible — because the whole environment is declared in code, tearing it down and rebuilding it is routine, saving the cost of idle resources
Destroy operations are free while running resources are expensive
explain: Codified environments can be treated as ephemeral: destroy eliminates idle cost, apply rebuilds deterministically — the economic payoff of reproducibility. D is confused — destroy itself isn't the saving; not paying for idle hours is. A is invented — Terraform has no pricing power. B is nonsense — state files are tiny JSON.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A configuration declares `source = "aws"` inside required_providers and terraform init fails to find the provider. What is wrong?
options: Provider plugins are built into the CLI, so required_providers is unnecessary
The source address must be a full HOSTNAME/NAMESPACE/TYPE address like "hashicorp/aws" (hostname defaults to registry.terraform.io) — a bare "aws" is not a valid source
The source argument belongs in the provider block, not required_providers
Init cannot install providers; they must be downloaded manually
explain: Provider source addresses have the form [<HOSTNAME>/]<NAMESPACE>/<TYPE>; "hashicorp/aws" resolves via registry.terraform.io. A bare "aws" matches no address. A is wrong — providers are separate plugins (only terraform.io built-in providers are special-cased, and explicit source is still best practice). C is wrong — source lives in required_providers. D is wrong — init installs providers automatically.

q: A team needs the ID of an existing, manually created VPC to place new subnets in it. They must not let Terraform modify or delete that VPC. Which block is correct?
options: A resource block for the VPC, since Terraform needs to manage anything it references
An import block to take over the VPC, then a resource block
A data source (data "aws_vpc") — it reads the existing VPC without managing its lifecycle
A variable holding a hardcoded VPC ID copied from the console
explain: Data sources read existing infrastructure without adopting management of it — the defining resource-vs-data-source split: resources are managed, data sources are read-only. A would make Terraform own (and potentially replace) the VPC. B is for bringing resources under management — the opposite of the requirement. D works but is brittle; the data source looks it up dynamically by filter.

q: A configuration creates an aws_db_instance and a data source reads that same instance's endpoint. During plan, the data source shows "(known after apply)" instead of failing. Why?
options: Data sources are always read during apply, never during plan
The plan failed silently and Terraform is guessing
depends_on forces all data sources to wait until apply
When a data source depends on values that aren't known until apply, Terraform defers reading it until apply instead of failing the plan
explain: Terraform reads data sources during plan when possible, but if their configuration depends on not-yet-known values (like a resource being created in the same apply), the read is deferred to apply — that's the documented behavior, not an error. A is wrong — plan-time reads are the norm. B is wrong — nothing failed. C is wrong — depends_on can force ordering, but the deferral here comes from unknown values, not depends_on.

q: A configuration uses count = 3 on aws_instance.web. The engineer needs the ID of the second instance for an output. What is its correct address?
options: aws_instance.web[1] — count instances are zero-indexed
aws_instance.web[2], because counting starts at 1
aws_instance.web.1 in dotted notation
aws_instance.web["1"] with a string index
explain: Count-based instances are addressed with zero-based numeric indices: [0], [1], [2] — so the second is [1]. B assumes one-based indexing, which HCL doesn't use. C invents a dotted syntax that doesn't exist. D uses a string index, which is the for_each style, not count.

q: required_providers constrains the AWS provider to ">= 4.0, < 6.0". Versions 4.67, 5.12, 5.90, and 6.1 exist in the registry. Which does terraform init install?
options: 6.1, because init always prefers the absolute latest
It prompts the engineer to choose interactively
4.67, the oldest version satisfying the constraint, for maximum stability
The newest available version within the constraint — 5.90
explain: Init selects the newest version satisfying all constraints (here, the 5.x line's latest: 5.90); 6.1 is excluded by < 6.0. C is wrong — Terraform never prefers oldest. A ignores the constraint. B is wrong — init is non-interactive about version selection.

q: A terraform block contains `required_version = ">= 1.5"`. A teammate claims this pins the AWS provider to at least 4.x. What does required_version actually constrain?
options: The provider plugin versions used by the configuration
The module versions downloaded by init
The Terraform CLI/Core version itself — provider versions are constrained separately in required_providers
The state file format version
explain: required_version gates which Terraform CLI versions may work on the configuration (failing fast on too-old/new binaries); it says nothing about providers. The teammate confuses it with required_providers version constraints (A). B is wrong — module versions are pinned in module blocks. D is wrong — state format is managed by Terraform automatically.

q: An engineer clones a Terraform repository fresh and needs the AWS provider plugin and the child modules downloaded before planning. Which single command does this?
options: terraform plan, which downloads everything it needs automatically
terraform get, which installs both providers and modules
terraform validate, which initializes the working directory
terraform init — it initializes the backend, installs provider plugins, and downloads modules
explain: Init is the setup command: backend initialization, provider installation, and module installation. A is wrong — plan assumes an initialized directory. B is wrong — get handles only modules, not providers (and init covers it). C is wrong — validate checks configuration validity; it doesn't install anything.

q: When terraform apply runs, which component actually translates the HCL resource declarations into AWS API calls that create real objects?
options: The provider plugin — Terraform core builds the plan and orchestrates, while each provider implements resource CRUD against its cloud's APIs
The state file, which replays recorded API calls
HCP Terraform, which proxies all cloud operations
The provisioner subsystem, which shells out to the AWS CLI
explain: The architecture split: core handles configuration language, graph, and state; provider plugins own the API translation for their platform's resources. B is wrong — state records results, never actions. C is wrong — HCP runs the same core+providers remotely; it isn't a translation layer. D is wrong — provisioners run scripts on/near resources; they don't implement resource CRUD.

q: Resources must be created in both us-east-1 and eu-west-1 in one configuration. How should the provider be configured?
options: Install Terraform twice, once per region
Declare two aws provider blocks — a default one and one with alias = "west" — and select the non-default per resource with the provider meta-argument (provider = aws.west)
Use one provider block and set the region per resource with a region argument
Create two state files; the region follows the state file
explain: Multiple provider configurations use aliases; resources opt into the non-default via the provider meta-argument. This is the documented multi-region pattern. A is absurd — regions aren't CLI installs. C is wrong — region is a provider-level setting, not per-resource. D confuses state isolation with provider configuration.

q: In `aws_instance.web.id`, the engineer set ami in the resource block but never set id anywhere. What is the difference between ami and id here?
options: There is none — both are configurable values
ami is set in variables while id is set in the resource block
Arguments (like ami) declare desired configuration; attributes (like id) are read-only values the provider exports after creating the resource, referenced but never assigned
id is an argument that Terraform auto-fills from the AMI
explain: The argument/attribute split: you write arguments to express intent; the provider returns attributes (IDs, endpoints, ARNs) that you can reference elsewhere but cannot set. A erases a foundational distinction. B invents a variables-vs-block split. D reverses the direction — nothing auto-fills arguments from attributes.

q: A team wants every deploy to use the newest patched Ubuntu AMI without editing configuration files each month. What is the right approach?
options: Hardcode the current AMI ID in a variable default and update it monthly
Declare a resource block for the AMI so Terraform manages its lifecycle
Store AMI IDs in the state file and let refresh update them
A data source (data "aws_ami" with filters and most_recent = true) — it resolves the latest matching AMI dynamically at plan time
explain: Data sources query the provider at plan time; most_recent selects the newest match, so new images flow in with no code edits. A is manual toil that defeats the purpose. B is wrong — you don't manage public AMIs as resources. C is wrong — state records results; it doesn't resolve AMI lookups.

q: A data "aws_ami" block filters for an AMI name that matches nothing in the region. What happens at plan time?
options: The plan fails — a data source that cannot be read is an error, so the filters must be fixed
The data source returns an empty string and the plan continues with a warning
Terraform creates a placeholder AMI so the plan can proceed
The data source is silently skipped and dependent resources are dropped from the plan
explain: Data source reads are real API queries; zero matches is a read error that fails the plan — Terraform won't guess. B is wrong — there's no lenient empty-string fallback. C is wrong — data sources never create anything. D is wrong — failures propagate, they don't silently prune the graph.

q: A root module calls three child modules, each with its own required_providers. The engineer wants one view of every provider the whole configuration requires and which module declared each requirement. Which command shows this?
options: terraform version, which lists every provider in the dependency tree
terraform providers — it shows the provider requirements tree across the root and all child modules
terraform init, which prints the full provider inventory
terraform state list, which includes provider addresses
explain: terraform providers is built for exactly this: the tree of provider requirements by module. A is wrong — version shows the CLI version plus installed provider versions, not requirements by module. C is wrong — init installs; it doesn't render a requirements report. D is wrong — state list shows managed resource instances, not provider requirements.

q: An engineer saves a plan with terraform plan -out=deploy.tf. The next terraform plan in that directory fails with a strange syntax error. What went wrong?
options: Plan files must be saved with an absolute path, not a relative one
-out requires the saved plan to be applied before any new plan runs
The .tf suffix makes Terraform parse the plan file as configuration — saved plans must not use .tf (the convention is a name like tfplan)
Two plan files cannot exist in the same directory
explain: The .tf extension is reserved for HCL configuration; Terraform tried to parse the binary plan artifact as code. Name plan files without .tf (tfplan is the convention). A is wrong — relative paths are fine. B invents an ordering requirement. D is wrong — multiple plan files coexist fine, they're just confusing.

q: A pipeline step must alert when infrastructure drifts but fail the build only on real errors. It runs `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode`. How should it interpret the exit codes?
options: 0 = error, 1 = changes present, 2 = no changes
Exit codes are identical with or without the flag, so the flag is useless
0 = succeeded with empty diff (no changes), 1 = error, 2 = succeeded with non-empty diff (changes present)
The flag only affects terraform apply, not plan
explain: The documented mapping: 0 clean, 1 error, 2 successful plan with changes — which is exactly the drift signal (2 means alert, 1 means fail). A scrambles the mapping. B is wrong — without the flag, plan exits 0 whether or not changes exist, which is why the flag exists. D is wrong — it's a plan flag.

q: An engineer commits tfplan files to git for "review history," and a database password appears in a pull request diff. How did this happen, and what is the rule?
options: Saved plan files embed all planned values, including sensitive ones, in cleartext — treat plan files as secrets and never commit them
Plan files are encrypted, so the password must have leaked from the state file instead
Only non-sensitive values are stored in plan files; the password came from a tfvars file
Committing plan files is safe because git redacts secrets automatically
explain: A saved plan is a complete execution artifact containing every planned value in cleartext, secrets included — it must be handled like a credential (short-lived, access-controlled, never in VCS). B is wrong — no encryption is applied. C is wrong — sensitivity doesn't exclude values from the plan. D invents git behavior that doesn't exist.

q: An engineer runs `terraform plan tfplan` where tfplan is a plan saved earlier with -out. What does Terraform do?
options: It generates a fresh plan and overwrites tfplan
It displays the contents of the saved plan without modifying it or re-planning
It applies the saved plan immediately
It errors, because plan cannot take a file argument
explain: Given a saved plan file, plan becomes a viewer: it renders what was planned, read-only. This is the documented way to inspect a planfile. A is wrong — the file is never overwritten by this. C is wrong — only apply executes a plan file. D is wrong — the file argument is explicitly supported.

q: The team wants to decommission a whole environment. The lead runs terraform destroy, sees a proposed plan, and is asked to confirm. What is true about this flow?
options: Destroy has no preview; it deletes immediately
Destroy requires -target for every resource
Destroy shows a plan and prompts for confirmation (use -auto-approve in automation); the same preview is available anytime via terraform plan -destroy
Destroy skips the state file and deletes by tag
explain: Destroy is plan-then-confirm like apply; -auto-approve is the automation answer, and plan -destroy previews without the prompt. A is wrong — the confirmation is the safety gate. B is wrong — destroy defaults to everything in state. D is wrong — destroy is entirely state-driven.

q: A variable is declared type = number, but a tfvars file passes "three". At which point does Terraform report this, and why so early?
options: Only at apply, when the provider rejects the value
terraform fmt reports it while formatting
It is silently coerced to 3
terraform validate catches the type mismatch statically, before any provider or cloud interaction
explain: Validate's job is exactly this class of error: type mismatches, missing required arguments, invalid references — caught without touching providers or state. A is wrong — that would waste a whole plan cycle on a checkable error. B confuses formatting with validation. C is wrong — "three" isn't convertible; Terraform errors rather than guesses.

q: A CI job runs `terraform fmt -check -recursive` and fails the build when files aren't canonically formatted. What does -check actually do?
options: It checks formatting and exits non-zero listing the offending files, without rewriting anything
It rewrites the files and exits 0
It exits 0 when files need formatting, since the check itself succeeded
-recursive is the default, so the flag is redundant
explain: -check is the read-only gate: exit 0 if all formatted, non-zero (listing filenames) otherwise — and it implies -write=false. B describes plain fmt. C inverts the exit-code contract. D is wrong — fmt is non-recursive by default; -recursive is what reaches subdirectories.

q: A scheduled automation pipeline hangs every night at the terraform apply step, waiting on a "Do you want to perform these actions?" prompt. What is the correct fix?
options: Add -input=false, which suppresses the approval prompt
Approvals can only be skipped in HCP Terraform, not in CLI automation
Apply never prompts, so the hang must be a provider issue
Add -auto-approve — interactive apply prompts for confirmation by default, and automation must explicitly opt out of the prompt
explain: The confirmation prompt is the default safety behavior; -auto-approve is the documented automation flag. C denies the premise — the prompt is real. A confuses -input=false (skips variable prompts) with approval. B is wrong — -auto-approve is a core CLI flag.

q: After applying, a deploy pipeline needs the RDS endpoint to render an application config file. What is the reliable way to get it?
options: Parse the human-readable plan output from the last apply
Outputs are only displayed during apply, so re-run apply
terraform output -raw db_endpoint — output values are stored in state and readable anytime via the output command
Use terraform console to re-plan the database module
explain: Output values persist in state precisely so downstream automation can consume them; -raw gives the plain string for scripting. A is brittle — plan text is a UI, not an interface. B is wrong — outputs live on in state. D misuses console, which evaluates expressions interactively, not as a value fetcher for pipelines.

q: A complex for expression is producing the wrong list of subnets, and the engineer wants to experiment with variations quickly without running full plans. What should she use?
options: terraform console — an interactive REPL that evaluates expressions against the current state and configuration
terraform plan -target on the expression
terraform apply with -refresh-only to test the expression
Edit the state file until the expression works
explain: Console exists for exactly this: an interactive REPL that evaluates HCL expressions with real state values loaded, without changing anything. B is wrong — -target selects resources, not expressions. C is wrong — refresh-only syncs state from reality; it doesn't evaluate HCL. D is wrong — hand-editing state is unsupported and dangerous.

q: The team is importing dozens of existing subnets and wants Terraform to draft the corresponding resource blocks automatically instead of hand-writing each one. Which workflow does this?
options: Write import blocks, then run terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf — Terraform generates resource configuration for the imported objects, which the team reviews and refines
terraform import writes the resource blocks automatically
Import blocks generate configuration on every plan without any extra flag
Configuration can only ever be hand-written; Terraform cannot generate it
explain: -generate-config-out is the config-generation companion to import blocks: it drafts the resource blocks from the discovered objects for review. B is wrong — CLI import only binds state, writing no config. C is wrong — generation requires the explicit flag. D denies a documented feature.

q: The team widens a module's version constraint to allow v3, but terraform init keeps installing v2.9. What will actually pick up the new version?
options: terraform init always installs the newest allowed version, so this is a bug
terraform init -upgrade — plain init reuses the locked selections; -upgrade tells it to select the newest versions allowed by the constraints
Deleting .terraform/modules by hand before every init
terraform apply, which upgrades modules automatically
explain: Init is conservative by design: it honors the lock file's recorded selections. -upgrade is the explicit 're-resolve to newest allowed' for providers and modules. A misstates init's contract. C is a hack that doesn't change selection logic. D is wrong — apply never changes module/provider versions.

q: The team must bring 30 existing S3 buckets under Terraform management and wants the imports peer-reviewed before any state changes. Which approach fits?
options: Run terraform import 30 times; each import is automatically reviewed
Write import blocks — imports become part of the plan, so reviewers see exactly what will be adopted in the pull request, and a normal apply executes them
Import blocks execute immediately on save, so no review is possible
Delete and recreate the buckets so no import is needed
explain: Config-driven import is plannable: the plan shows each import action for review, and apply performs them — unlike the CLI command, which mutates state immediately with no preview. A is wrong — CLI import has no review step. C describes the opposite of import-block behavior. D is destructive and unnecessary.

q: A variable must hold an object with a name (string) and enabled (bool) — nothing else, with types enforced. Which declaration is correct?
options: type = map(string), which enforces both keys and value types
type = tuple([string, bool]), which names the fields
type = list(object({ name = string, enabled = bool })), for a single object
type = object({ name = string, enabled = bool }) — an object type constrains both attribute names and their types
explain: object({...}) is the structural type: fixed attribute names each with a declared type. A allows any string keys with string values only — wrong shapes pass. B is positional, not named. C describes a list of such objects — wrong cardinality for a single value.

q: TF_VAR_region is set to us-east-1 in the environment, but the command includes -var 'region=eu-west-1'. Which value wins, and why?
options: -var 'region=eu-west-1' — command-line -var flags outrank TF_VAR_ environment variables in the precedence chain
TF_VAR_region, because environment variables are the highest precedence
Terraform errors on the conflict and asks the user to pick
Whichever was set most recently in time
explain: The precedence order (highest first): -var / -var-file flags, then *.auto.tfvars, then terraform.tfvars, then environment variables, then defaults. Flags beat env vars deliberately so automation can override ambient config. B inverts the order. C is wrong — no conflict error exists; precedence resolves it. D confuses shell timing with Terraform's fixed chain.

q: Company policy requires every resource name to start with the environment prefix, e.g. "prod-". Where should this rule be enforced so violations are rejected early with a custom error?
options: In a comment above each resource block reminding authors
In the variable's type constraint, which supports regex patterns
With a Sentinel policy, which is the only mechanism that can validate strings
In a validation block on the variable using a regex condition (e.g. can(regex("^prod-", var.name))) with an error_message — evaluated during plan
explain: validation blocks are the config-native input guard: evaluated at plan with custom error messages. A relies on human vigilance. B is wrong — type constraints check shapes (string, number), not string patterns. C is wrong — Sentinel is the HCP-side policy engine; validation blocks are the in-configuration mechanism.

q: A database password variable is marked sensitive = true. It's hidden in plan output, but the engineer later finds it in plaintext inside terraform.tfstate. What is the correct understanding?
options: sensitive = true is broken and should be reported as a bug
Marking the output sensitive instead would have encrypted the state
sensitive only redacts display in CLI output and logs — state still stores the value in cleartext, so the state backend itself must be encrypted and access-controlled
Sensitive values are never written to state at all
explain: sensitive is a display control, not encryption: plan/UI/logs redact, but state is the system of record and holds real values. Protecting secrets means securing the backend (encryption at rest, tight IAM). A misdiagnoses documented behavior as a bug. B is wrong — output sensitivity also only redacts display. D is false — Terraform must persist actual values to manage resources.

q: Twenty resources need the same computed tag map built from var.project and var.environment. The team wants it defined once, not user-overridable. What is the right construct?
options: A variable with a default, which users can override per workspace
A local value — locals { common_tags = {...} } — computed once from other values and referenced as local.common_tags; locals are internal, not inputs
An output value, which other resources can read
A data source that computes the tags
explain: Locals are for internal computed values: derived from variables/resources, defined once, referenced as local.<name>, and not settable from outside. A makes it an input, inviting accidental override. C is wrong — outputs expose values from a module outward; they don't define shared internals. D misuses data sources, which read external objects.

q: The team manages one S3 bucket per product team and wants addresses like aws_s3_bucket.teams["payments"]. The input is a map of team names to settings. Which meta-argument and references achieve this?
options: for_each = var.teams, with each.key and each.value inside the block — for_each over a map creates one instance per key, addressable by key
count = length(var.teams) with each.key for the name
for_each over the map, referenced as aws_s3_bucket.teams[0]
count with element(keys(var.teams), count.index) and string addresses
explain: for_each on a map yields key-addressed instances (["payments"]) with each.key/each.value — the idiom for named collections. B is wrong — each.* only exists with for_each. C mixes metaphors — numeric indexing is count's style. D is the old count workaround: fragile (renames shift indices) and doesn't give key addresses.

q: A database read replica should only exist in production, not in dev or staging. Which pattern implements this conditional resource?
options: count = var.is_prod, passing the boolean directly as the count
count = var.env == "prod" ? 1 : 0 — the conditional (ternary) expression yields 1 or 0, creating the resource or nothing
for_each = var.env, iterating over the environment name
A provisioner that deletes the replica in every non-production environment
explain: The ternary-to-count idiom is the standard conditional-resource pattern: 1 creates it, 0 skips it. A is wrong — count requires a number; booleans don't implicitly convert. C is wrong — for_each needs a map or set of strings, not a single string. D is imperative demolition instead of declarative conditionality.

q: A security group needs a variable-driven list of ingress rules — sometimes 2, sometimes 10. How should the repeated nested ingress blocks be generated?
options: count on the ingress nested block
A for_each directly on the nested block type
A dynamic "ingress" block with for_each over the rule list and a content block using ingress.value — dynamic blocks generate repeatable nested blocks
Nested blocks can't be generated; write each one literally
explain: dynamic blocks exist for exactly this: for_each over a collection, content describing each generated nested block, iterator (ingress.value) per element. A is wrong — count/for_each aren't valid on nested block types. B is wrong for the same reason — the meta-arguments belong on the dynamic wrapper. D denies a core language feature.

q: An external cost-allocation tool updates the CostCenter tag on resources out-of-band. Every terraform apply reverts the tag, generating noise and fighting the tool. How should Terraform treat the tags?
options: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }, which also freezes tag values in place
Remove the tags argument from the configuration entirely
Mark the tags variable sensitive so Terraform ignores changes to it
lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags] } — Terraform stops reconciling that attribute, leaving the external tool's values alone
explain: ignore_changes declares attributes Terraform should stop managing — the answer to out-of-band writers. A is wrong — prevent_destroy blocks destruction only, not updates. B would make Terraform plan tag removal. C is wrong — sensitive only redacts display.

q: A TLS certificate resource has a unique-name constraint, so destroying the old one before creating the new causes an outage window. How should replacement be ordered?
options: lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } — the replacement is created first, then the old one is destroyed
Destroy-first is the default and cannot be changed
create_before_destroy only works with count-based resources
Order the resources with depends_on instead
explain: create_before_destroy flips the replacement order for exactly this class of problem (unique names, zero-downtime swaps). B is wrong — destroy-first is the default, but it is changeable. C invents a count restriction. D is wrong — depends_on orders distinct resources; it doesn't change a single resource's replacement sequence.

q: A golden-image pipeline publishes a new AMI on the first of each month. The team's instances should be replaced to pick up each new image. How is this expressed?
options: depends_on = [data.aws_ami.golden], which forces replacement whenever the image changes
lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [data.aws_ami.golden.id] } — when the resolved AMI ID changes, Terraform plans replacement of the instance
Manually taint the instances on the first of each month
ignore_changes on the ami argument, so new images flow in silently
explain: replace_triggered_by watches the referenced value and converts its change into a replacement plan — the declarative 'replace me when that changes'. A is wrong — depends_on only orders operations. C is manual toil this automates. D is the opposite — ignore_changes would freeze the old AMI.

q: A module outputs a bucket website endpoint, and the team wants apply to fail loudly with a custom error if the endpoint doesn't use HTTPS. Which language feature enforces this guarantee on the output?
options: A validation block inside the output block
A variable validation in the calling module
An output postcondition — postcondition { condition = startswith(var.website_endpoint, "https://") ... } with an error_message, checked when the output is produced
A check block, which is the only place output conditions are allowed
explain: Outputs support preconditions and postconditions: boolean conditions with custom error messages evaluated as the value is produced. A is wrong — validation blocks exist only on variables. B guards the wrong boundary (the caller's input, not this module's promise). D is wrong — check blocks are separate post-apply assertions, not output guards.

q: Instance types vary by environment: var.instance_types is a map like { dev = "t3.micro", prod = "m5.large" }, but a new environment "test" has no entry yet. Which expression safely falls back to "t3.micro"?
options: var.instance_types[var.env], which returns null for missing keys
var.instance_types.var.env using dotted access
element(values(var.instance_types), 0), which picks a default
lookup(var.instance_types, var.env, "t3.micro") — lookup returns the default when the key is absent instead of erroring
explain: lookup(map, key, default) is the safe-access function: missing key yields the default. A is wrong — direct index into a map with a missing key is an error, not null. B invents dotted map access. C grabs an arbitrary first value — not a default, and nondeterministic in intent.

q: A company keeps its reusable Terraform modules in a private GitHub repository. Which module source address correctly references the vpc module in that repo?
options: source = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf-modules.git//vpc" — the git:: prefix with an optional //subdirectory selects modules from version control
source = "acme/vpc/aws", which only works for the public registry
source = "./vpc", which reaches private GitHub repos automatically
source = "https://github.com/acme/tf-modules/vpc.zip", which Terraform unpacks as a module archive
explain: Git sources use the git:: (or plain git-URL) scheme with // to select a subdirectory — the standard for private-repo modules (SSH URLs work too). B is the public-registry shorthand, unusable for private code. C is a local filesystem path — it can't reach GitHub. D invents zip-URL module fetching; HTTP sources fetch single files, not module trees.

q: A module block has no version argument. A fresh terraform init on a new machine installs v3.0.0 of the module, whose interface changed, and production breaks. What is the best-practice fix?
options: Pin the version in required_providers instead
Add a version constraint to the module block (e.g., version = "~> 2.0") so future installs stay on a compatible line; use init -upgrade deliberately when ready to move
Delete the lock file so init always picks the newest
Move the version pin into variables.tf
explain: Module version constraints bound what init may select on fresh installs; without one, 'latest' is a moving target. -upgrade makes version moves explicit and reviewable. A is wrong — required_providers constrains providers, not modules. C makes the problem worse (guarantees newest). D is wrong — versions aren't variables.

q: The root module needs the VPC ID created inside child module "vpc" to pass to another module. The child declares output "vpc_id". What is the correct reference in the root?
options: var.vpc_id, since child outputs become root variables
module.vpc.output.vpc_id with the explicit output segment
module.vpc.vpc_id — module outputs are referenced as module.<NAME>.<OUTPUT>
data.vpc.vpc_id, because child outputs are read as data sources
explain: The reference syntax is module.<name>.<output-name>; it requires the child to declare that output. A confuses outputs with input variables. B invents an extra '.output' segment. D misuses data sources, which read external objects, not module outputs.

q: A module block passes bucket_suffix = "-logs", but no variable named bucket_suffix is declared in the child module. What happens?
options: The extra value is silently dropped
Terraform declares the variable implicitly from usage
It is applied as a tag to every resource in the module
Terraform errors with an unsupported argument message — module block arguments must match declared input variables
explain: Module calls are strictly typed against the child's declared variables; undeclared arguments are a static error, which is what catches typos in input names. A would hide misconfigurations. B would make interfaces unpredictable — Terraform requires explicit declarations. C invents tag coercion.

q: A module "vpc" is instantiated with for_each over a map of environments { dev, prod }. How does the root reference the prod instance's vpc_id output?
options: module.vpc["prod"].vpc_id — for_each on a module creates key-addressed instances, each with its own outputs
module.vpc[1].vpc_id, since modules are indexed numerically
module.vpc.prod.vpc_id in dotted notation
module.vpc.vpc_id["prod"], indexing the output itself
explain: Module instances follow the same addressing as resources: for_each gives string-keyed instances (module.vpc["prod"]), each exposing the module's outputs. B applies count-style indexing to a for_each expansion. C invents dotted instance access. D reverses the nesting — the instance is indexed, not the output.

q: The team raises a child module's version constraint from ~> 1.0 to ~> 2.0, but terraform init still installs the 1.x module. What command picks up the new version?
options: terraform get -update, which is the modern replacement for init
terraform refresh, which updates module sources
terraform apply, which refreshes module versions automatically
terraform init -upgrade — plain init honors the recorded (locked) selections; -upgrade re-resolves modules and providers to the newest allowed
explain: -upgrade is the explicit 're-resolve dependencies' switch for both providers and modules; without it init stays conservative. C is wrong — apply never changes dependency versions. A is wrong — get only installs modules (init supersedes it) and doesn't manage providers. B is wrong — refresh updates state from reality, not module code.

q: A developer adds a second module block to the configuration and immediately runs terraform plan, which fails with "Module not installed". What went wrong?
options: Plan installs modules automatically, so the source address must be invalid
The state file must be refreshed before new modules can be planned
terraform init must be re-run — init installs modules, and newly added module blocks aren't downloaded until it runs again
Module blocks require an explicit version argument before init will fetch them
explain: Init is what downloads modules; adding a module block changes the dependency set, so init must run again before plan can proceed. A is wrong — plan never installs anything. B is wrong — refresh concerns state, not module code. D is wrong — version is optional (though pinning is best practice).

q: An engineer writes source = "terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws" for a public module. What do the three segments represent?
options: Cloud provider / service / resource type
Version / module name / submodule
Git organization / repository / ref
NAMESPACE / NAME / PROVIDER on the Terraform Registry (default host registry.terraform.io)
explain: Registry addresses are NAMESPACE/NAME/PROVIDER — who published it, the module name, and which provider it's built for. A maps it to cloud concepts. B invents a version segment (version is a separate argument). C describes a VCS address, not registry shorthand.

q: Root module A calls child module B, which calls grandchild module C. The root needs an endpoint that only module C's resources know. How does the value reach the root?
options: Each level re-exports it: C declares the output, B declares an output referencing module.c.<output>, and A references module.b.<output> — outputs don't bubble up automatically
The root references module.b.module.c.endpoint directly
Outputs propagate upward automatically through nesting
The root reads it with a data source pointed at module C
explain: Module boundaries are opaque: only a module's own declared outputs are visible to its caller, so values must be explicitly re-exported level by level. B invents chained module addressing (only one level is addressable). C denies the encapsulation rule. D misuses data sources for intra-configuration values.

q: A team wants a git-sourced module pinned to release tag v2.1.0, not the branch tip. How is the tag expressed in the source address?
options: With the version argument: version = "v2.1.0" alongside the git source
With a ref query parameter: source = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf-modules.git//vpc?ref=v2.1.0"
Tags are followed automatically; no syntax is needed
By naming the branch v2.1.0, since only branches are addressable
explain: ?ref= pins any git ref — tag, branch, or commit SHA — and tags are the immutable choice for releases. A is wrong — the version argument works only with registry sources, not VCS. C is wrong — default is the branch tip, a moving target. D is wrong — tags are addressable and preferable to branches.

q: Module "app" needs an IAM role created by module "iam" to exist first, but app takes no inputs from iam, so there's no data reference between them. How is the ordering enforced?
options: It can't be — modules without data flow apply in random order
depends_on is not allowed inside module blocks
depends_on = [module.iam] in the app module block — the meta-argument works on modules for exactly these hidden ordering dependencies
Add a provisioner to module app that waits for the role
explain: depends_on accepts module addresses too, creating explicit ordering where no data reference implies one. A is wrong — graph order is deterministic; the issue is only missing edges. B is wrong — the restriction some expect doesn't exist. D is a fragile imperative hack for a declarative ordering need.

q: A child module must create some resources in us-east-1 and others in eu-west-1. The root has aws and aws.west provider configurations. How does the module get both?
options: Child modules automatically inherit all of the parent's aliased providers
The child declares its own provider blocks with matching aliases
The module block maps them explicitly: providers = { aws = aws, aws.west = aws.west } — aliased configurations are passed, never implicitly inherited
Pass the region names as string variables and let the module configure providers from them
explain: Only default (unaliased) provider configurations are implicitly inherited; aliased ones must be passed via the providers argument mapping child provider names to parent configurations. A states the common misconception the question tests. B creates separate, independent provider configs in the child — not the parent's. D is wrong — modules cannot configure providers from variables (provider configuration must be static).

q: A new team member asks what terraform.tfstate actually contains. Which description is accurate?
options: The bindings between resource addresses in configuration and real remote object IDs, plus dependencies, outputs, and metadata like serial and lineage
A copy of all the .tf configuration files
The cloud credentials used by the last apply
Only the output values, for use by downstream automation
explain: State is Terraform's ledger: which real object each address manages, how they're ordered, computed outputs, and integrity metadata (serial/lineage). B is wrong — config lives in .tf files; state records results. C is wrong — credentials are never stored in state. D is too narrow — outputs are one section of a much larger record.

q: The team stores state in an S3 bucket without versioning. A faulty automation overwrites the state object with garbage, and the last known-good state is unrecoverable. Which backend practice would have saved them?
options: DynamoDB state locking, which prevents concurrent writes
The -backup flag on apply, which versions remote state automatically
Storing the state file in the same repository as the configuration
Enabling versioning on the state bucket — every state write becomes a recoverable version, so a corrupted state can be rolled back
explain: S3 versioning on the state bucket is the standard remote-state safety net: prior state versions survive overwrites and can be restored. A is wrong — locking prevents concurrent writers, not bad writes. B is wrong — -backup only backs up local state files. C is wrong — state must never live in version control.

q: The team is moving from local state to an S3 backend. They update the backend block and run terraform init. Which flag carries the existing state into the new backend, and what happens without it?
options: -reconfigure carries the state over automatically
No flag is needed; init always migrates state
-migrate-state — it copies the existing state to the new backend (after confirmation); without it (e.g., -reconfigure), Terraform ignores the old state and plans to recreate everything
terraform state push performs the migration during init
explain: -migrate-state is the explicit 'move my state' instruction. -reconfigure means 'forget the old backend config' — Terraform then sees empty state and proposes creating duplicates of everything already running. A confuses the two flags. B is wrong — init never migrates unprompted. D misuses state push, which overwrites remote state with a local file.
