q: The backend "s3" block is written with an empty body, and the bucket, key, and region are supplied at init time via -backend-config="prod.hcl". Why is this pattern recommended?
options: Backend blocks cannot contain arguments, so this is the only valid syntax
Partial backend configuration keeps environment-specific and credential values out of versioned code — the backend type is declared in config, the sensitive details are supplied per environment
-backend-config only works with CLI workspaces
Hardcoding credentials in the backend block is required for init to succeed
explain: Partial configuration separates the declared backend type (safe to version) from per-environment credentials/names (supplied via files, env vars, or flags) — no secrets in git. A is wrong — backend blocks normally hold their arguments inline. C invents a workspace restriction. D states the anti-pattern this technique avoids.

q: One configuration must manage dev, staging, and prod with completely separate infrastructure but a single S3 backend. Which approach isolates their states?
options: terraform workspace new dev/staging/prod — CLI workspaces keep separate state files (e.g., env:/prod/...) within the same backend, selected via workspace select
CLI workspaces share one state file, so this can't be done
Workspaces exist only in HCP Terraform
Copy the configuration directory three times
explain: CLI workspaces are state isolation within one backend: each workspace gets its own state object under a key prefix, while the configuration stays identical. B inverts the definition — separation is the whole point. C confuses CLI workspaces with HCP workspaces (different concept). D is the duplication this feature eliminates.

q: A resource is renamed from aws_s3_bucket.logs to aws_s3_bucket.audit_logs. The bucket must not be recreated. What is the safe operation?
options: Run apply — Terraform matches renames by resource type automatically
terraform state mv 'aws_s3_bucket.logs' 'aws_s3_bucket.audit_logs' (or the equivalent moved block) — rebinds the existing object to the new address
terraform state rm the old address, then apply
Edit the state JSON to rename the address
explain: state mv (or declarative moved blocks) retargets the binding: same remote object, new address — no disruption. A is wrong — Terraform sees a deletion plus an addition and plans destroy/create. C would orphan the bucket from management, then apply would create a duplicate. D is the unsupported hand-edit path.

q: A VM was deleted in the cloud console weeks ago, and the team wants Terraform to simply forget about it — no destroy planned, no replacement. The config block is already removed. What completes this?
options: terraform refresh, which deletes stale bindings automatically
terraform plan -destroy, scoped to the missing VM
terraform state rm 'aws_instance.old' — removes the state binding so Terraform stops tracking it; the (already deleted) object needs no destroy
terraform state mv to a trash address
explain: state rm unbinds: Terraform forgets the object without touching reality — right when reality is already gone or intentionally unmanaged. A is wrong — refresh updates attributes; it doesn't drop bindings for missing objects silently. B would plan destruction of things still tracked. D invents a trash-address pattern.

q: An engineer hand-edits terraform.tfstate to 'fix' a resource ID, and the next apply behaves erratically. What is the rule about manual state edits?
options: Hand-editing is the documented way to fix state discrepancies
JSON edits are safe as long as the file stays valid JSON
The state file is write-through, so edits apply cleanly
Manual edits are unsupported — state has integrity metadata (serial, lineage, checksums) and Terraform expects to be its only writer; use state mv/rm, refresh, or import workflows instead
explain: Terraform owns the state file's format and integrity fields; hand edits risk corruption that surfaces as bizarre plans. The supported mutation paths are the state subcommands and config-driven workflows (moved/import blocks). A–C all bless a practice HashiCorp explicitly warns against.

q: A security review finds a database password in plaintext inside the S3 state object, even though the variable was marked sensitive. What must the team do?
options: Treat state as sensitive data: enable encryption at rest on the backend, restrict access with tight IAM, and consider designs that keep secrets out of state (write-only attributes, secret stores referenced at runtime)
Marking it sensitive was the mistake — remove the flag and the password won't be stored
S3 encrypts everything by default, so no action is needed
State files never contain secret values; the finding must be a false positive
explain: sensitive redacts display only — state necessarily holds real values, so the backend must be hardened (SSE, IAM, versioning/locking) and secret-handling designs preferred. B inverts cause and effect. C over-relies on defaults while ignoring access control. D denies how Terraform works.

q: For an audit, the team needs a point-in-time copy of the current remote state without changing anything. Which command produces it?
options: terraform state show, which exports the full state
terraform state pull — downloads the current remote state as JSON (e.g., redirected to a backup file) without modifying anything
terraform state push, which backs the state up to the backend
Copying terraform.tfstate locally, which is always the latest
explain: state pull is the read-only download: snapshot the remote state for inspection or backup. A shows one resource's attributes, not the whole state. C is dangerous — push overwrites remote state with a local file. D is wrong — the local file may be a stale cache; pull is authoritative.

q: Someone relaxed an S3 bucket policy in the console during an incident. The next terraform plan proposes tightening it back, with no .tf edits. Why?
options: Plans read the console audit log and automatically revert manual actions
Bucket policies are immutable, so Terraform restores them
Plan refreshes state by default — it detected the out-of-band policy change as drift and proposes reconciling it to the configuration
A refresh-only apply ran automatically in the background
explain: Refresh-on-plan is the default: Terraform re-reads managed objects before diffing, so console edits surface as proposed reversions. A invents audit-log integration. B is wrong — policies are mutable; that's why drift was possible. D is wrong — no background apply runs on its own.

q: After changing the S3 backend's bucket name, an engineer runs terraform init -reconfigure. The next plan proposes creating every resource from scratch, even though all of it already exists. What went wrong?
options: Init failed to detect the new bucket
The state file was corrupted by the bucket rename
-reconfigure merges old and new state, creating duplicates

-reconfigure tells Terraform to ignore any existing state and use the new backend fresh — the old state was left behind, so Terraform thinks nothing exists; -migrate-state should have been used to carry it over
explain: The two flags answer different questions: -migrate-state = 'move my state to the new backend'; -reconfigure = 'forget the old backend'. With reconfigure, the prior state is abandoned and every real object looks unmanaged — hence create plans for existing infra. A misdiagnoses. B is wrong — nothing corrupted. C inverts -reconfigure's meaning.

q: A VM's OS is corrupted beyond repair. The configuration hasn't changed and shouldn't — the team just needs that one instance recreated. What is the current best-practice command?
options: terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web — flags the instance for replacement on the next apply (the -replace flag superseded terraform taint)
terraform taint, which remains the recommended approach
Edit the configuration to force a change, apply, then revert
terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.web followed by apply
explain: -replace is the modern replacement workflow: declarative, plannable, and visible in the plan — taint is deprecated in favor of it. B is outdated. C is hacky config churn. D works but is two manual steps with a window where the resource doesn't exist, and bypasses plan review.

q: An apply fails with a cryptic provider 403 error. The team needs full debug logs, including HTTP traces, saved to a file for a support ticket. How?
options: terraform apply --verbose, which enables debug output
Set TF_LOG=DEBUG (levels: TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR) and TF_LOG_PATH to a file — Terraform writes detailed operational logs there
Debug logs are written automatically to terraform.log
Set TF_DEBUG=1, the universal debug flag
explain: TF_LOG controls verbosity with the documented level ladder (TRACE most verbose); TF_LOG_PATH captures it to a file — the standard provider-debugging recipe. A invents a --verbose flag. C is wrong — no automatic log file exists. D invents a flag name.

q: The team is upgrading Terraform CLI from 1.5 to 1.9 across all machines and CI. What is the safe upgrade practice?
options: Each engineer upgrades whenever convenient; mixed versions are fine
The state file must be manually converted before the new CLI can read it
Read the CHANGELOG for breaking changes, upgrade together, and test in non-production first — newer CLIs auto-upgrade the state format, and old CLIs can't read new-format state
Upgrades never affect state, so just upgrade production first
explain: The documented cautions: state format upgrades are one-way (a newer CLI writes state older CLIs reject), so the fleet moves together after reviewing breaking changes in a safe environment. A risks the one-way state trap. B is wrong — Terraform handles state upgrades itself. D inverts safe rollout order.

q: After every apply, the team wants Terraform to continuously verify that the application load balancer returns HTTP 200, warning — but not blocking — if it doesn't. Which construct does this?
options: A provisioner that curls the endpoint during apply
A variable validation on the ALB's DNS name
An output precondition, which blocks apply on failure
A check block — assert { condition = data.http.alb.status_code == 200 ... } — evaluated after apply and on every refresh; failures warn without blocking operations
explain: check blocks are post-apply assertions for ongoing health: they re-evaluate on plan/apply and surface warnings without halting workflows. A runs once at provision time and can fail the apply. B validates inputs, not runtime health. C is wrong — preconditions block; checks deliberately don't.

q: Terraform fails with 'Error: Cycle: aws_security_group.a, aws_security_group.b'. What does this mean and how is it fixed?
options: A dependency cycle — A depends on B and B depends on A, so no valid ordering exists; break it by removing one direction of the dependency (e.g., referencing via data source or restructuring)
A transient error; re-running with higher -parallelism resolves it
Too many resources; split the configuration
Remove all depends_on blocks and let Terraform retry
explain: Cycles are graph errors, not transient: the dependency arrows form a loop with no topological order. The fix is structural — eliminate one edge. B is wrong — parallelism doesn't create ordering. C misdiagnoses scale. D is wrong — depends_on didn't cause it; removing ordering hints can't fix a genuine loop (and may be the loop's cause, not cure).

q: An apply fails halfway — 8 of 15 resources were created before a quota error stopped it. What is the correct recovery?
options: Taint all 8 created resources so they're recreated cleanly
Fix the quota issue and re-run apply — state recorded the 8 successes, so Terraform resumes by creating only the remaining 7
Delete the state file and start over to avoid a split-brain
State automatically rolled back, so just fix and re-apply from zero
explain: State is the resume ledger: completed work is recorded, so re-apply is idempotent continuation, not a redo. A would pointlessly destroy good resources. C destroys the only record of what exists. D is wrong — Terraform has no transactional rollback; partial progress persists by design.

q: An engineer runs plan against production and sees 'No changes,' yet the console clearly shows drifted settings. A colleague asks: 'Which workspace are you in?' — it's 'default,' but production lives in workspace 'prod'. Why does this explain the empty plan?
options: Plans are cached per directory, so it showed a stale result
Refresh is disabled in the default workspace
CLI workspaces isolate state — 'default' and 'prod' track completely separate infrastructure, so the plan compared the wrong state against the config
The state file is corrupted in the default workspace
explain: Each workspace is a separate state binding: planning in 'default' diffs config against default's reality, which is empty/clean — prod's drift lives in prod's state. terraform workspace select prod fixes it. A is wrong — plans aren't cached. B is wrong — refresh isn't workspace-dependent. D jumps to corruption without evidence.

q: A very large database regularly exceeds the AWS provider's default creation timeout, failing applies that would otherwise succeed. How should the configuration accommodate this?
options: Increase -parallelism so the database creates faster
Pass a -timeout flag to apply
Timeouts apply to plans, not resource creation, so nothing can be done
Add a timeouts block to the resource (e.g., timeouts { create = "90m" }) to override the provider's default per-operation timeout
explain: The timeouts meta-block overrides default per-operation (create/update/delete) timeouts for slow resources — the documented escape hatch. A is wrong — parallelism doesn't speed one resource. B invents a CLI flag. C is wrong — timeouts govern provider operations during apply.

q: After importing existing resources with import blocks and applying, the next plan still proposes several updates. What does this indicate?
options: The import was inaccurate — the configuration doesn't match the real resource attributes, so update the config to reflect reality; an empty plan confirms the import is faithful
The import failed silently and must be retried
Removing the import blocks will clear the proposed updates
Plans always show updates after any import; this is expected and ignorable
explain: Import binds the object; the config must then describe it truthfully. Proposed updates = config/reality mismatch to reconcile (write config to match, or accept the update). A clean plan is the verification signal. B is wrong — failed imports error loudly. C is wrong — import blocks are inert post-import; removal changes nothing. D normalizes what is actually a mismatch to fix.

q: A CI job dies at the module-download step: 'permission denied (publickey)' while fetching a private module repository. The job's Terraform configuration is valid. What should the team fix?
options: The module needs a version argument before git will authenticate
The CI environment has no SSH key or token for the private repo — init delegates fetching to git, which needs its own credentials
The Terraform version in CI is too old for git module sources
HCP Terraform must approve all private module downloads
explain: Init shells out to git/ssh for VCS sources — Terraform credentials don't apply; the machine needs a deploy key or token with repo access. This is the classic CI failure. A confuses versioning with auth. C is wrong — git sources are long-standing functionality. D is irrelevant to CLI-driven init.

q: A local-exec provisioner calls an API to register a DNS record, but it intermittently runs before the DNS zone resource exists — there's no attribute reference linking them. How is reliable ordering established?
options: Provisioners always run after all resources, so this shouldn't happen
depends_on on the resource containing the provisioner, listing the zone — explicit ordering for dependencies with no data flow
Add a sleep to the provisioner script
depends_on passes the zone's attributes into the provisioner
explain: depends_on creates ordering edges where no data reference implies one — the textbook hidden-dependency fix. A is wrong — provisioners run with their resource, ordered only by the graph. C is a flaky timing hack. D is wrong — depends_on orders; it doesn't pass data (references do that).

q: A data source reads an attribute of a resource being created in the same configuration. During plan, its values show as '(known after apply)'. What is happening?
options: The plan is broken; data sources can't reference managed resources
The data source must be given depends_on to read at plan time
Plan always fails when data sources reference new resources
Terraform defers the data source read until apply, when the dependency's values exist — plan proceeds with unknowns rather than failing
explain: Unknown-value deferral: when a data source's inputs aren't known until apply, its read waits for apply — the plan shows placeholders instead of erroring. A is wrong — this is supported and common. B is wrong — depends_on doesn't make unknown values known. C is wrong — no failure occurs.

q: A team using CLI workspaces (dev/stage/prod states in one backend) migrates to HCP Terraform and expects one HCP workspace with three CLI workspaces inside it. What must they understand?
options: HCP workspaces and CLI workspaces are different concepts — an HCP workspace holds one state, one configuration, and its run history; use one HCP workspace per environment instead
CLI workspaces sync into HCP workspaces automatically
HCP Terraform has no workspace concept
One HCP workspace can contain multiple CLI workspaces natively
explain: The name collision is the trap: CLI workspaces = multiple states in one backend; HCP workspaces = one managed unit (config + state + runs + variables). Migration means one HCP workspace per environment. B–D all assume a mapping that doesn't exist.

q: A regulated company uses HCP Terraform but policy forbids their infrastructure plans from executing on shared SaaS workers — runs must happen inside their own network. Which execution mode fits?
options: Remote execution, which runs on customer networks by default
Agent execution — HCP Terraform agents run in the company's own infrastructure, polling HCP for work while keeping execution local
Local execution, which is the agent mode under a different name
Execution modes are assigned randomly per run
explain: Agents are the private-network answer: they execute plans/applies inside your perimeter while HCP orchestrates. A is wrong — remote = HashiCorp's workers. C conflates local execution (runs on the operator's machine via CLI) with agents. D is nonsense.

q: A developer merges a change to main. The VCS-connected workspace has auto-apply disabled. What happens next?
options: HCP Terraform runs the plan and then pauses — with auto-apply off, someone must manually confirm before anything is applied
The merge is rejected until auto-apply is enabled
The run applies immediately; auto-apply only affects CLI-driven runs
VCS-connected workspaces cannot run at all without auto-apply
explain: Auto-apply is the per-workspace 'proceed without asking' toggle: off means runs stop at the confirmation step after planning — the standard prod posture. B is wrong — merges aren't gated on the setting. C inverts the toggle's meaning. D is wrong — manual confirmation is the default behavior.

q: AWS access keys must be available to Terraform runs in an HCP workspace. How should they be configured?
options: As terraform variables, since providers read variables directly
As regular variables with the HCL checkbox enabled
Hardcoded in the provider block for reliability
As environment variables marked sensitive — providers read credentials from the environment; the sensitive flag redacts them in the UI and logs
explain: The variable-category split: provider credentials go in environment variables (that's how provider SDKs consume them); sensitive hides them in UI/logs. A is wrong — terraform variables become HCL inputs, not env credentials. B misuses the HCL checkbox (for structured values, not secrets). C puts secrets in versioned code.

q: Thirty workspaces each define the same AWS credentials as workspace variables, and every rotation means thirty manual edits. What is the intended solution?
options: Variable sets — define the shared variables once and attach the set to all thirty workspaces; rotate in one place
Copying the variables is required; there is no sharing mechanism
Variable sets are scoped to a single workspace
Commit a terraform.tfvars file to each repo instead
explain: Variable sets are the multi-workspace sharing primitive: one definition, many attachments, single rotation point. B denies the feature. C inverts its scope — sharing is its purpose. D scatters secrets across repos, the problem restated.

q: A Sentinel policy requiring resource tags is set to advisory during rollout, while the encryption policy is hard-mandatory. A run violates both. What happens?
options: Advisory policies can't fail; only mandatory ones evaluate
Soft-mandatory is the only level that can be overridden
Both policies block the run until fixed
The advisory tag failure only warns in the UI without blocking; the hard-mandatory encryption failure stops the run until fixed (unless the policy set explicitly allows overrides)
explain: Enforcement levels (verified in HCP docs): advisory never interrupts — informational only; soft-mandatory stops but is overridable with permission; hard-mandatory stops and requires a fix unless the policy set enables overrides. C treats advisory as blocking. A is wrong — advisory policies do evaluate and report. B is wrong — policy-set-level overrides can cover hard-mandatory too.

q: A compliance policy must apply to production workspaces only, not to the dozen development workspaces. How should the policy set be scoped?
options: Policies are always organization-global; the code must check workspace names
Scope the policy set to specific projects/workspaces when connecting it — and keep the policy code itself in a VCS-connected policy set for versioning
Create a separate HCP organization per environment
Enforcement levels provide the scoping
explain: Policy sets support scoped application: global, per-project, or per-workspace — the administrative answer to 'prod-only rules.' VCS-connected sets version the policy code alongside. A forces policy code to do admin work. C is organizational overkill. D confuses enforcement strength with targeting.

q: The network team's workspace applies successfully, and the app team's workspace should automatically start a run afterward to pick up the new VPC outputs. What connects them?
options: Remote state sharing, which triggers runs automatically
Run triggers — the app workspace lists the network workspace as a source, so successful applies there queue runs downstream
Both workspaces must be merged into one
Workspace variables with the same names
explain: Run triggers chain workspaces operationally: source apply → downstream run queued. A is wrong — remote state sharing gives data access, not run orchestration. C destroys the separation the design wants. D is wrong — variable names don't trigger anything.

q: The app workspace reads the network workspace's state via terraform_remote_state, but the read fails with a 403 error. What is the likely cause?
options: The network workspace hasn't enabled remote state sharing for the app workspace — HCP workspaces must explicitly permit state consumers
terraform_remote_state only works with the local backend
The app workspace needs the network workspace's API token copied into its variables
Cross-workspace reads require both workspaces to run the same Terraform version
explain: Remote state access is permissioned: the source workspace must share its state (global sharing or named consumers in HCP). A 403 means that grant is missing. B is wrong — the data source is designed for remote backends. C is wrong — auth uses the reading workspace's own identity, not copied tokens. D invents a version requirement.

q: FinOps wants to see the projected monthly cost impact of an infrastructure change before it is applied. Where does this appear in HCP Terraform?
options: In the Sentinel policy output, which estimates costs
In the run itself — HCP's cost estimation phase shows projected cost changes between plan and apply, reviewable before confirming
Only after apply, in the billing dashboard
Cost estimation replaces the plan phase
explain: Cost estimation is a native run phase (after plan, before policy check/apply): it diffs projected costs so approvers see the money impact pre-apply. A confuses policy-as-code with cost projection. C misses the pre-apply purpose. D is wrong — estimation follows the plan; it doesn't replace it.

q: The dev workspace should apply automatically when its branch merges; production must wait for a human to review the plan and click apply. How is this configured?
options: Auto-apply is organization-wide, so this split is impossible
Production uses CLI-driven runs instead
Per-workspace auto-apply setting — enabled on dev for merge-to-apply, disabled on prod so runs pause for manual confirmation
Manual apply is unavailable in VCS-connected workspaces
explain: Auto-apply is a per-workspace toggle: on = runs proceed through apply without intervention; off = runs wait at the confirmation step. That toggle is exactly the dev/prod split. A is wrong — it's not org-wide. B is a workaround, not the setting. D is wrong — manual confirmation is the default behavior.

q: A platform team wants to share vetted internal modules across the company with versioning and access control, not via copy-pasted git URLs. What does HCP Terraform provide?
options: The public registry, which supports private modules
Git submodules, managed by HCP
A shared workspace that all teams apply from
The private registry — publish versioned modules (and providers) from VCS tags, consumable via normal registry source addresses with organization access control
explain: HCP's private registry is the internal distribution channel: VCS-tagged releases become immutable versions, consumed with registry source syntax and governed by org permissions. A is wrong — public registry is public. B is a git mechanism, not a registry. C confuses workspaces (execution units) with module distribution.

q: A team lead declares, 'We practice Infrastructure as Code — all our server build procedures are documented step-by-step in the company wiki.' An engineer disagrees. Why is the engineer right?
options: Wikis cannot be version controlled, so the procedures fail audit requirements
A wiki documents steps for humans to perform; IaC requires executable, machine-readable definitions that a tool can apply directly to produce infrastructure
Documentation is forbidden under IaC — everything must be memorized by the team
IaC only applies to cloud infrastructure, and the wiki covers on-premises servers
explain: The 'code' in IaC means definitions a machine can execute: Terraform reads .tf files and provisions real infrastructure. A wiki describes what a human should do — it cannot provision anything itself and reintroduces human error and drift. A is wrong — wikis can be versioned; versioning isn't the missing piece, executability is. C is absurd — IaC teams document heavily; the config itself is documentation. D is wrong — IaC covers on-premises and SaaS resources too, via providers.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team practices immutable infrastructure: every change, even flipping a log level, means building a new machine image and replacing servers. A frustrated engineer asks whether something is misconfigured. What is the exam-correct answer?
options: Yes — immutable infrastructure still allows in-place patching for trivial changes; full rebuilds are only for major releases
The team should abandon immutable infrastructure entirely, since it is never appropriate for production

Nothing is misconfigured — this is the deliberate trade-off of immutable infrastructure: slower, heavier changes in exchange for reproducibility and drift-free servers, with every change flowing through the same build-and-replace pipeline
The team should use immutable infrastructure in development and mutable patching in production, where speed matters most
explain: Immutable infrastructure's core bargain is that change happens only by replacement — even tiny edits go through the full pipeline. That cost buys servers that are never snowflakes and always reproducible. A contradicts the definition of immutable (no in-place mutation). B is too absolute — immutable infra is a mainstream production pattern. D is backwards: production is where reproducibility matters most.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A company manages firewalls in Terraform but still changes DNS records through support tickets. A ticketed DNS change causes an outage. What does this incident demonstrate about IaC adoption?
options: IaC's benefits — review, reproducibility, audit trail — apply only to what is actually defined in code; the ticket-driven DNS changes keep every risk of the old manual process
Terraform should have automatically detected and reverted the DNS change
Terraform cannot coexist with any manual process, so the team must migrate DNS immediately or abandon Terraform
This proves Infrastructure as Code does not work for networking components
explain: IaC protects the surface it covers. The DNS records were never declared in configuration, so no review, plan preview, or version history applied to them — partial adoption leaves partial risk. B is wrong — Terraform only manages resources declared in its configuration; it has no awareness of unmanaged DNS. C overstates it — coexistence is common during migrations; the point is the unmanaged part keeps manual-process risk. D generalizes one gap into a verdict on all networking.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team happily rebuilds stateless app servers from new images weekly, following immutable infrastructure. The DBA asks how this applies to the production database. What is the correct guidance?
options: Delete and recreate the database on the same schedule as the app servers; the data will be preserved automatically
Databases cannot be managed by Terraform at all and must stay manual
Rebuild the database servers but keep the old disks attached forever to avoid data decisions

Manage the database resource in Terraform, but pair any replacement with a deliberate data strategy — backups, restore, or migration — because Terraform provisions the infrastructure, not the rows inside it
explain: Immutable replacement is safe for stateless servers precisely because they hold no unique data. A database's value is its data, which Terraform does not manage — recreating the resource destroys the data unless a backup/restore or migration strategy runs alongside. A guarantees data loss. B is false — managed databases are routine Terraform resources. C is hand-waving that accumulates orphaned disks and never answers the data question.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team's servers have auto-generated names like i-0a1b2c3d, no engineer is attached to any individual machine, and a failed server is replaced from code without investigation or mourning. Which concept does this describe?
options: Cattle, not pets — servers are disposable and interchangeable, rebuilt from code rather than hand-tended as unique individuals
High availability — the servers are engineered to never fail
Elasticity — the fleet automatically scales with demand
Immutable backups — every server is snapshotted before any change
explain: Cattle-vs-pets is the mindset behind immutable IaC: machines are identical, replaceable units, so failure is handled by replacement, not surgery. B confuses disposability with fault tolerance — these servers do fail; the team just doesn't care. C is about scaling capacity up and down, not about replaceability. D invents a practice; snapshots are a backup tactic, not the philosophy described.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A typo in a shared Terraform module used by 50 workspaces causes a misconfiguration to roll out everywhere at once. A manager concludes shared modules are too dangerous. What is the exam-correct lesson?
options: Shared modules should be banned; every workspace must maintain its own copy of the configuration
IaC eliminates human error, so this incident must be a Terraform bug rather than a process failure
Automation amplifies both good and bad changes — widely reused code needs proportionally stronger review and testing, because one mistake now replicates everywhere at machine speed
The team should apply changes manually to each workspace so errors stay contained
explain: IaC doesn't remove human error; it scales whatever humans write — rigor must scale with reuse. The fix is versioned modules, plan review, and testing, not abandoning reuse. A and D retreat to copy-paste, which reintroduces drift and multiplies maintenance. B misattributes the cause: Terraform faithfully applied exactly what was written.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A platform team manages GitHub repositories, DNS zones, and Datadog monitors with Terraform — no virtual machines involved. A newcomer asks whether this is a misuse of the tool. What is the correct answer?
options: No — Terraform manages anything with an API through providers, not just compute; repositories, DNS, and SaaS services are legitimate IaC targets
Yes — Terraform is only for virtual machines and networks; SaaS services must be managed in their own consoles
Yes — providers only exist for the major cloud vendors
No, but these resources cannot benefit from state locking or plan previews
explain: Providers are Terraform's integration layer, and thousands exist for SaaS, DNS, identity, and on-premises systems — IaC is about managing infrastructure-as-defined-by-APIs. B and C falsely narrow the provider ecosystem to compute. D is wrong — every managed resource gets the full workflow: state, locking, plans, and drift detection.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Eight months after the initial Terraform rollout, the team faces its first region expansion, a mass certificate rotation, and a 3x traffic scaling event. A manager calls these 'operations work' that sits outside Terraform. What is the exam-correct response?
options: Terraform cannot update existing resources, only create them
IaC covers the full infrastructure lifecycle — day-2 operations like scaling, patching, and rotations are also expressed as code changes, not just the initial build
Console changes are automatically imported into the Terraform configuration
Day-2 operations are the cloud provider's responsibility once Terraform provisions the resources
explain: IaC's value compounds in day-2 operations: every ongoing change goes through the same review-plan-apply loop as the initial build. Hand-editing after provisioning reintroduces exactly the drift IaC was adopted to kill. A is false — updates are core to Terraform. C is false — nothing auto-imports; unmanaged changes become drift. D abdicates responsibility the team still owns.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A scheduled nightly terraform apply keeps undoing a temporary firewall exception the security team added in the cloud console during an active investigation. The security team calls this a Terraform bug. What is actually happening?
options: Terraform continuously reconciles real infrastructure toward the declared desired state, so a console fix that never lands in code will be undone by the next run
Terraform randomly reverts manual changes to punish console usage
The state file was corrupted by the manual change
Scheduled applies always destroy and recreate every resource
explain: This is desired-state reconciliation working as designed: Terraform's source of truth is the configuration, so the next run converges reality back to it — including reverting the undeclared fix. The lesson is to commit the fix in code. B invents malice; the behavior is deterministic convergence. C is wrong — the state wasn't corrupted, it was simply never told about the change. D is false — only drifted resources are corrected, not everything.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A junior engineer wants to try a risky network redesign but fears breaking staging. A senior engineer tells her to prototype it on a branch — worst case, she deletes the branch and nothing ever happened. Which 'as code' property makes this safe?
options: Code comments, which document why each resource exists
Syntax highlighting, which makes configuration easier to read
Version control — the redesign lives on a disposable branch carrying its own complete infrastructure definition, so experiments can be created and abandoned without touching staging
Compilation, which converts HCL into machine code for faster applies
explain: Because infrastructure is defined in version-controlled code, a branch is a complete, disposable infrastructure definition — the redesign can be applied to an isolated environment and abandoned by deleting the branch, with staging never at risk. A and B describe readability aids, not environment mechanics. D invents a compilation step Terraform doesn't have.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team keeps its architecture diagrams in the same repository as its Terraform configuration, updated in the same pull requests as the infrastructure changes. Why is this better than a separate wiki page?
options: Diagrams in a repository load faster than wiki pages
The documentation evolves atomically with the change it describes — the diagram and the infrastructure can never drift apart, because they are reviewed and merged together
Terraform renders the diagrams automatically during apply
Wikis cannot contain images
explain: Colocating docs with code means the doc update ships in the same reviewed change as the infra update — documentation drift becomes structurally impossible rather than a matter of discipline. A is a trivial performance claim, not the reason. C is false — Terraform doesn't render diagrams. D is false — wikis handle images fine.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: After adopting Terraform, a manager asks whether engineers are now forbidden from ever opening the cloud console again. What is the exam-correct answer?
options: Yes — any console access violates Infrastructure as Code principles
No — the console remains useful for reading state and investigating; IaC prohibits unmanaged changes, not looking
Yes — the cloud provider disables console access once Terraform manages the account
No — but console access is only permitted during incidents
explain: IaC bans unmanaged mutation, not observation. Reading the console to investigate, verify, or learn is normal; the rule is that changes flow through code so they are reviewed and recorded. A overstates the practice into a ban that doesn't exist. C invents a provider behavior. D invents a restriction — routine read access is fine anytime.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A provider developer tests a custom AWS provider build locally using dev_overrides. It works, so they merge — but the HCP Terraform run for that commit downloads the official registry provider, and the custom fix goes untested. What explains the difference?
options: dev_overrides only affect the local Terraform CLI; remote runs in HCP Terraform never read the engineer's CLI configuration file
HCP Terraform does not support the AWS provider
The dev_overrides block must be committed to version control to affect remote runs
Remote runs require the provider binary to be uploaded as a run artifact
explain: dev_overrides live in the CLI configuration file (~/.terraformrc) on the engineer's machine — they reroute local plugin loading for development. HCP Terraform runs execute on HashiCorp's infrastructure with its own plugin installation, which ignores local CLI config. B is false. C is wrong — dev_overrides must never be committed; they're a local-dev-only escape hatch. D invents an artifact mechanism.

q: A required_providers entry declares source = "hashicorp/random" with no version argument. A reviewer flags the configuration as invalid, insisting every provider entry must pin a version. Is the reviewer correct?
options: No — the version argument is optional; without it Terraform accepts any available version, though leaving it unpinned is poor practice
Yes — required_providers entries without a version constraint cause terraform init to fail
No — but Terraform will refuse to install the provider until a version is added
Yes — a source without a version is only valid for providers in the hashicorp namespace
explain: The version argument is optional: omitted, the constraint is unconstrained and Terraform selects the newest available release. The reviewer confuses best practice (always pin) with validity. B invents an init failure. C invents a refusal — init proceeds happily. D invents a namespace-specific rule that doesn't exist.

q: An engineer runs terraform login to authenticate the CLI with HCP Terraform, then later wants to confirm the credential was fully removed after running terraform logout. Which file should they check?
options: .terraform.lock.hcl in the working directory
~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json, where the CLI stores API tokens for configured hosts
terraform.tfstate, which records the login session
~/.aws/credentials, which Terraform shares with the AWS CLI
explain: terraform login writes host credentials to credentials.tfrc.json in the CLI config directory, and terraform logout removes the entry for that host — checking the file confirms removal. A is the provider dependency lock file, unrelated to user auth. C never holds user credentials. D is the AWS CLI's file, unrelated to HCP Terraform tokens.

q: An engineer needs to free disk space on a build machine and is eyeing two candidates: the .terraform/ directory and .terraform.lock.hcl. Which is safe to delete, and why?
options: Both are safe to delete; Terraform regenerates everything from configuration alone
Delete .terraform.lock.hcl but keep .terraform/, because the lock file is only a cache
Delete .terraform/ but keep .terraform.lock.hcl — .terraform/ is a local installation cache that terraform init restores, while the lock file records the pinned provider versions the team agreed on
Neither can be deleted without corrupting the state file
explain: .terraform/ holds downloaded providers and modules — a pure cache that init rebuilds. The lock file is the team's record of exactly which provider builds were selected and verified; deleting it loses those pins and the next init may select different versions. A wrongly treats the lock file as disposable. B reverses the two. D confuses working-directory files with state, which lives separately.

q: An engineer hesitates to re-run terraform init on an already-initialized working directory, fearing it will upgrade all providers to their newest versions. What actually happens?
options: Re-running init is safe and idempotent — it reinstalls anything missing but keeps the locked provider selections; only init -upgrade changes versions
Init always upgrades to the newest allowed versions, so the fear is justified
Init deletes the state file and starts over
Init refuses to run twice in the same directory
explain: Init honors the existing lock file and backend state; it only fills in what's missing. Version changes require -upgrade (or edited constraints). B describes -upgrade behavior, not plain init. C confuses init with a destructive operation — init never touches state content. D is false — re-init is routine.

q: A provider publishes 2.4.0-beta1. A configuration constrains the provider to >= 2.0. The team runs terraform init expecting the beta to be selected, but Terraform installs 2.3.0 instead. Why?
options: Beta versions are only available from a network mirror, never the public registry
Terraform selects prerelease versions only through an exact version constraint (= 2.4.0-beta1 or the bare version); inexact operators like >= never match prereleases
The lock file always blocks prerelease versions
Prerelease versions require terraform init -upgrade to be selected
explain: Documented version-constraint behavior: prereleases (the -suffix versions) are excluded from range matching and are selected only by exact pins. A invents a mirror restriction. C is wrong — the lock file records whatever was selected, it doesn't filter prereleases. D confuses -upgrade (which still respects the same matching rules).

q: A root module calls a child module that uses the random provider, but the root configuration never mentions random. The engineer asks whether the child module directory needs its own terraform init. What is the answer?
options: Yes — each module directory must be initialized separately before use
No — running terraform init in the root installs providers for the entire module tree, including child modules
Yes — but only for providers not used by the root module
No — child modules download their own providers automatically during plan
explain: Init operates on the whole configuration: it walks the module tree and installs every provider any module requires. Per-module init is not a thing. A and C invent a per-directory init requirement. D is wrong — plan never installs providers; that's init's job.

q: A configuration needs two Docker providers: kreuzwerker/docker and a company's internal fork published as acme/docker. Both have type 'docker'. How does Terraform tell them apart?
options: It cannot — two providers with the same type always conflict
By the namespace portion of the source address (kreuzwerker vs acme); each required_providers entry maps a distinct source to its own local name
By the version constraint; different versions imply different providers
The second source address is ignored and both use kreuzwerker/docker
explain: A provider source address is hostname/namespace/type — the namespace (organization or user) distinguishes same-type providers, and each gets its own local name in required_providers. A is false — this is exactly what namespaces are for. C confuses versions with identity. D invents silent ignoring.

q: A team wants any 2.x provider release but never 3.0. Two engineers propose version = "~> 2.0" and version = "~> 2.0.0". Which is correct for the goal, and why?
options: "~> 2.0" — it allows >= 2.0, < 3.0, while "~> 2.0.0" would restrict to >= 2.0.0, < 2.1.0
"~> 2.0.0" — the extra precision is required to exclude major versions
Both are identical; the trailing .0 is cosmetic
"~> 2.0" — it allows >= 2.0 with no upper bound
explain: The pessimistic operator allows only the rightmost component to increment: ~> 2.0 spans 2.x (up to but not including 3.0), while ~> 2.0.0 spans only 2.0.x. B inverts the semantics. C ignores the documented difference. D drops the upper bound that ~> always implies.

q: An engineer on Windows creates ~/.terraformrc to configure a provider mirror, but Terraform ignores it. What is wrong?
options: CLI configuration files are not supported on Windows
On Windows the CLI configuration file is %APPDATA%/terraform.rc, not ~/.terraformrc
Provider mirrors can only be configured with environment variables
The file must be named terraform.rc only on Linux
explain: The CLI config file location is platform-specific: ~/.terraformrc on Linux/macOS, %APPDATA%/terraform.rc on Windows. A is false — Windows is fully supported. C is wrong — the config file is the standard place for provider_installation blocks. D reverses the platforms.

q: A registry module released version 2.0. The constraint allows it, but plain terraform init keeps installing 1.9. The engineer wants to update modules without touching providers or backend settings. Which command fits?
options: terraform init -upgrade, which upgrades everything including providers
terraform get -update, which updates installed modules only
terraform plan -refresh-only, which updates module versions as a side effect
terraform providers lock, which upgrades modules to their newest versions
explain: terraform get installs/updates modules only — providers and backends are untouched — and -update permits upgrading already-installed modules. A would also upgrade providers, which the engineer wants to avoid. C confuses refresh-only (state refresh, no config changes) with module installation. D manages provider hashes in the lock file, not modules.

q: An engineer runs terraform init -backend-config=base.hcl -backend-config=prod.hcl, and both files set the S3 key. Which value wins?
options: The first file wins; later -backend-config flags are ignored
Terraform errors out on duplicate backend keys across files
The last flag wins — multiple -backend-config options merge in order, with later values overriding earlier ones
The values are concatenated together
explain: Backend configuration from multiple -backend-config flags (and files) merges in order, later overriding earlier — the standard pattern is a shared base file plus an environment-specific override. A reverses the precedence. B is wrong — merging, not erroring, is the documented behavior. D invents concatenation.

q: A CI pipeline runs terraform init without -input, and the backend configuration is incomplete. The engineer adds -input=false expecting init to fill in defaults. What actually happens?
options: Init prompts anyway; -input=false only affects apply
Init fails fast with an error instead of hanging on a prompt — -input=false disables interactive prompts, so missing backend settings become an error rather than a question
Init skips backend configuration entirely and uses local state
Init waits 30 seconds for input and then continues with empty values
explain: -input=false makes Terraform non-interactive: anything that would prompt becomes an error, which is exactly what automation wants — fail loudly instead of hanging forever. A is wrong — -input applies to init too. C confuses -input=false with -backend=false. D invents a timeout behavior.

q: A CI pipeline runs terraform plan -out=tfplan -var=instance_type=t3.large. A later step runs terraform apply -var=instance_type=t3.xlarge tfplan, expecting the larger instance type. What happens?
options: t3.xlarge is applied — -var flags at apply time override the values used at plan time
t3.large is applied silently — the extra -var flag is quietly ignored
The apply errors out: -var and -var-file cannot be used with a saved plan, because the plan already includes the variable values set when it was created
Terraform prompts the operator to choose between t3.large and t3.xlarge
explain: A saved plan bakes in all input values, so Terraform rejects -var/-var-file at apply time with an explicit error rather than guessing — re-plan with the new value instead. A states the exact misconception the error prevents. B is wrong — it errors, it doesn't silently ignore. D invents a prompt; there is none.

q: A security team wants to run custom automated checks against proposed infrastructure changes, but the company does not use Sentinel. Which command gives them the plan in a machine-readable format their tooling can consume?
options: terraform plan -out=tfplan, because plan files are already JSON
terraform show tfplan piped through grep, which is the supported machine interface
terraform show -json tfplan, which renders the saved plan as JSON for external tooling
terraform output -json, which includes the planned changes
explain: terraform show -json converts a saved plan (or state) to JSON — the documented machine-readable interface that policy tools and custom checks consume. A is wrong — plan files are a binary-ish internal format, not JSON. B is fragile text scraping, not a supported interface. D is wrong — output shows values from state, not planned changes.

q: A team wants destroying the dev environment to go through the same review-then-execute discipline as creating it — a reviewed proposal first, execution second. Which workflow does this?
options: terraform destroy -auto-approve in the CI pipeline
Comment out every resource block and run terraform apply
terraform plan -destroy, review the screen output, then run terraform destroy as a separate step
terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.tfplan, review the saved plan, then terraform apply destroy.tfplan — the destroy executes exactly the reviewed proposal
explain: A saved destroy plan is the reviewable contract: reviewers approve the exact destroy actions, and apply executes that plan verbatim. A skips review entirely. B is a clumsy equivalent that still needs review of an unsaved plan. C re-plans at destroy time, so what runs may differ from what was reviewed.

q: A compromised EC2 instance must be destroyed immediately, but the other 200 resources must not be touched. Which single command destroys only that instance?
options: terraform apply -destroy -target=aws_instance.compromised
terraform destroy, because destroy always asks which resources to keep
terraform state rm aws_instance.compromised, which deletes the instance from the cloud
terraform plan -target=aws_instance.compromised, which destroys the target during planning
explain: Combining -destroy with -target limits the destroy plan to the targeted resource — one command, surgical. B would destroy everything. C is a dangerous confusion — state rm only forgets the resource in state; the live instance keeps running unmanaged. D is wrong — plan never destroys anything.

q: A team's plan makes so many concurrent API calls that the cloud provider rate-limits them mid-plan. How can they reduce the concurrency of Terraform's operations?
options: terraform plan -parallelism=5 (or any value below the default 10) — it caps how many resource operations run concurrently
terraform plan -target=aws_instance.one, because targeting eliminates all API calls
terraform plan -refresh=false, which disables parallelism entirely
Set TF_LOG=DEBUG, which slows API calls enough to avoid rate limits
explain: -parallelism directly controls operation concurrency (default 10); lowering it is the documented answer to provider rate limiting. B is wrong — targeting narrows scope but doesn't cap concurrency. C confuses refresh with parallelism. D is wrong — log verbosity doesn't throttle API calls.

q: After an engineer resizes a database in the cloud console, a teammate runs terraform output db_instance_type expecting the new size. They see the old size. Why?
options: terraform output displays values from the configuration files, not from real infrastructure
The console change corrupted the state file, freezing the old value
terraform output reads from the state file without refreshing — it never contacts the provider, so console changes are invisible until a refresh updates the state
terraform output requires a -refresh=true flag to see current values
explain: output is a state reader, not a live query: no refresh happens, so it reports the last-recorded values. A is wrong — outputs come from state, not config. B misdiagnoses normal behavior as corruption. D invents a flag that doesn't exist.

q: Two engineers debate: one claims -refresh=false and -refresh-only are opposites. What is the exam-correct resolution?
options: They are opposites — one refreshes state and the other does not
They are two names for the same behavior
-refresh-only is the default mode of every plan
They control different things — -refresh=false skips the refresh step during a normal plan/apply, while -refresh-only is a plan mode that only refreshes state and proposes no infrastructure changes
explain: -refresh=false modifies a normal run (plan/apply proceed, just without pre-refresh); -refresh-only changes the run's purpose entirely (reconcile state with reality, change nothing). They are different axes, not opposites. A states the misconception. B conflates them. C is wrong — normal planning is the default.

q: For a cost-allocation deadline, an engineer manually adds Owner tags to 40 resources in the cloud console. The tags are correct, and the team wants them recorded in state without Terraform modifying the tags themselves. Which workflow does this?
options: terraform plan -refresh-only -out=refresh.tfplan, then terraform apply refresh.tfplan — state is updated to match the real tags, with no resource changes proposed
terraform apply -refresh=false, which writes the console tags into the state file
terraform state pull > backup.tfstate, which syncs the state file with the cloud
Delete and re-import all 40 resources so the tags are captured
explain: Refresh-only mode exists to reconcile state with reality: the plan proposes zero infrastructure changes and the apply persists the refreshed state — the tags are adopted, not touched. B does the opposite, skipping refresh. C only downloads the state file; it doesn't update it from the cloud. D is needless surgery for a bookkeeping update.

q: An engineer runs a targeted apply (terraform apply -target=aws_instance.urgent) for an emergency fix. The fix is deployed. What should they do next to make sure the rest of the configuration is still converged?
options: Nothing — a targeted apply always converges the entire configuration
Delete the state backup so the next run starts clean
Run a full, non-targeted plan to surface any pending changes the targeted run skipped, and apply if needed
Run terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.urgent to clean up the targeting
explain: -target deliberately narrows the operation, so other pending changes are deferred, not resolved — a follow-up full plan is the documented way to confirm everything else is converged. A is the dangerous misconception: targeting skips, not includes, the rest. B destroys the safety net for no reason. D would destroy the just-fixed resource.

q: An instance is behaving erratically and the team wants it replaced. They know terraform taint is deprecated. What is the current command to force replacement on the next apply?
options: terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.flaky, which marks the resource for destroy-and-recreate
terraform taint aws_instance.flaky, because deprecation warnings can be ignored
Delete the resource from the state file with terraform state rm and re-import it
terraform plan -replace=aws_instance.flaky, because -replace only works on plan, never apply
explain: -replace is the supported successor to taint and works on both plan and apply, flagging the resource for replacement. B ignores a real deprecation (taint deprecated since 0.15.2). C is destructive surgery — state rm orphans the live instance. D is wrong about the flag's availability; it works on apply too.

q: A solo developer uses local state and wonders when terraform plan -lock=false is acceptable. What is the exam-correct guidance?
options: Always — state locks are advisory and Terraform works fine without them
-lock=false is required for all CI pipelines to avoid hangs
Only for local, single-operator workflows — disabling the lock on shared remote state risks concurrent runs corrupting the state file
-lock=false speeds up plans by skipping the refresh phase
explain: Locking exists to prevent concurrent state writes; with one operator and local state there is nothing to collide with, but on shared remote state disabling it invites corruption. A is wrong — locks are enforced, not advisory. B is wrong — CI should use -lock-timeout, not disable locking. D confuses locking with refresh.

q: An engineer notices that terraform apply with zero configuration changes still takes two minutes and rewrites the state file. Why isn't it instantaneous?
options: Terraform always recreates at least one resource per apply
This indicates a corrupted state file slowing down the run
The time is spent entirely on state locking overhead
Apply still runs the refresh phase — reading real infrastructure to confirm nothing drifted — and persists the refreshed state, even when no changes result
explain: No-change doesn't mean no-work: refresh performs API reads for every managed resource and the state is rewritten with the results. A is false — zero-change applies create nothing. B misdiagnoses normal behavior as corruption. C overstates locking, which is a small fraction of the time.

q: A CI pipeline is split into two jobs: 'plan' on pull requests and 'apply' after merge. How should the pipeline guarantee the apply executes exactly the plan reviewers approved?
options: Re-run terraform plan in the apply job — plans are deterministic so it will match
Copy the .tf files to the apply job and run terraform apply without a plan file
terraform plan -out=tfplan in the plan job, pass tfplan between jobs as an artifact, and run terraform apply tfplan — the saved plan is the reviewed contract
Run terraform apply -auto-approve in the plan job so no second job is needed
explain: The saved plan file is the mechanism for plan/apply separation: it freezes the reviewed changes and apply executes that exact plan (erroring if config drifted since). A is unreliable — re-planning can produce a different plan. B applies whatever the current code says, not what was reviewed. D collapses the separation the pipeline was designed to enforce.

q: An engineer deletes an aws_s3_bucket resource block and adds removed { from = aws_s3_bucket.logs } with no lifecycle nested block, then applies. The bucket — full of data — is deleted. What went wrong?
options: removed blocks always delete the real object; there is no way to keep it
The engineer should have used terraform state rm instead, which never deletes anything
removed blocks only work on resources with count or for_each
Nothing in the configuration was wrong except the missing lifecycle { destroy = false } — a removed block defaults to destroy = true, so Terraform deleted the bucket
explain: The removed block's default is destroy = true: without explicitly opting out, Terraform destroys the object it stops managing. The safe form is lifecycle { destroy = false }. A is wrong — destroy = false preserves the object. B is true about state rm but misses the point: the removed block is the reviewable way, it just needs the lifecycle setting. C invents a count/for_each restriction.

q: A team wants to stop managing a legacy resource, and the change must go through pull-request review like any other infrastructure change. Which approach fits, and why?
options: terraform state rm, because it is instantaneous and needs no review
A removed block with lifecycle { destroy = false } — it is declarative, appears in the plan for review, and is version controlled, unlike the imperative state rm
Delete the resource block and apply immediately without any other change
Comment out the resource block, which Terraform treats as a removal request
explain: removed blocks bring 'stop managing this' into the normal code-review workflow: the plan shows the removal before anything happens. state rm (A) acts immediately on shared state with no plan and no review trail. C without a removed block would plan to destroy the resource. D is wrong — commenting out a block is identical to deleting it: Terraform plans destruction.

q: A resource was renamed from aws_instance.a to aws_instance.b last quarter (with a moved block), and now must be renamed again to aws_instance.c. How should the configuration record both renames?
options: Only one moved block is allowed per configuration, so the old one must be deleted first
Chain two moved blocks — from a to b, and from b to c — so users upgrading from either old address converge on aws_instance.c
moved blocks cannot be chained; the engineer must use terraform state mv for the second rename
Delete both moved blocks and let Terraform recreate the resource at the new address
explain: HashiCorp documents chaining moved blocks for exactly this: each link maps one historical address forward, so configurations at any previous address upgrade cleanly to the final one. A invents a one-block limit. C is wrong — chaining is the recommended pattern, and state mv would bypass review. D would destroy and recreate a live resource.

q: A check block's assert condition fails during terraform apply. The apply continues and finishes successfully, with a warning in the output. An engineer calls this a bug. Is it?
options: No — check blocks never block operations; a failed assertion produces a warning so the condition is visible, while the apply proceeds
Yes — any failed assert must halt the apply immediately
Yes — check blocks are only evaluated during terraform validate, never during apply
No — but the warning means the state file was not updated
explain: check blocks are observability, not gates: they surface failing conditions as warnings without stopping the run, and HCP Terraform re-evaluates them during health assessments. B confuses checks with preconditions/postconditions, which do halt execution. C is wrong — checks evaluate during plan and apply. D is wrong — state updates normally; only the warning is added.

q: A team writes check blocks asserting their service endpoints stay healthy. Where do these assertions get evaluated on an ongoing schedule, without anyone running Terraform manually?
options: terraform validate, which runs checks on every commit
Sentinel policies, which evaluate check blocks during plan
The Terraform CLI's built-in cron scheduler
HCP Terraform health assessments — continuous validation periodically evaluates check blocks against live infrastructure and reports drift
explain: Continuous validation in HCP Terraform runs health assessments on a schedule: check-block validation plus drift detection, with results surfaced in the workspace UI. A is wrong — validate is a static syntax check. B confuses Sentinel (policy-as-code on plans) with check blocks (assertions on live infra). C invents a CLI scheduler.

q: A resource has a lifecycle precondition that fails. At what point does the run stop?
options: After apply — preconditions are verified against the created infrastructure
At plan time — preconditions are evaluated before Terraform plans the resource's actions, so a failure blocks the plan itself
Preconditions are only evaluated during terraform validate
Preconditions never stop a run; they only emit warnings like check blocks
explain: Preconditions are plan-time gates: they evaluate before the resource is planned, and failure stops the run before anything is created — that's what makes them useful for catching invalid inputs early. A describes postconditions, which evaluate after apply. C is wrong — validate doesn't evaluate lifecycle conditions. D confuses preconditions with check blocks.

q: A resource defines lifecycle { postcondition { condition = self.private_ip != "" ... } }. What does self refer to, and when is it evaluated?
options: self refers to the root module, evaluated at plan time
self refers to the provider configuration, evaluated during init
self refers to the resource instance being created, evaluated after apply — so the condition can assert on the real provisioned attributes
self is not permitted in postconditions; only preconditions may use it
explain: In postconditions, self is the resource instance after apply, letting authors assert on actual provisioned values (like an assigned IP). A confuses self with the module scope. B invents provider/init involvement. D reverses the truth — self is available in both, and is most useful in postconditions.

q: An engineer writes dynamic "provisioner" { for_each = var.scripts ... } hoping to generate repeated provisioner blocks. What happens?
options: Terraform errors — dynamic blocks cannot generate meta-argument blocks like provisioner or lifecycle; those must be written statically
It works — one provisioner block is generated per element of var.scripts
It works, but only for local-exec provisioners
The provisioners are generated but only run on destroy
explain: Documented limitation: dynamic blocks generate only nested block types belonging to the resource/data source/provider — never meta-arguments (lifecycle, provisioner), which Terraform must process before expressions are safe to evaluate. B states the hoped-for behavior that doesn't exist. C invents a provisioner-type exception. D invents destroy-only generation.

q: A provider's resource type nests blocks two levels deep (e.g., origin groups containing origins). Can a dynamic block generate the inner blocks dynamically too?
options: No — dynamic blocks cannot be nested under any circumstances
Yes — but only one dynamic block is allowed per resource
No — nested structures must be written out statically
Yes — a dynamic block can be nested inside the content portion of an outer dynamic block, with each level getting its own iterator
explain: HashiCorp documents nesting dynamic blocks inside the content of an outer dynamic block for multi-level structures — each level iterates its own collection with its own iterator. A and C deny a documented capability. B invents a one-per-resource limit.

q: A dynamic block has for_each = [] because the input list is empty. What happens?
options: Terraform raises an error: for_each must not be empty
Zero blocks are generated — an empty for_each simply produces no nested blocks, with no error
One empty block is generated as a placeholder
The entire resource is skipped
explain: Empty collections are the standard way to make a nested block conditional: zero elements means zero blocks, cleanly. A invents an error that doesn't exist (this is also why var.enable ? [1] : [] is the idiom for optional blocks). C invents placeholder blocks. D confuses block generation with resource creation.

q: A variable marked sensitive flows into a resource argument and then into an output. The output was not marked sensitive. What does Terraform do with the output value, and where does the secret still live?
options: Terraform strips the sensitive marking at the output; the value is safe everywhere
The output is automatically treated as sensitive because the marking propagates through references — but the value is still stored in plaintext in the state file
Terraform refuses to plan until every downstream output is manually marked sensitive
Sensitive values are encrypted in the state file automatically
explain: Sensitivity propagates: any expression touching a sensitive value becomes sensitive, so the output is redacted in UI output automatically. But redaction is display-only — the state file still holds the plaintext value, which is why state access must be guarded. A is dangerously wrong — nothing strips the marking. C invents a plan failure. D is the classic misconception: Terraform never encrypts state itself.

q: A configuration calls provider::terraform::encode_tfvars({ name = "web" }). Terraform errors that the function is not available. What must be declared for this provider-defined function to work?
options: Nothing — provider-defined functions are built in and always available
A provider "terraform" block with credentials
The function must be defined as a local value first
The terraform provider in required_providers with source = "terraform.io/builtin/terraform" — the function belongs to that provider and must be declared as a dependency
explain: Provider-defined functions live in providers: the call syntax is provider::<local-name>::<function>, and the provider must be declared in required_providers — here the built-in terraform provider. A is wrong — they're provider capabilities, not built-ins. B confuses declaration with a configured provider block (no credentials exist for it). C invents a locals requirement.

q: A team uses a terraform_data resource to run a provisioner that installs software, and they want the provisioner to re-run whenever the content of deploy.sh changes. Which pattern does this?
options: terraform_data with input = filesha256("deploy.sh") and triggers_replace referencing that input — a content change forces replacement, which re-runs the provisioner
count = filesha256("deploy.sh") on the terraform_data resource, since count accepts a hash directly
A plain variable holding the file content — variables alone trigger replacement when they change
terraform_data with prevent_destroy, which forces re-provisioning on every apply
explain: terraform_data's input stores arbitrary values in state and triggers_replace names values whose change forces replacement — the file hash changing replaces the resource, re-running its provisioners. B is wrong — count needs a whole number. C is wrong — variable changes alone don't force replacement. D inverts prevent_destroy, which blocks destruction rather than causing it.

q: A configuration consumes both the public terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws module and the company's private app.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws module. An engineer asks why only the private one spells out a hostname. Why?
options: Private modules use a different source type that requires a hostname
The hostname is optional everywhere and the private address is just verbose by convention
Public modules are exempt from version pinning, so their addresses are shorter
The public registry is Terraform's default hostname, so it is omitted by convention — private registries must name their host explicitly
explain: Source addresses are hostname/namespace/name/provider; registry.terraform.io is the assumed default, so public modules show only three parts while private ones need all four. A invents a separate source type. B is wrong — the hostname is required for non-default registries. C confuses address length with versioning.

q: A Git repository holds three modules in subdirectories: modules/vpc, modules/eks, and modules/rds. How does a module block address only the vpc module?
options: Git sources cannot address subdirectories — each module needs its own repository
source = "git::https://github.com/acme/infra.git//modules/vpc" — the double slash separates the repository URL from the subdirectory path
source = "git::https://github.com/acme/infra.git/modules/vpc" — a single slash selects the subdirectory
terraform init prompts for which subdirectory to use
explain: The // subdir separator is the documented syntax for addressing part of a repository — single-slash is just a (nonexistent) URL path. A denies a standard monorepo pattern. C uses the wrong separator. D invents an interactive prompt.

q: A team edits a local-path module (source = "./modules/vpc") and re-runs plan. A teammate insists they must run terraform init -upgrade first. Is that necessary?
options: Yes — init -upgrade is required after any module change
No — but they must delete .terraform/modules first or the old copy is used
No — local path modules are read fresh from disk on every run; -upgrade only matters for versioned registry sources
Yes — otherwise the plan uses the version recorded in the lock file
explain: Local modules aren't versioned or cached by version — Terraform reads them directly each run, so edits take effect immediately. A invents an -upgrade requirement. B confuses the download cache with local paths. D confuses module versions with the provider lock file.

q: A root module needs the ID of a subnet created inside a child module. The engineer tries module.vpc.aws_subnet.private.id and it fails. What is the correct approach?
options: The child module must expose the value through an output block; the root then references module.vpc.subnet_id — resources inside a module are only reachable via its outputs
Use terraform_remote_state to read the child module's state directly
Reference it as data.aws_subnet.private inside the root module
Module internals are unreachable by design; duplicate the resource in the root
explain: Module encapsulation: only declared outputs cross the module boundary — internal resource addresses aren't visible outside. B misuses remote state (for separate configurations, not child modules). C invents a data source shortcut. D defeats modularization entirely.

q: A platform engineer notices their no-code-ready module contains provider blocks, which reusable modules normally must not have. They ask whether to remove them. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes — remove them; no-code modules follow the same rules as every other module
No — but the module will fail because providers are forbidden in the private registry
No — and hardcode credentials in those provider blocks so deployments never need variables

No — no-code modules are the exception: they must be self-contained, including provider configuration, because no root module will configure providers for them (credentials still come from variable sets, never hardcoded)
explain: No-code modules deploy without any calling configuration, so they carry their own provider blocks — HashiCorp documents this explicitly — while credentials are supplied via variable sets. A applies the general rule to the documented exception. B invents a registry prohibition. C is a security anti-pattern: credentials never belong in module code.

q: An engineer hot-fixes a bug by editing files directly inside .terraform/modules/vpc. The fix works, but vanishes after the next terraform init. Why?
options: Terraform detects manual edits and reverts them as a security measure
Module edits require terraform apply -refresh-only to persist
The engineer edited the wrong copy; the active copy lives in the state file
.terraform/modules is a download cache — init re-installs modules from their source, discarding local edits; the fix belongs in the module's source (a new registry version or the source repo)
explain: .terraform is disposable cache, not source of truth — init re-fetches per the recorded source/version. The durable fix is a new module version or a commit to the source repo. A invents edit detection. B confuses refresh-only with module installation. C invents module storage in state.

q: A team renames a module call from module "app" to module "frontend". Without any refactoring block, Terraform plans to destroy and recreate every resource in the module. How do they avoid that?
options: Run terraform state mv once per resource — moved blocks cannot target modules
Delete the module and re-import each resource with import blocks
Add moved { from = module.app to = module.frontend } — moved blocks operate on whole module calls, not just individual resources
Module renames are always destructive; schedule a maintenance window
explain: moved blocks accept module addresses, remapping every resource inside in one declaration — the reviewable equivalent of many state mv calls. A is wrong — per-resource state mv works but bypasses review and is tedious. B is needless surgery. D surrenders to destruction that refactoring blocks exist to prevent.

q: A team deletes a module block for a decommissioned project. Terraform plans to destroy 30 resources, but another team is adopting the infrastructure and it must keep running. What replaces the module block?
options: Nothing — deleting the block already keeps the resources running
terraform state rm for each of the 30 resources, run by hand before the next apply
removed { from = module.legacy } with no lifecycle block — the default keeps resources alive
removed { from = module.legacy lifecycle { destroy = false } } — the module's resources leave Terraform management intact instead of being destroyed
