explain: removed blocks accept whole-module addresses, and destroy = false is what keeps the real objects alive while management ends. A is wrong — deleting the block plans destruction. B works but is imperative and unreviewed. C is the trap — the removed default is destroy = true.

q: A child module must create resources in two AWS regions. The root defines provider "aws" and provider "aws" { alias = "eu" }. How does the root give the module access to the aliased provider?
options: providers = { aws = aws.eu } inside the module block — the aliased configuration is passed explicitly to the child module
The module automatically inherits all aliased providers from the root
The child module declares its own provider "aws" { alias = "eu" } block with the region
Add a second terraform block in the child module for the aliased provider
explain: The providers meta-argument explicitly maps provider configurations into the module — child modules never implicitly receive aliased providers (only the default configuration is inherited). B states the common misconception. C violates the rule against provider blocks in reusable modules. D invents a second terraform block mechanism.

q: An engineer's CLI fails to download private registry modules with 401 Unauthorized, though their token is valid. Where does Terraform look for private registry credentials?
options: The backend block, which authenticates all registry access
The CLI configuration file's credentials block for app.terraform.io (written by terraform login) — CI systems populate it non-interactively instead of logging in
The required_providers block, which accepts a token argument
A TF_VAR_registry_token environment variable
explain: Registry auth lives in CLI config: credentials "app.terraform.io" { token = ... } — login writes it, automation writes it directly. A confuses state-backend auth with registry auth. C invents a token argument on required_providers. D invents an env var convention.

q: A registry module validates its instance_type variable against an allowed list. A caller passes "db.mega.xlarge", which is not allowed. When does the failure surface?
options: During terraform init, which validates all module inputs
At plan time — variable validation runs before any infrastructure changes, failing fast with the validation error message
During apply, after the resources are created
Never — variable validation blocks are advisory only
explain: Variable validation is a plan-time gate: invalid inputs fail before anything is provisioned, which is the point of declaring them. A is wrong — init installs modules, it doesn't evaluate variables. C defeats the purpose of early validation. D confuses validation with check blocks.

q: A module author force-pushes the v1.2.0 Git tag to fix a bug after publishing to the private registry. What do consumers who pin version = "1.2.0" get on their next init?
options: The fixed code — the registry tracks the tag, so it follows the force-push
An error, because the registry detects the tag changed
The registry automatically deletes the compromised version
The original v1.2.0 — published registry versions are immutable snapshots; re-tagging does not change what was published, and consumers must wait for v1.2.1
explain: Registry versions are immutable: publishing snapshots the code at the tag, so later tag moves don't affect the published artifact — the fix needs a new version. A describes tag-following, which registries deliberately don't do. B invents tag-change detection. C invents automatic deletion.

q: Resources aws_instance.web["a"] and aws_instance.web["b"] must move into module.servers without recreation. Which state mv invocation preserves the for_each instance keys?
options: terraform state mv 'aws_instance.web' 'module.servers.aws_instance.web' — keys are re-derived automatically
terraform state mv cannot move for_each instances; use import blocks instead
terraform state mv 'aws_instance.web["a"]' 'module.servers.aws_instance.web["a"]' — each instance address, key included, maps to its new address
terraform state mv 'aws_instance.web[*]' 'module.servers.aws_instance.web[*]' — wildcards move all instances at once
explain: state mv works on full resource addresses including instance keys — each instance is moved individually with its key intact. A drops the keys, which is an invalid address mapping. B is wrong — for_each instances move fine. D invents wildcard support that state mv doesn't have.

q: A team is splitting a monolithic state: database resources must move from the main local state file to a separate state file for the data team. Which command moves them selectively?
options: terraform state mv -state=terraform.tfstate -state-out=database.tfstate aws_db_instance.main aws_db_instance.main — reads one state file, writes the resource into another
terraform state pull > database.tfstate, which extracts only the database resources
terraform state push database.tfstate, which moves resources out of the current state
Copy terraform.tfstate to database.tfstate and delete the unwanted JSON blocks by hand
explain: -state and -state-out let state mv operate across two state files — the selective move primitive for state splits. B is wrong — pull downloads the whole state. C is wrong — push replaces the entire state. D is dangerous hand-editing of state JSON.

q: After running terraform state mv against local state, an engineer asks what safety net exists if the addresses were wrong. What is the answer?
options: None — state mv is irreversible, which is why it requires -auto-approve
Terraform writes terraform.tfstate.backup before modifying the state, and best practice is to take your own backup (terraform state pull) first anyway
The previous state is recoverable from the plan file
Backups are only created for remote state backends
explain: Local state operations write a .backup file automatically — plus a manual state pull before surgery is the professional habit. A is wrong on both counts (backups exist; no -auto-approve on state mv). C is wrong — plans don't contain prior state. D reverses reality: local state gets file backups; remote backends rely on versioning.

q: An engineer points a configuration at a completely fresh S3 bucket and key for an isolated experiment, then runs terraform init -reconfigure. The experiment starts with empty state while the original state is untouched. Is this expected?
options: No — this is a bug; init always migrates state when the backend configuration changes
No — -reconfigure only works with the local backend
No — the engineer forgot terraform init -upgrade, which is required for backend changes
Yes — -reconfigure points Terraform at the new backend configuration without migrating any state; copying state over is what -migrate-state is for
explain: -reconfigure means 'use the new backend settings, leave state alone'; -migrate-state means 'copy existing state into the new backend'. The experiment scenario is exactly what -reconfigure is for. A mislabels documented behavior as a bug. B invents a backend restriction. C confuses provider/module upgrades with backend migration.

q: A team sets use_lockfile = true in their S3 backend configuration. What changes about state locking?
options: State is no longer locked during operations
The S3 bucket must now have versioning disabled for locking to work
Terraform coordinates locking with a lock file object in the bucket itself, instead of a DynamoDB table — DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated
Locking now requires a separate aws_dynamodb_table resource in the configuration
explain: Since 1.10 the S3 backend supports native lock files (use_lockfile), and DynamoDB locking was deprecated in 1.11 — no sidecar table needed. A is wrong — locking still happens. B invents a versioning requirement. D describes the old DynamoDB pattern this replaces.

q: Two CI jobs occasionally overlap and the loser fails with 'Error acquiring state lock'. The team wants the loser to wait its turn instead of failing. Which flag does this?
options: terraform plan -lock-timeout=5m — Terraform waits up to five minutes for the lock instead of failing immediately
terraform plan -lock=false, which makes locking failures impossible
terraform force-unlock, run automatically before every plan
Delete the lock object from the backend between runs
explain: -lock-timeout is the graceful answer: wait for the legitimate holder to finish. B is unsafe — disabling locks invites concurrent-write corruption. C is dangerous automation — force-unlock is for crashed runs, and unlocking a live run corrupts state. D is manual lock-breaking with the same corruption risk.

q: An engineer restores a state backup with terraform state push backup.tfstate and gets an error about lineage mismatch. What does this mean?
options: The backup file is corrupted and unusable
terraform state push is read-only and cannot restore backups
push guards against overwriting a different state lineage — the backup's lineage UUID doesn't match the current state's, so -force is required to override it deliberately
The backup was taken with a different Terraform version
explain: Every state has a lineage UUID; push refuses to replace a state with a different lineage unless -force acknowledges the intent — protection against restoring the wrong backup. A misdiagnoses a safety check as corruption. B is wrong — push writes state. D is wrong — version isn't what lineage tracks.

q: A team isolates production with terraform workspace new prod. During a late-night session, an engineer applies a development change while accidentally selected into prod. What does this incident reveal about workspaces?
options: Workspaces provide access control, so this should have been impossible
Workspaces isolate state only — every workspace shares the same backend configuration and credentials, so selecting the wrong workspace applies real changes to the wrong environment
Each workspace needs its own backend block to be truly separate
Workspaces cannot share module code, which caused the confusion
explain: The classic workspace footgun: state separation without any guardrail on which workspace is active — one select command chooses the blast radius. A is the dangerous misconception: workspaces are not a security boundary. C is wrong — one backend block serves all workspaces. D is wrong — modules are shared normally.

q: A configuration declares terraform { cloud { organization = "acme" workspaces { name = "prod" } } }. A teammate asks where the backend "remote" block is. What is the answer?
options: The configuration is broken — a backend block is always required
The cloud block only enables local execution; remote state needs backend "remote"
The cloud block is the HCP Terraform integration — it configures remote execution and state natively, and backend "remote" is the older alternative for the same thing
Both blocks are required together or init fails
explain: The cloud block is the native HCP Terraform backend: remote operations and remote state without a separate backend stanza. backend "remote" is the legacy equivalent. A is wrong — exactly one of them is used. B inverts the cloud block's purpose (it's for remote execution). D invents a dual requirement.

q: A variable is declared with sensitive = true and applied. An auditor asks where the plaintext value can still be found by someone with repository and state access. What is the honest answer?
options: Nowhere — Terraform encrypts sensitive values everywhere they are stored
Only in the plan file, which should be deleted after apply
The values are hashed in the state file, so they cannot be recovered
In the state file — sensitive only redacts display output; the state still holds the plaintext value, which is why state access must be tightly controlled
explain: sensitive is a display mask, not encryption: state, and plan files, contain the real values in cleartext. Anyone asserting otherwise misunderstands the threat model. A states the classic misconception. B is wrong — the state file is the durable copy. C invents hashing.

q: A configuration tags resources with Name = "web-${terraform.workspace}". When applied in a fresh working directory where no workspace was ever created, what does the tag resolve to?
options: web-default — terraform.workspace returns the current workspace name, and every working directory starts in the "default" workspace
web- — the interpolation is empty until a workspace is created
An error — terraform.workspace may only be used inside modules
web-prod — fresh directories default to a workspace named prod
explain: terraform.workspace is simply the active workspace's name, and "default" always exists — it's the workspace you're in until you create and select another. B invents empty interpolation. C invents a usage restriction. D invents a prod default.

q: A team configures backend "remote" with workspaces { prefix = "network-" } and runs terraform workspace new prod. What is the resulting remote workspace called?
options: prod — the prefix is only a display label
network- — the workspace name is ignored when a prefix is set
network-prod — the prefix is prepended to the local workspace name to form the remote workspace name
An error — prefix and workspace names cannot be combined
explain: With a prefix, Terraform maps each local workspace name to a remote workspace named <prefix><name> — so network-prod. This is how one configuration fans out to many remote workspaces. A ignores the prefix semantics. B drops the name. D invents an incompatibility.

q: A team renames a for_each key from "blue" to "green" on aws_instance.web. Without intervention, Terraform plans to destroy the blue instance and create a green one. Which state mv remaps the existing instance to its new key?
options: terraform state mv 'aws_instance.web' 'aws_instance.web' — a no-op move refreshes the keys
No state command can do this; the instance must be recreated
terraform state mv 'aws_instance.web["blue"]' 'aws_instance.web' — dropping the key merges it back
terraform state mv 'aws_instance.web["blue"]' 'aws_instance.web["green"]' — the instance keeps its identity under the new key
explain: Instance keys are part of the address: moving blue→green tells Terraform the existing object is now the green instance — no destroy, no create. A is a literal no-op. B is wrong — key remaps are a routine state mv use. C produces an invalid address mapping.

q: Three instances are degraded and all three must be replaced in a single apply. How does the engineer flag all of them for replacement?
options: terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.a -replace=aws_instance.b -replace=aws_instance.c — the flag can be repeated for each target
terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.a,aws_instance.b,aws_instance.c — comma-separated in one flag
terraform taint aws_instance.a aws_instance.b aws_instance.c — taint accepts multiple addresses
Only one resource can be replaced per apply; run three applies
explain: -replace is repeatable, one flag per address. B invents comma-separated syntax. C is wrong twice over — taint is deprecated and takes one target. D invents a one-per-apply limit that doesn't exist.

q: An engineer imports a manually created database but types the wrong identifier. The import succeeds — attached to the wrong database. What is the lesson about import IDs?
options: Terraform validates identifiers against the cloud API before importing, so this cannot happen
Wrong IDs are harmless — terraform refresh corrects them automatically
Import IDs are just labels; any unique string works
Terraform trusts the given ID blindly — always verify the identifier against the provider first, because a wrong ID binds state to the wrong real object
explain: Import performs no 'is this the object you meant' check — the ID is taken at face value, so a typo adopts the wrong infrastructure. A invents validation that doesn't exist. B is wrong — refresh reads whatever the state points at. C confuses import IDs with resource labels.

q: After a Terraform panic, an engineer finds crash.log in the working directory and asks whether any logging had to be configured beforehand to get it. What is the answer?
options: Yes — crash logs are only written if TF_LOG was set before the run
No setup was needed — Terraform writes crash.log automatically on panic, unlike regular TF_LOG output which must be enabled before the run
Yes — the -debug flag must be passed for crash logs to be produced
No — but the crash log is written to the state backend, not the working directory
explain: crash.log is automatic on panic — no prior configuration required. That distinguishes it from TF_LOG logging, which only captures what happens after it's enabled. A and C invent prerequisites. D invents backend storage for a local diagnostic file.

q: Plan output shows: 'Warning: the aws_s3_bucket_object resource is deprecated, use aws_s3_object instead.' The team is tempted to ignore it since everything still works. What is the correct response?
options: Ignore it — deprecation warnings never lead to removals
Downgrade the provider immediately to silence the warning
Deprecation means the resource was already removed; the plan is lying
Schedule the migration — deprecated means the old name is slated for removal in a future provider version, so ignoring it just defers a breaking change
explain: Deprecation is advance notice of removal: the migration is inevitable, and doing it deliberately beats doing it during an emergency upgrade. A is the complacency the warning exists to prevent. B treats the symptom. C misreads 'deprecated' as 'removed'.

q: An engineer runs terraform workspace select prod on a fresh clone, but no prod workspace exists yet. What happens?
options: Terraform creates the prod workspace automatically and selects it
Terraform silently selects the default workspace instead
Terraform errors — select only switches to workspaces that already exist; create it first with terraform workspace new prod
Terraform deletes the current workspace and retries
explain: select is switch-only; new is create-and-switch. A confuses select with new. B invents silent fallback. D invents deletion.

q: Friday's apply created 50 resources in the wrong region. The team asks how to 'roll back' the apply. What is the exam-correct answer?
options: Run terraform rollback to undo the apply
There is no apply rollback — revert or correct the configuration and apply again; the next run converges reality to the corrected desired state
Restore the pre-apply state backup, which also deletes the wrong-region resources
Delete the state file so Terraform forgets the mistake
explain: Terraform has no rollback command: correction is forward-only — fix the config, re-apply, and the unwanted resources are destroyed as part of converging on the corrected state. A invents a command. C is the classic trap — restoring state doesn't un-create real infrastructure, it just blinds Terraform to it. D orphans everything.

q: A terraform destroy fails halfway through with a cloud API error. Some resources are gone from the cloud but remain in state. What is the correct recovery?
options: Run terraform state rm for the leftover resources to clean up the state
Delete the state file and start over — the state is now untrustworthy
The remaining resources are orphaned forever and must be deleted in the console
Fix the underlying API issue and re-run the destroy — Terraform reconciles from the current state, so completed deletions stay deleted and the rest are retried
explain: State is the record of what was accomplished: re-running destroy retries only what remains. A would orphan the leftovers (state forgets them, cloud keeps them). B destroys the record of progress. C gives up on the exact reconciliation Terraform is designed to do.

q: After upgrading the AWS provider, terraform validate fails: an argument the configuration uses was removed in the new provider version. The plan had been fine for months. What happened?
options: The state file was corrupted by the upgrade
Validate caches old provider schemas until terraform init -upgrade is run
The new provider version removed or renamed the argument — provider upgrades can change schemas, so the configuration must be updated per the provider's upgrade guide
Terraform validate does not support provider upgrades and must be skipped
explain: Providers evolve their schemas: upgrades can remove or rename arguments, and validate (using the newly installed schemas) catches it. The discipline is reading the provider CHANGELOG/upgrade guide before upgrading. A misdiagnoses a schema change as corruption. B invents schema caching. D invents a validate limitation.

q: A teammate asks what the HCP Terraform run list's 'Cancel' button does to a run that is mid-apply, and whether it is safe. What is the accurate answer?
options: Cancel rolls back all changes the apply made so far
Cancelling a run stops new operations from starting; completed changes stay in place and in state — it is not a rollback, and a follow-up run reconciles the rest
Cancel is only available before the plan finishes
Cancelling corrupts the state file and requires a restore
explain: Cancellation is graceful-stop, not rollback: in-flight operations finish or stop, everything completed is recorded, and the next run converges the remainder. A invents rollback semantics Terraform doesn't have. C is wrong — runs can be cancelled mid-apply. D invents corruption.

q: An engineer hits Ctrl+C during a long terraform apply. What is the state of the world afterward?
options: The state file is corrupted and must be restored from backup before anything else runs
Terraform rolls back every change the apply made, leaving zero trace
Terraform stops starting new operations and records what completed — re-running apply reconciles the rest, because interrupted applies are recoverable by design
All in-flight resources are left in an unknown state that only console deletion can fix
explain: Terraform handles interrupts gracefully: it stops, persists completed work to state, and the next run continues convergence — idempotent recovery, not disaster. A overstates the damage. B invents rollback. D ignores that completed operations are properly recorded.

q: An engineer runs terraform plan -replace=aws_instance.web -out=tfplan, reviews it, then runs terraform apply tfplan. Is the forced replacement honored?
options: No — -replace must be given on the apply command, not the plan command
No — -replace cannot be combined with -out
Yes — the replacement intent is recorded in the saved plan, so applying the plan file carries it out
Only if -auto-approve is also passed to the apply
explain: -replace is a planning input like variables: plan records it in the plan file and apply executes it. A invents an apply-only restriction. B invents a flag incompatibility. D confuses approval with replacement semantics.

q: A plan shows changes to resources nobody on the team touched, and no configuration was edited. What are the usual suspects the team should investigate before applying?
options: Drift from out-of-band console changes, a provider or module version that shifted, or a teammate's unreviewed commit — investigate first, because the plan is reporting real inputs
This is always a Terraform bug; file an issue and apply anyway
The state file is corrupted; restore from backup immediately
Plans always show random changes; only the summary counts matter
explain: Unexplained plan changes have three mundane causes — drift, version shifts, or someone else's change — and the discipline is to identify which before approving. B abdicates investigation. C jumps to the rarest cause. D normalizes ignoring the plan, the opposite of the workflow's purpose.

q: A team wants an external security scanner to evaluate the planned changes after planning completes but before anything is applied. Which run task stage fits, and what does it receive?
options: Pre-plan — it receives the configuration before Terraform plans
Post-apply — it receives the final state after everything is done
Pre-apply — it runs before the plan is created
Post-plan — it fires after plan creation and receives the plan JSON, which is exactly what a scanner needs to evaluate
explain: Post-plan is the stage for plan analysis: HCP Terraform delivers the plan JSON to the task endpoint. Pre-plan (A) fires before any plan exists. Post-apply (B) is after the fact. C misdescribes pre-apply, which runs after planning, before apply — usable, but post-plan is the stage designed around plan content.

q: A run task fails, yet the run continues to apply with only a warning in the UI. A teammate asks what enforcement level this was, and which level would have stopped the run. What is the answer?
options: Advisory — it can never block a run; a mandatory task would have stopped the run on failure
Mandatory — it blocks only applies, not plans
Advisory — it blocks the run unless someone clicks continue
There are no enforcement levels; all run tasks are advisory
explain: Advisory tasks warn without blocking; mandatory tasks transition the run to an errored state on failure (including timeouts). B misdescribes mandatory. C inverts advisory. D denies the documented two levels.

q: An HCP Terraform workspace shows a health assessment result. Which two things did the assessment actually evaluate?
options: Sentinel policy results and cost estimation deltas
Terraform test execution and plan output
State locking status and backup freshness
Check block validation and resource drift detection — the assertions in configuration plus real-world vs state comparison
explain: Health assessments (continuous validation) do exactly two things: evaluate check blocks against live infrastructure and detect drift between real objects and state. A confuses governance/cost features with health. B confuses test-framework runs with assessments. C invents lock/backup checks.

q: An organization admin wants one view of every EC2 instance managed across 200 HCP Terraform workspaces, without opening each workspace. Which feature provides this?
options: Explorer — organization-wide visibility into resources managed across workspaces, collected from runs
Run tasks — they aggregate resource inventories as a side effect
Variable sets — they list every resource their variables touch
The private registry — it indexes all managed resources
explain: Explorer is the fleet-wide resource inventory: it aggregates what runs report across the organization for searching and filtering. B misattributes inventory to run tasks. C confuses variables with resources. D confuses the module/provider registry with resource tracking.

q: A platform team wants cost overruns blocked before infrastructure is created, not discovered in next month's bill. Which HCP Terraform combination does this?
options: Cost estimation appears on the billing page after apply; nothing can block beforehand
Estimated cost changes are shown on the run before apply, and Sentinel policies can evaluate them to stop over-budget plans
Cost estimation automatically cancels expensive runs with no configuration needed
Cost data is only available through the CLI, not in runs
explain: Cost estimation surfaces projected deltas on the run, and policy-as-code (Sentinel) turns those numbers into a gate. A is wrong — estimates appear pre-apply. C invents automatic cancellation. D is wrong — estimates are a first-class run feature.

q: A priority global variable set and a workspace-specific variable define the same key with different values. A run uses one of them. Which one, and why?
options: The workspace variable — workspace scope always beats global scope
The values are merged together
It is an error — duplicate keys across scopes are rejected
The priority global variable set — priority sets outrank everything below them, including workspace-specific variables
explain: Priority variable sets sit at the top of the precedence order by design — they override even workspace-specific values. A states the non-priority rule, which priority overrides. B invents merging. C invents an error; conflicts resolve by precedence.

q: Two non-priority workspace-scoped variable sets applied to the same workspace define the same key. How does HCP Terraform choose the winning value?
options: The variable set edited most recently wins
The larger variable set wins
A random one is chosen and flagged for review
Lexical ordering of the variable set names — the alphabetically-first set wins, regardless of edit recency
explain: Documented tie-break: at the same precedence level, conflicting keys resolve by lexical (Unicode code-point) ordering of variable set names — deterministic, not recency-based. A states the intuitive-but-wrong rule. B invents size-based precedence. C invents randomness.

q: A project-owned project-scoped variable set and an organization-owned project-scoped variable set define the same key. Which value does a workspace in that project use?
options: The project-owned set — at the same scope, project-owned variable sets take precedence over organization-owned ones
The organization-owned set — organization scope always wins
The workspace's own variables, which must exist for either to apply
Neither — the conflict fails the run
explain: Ownership is part of precedence: project-owned sets outrank organization-owned sets at the same scope, letting teams specialize shared defaults. B inverts the rule. C invents a requirement. D invents a failure mode — precedence resolves it.

q: A security team mandates zero long-lived cloud credentials stored in HCP Terraform. Which feature meets this, and how does it work?
options: Variable sets with short TTLs — credentials expire automatically
SSH agent forwarding through the run workers
Dynamic provider credentials — HCP Terraform mints short-lived, just-in-time credentials per run via an OIDC trust relationship, so nothing long-lived is stored
Storing credentials in the private registry instead of workspaces
explain: Dynamic provider credentials use workload identity (OIDC): each run gets unique, time-bound credentials with no rotation burden and no static secrets at rest. A invents TTLs on variable sets. B is irrelevant to provider auth. D moves the secret without eliminating it.

q: A platform team wants developers with no Terraform knowledge to deploy approved infrastructure patterns. How do they make a private registry module available for this?
options: Share the module's Git URL and hope developers learn the syntax
Grant every developer workspace admin so they can write configuration
Add the module to the no-code provisioning allowlist — it earns the No-Code Ready badge, and each deployment creates a workspace that runs the module with UI-supplied variable values
Email the .tf files to developers for local applies
explain: No-code provisioning is the self-service path: allowlisted modules get the badge and a Provision Workspace flow; HCP Terraform creates the workspace and starts the run automatically. A and D abandon the self-service goal. B grants dangerous permissions instead of a safe workflow.

q: A hard-mandatory Sentinel policy fails. An admin with the Manage Policy Overrides permission tries to override it and cannot. Why is this the expected behavior?
options: Admins can always override any policy — this must be a UI bug
Only soft-mandatory policies exist; hard-mandatory is not a real level
Policy overrides require the Terraform CLI, not the UI
Hard-mandatory failures cannot be overridden unless the policy set itself enables the 'can be overridden' option — the set-level switch takes precedence over the individual policy level
explain: Hard-mandatory is intentionally non-overridable by default; only the policy set's explicit override allowance lifts that, by design taking precedence. A denies the documented behavior. B denies the three enforcement levels. C invents a CLI-only restriction (CLI override exists only for soft-mandatory).

q: A Sentinel policy check shows status 'Errored' and the Override & Continue button is missing. The policy author insists the logic is correct. What is the most likely explanation?
options: 'Errored' and 'Failed' are the same thing — the button appears after refresh
Waiting a few minutes always resolves errored checks
The run will proceed on its own; errored checks never block
'Errored' means the policy itself could not be evaluated — a syntax error or unimported library, for example — and only Failed soft-mandatory checks can be overridden, so the policy must be fixed
explain: Errored ≠ Failed: an errored policy never produced a verdict (broken code, missing import), so there is nothing to override — fix the policy. A conflates the two statuses. B invents self-healing. C is wrong — errored checks have no enforcement level and block like failures.

q: A bank's auditors ask who changed the production firewall rules last Tuesday and exactly what changed. The platform team answers by linking a merged pull request that shows the plan output and the diff. Which IaC property makes this possible?
options: Every infrastructure change is a reviewed, timestamped commit, so the full history of who changed what and when is built into the workflow
Terraform automatically emails auditors before every apply
The state file records the identity of whoever ran apply
Provider APIs keep a permanent log that Terraform can replay on demand
explain: A is correct: with IaC, infrastructure changes flow through version control, so the commit history is a built-in audit trail of author, time, and exact diff. B is a misconception — Terraform sends no auditor emails. C is wrong — the state file tracks resource attributes, not user identity. D is wrong — providers do not keep Terraform-replayable permanent logs; the audit trail lives in version control, not the provider API.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A scheduled job runs terraform apply every 30 minutes as a compliance enforcement loop. A manager fears this will pile up duplicate resources. Why is the fear unfounded?
options: Each apply replaces all resources, so duplicates never accumulate
Idempotence — apply converges real infrastructure toward the declared desired state; when nothing has drifted, the run changes nothing
The state lock prevents the second and later runs from doing anything
Scheduled applies automatically run in refresh-only mode
explain: B is correct: idempotence means repeated applies converge on the same end state — a no-drift run is a no-op, so enforcement loops are safe. A is wrong: apply does not replace everything each run. C is wrong: the state lock serializes concurrent runs; sequential runs each acquire it normally. D is false: a scheduled apply is a normal apply, not refresh-only.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Someone deletes a VM directly in the cloud console. The next terraform plan proposes to recreate exactly one VM and change nothing else. What detected the out-of-band deletion?
options: The provider sent Terraform a deletion webhook
The configuration file auto-updated to remove the VM
Refresh compared real infrastructure against the state and detected drift from the desired configuration
The dependency lock file flagged the missing resource
explain: C is correct: before planning, Terraform refreshes — querying real infrastructure and comparing it to the state — so manual changes surface as drift in the plan. A is wrong: providers do not push webhooks to Terraform. B is backwards: the configuration never auto-updates; it remains the source of truth. D is wrong: the lock file pins provider versions and hashes, it tracks nothing about resources.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team's change process is: open a pull request, get the plan posted as a review comment, require two approvals, merge, then apply. What is this called?
options: A GitOps-style review workflow — infrastructure changes are proposed, reviewed, and approved as code before they are applied
Blue-green deployment
Canary release
ClickOps
explain: A is correct: treating infrastructure changes like software changes — PR, review, merge — is the GitOps collaboration model IaC enables. B and C are application deployment strategies (parallel environments, gradual rollout), not change-review workflows. D names the manual console-clicking practice this workflow replaces.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A startup runs dev on AWS and prod on Azure. An engineer asks why the team chose Terraform instead of CloudFormation for AWS plus ARM templates for Azure. What is the strongest answer?
options: Terraform provisions resources faster than native tools
Cloud providers charge lower API rates for Terraform calls
Terraform templates can be imported directly into CloudFormation
Providers give one consistent workflow and language across clouds instead of learning and maintaining a different native tool per cloud
explain: D is correct: the provider plugin model abstracts each cloud's API behind one language and workflow, which is Terraform's multi-cloud value proposition. A is wrong: speed is not the differentiator. B is false: API pricing does not depend on the client. C is false: there is no CloudFormation import path for Terraform templates.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A platform team publishes hardened, pre-approved Terraform modules so product teams can provision databases and queues themselves without deep cloud networking knowledge. Which IaC-enabled concept is this?
options: Multi-tenancy
Self-service infrastructure — a platform team codifies guardrailed patterns so product teams provision safely without being cloud experts
GitOps
Policy as code
explain: B is correct: reusable modules let a platform team package expertise into self-service building blocks with guardrails baked in. A is about shared infrastructure, not enablement. C is the change-review workflow, not the consumption model. D is compliance checking of plans — related, but it does not describe teams provisioning for themselves.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A plan shows the monthly cost delta of proposed changes, and finance reviews it before apply. Which IaC benefit does this illustrate?
options: Terraform negotiates discounted cloud pricing
Cost reports replace the need for plan review
Shift-left cost visibility — the financial impact is reviewed before anything is provisioned instead of discovered on the bill
Apply is automatically blocked until finance approves
explain: C is correct: because the plan enumerates every change up front, its cost impact can be reviewed pre-deployment — finance sees the bill before it exists. A is false: Terraform negotiates nothing. B is backwards: the cost estimate derives from the plan, it does not replace it. D is wrong: there is no built-in finance approval gate; review is a process the team adds.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A team debates managing 200 cloud resources with Terraform versus a long bash script calling the cloud CLI. Why is Terraform's declarative model the better fit at this scale?
options: You declare the desired end state and Terraform computes ordering, dependencies, and parallelism; an imperative script must hand-code every step and its order
Bash cannot call cloud APIs
Terraform scripts execute faster than bash
Declarative code does not need a state file
explain: A is correct: declarative IaC outsources the how — dependency graph, ordering, parallelism, retries — to the engine, while imperative scripts encode every step by hand and rot as scale grows. B is false: bash calls APIs fine. C is wrong: execution speed is not the argument. D is backwards: Terraform's declarative model depends on the state file to know current reality.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: After a regional outage, a team rebuilds its entire environment in a new region by running the same Terraform configuration with a different region variable. Which benefit made this recovery practical?
options: High availability
Automatic failover
Backup restoration
Reproducible disaster recovery — the whole environment is rebuilt from versioned code instead of reconstructed by hand
explain: D is correct: because the environment is fully described in code, disaster recovery is re-provisioning from a known-good definition, not archaeology. A and B are architecture properties (surviving failure, automatic switchover), not rebuild-from-code. C is wrong: no backup was restored — the infrastructure was recreated from configuration.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A security team wants every firewall change checked against corporate policy before it is deployed. How does an IaC workflow enable this?
options: Terraform encrypts all firewall rules at rest
Policy as code — planned changes are checked against codified rules before apply, so violations are caught pre-deployment
Providers automatically refuse insecure rules
Security groups cannot be managed by Terraform
explain: B is correct: because changes exist as a machine-readable plan before apply, policy engines can evaluate them and block violations before anything is created. A confuses encryption with authorization. C is false: providers provision what they are told; they do not judge security posture. D is false: security groups are routinely managed by Terraform.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Which task is OUTSIDE Terraform's core scope as an infrastructure provisioning tool?
options: Provisioning cloud networks, VMs, and load balancers
Managing DNS records through a provider
Coordinating create and destroy ordering across dependent resources
Ongoing OS-level configuration management such as patching packages and editing application configs — the domain of tools like Ansible or Chef
explain: D is correct: Terraform provisions infrastructure; continuous OS and application configuration management belongs to tools like Ansible or Chef — Terraform provisioners are a last resort, not a config-management engine. A, B, and C are all squarely inside Terraform's scope: provisioning resources, managing them via providers, and ordering operations across the dependency graph.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: Dev, staging, and prod each use the same configuration but keep completely separate state files, so an experiment in dev can never touch production resources. What principle does this illustrate?
options: Workspace sharing
Remote state coupling
Blast-radius isolation — separate states ensure a change in one environment cannot affect another's infrastructure
State locking
explain: C is correct: state separation bounds the blast radius — an apply can only ever touch what its state tracks. A is vague and wrong: nothing is shared here. B is the opposite: coupling states together increases blast radius. D is about concurrency (preventing simultaneous writes), not about isolating environments.
domain: Domain 1: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform

q: A configuration defines data.aws_ami.ubuntu and an aws_instance using its ID. The plan shows the AMI ID as (known after apply) instead of a concrete value. Why was the data source read deferred until apply?
options: Data sources are always read during apply, never during plan
The data source block contains a syntax error
The data source depends on a managed resource, so Terraform must wait until apply when that resource exists before it can read
Refresh is disabled for data sources
explain: C is correct: data sources are read during plan only when all their inputs are known; if they depend on a resource being created, the read is deferred until apply. A is false: plan-time reads are the norm when inputs are known. B is wrong: a syntax error would fail the plan outright. D is wrong: refresh concerns managed resources in state, not data-source read timing.

q: A root module contains module 'app' { source = './app' depends_on = [module.db] }. What does this depends_on guarantee?
options: Ordering only — every resource in module app waits for module db's resources; no data is passed and no values are shared
module app automatically receives module db's outputs as inputs
Resources in both modules are created in parallel for speed
module db is destroyed before module app is created
explain: A is correct: depends_on affects only ordering in the dependency graph; it never passes data — outputs must be wired explicitly through input variables. B is the classic trap: ordering is not data flow. C is the opposite of what depends_on does. D scrambles the ordering into nonsense.

q: A reviewer flags depends_on = [aws_db_instance.main] written INSIDE a shared child module. The reference resolves, so why is this still bad practice?
options: depends_on is not allowed inside child modules
It creates a hidden dependency — callers cannot see the ordering requirement, so the module is harder to reuse and reason about; dependencies should flow through input variables
It makes the module execute faster
Child modules cannot reference any resources at all
explain: B is correct: an in-module depends_on hides an ordering edge from the caller, making the module's requirements invisible and its reuse surprising — the fix is to accept the dependency as an input variable. A is false: it is syntactically allowed. C is backwards: extra edges slow planning, not speed it. D is false: child modules reference their own resources constantly.

q: Three subnets are built from ['10.0.1.0/24', '10.0.2.0/24', '10.0.3.0/24']. Removing the middle CIDR from the list must NOT recreate the other two subnets. Which construct achieves this?
options: count = 3 with count.index selecting the CIDR
count with the list, letting Terraform reorder
depends_on chaining the subnets together
for_each over the CIDR strings so each subnet is keyed by its stable address instead of a shifting index
explain: D is correct: for_each keys instances by the CIDR string itself, so removing one element only destroys that instance. A is the trap: with count, removing the middle element shifts every later index and recreates those subnets. B suffers the same index-shift problem. C only affects ordering, not instance identity.

q: A resource uses for_each over var.clusters, a map of objects each containing instance_type. Inside the resource block, how do you reference the current instance's type?
options: var.clusters.instance_type
each.value.instance_type — each.value is the object for the current key
count.index.instance_type
each.key.instance_type
explain: B is correct: with for_each over a map, each.key is the map key and each.value is the corresponding object, so each.value.instance_type reads the current one. A addresses the whole map, not one element. C is invalid: count and for_each are mutually exclusive. D is wrong: each.key is the key string, which has no instance_type attribute.

q: An output must list the private IP of every aws_instance.web created with count. Which expression is correct?
options: aws_instance.web[*].private_ip — the full splat collects the attribute from every instance
aws_instance.web.private_ip
aws_instance.web[private_ip]
element(aws_instance.web, private_ip)
explain: A is correct: the full splat [*] projects an attribute across all instances of a multi-instance resource into a list. B is wrong: without an index you cannot address a multi-instance resource. C is invalid syntax. D is wrong: element() takes a numeric index, not an attribute name.

q: A resource sets subnet_id = aws_subnet.main.id, and the author also adds explicit depends_on = [aws_subnet.main] 'for safety'. What is true of the explicit depends_on?
options: It is required — Terraform cannot infer the dependency
It is recommended for every interpolated reference
It is unnecessary — the interpolation already creates an implicit dependency; the explicit depends_on adds nothing
It will cause a dependency cycle error
explain: C is correct: referencing aws_subnet.main.id already inserts an implicit graph edge, so the explicit depends_on is redundant noise. A and B reflect the misconception that implicit dependencies are unreliable — they are the primary mechanism. D is wrong: a duplicate edge is harmless, not a cycle.

q: The root configures two aws provider configurations: the default (production account) and an aliased sandbox one. How does the sandbox S3 bucket resource select the sandbox configuration?
options: Define a second terraform block for the sandbox account
depends_on = [aws.sandbox]
Provider aliases are inherited automatically from the directory name
provider = aws.sandbox on the resource — the provider meta-argument selects a non-default (aliased) provider configuration
explain: D is correct: the provider meta-argument binds a resource to a specific (possibly aliased) provider configuration. A is wrong: there is one terraform block per module; accounts are provider configurations, not blocks. B is invalid: depends_on expresses ordering between resources, not provider selection. C is the misconception: aliases are never inherited implicitly.

q: An engineer adds prevent_destroy = true to the production database resource, then a teammate runs a plan that would destroy it. What happens?
options: The destroy proceeds with a warning
Only the database is skipped while the rest applies
Terraform prompts for an extra confirmation
The plan fails with an error — prevent_destroy rejects any plan that would destroy the resource
explain: D is correct: prevent_destroy is a hard guard — any plan containing the resource's destruction errors out before anything is applied. A is the dangerous misconception: there is no warn-and-continue. B is wrong: the whole plan fails, not just one resource. C is wrong: no extra prompt exists; it is an error, not a confirmation.

q: An external cost-allocation tool rewrites resource tags nightly, so every morning's plan shows tag-only diffs. How should the team silence this noise in configuration?
options: lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags] } — Terraform stops proposing updates for the tags attribute
Add depends_on pointing at the tagging tool
Remove the resources from state with state rm
Set tags to null in the configuration
explain: A is correct: ignore_changes tells Terraform to disregard external modifications to listed attributes. B is nonsense: depends_on cannot reference an external SaaS tool. C is the trap: state rm would make Terraform plan to recreate the resources. D does not help: null still differs from the externally-set tags.

q: The team wants new EC2 instances automatically whenever data.aws_ami.ubuntu resolves a newer AMI. Which lifecycle configuration does this?
options: depends_on = [data.aws_ami.ubuntu]
create_before_destroy = true
lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [data.aws_ami.ubuntu] } — a change in the data source forces replacement of the instance
ignore_changes on the ami argument
explain: C is correct: replace_triggered_by forces resource replacement when the referenced object changes — exactly the AMI-rotation pattern. A is the trap: depends_on only orders operations, it never triggers replacement. B controls replacement ordering, not what triggers it. D is the opposite: it would suppress the AMI change entirely.

q: A local-exec provisioner must re-run whenever var.script_version changes. The team wants the modern built-in pattern rather than the legacy null provider. What should they use?
options: count on the provisioner block
depends_on = [var.script_version]
A data source holding the version
A terraform_data resource with triggers_replace = { version = var.script_version } — the built-in replacement for null_resource, recreated when its triggers change
explain: D is correct: terraform_data is the built-in successor to null_resource; changing triggers_replace forces recreation, which re-runs its provisioners. A is invalid: provisioners accept no count. B is invalid: depends_on cannot reference variables. C is wrong: data sources are read, not recreated, so they trigger nothing.

q: For terraform state show, what is the correct address of the SECOND instance of aws_instance.api created with count = 3?
options: aws_instance.api.2
aws_instance.api[1] — count instances are zero-indexed
aws_instance.api[2]
aws_instance.api.second
explain: B is correct: count instances are addressed [0], [1], [2], so the second is [1]. A uses dot-index syntax, which does not exist. C is the classic off-by-one: [2] is the third instance. D invents a named-instance syntax that count does not provide.

q: A CI job only needs terraform validate, but terraform init fails because the pipeline has no backend credentials. The backend configuration itself is unchanged and valid. What is the correct init invocation?
options: Skip init entirely and run validate
terraform init -backend=false — install providers and modules without configuring the backend
terraform init -reconfigure
Delete the backend block from the configuration
explain: B is correct: -backend=false skips backend initialization while still installing providers and modules, which is all validate needs. A is wrong: validate requires an initialized working directory. C is the trap: -reconfigure still configures the backend, so it still needs credentials. D mutates committed configuration to work around a pipeline concern.

q: The provider constraint allows ~> 5.0, the lock file pins 5.1, and the team wants 5.4 without editing any configuration files. Which command does this?
options: terraform init -upgrade — re-resolves providers within the allowed constraints and updates the lock file
Edit the lock file's version number by hand
terraform apply -upgrade
Delete the .terraform directory only
explain: A is correct: -upgrade tells init to select the newest versions permitted by the constraints and record them in the lock file. B is dangerous: hand-edited hashes will fail verification. C is invalid: apply has no -upgrade flag. D is wrong: reinstalling without -upgrade selects the same locked 5.1.

q: A deploy script needs the db_endpoint output as plain text — no quotes, no formatting — to build a connection string. Which command prints a single string output value raw?
options: terraform output -raw db_endpoint — prints the string value with no quotes or extra formatting
terraform output with no arguments
terraform show -raw db_endpoint
echo $db_endpoint
explain: A is correct: output -raw renders one string output as plain text for scripting. B is wrong: bare output lists every output as name/value pairs, not one raw value. C is invalid: show has no per-output -raw form. D invents a shell variable that does not exist.

q: A pipeline is split: job A builds the plan, a human approves, then job B must execute exactly what was reviewed — nothing more, nothing less. Which workflow guarantees this?
options: Re-run terraform plan in job B and apply immediately
terraform apply -var-file in job B
Copy the state file from job A to job B
terraform plan -out=tfplan in job A, then terraform apply tfplan in job B — the saved plan file guarantees byte-identical execution of the reviewed changes
explain: D is correct: a saved plan file captures the exact reviewed change set, and applying the file executes precisely that. A is the trap: a fresh plan in job B can differ if anything changed meanwhile. B only supplies variables, not the approved change set. C copies state, which records reality — not the approved plan.

q: An engineer suspects someone changed infrastructure in the console and wants state synced with reality without modifying any infrastructure. Which command pair does this?
options: terraform plan -refresh-only followed by terraform apply -refresh-only — reconciles state with real infrastructure while proposing no infrastructure changes
terraform destroy -target on the suspect resources
terraform state rm on everything suspect
terraform refresh -force
explain: A is correct: refresh-only mode updates the state to match reality and never proposes creates, updates, or deletes. B is destructive: it would delete the resources. C orphans them: Terraform would then plan to recreate everything. D is invalid: refresh takes no -force flag, and the standalone refresh command is superseded by refresh-only mode.

q: A nightly automation pipeline must run terraform apply with no human at the keyboard. Which flag provides the non-interactive approval?
options: Pipe the word yes into terraform apply
terraform apply -auto-approve — skips the interactive confirmation prompt, intended for automation
Set TF_INPUT=yes
Add -target for every resource
explain: B is correct: -auto-approve is the designed mechanism for non-interactive applies. A is a fragile hack, not the supported flag. C is wrong: TF_INPUT controls whether Terraform may prompt for input values, not the approval. D is unrelated: targeting limits scope, it does not approve anything.

q: Without any cloud credentials available, what class of problems can terraform validate still catch?
options: Whether the plan matches real infrastructure
Whether the provider API credentials have sufficient permissions
Syntax, block structure, and static type errors in the configuration — no state access or provider credentials required
Corruption in the state file
explain: C is correct: validate performs static configuration checks only, which is why it runs without credentials or state. A is wrong: comparing against reality requires plan/refresh with credentials. B obviously needs credentials to test. D is wrong: validate never reads the state file.

q: A hotfix must update only aws_instance.bastion right now; everything else waits for the normal change window. Which flag scopes the run to that resource, and what is the caution?
options: terraform plan -refresh-only
-destroy -target is the only way to scope a run
There is no way to scope a run to one resource
-target=aws_instance.bastion — limits the plan and apply to the target and its dependencies, but routine targeting risks leaving other drift unaddressed
explain: D is correct: -target scopes plan and apply (including dependencies), with the well-known caution against habitual use. A is a different mode entirely: refresh-only never changes infrastructure. B is wrong: -target works with plan and apply, not only destroy. C is false: targeted runs are a documented feature.

q: Only a module source changed; the backend and providers are already initialized. What is the lightest command to update just the modules?
options: terraform get -update — downloads and updates modules without re-initializing the backend or reinstalling providers
terraform init -reconfigure
terraform plan -update
terraform apply -get
explain: A is correct: get is the module-only subset of init, and -update forces re-download of changed sources. B is the trap: -reconfigure needlessly resets backend configuration. C and D are invalid: neither plan nor apply has an -update flag.

q: Developers work on macOS ARM laptops while CI runs on Linux AMD64. How can the team guarantee both platforms install the same verified provider builds?
options: Commit the .terraform directory to version control
terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64 — records hashes for each platform in the dependency lock file
Run init -upgrade on each machine separately
Vendor the provider binaries by hand into the repo
explain: B is correct: providers lock adds per-platform hashes to the lock file so every platform installs the identical verified build. A is wrong: .terraform is a local cache and must not be committed. C does not add platforms — each machine would lock only its own. D is unnecessary manual work the lock file already handles.

q: A CI run hangs waiting for someone to type a variable value. Which flag makes Terraform fail fast instead of prompting?
options: TF_AUTO=yes
terraform plan -auto-approve
terraform plan -input=false — disables interactive prompts so missing input becomes an error instead of a hang
Provide an empty tfvars file
explain: C is correct: -input=false is the standard automation guard against interactive prompts. A is an invented variable. B is the trap: -auto-approve skips the approval prompt, not variable input prompts. D does not help: Terraform still prompts for variables with no value.

q: An apply manages 400 independent resources and crawls at the default concurrency. Which flag raises the number of simultaneous operations?
options: -target each resource in batches
count = 50 on the slowest resources
-parallelism=50 — sets how many resource operations Terraform runs concurrently (default 10)
-refresh=false always speeds up applies
explain: C is correct: -parallelism controls concurrent operations (default 10). A is wrong: targeting scopes the run; it does not parallelize it. B confuses resource replication (count) with operation concurrency. D is wrong: -refresh=false affects the plan refresh phase, not apply concurrency — and skipping refresh trades accuracy for speed.

q: A plan over a 5,000-resource state spends 20 minutes just refreshing. For a quick what-if on configuration changes, which flag skips the refresh phase?
options: -refresh-only
-target everything
-refresh=false — plans against the stored state without re-querying providers, trading accuracy for speed
-parallelism=100
explain: C is correct: -refresh=false skips provider refresh and plans from state as-is — fast but potentially stale. A is the opposite mode: refresh-only performs nothing but refresh. B does not skip refreshing. D raises concurrency but still refreshes every resource.

q: A variable instance_type must start with 't3.'; invalid values should fail fast with a clear message during plan. How is this enforced in configuration?
options: A validation block inside the variable with a condition on the value and a custom error_message — Terraform rejects invalid values before any infrastructure changes
Check the value inside a provisioner
Add depends_on referencing the variable
Variables cannot be validated; document the rule in the README
explain: A is correct: validation blocks evaluate a condition and surface error_message at plan time. B is wrong: provisioners run during apply — far too late — and are the wrong tool. C is invalid: variables accept no depends_on. D is the misconception: variable validation has existed since 0.13.

q: A variable declares default = 'us-east-1', but a caller explicitly passes null and the provider then errors on the null region. How can the module author make null fall back to the default?
options: Nothing — an explicit null always overrides the default
Add a validation block
Set nullable = false — a null assignment then falls back to the default value instead of remaining null
Set sensitive = true
explain: C is correct: nullable = false restores the pre-1.0-style behavior where null means 'use the default'. A describes the default behavior without the setting — the very problem being fixed. B only rejects values; it cannot substitute one. D is unrelated: sensitivity controls redaction, not null handling.

q: A variable's type is an object, and its tags attribute should be optional, defaulting to an empty map when the caller omits it. Which type-constraint syntax does this?
options: Make tags a required attribute
Declare the whole variable as type = any
Set default = null on the object
tags = optional(map(string), {}) inside the object type constraint — optional attributes with defaults are supported in type constraints
explain: D is correct: optional() marks an object attribute optional and supplies its default when omitted. A defeats the requirement. B is the trap: any abandons all type safety. C only defaults the entire object to null; it does not give the attribute a default.

q: A root module passes a sensitive variable into a child module, and the child exposes it through an output. The plan errors. What must the child module do?
options: Mark the output sensitive = true — sensitivity must propagate; an output carrying a sensitive value is rejected unless it is also marked sensitive
Remove sensitive = true from the variable
Wrap the output value in nonsensitive()
Sensitive values cannot cross module boundaries
explain: A is correct: Terraform tracks sensitivity through expressions, and a non-sensitive output exposing a sensitive value is an error — the output must declare sensitive = true. B is the dangerous shortcut: it strips protection instead of propagating it. C deliberately unveils the value — the opposite of what is wanted. D is false: sensitive values flow through modules freely as long as sensitivity is honored.

q: An engineer needs a non-sensitive identifier derived from a sensitive value, for use as a for_each key where sensitive values are forbidden. Which function explicitly removes the sensitive marking?
options: Sensitive values can never be transformed or used
nonsensitive() — explicitly unveils the value so it can be used where sensitive values are not allowed
tostring()
sensitive()
explain: B is correct: nonsensitive() is the deliberate opt-out that returns the raw value, placing responsibility on the author. A is false: transformation is allowed with care. C is the trap: tostring() preserves the sensitive marking. D does the opposite: it applies the marking.

q: A configuration reads an optional first list element's name, falling back to a default when the list is empty. Which function returns the first argument that evaluates without error?
options: coalesce()
can()
try() — evaluates each argument in order and returns the first one that succeeds, so a missing index falls back instead of failing
merge()
explain: C is correct: try() catches evaluation errors per argument, making it the tool for uncertain traversals. A is the trap: coalesce() picks the first non-null value but still errors on an invalid index. B returns only true/false, not the value. D combines maps and objects — unrelated.

q: Inside a variable validation block, an engineer needs a true/false test of whether a string parses as a number before converting it. Which function returns true when its expression succeeds and false on error?
options: try()
length()
tobool()
can() — returns a boolean indicating whether the expression evaluated successfully, ideal for validation conditions
explain: D is correct: can() is designed for exactly this — a boolean success probe for validation and conditionals. A returns the value itself, not a boolean. B measures string length, which says nothing about numeric parsing. C converts values and errors on failure rather than returning false.

q: An engineer wants the first non-null value among var.primary, var.fallback, and a literal default. Which function implements first-non-null-wins?
options: coalesce() — returns the first argument that is neither null nor empty string
merge()
compact()
distinct()
explain: A is correct: coalesce() scans its arguments and returns the first usable one. B is the trap: merge() combines maps, it does not select among scalars. C removes null/empty elements from a list but returns a list. D deduplicates list elements — unrelated to fallback selection.

q: A security group needs one ingress block per port in var.ingress_ports, a list that changes per environment. Which construct generates repeated nested blocks from a collection?
options: count on the security group resource
A dynamic block — dynamic 'ingress' with for_each over the list and a content block describing each rule
for_each on the provider block
A provisioner loop over the ports
explain: B is correct: dynamic blocks generate nested blocks from a collection, with each element available inside content. A is the trap: count would duplicate the entire security group, not its ingress rules. C is invalid: providers accept no for_each. D is wrong: provisioners execute scripts; they cannot author configuration blocks.

q: A cleanup script must run when a resource is destroyed — for example, deregistering it from an external inventory. How is a provisioner configured for destroy time?
options: Use a normal provisioner — they run on destroy by default
Set when = create
Set when = destroy on the provisioner — creation-time is the default, so destroy-time execution must be opted into explicitly
Provisioners cannot run on destroy
explain: C is correct: provisioners default to running at creation; when = destroy opts into destroy-time execution. A states the exact misconception the question traps. B selects creation-time explicitly — the default behavior, not what is asked. D is false: destroy-time provisioners are a documented feature.

q: A bootstrap script must execute ON the newly created VM, not on the operator's laptop. Which provisioner type and requirement apply?
options: local-exec — it runs on the remote host
remote-exec — it needs no connection information
Both provisioners always run locally
remote-exec with a connection block — remote-exec runs on the target host via the connection settings, while local-exec runs on the machine executing Terraform
explain: D is correct: remote-exec connects to the target (needing a connection block with host/credentials) whereas local-exec runs where Terraform runs. A reverses the two. B is wrong: without connection info remote-exec cannot reach the host. C is false: that describes only local-exec.

q: A user_data boot script needs per-environment values interpolated into it. Which approach renders a template file with variables for use as user_data?
options: templatefile() — renders a file template with the given variables, the standard approach for parameterized user_data scripts
A heredoc cannot interpolate variables
file() with variable references inside
Only provisioners can inject variables
explain: A is correct: templatefile(path, vars) renders the template with variables available for interpolation. B is false: heredocs do interpolate. C is the trap: file() reads raw content with no templating. D is wrong: user_data templating needs no provisioners.

q: A monorepo keeps its VPC module at modules/vpc inside a git repository. Which source address correctly points a module block at that subdirectory?
options: git::https://example.com/repo.git/modules/vpc
https://example.com/repo.git?modules/vpc
git::https://example.com/repo.git//modules/vpc — the double slash separates the repository URL from the subdirectory path
app.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws
explain: C is correct: for go-getter style git sources, // marks where the repo address ends and the subdirectory begins. A is the trap: a single slash becomes part of the repo URL and fails. B uses the wrong separator entirely. D is registry syntax, which does not apply to git sources.

q: A module is sourced from git and the team wants to pin it to the v2.1.0 tag. Which mechanism pins a git-sourced module to a tag?
options: version = '2.1.0' in the module block
Edit the dependency lock file
The double-slash subdirectory syntax
Append ?ref=v2.1.0 to the git source URL — the ref query selects the tag, branch, or commit
explain: D is correct: git sources are pinned with the ?ref= query parameter. A is the trap: the version meta-argument works only for registry sources, not git. B is wrong: the lock file records provider versions and hashes, not module versions. C addresses subdirectories, not versions.

q: A registry module declares version = '~> 3.0'. Which releases may Terraform select?
options: Any 3.x release (>= 3.0, < 4.0) but not 4.0 — the pessimistic operator allows minor and patch movement while capping the major version
Any version >= 3.0, including 4.0 and beyond
Exactly 3.0 and nothing else
3.0 through 3.9 only, excluding 3.10
explain: A is correct: ~> 3.0 means >= 3.0, < 4.0, so 3.10 and 3.99 are fine but 4.0 is excluded. B describes the >= operator, the classic confusion. C describes the = operator. D is the misconception that 3.10 is somehow beyond 3.9 — semver ordering allows it.

q: Module 'app' needs the VPC ID produced by module 'vpc'. How does the app module block reference that output?
options: var.vpc.vpc_id
module.vpc.vpc_id — module outputs are addressed as module.<module-name>.<output-name>
data.vpc.vpc_id
output.vpc_id
explain: B is correct: module.<name>.<output> is the addressing scheme for child-module outputs. A is wrong: var.* addresses input variables, not other modules' outputs. C is wrong: data.* addresses data sources. D invents an output.* prefix that does not exist.

q: The team needs one instance of the 'env' module per entry in var.envs, a map keyed by environment name, so removing 'staging' never disturbs 'prod'. Which module-block construct does this?
options: count = 3 on the module block
Hand-write one module block per environment
for_each = var.envs on the module block — each.key and each.value distinguish the instances by their stable map keys
Modules cannot use for_each
explain: C is correct: for_each on a module block creates one instance per map key, immune to the index-shift problem. A is the trap: count indexes would shift and recreate environments when one is removed. B is manual toil that for_each eliminates. D is false: modules have supported for_each for years.

q: A child module's resources must be created in the aliased provider configuration aws.west, which is defined in the root. Which module-block argument wires the child's default provider to that alias?
options: Add provider = aws.west to the child module's source code
Nothing — aliases are inherited automatically
Declare required_providers in the child
providers = { aws = aws.west } in the module block — the caller maps the child's expected provider to the aliased configuration
explain: D is correct: the providers meta-argument in the calling module block maps provider requirements to specific configurations, including aliases. A hardcodes the alias inside the child, destroying its reusability. B is the misconception: aliases are never inherited implicitly. C only declares which providers the child needs; it does not select configurations.

q: A shared child module contains terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = 'hashicorp/aws', configuration_aliases = [aws] } } }. What does configuration_aliases declare?
options: That the module expects the caller to pass in an aliased aws provider configuration via the providers argument
That Terraform creates the alias automatically
That the module pins the aws provider version
That the module enables for_each on itself
explain: A is correct: configuration_aliases is the child's declaration that it needs an additional (aliased) provider configuration supplied by the caller. B is wrong: aliases are defined in the root module, never auto-created. C is the trap: version pinning is the version argument, not configuration_aliases. D is unrelated: for_each needs no provider declaration.

q: A private registry on HCP Terraform hosts org 'acme's AWS VPC module. What is the correct module source address?
options: acme/vpc/aws
app.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws — <hostname>/<namespace>/<name>/<provider>
registry.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws
git::acme/vpc
explain: B is correct: private registry addresses are HOST/NAMESPACE/NAME/PROVIDER, with the HCP Terraform hostname first. A is the trap: omitting the hostname makes it unresolvable. C points at the public registry host, not the organization's private one. D mixes the git protocol with a registry-style path.

q: A reviewer rejects a published module as unmaintainable because it is a single 900-line file with no documentation. What is the conventional module structure reviewers expect?
options: A single main.tf is sufficient for any module
Provider binaries must be vendored inside the module
main.tf, variables.tf, and outputs.tf separating concerns, plus a README.md documenting usage — the standard layout consumers expect
Modules must be written as a single file by policy
explain: C is correct: the community convention splits resources, inputs, and outputs into dedicated files with a README, making modules discoverable and reviewable. A is the misconception being corrected: it works but does not scale for shared modules. B is wrong: providers are installed by Terraform, never vendored. D invents a rule that does not exist.

q: In a monorepo, the app configuration at live/prod needs the VPC module at modules/vpc in the same repo. Which source value is correct?
options: An absolute HTTPS URL
git::./modules/vpc
module.vpc
source = '../modules/vpc' — a relative local path, the standard approach for monorepo-local modules
explain: D is correct: plain relative paths address local filesystem modules. A is for remote sources. B is the trap: git:: requires a repository URL, not a local path. C invents a module.* source syntax that does not exist.

q: A team outgrows raw git URLs for modules: they want version constraints, a browsable catalog, and generated documentation. Which source type provides all three?
options: A registry (public or private) — versioned releases with constraint resolution, a searchable catalog, and auto-generated docs
Raw git URLs — they version modules better than registries
Local filesystem paths
HTTP tarball URLs in all cases
explain: A is correct: registries add versioning semantics, discovery, and docs on top of module distribution. B is the trap: git URLs work but provide no constraint resolution or docs UI. C offers no versioning at all. D overstates: tarballs are a valid source but bring none of the catalog benefits.

q: A monitoring module should exist only when var.monitoring is true, and the root must reference its endpoint output safely. Which pattern works?
options: Delete the module block from the files when monitoring is off
count = var.monitoring ? 1 : 0 on the module block, referencing module.monitoring[0].endpoint — the indexed instance exists only when created
for_each directly on the boolean variable
Modules cannot be created conditionally
explain: B is correct: count on a module block makes it conditional, and [0] addressing is safe because the instance exists exactly when count is 1. A is manual toil that defeats IaC. C is invalid: for_each requires a map or set, not a boolean. D is false: conditional modules via count or for_each are standard.

q: An engineer needs to adopt a single existing S3 bucket into state immediately, without authoring an import block. Which command imports it ad hoc?
options: terraform state mv
terraform refresh
terraform plan -import
terraform import aws_s3_bucket.assets my-bucket — the CLI form takes the resource address plus the provider's native ID, with no block required
explain: D is correct: the terraform import CLI command adopts one existing object with no configuration block needed. A is wrong: state mv re-addresses already-tracked resources, it cannot adopt new ones. B only syncs state with reality. C invents a flag that does not exist.

q: An import block will adopt the existing EC2 instance i-0abc123 into aws_instance.web. Which fields must the import block contain?
options: Only the to address
Only the id
source and version
to = <resource address> and id = 'i-0abc123' — the target address plus the provider's native resource ID
explain: D is correct: import blocks require to (where it lands in configuration) and id (the provider-native identifier). A and B each omit a required half — without to there is no target, without id Terraform cannot find the object. C invents fields: import blocks take no source or version.
