q: An engineer runs terraform apply -refresh-only after a colleague changed infrastructure in the console, believing this 'fixed the drift'. What did the command actually change, and what happens on the next normal plan?
options: Only the state file — refresh-only reconciles state with reality but never modifies infrastructure or configuration, so the next plan still proposes changes to match the configuration
The configuration files were updated to match reality
The drifted resources were destroyed
The dependency lock file
explain: A is correct: refresh-only updates state to mirror reality; it changes no infrastructure and edits no configuration — the drift is recorded, not remediated, so the next plan still proposes reverting it. B is wrong: configuration is never auto-edited. C is wrong: nothing is destroyed in refresh-only mode. D is unrelated: the lock file tracks providers.

q: An engineer writes bucket = var.bucket inside the backend 's3' block to avoid hardcoding the state bucket name. What happens at init?
options: It works — backend blocks accept variables
It fails — backend blocks do not support variables, interpolations, or locals; use partial backend configuration and supply values via -backend-config at init
It works if the variable is set through TF_VAR_bucket
Backend blocks support locals but not variables
explain: B is correct: backend configuration is loaded before variables exist, so no variables, interpolation, or locals are allowed — partial config plus -backend-config (or a config file) is the supported pattern. A and C share the same misconception: TF_VAR_ does not help because variables are unavailable that early. D is false: locals are equally unsupported.

q: An apply crashed mid-run and the state lock was never released. The error output includes the lock ID. How should the engineer safely clear the stale lock?
options: Delete the state file and re-create everything
Run terraform init -reconfigure
terraform force-unlock <ID> — releases the stale lock, after first confirming no apply is actually still running
Restart the machine and wait for expiry
explain: C is correct: force-unlock removes the lock record; the caution is verifying no real run holds it, since unlocking a live apply risks state corruption. A is catastrophic overkill. B does not touch locks. D is the misconception: locks do not self-expire — waiting achieves nothing.

q: A refactor moves aws_s3_bucket.logs into a child module as module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.logs. How can the existing bucket be kept without destroy and recreate?
options: moved blocks are the only way and they only work in the root
Delete the resource and re-import it
Hand-edit the state JSON in a text editor
terraform state mv 'aws_s3_bucket.logs' 'module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.logs' — rewrites the state address so the existing bucket is adopted at its new address
explain: D is correct: state mv re-addresses the tracked object, so the next plan sees the real bucket already at the new address. A is wrong on both counts: state mv is the CLI alternative and works with module addresses. B is wasteful toil. C is dangerous: hand-editing risks corrupting state checksums and structure.

q: An engineer wants to quickly inspect the attributes Terraform currently tracks for a single resource. Which command prints them?
options: terraform state show aws_instance.web — prints the tracked attributes for that resource address
terraform console
terraform output
terraform get
explain: A is correct: state show renders one resource's state attributes. B evaluates expressions rather than dumping state. C is the trap: output shows only declared outputs, not resource attributes. D downloads modules — unrelated.

q: Configuration should tag resources with the current workspace name, e.g. Environment = <workspace>. Which built-in reference provides the active workspace name?
options: var.workspace
terraform.workspace — the built-in value exposing the current workspace name for interpolation
env.WORKSPACE
data.terraform_remote_state.workspace
explain: B is correct: terraform.workspace is the built-in reference to the active workspace name. A invents an input variable that does not exist by default. C invents an environment variable. D misuses the remote-state data source, which reads other states' outputs, not the current workspace name.

q: The app configuration needs the VPC ID that the network configuration already manages in its own state. Which data source reads another workspace's root outputs?
options: A module block pointing at the network directory
Importing the network state file by hand
The terraform_remote_state data source, configured with the same backend — it exposes the other configuration's root outputs
data.terraform_state
explain: C is correct: terraform_remote_state reads a remote backend's state outputs, the designed cross-configuration sharing mechanism. A is wrong: modules share configuration, not state. B is manual and fragile. D invents a data source name that does not exist.

q: State has become corrupted and the team must fix it by hand. What is the sanctioned workflow for manual state surgery?
options: Edit terraform.tfstate in place while a lock is held
Run terraform apply -refresh-only
Delete everything and re-create
terraform state pull, carefully edit the downloaded JSON, then terraform state push — with no concurrent runs in flight
explain: D is correct: pull/push is the supported manual-edit path, done while nobody else is operating on the state. A is dangerous: editing the live file risks corruption and races. B only refreshes values; it cannot repair structural corruption. C is the scorched-earth option, unnecessary when the state can be repaired.

q: What is the minimal valid backend 's3' block for storing state?
options: bucket, key, and region — the three required arguments that locate the state object
bucket alone
access_key and secret_key
dynamodb_table
explain: A is correct: bucket, key, and region are the required S3 backend arguments. B is incomplete: without key and region Terraform cannot locate the object. C is the misconception: credentials are supplied via environment or IAM, not as required backend arguments. D is optional (and the DynamoDB locking path is deprecated), not required.

q: How are resource attribute values stored in the state file, and what does that imply for state storage?
options: Encrypted by default with a Terraform-managed key
In cleartext — sensitive values are only redacted in CLI output, so the backend itself must provide encryption at rest and tight access controls
Irreversibly hashed
Only in memory, never on disk
explain: B is correct: state is JSON in cleartext, and sensitive marking only affects display — whoever can read the state can read the secrets, so backend-side encryption and access control are mandatory. A is the dangerous misconception: Terraform applies no default encryption to state contents. C is wrong: values must be readable for planning. D is false: state persists to the backend on disk.

q: The S3 backend declares key = 'network/terraform.tfstate'. After creating and selecting a non-default workspace and running apply, where does that workspace's state object live?
options: s3://bucket/network/terraform.tfstate — it overwrites the default workspace state
A separate bucket named after the workspace
s3://bucket/env:/staging/network/terraform.tfstate — non-default workspaces are namespaced under the backend's workspace key prefix
It shares the default state; workspaces do not isolate state
explain: C is correct: the S3 backend namespaces non-default workspaces under the workspace key prefix (default 'env:'), keeping states separate in one bucket. A would clobber the default state — workspaces exist to prevent exactly that. B is wrong: the bucket is shared. D contradicts the entire purpose of workspaces.

q: A shared module requires Terraform 1.5 or newer because it uses features older CLIs lack. How should the module declare this requirement so it is enforced before any operation?
options: In the required_providers block
With a comment at the top of main.tf
With a terraform_version input variable
terraform { required_version = '>= 1.5' } — Terraform checks the running CLI version against this constraint before init, plan, or apply
explain: D is correct: required_version is the enforced gate on the CLI version itself. A is the classic trap: required_providers constrains provider versions, not Terraform core. B is unenforced documentation. C invents a mechanism that does not exist.

q: A configuration must use the hashicorp/aws provider, version ~> 5.0. Which block declares both the source and the version constraint?
options: terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = 'hashicorp/aws', version = '~> 5.0' } } }
terraform { required_version = '~> 5.0' }
provider 'aws' { version = '~> 5.0' }
The dependency lock file alone
explain: A is correct: required_providers declares each provider's registry source and version constraint together. B is the trap: required_version constrains Terraform core, not providers. C is outdated: version inside provider blocks is deprecated and ignored. D is wrong: the lock file records selections; it does not declare requirements.

q: A team commits .terraform.lock.hcl to version control. A new hire asks why this generated file is tracked. What is the correct explanation?
options: It speeds up terraform apply
It records the exact selected provider versions and their hashes, so every machine installs identical, cryptographically verified providers
It stores a copy of the state
It is per-user and should actually be gitignored
explain: B is correct: the lock file pins provider selections with hashes, giving reproducible and tamper-evident installs across the team and CI. A is wrong: it is about consistency, not speed. C confuses it with terraform.tfstate. D states the exact misconception: the lock file is meant to be committed, unlike the .terraform directory.

q: The team wants to upgrade the AWS provider from 4.x to 5.x, a major version with breaking changes. What is the safe upgrade workflow?
options: Run init -upgrade and apply straight to production
Edit the lock file's version to 5.0 by hand
Read the provider CHANGELOG and upgrade guide for breaking changes, update the version constraint, run init -upgrade, and validate with plan in a non-production workspace first
Providers upgrade themselves automatically on the next apply
explain: C is correct: major upgrades demand changelog review, a constraint change, lock update, and a safe plan-first validation. A is reckless: prod-first with breaking changes. B is dangerous: hand-edited hashes fail verification and skip the changelog. D is false: nothing upgrades without an explicit init -upgrade and constraint change.

q: A provider crashes during apply and HashiCorp support asks for debug-level logs. How does the engineer enable detailed Terraform logging?
options: terraform plan -verbose
TF_DEBUG=1
Inspect the state file for log entries
Set TF_LOG=DEBUG (or TRACE) — the TF_LOG environment variable enables detailed logging, including provider RPC traffic at higher levels
explain: D is correct: TF_LOG controls Terraform's log verbosity (TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR). A is invalid: no -verbose flag exists. B invents the wrong variable name. C is wrong: the state file holds resource data, never logs.

q: A team debates constraining a provider with >= 5.0 versus ~> 5.0. Why is the pessimistic operator the safer default?
options: ~> 5.0 allows 5.x patches and minors but blocks 6.0, while >= 5.0 would silently admit a future breaking major release
>= 5.0 is actually the safer choice
The two operators are identical
~> 5.0 blocks all updates including patches
explain: A is correct: ~> 5.0 means >= 5.0, < 6.0, admitting fixes while excluding breaking majors; >= 5.0 leaves the door open to 6.0, 7.0, and beyond. B states the opposite of the safe practice. C is false: their upper bounds differ completely. D is false: ~> explicitly permits minor and patch updates.

q: An engineer must re-address dozens of resources with terraform state mv and wants to preview every move without touching state. Which flag previews the operation?
options: -auto-approve
-dry-run — prints the planned address changes without modifying state
-target
No preview exists; hand-edit the state JSON instead
explain: B is correct: state mv -dry-run shows what would change, the safe rehearsal for bulk moves. A is apply's flag, meaningless here. C scopes plan/apply operations, not state mv. D is wrong and dangerous: dry-run exists precisely so nobody hand-edits state JSON.

q: A datacenter has no internet access, so terraform init cannot reach the public registry. How can provider installation work in this air-gapped environment?
options: Providers cannot be installed without internet access
Commit one machine's .terraform directory to version control
Configure a filesystem mirror via the provider_installation block in the CLI configuration file, then init installs from the local mirror
Use init -backend=false
explain: C is correct: provider_installation in the CLI config file directs Terraform to a filesystem (or network) mirror for air-gapped installs. A is false: mirrors exist precisely for this. B is fragile and wrong: .terraform is a local cache, not a distribution mechanism. D is unrelated: -backend=false skips backend setup, not provider installation.

q: A plan succeeds but prints 'Warning: Argument X is deprecated and will be removed in a future version'. What does this mean and what should the team do?
options: The plan failed and nothing will apply
The warning can be ignored forever
The resource was already destroyed
The configuration still works for now, but the argument will be removed in a future major version — update the configuration before upgrading
explain: D is correct: deprecation warnings are advance notice — functionality remains until the removal version, so the fix belongs in the upgrade runbook. A confuses warnings with errors: the plan succeeded. B is the risky misconception: ignoring it guarantees a future breakage. C is false: nothing was destroyed; the plan completed.

q: Provider 5.2 introduced a regression and the team must return to 5.1, but terraform init -upgrade keeps them on 5.2. Why, and what is the correct downgrade path?
options: init -upgrade only moves versions upward within the constraints — set the constraint to permit 5.1 (e.g. version = '5.1') and run init again to reinstall the older version
Use terraform init -downgrade
Delete the lock file and nothing else
Downgrading a provider is impossible
explain: A is correct: -upgrade never selects a lower version; downgrading means constraining to the older version and re-running init. B invents a flag that does not exist. C alone is insufficient: without a constraint change, init re-selects the newest allowed. D is false: downgrades are routine via constraints.

q: After a local terraform apply, the working directory contains terraform.tfstate.backup. What is this file?
options: A backup of the configuration files
The pre-apply state snapshot — the local backend preserves the previous state version as .backup on every state-changing operation
The state lock file
It is created only by terraform destroy
explain: B is correct: the local backend keeps the prior state as .backup each time state is rewritten, giving a rollback point. A confuses it with configuration backups. C is wrong: locking uses a separate mechanism, not this file. D is false: every apply that changes state creates one, not just destroys.

q: A legacy configuration uses the template provider's data 'template_file' resources. During maintenance, what is the supported modern replacement?
options: Keep the template provider — it remains fully supported
Replace each template with a local-exec provisioner
Move the templates into the backend block
Replace data.template_file with the built-in templatefile() function — the template provider is archived and templatefile() is its successor
explain: D is correct: the template provider was archived; its functionality lives on as the built-in templatefile() function. A is the dangerous misconception: archived providers get no updates. B is the wrong tool: provisioners execute scripts, they do not render templates. C is nonsense: backends store state, not templates.

q: A team wants a nightly job that detects manual console changes without modifying anything. Which job design implements drift monitoring?
options: Run terraform apply every night
Run terraform plan -refresh-only and alert on any non-empty diff — it detects real-world drift while changing nothing
Run terraform destroy -target on drifted resources nightly
Run terraform fmt -check nightly
explain: B is correct: a refresh-only plan surfaces drift as a diff with zero infrastructure impact, ideal for a monitoring job. A is remediation, not monitoring — blind nightly applies can fight legitimate changes. C is destructive and absurd as a monitor. D checks file formatting, which has nothing to do with drift.

q: A team wants runs to execute on HCP Terraform but inside their own network, because the configuration manages private resources unreachable from the internet. Which execution mode fits?
options: Agent execution mode — agents running in the team's infrastructure poll HCP Terraform and execute runs locally
Local execution mode with state committed to git
Remote execution mode
VCS-driven workflow without agents
explain: A is correct: agents keep execution inside the private network while HCP Terraform orchestrates. B is wrong: local mode runs on the operator's machine, and state must never be committed to git. C is the trap: remote mode runs on HashiCorp's infrastructure, which cannot reach private resources. D does not solve the network problem: VCS triggering says nothing about where runs execute.

q: Every push to the infrastructure repository automatically queues a plan in the connected workspace, with no CLI involved. Which workflow is this?
options: CLI-driven workflow
VCS-driven workflow — the workspace is connected to a version control repo and HCP Terraform creates runs automatically on changes
API-driven workflow
Speculative-only workflow
explain: B is correct: VCS-driven workspaces trigger runs from repository events. A is wrong: CLI-driven runs start from terraform plan/apply on a workstation. C is wrong: API-driven runs originate from API calls, not git pushes. D confuses a run type (speculative plans) with the trigger mechanism.

q: A CI pipeline authenticates to HCP Terraform with a team API token. What determines what that token is allowed to do?
options: Team tokens can do anything in the organization
Team tokens can only read state
Whatever the team's permissions allow — the token inherits the team's permission scope, so least-privilege team membership controls what the token can touch
Team tokens can manage users and teams
explain: C is correct: a team token's power equals its team's permissions — scope the team minimally and the token is minimal. A is the dangerous misconception: only owner teams approach that. B is too narrow: permissions depend on the team, not the token type. D is wrong: user and team management is an organization-owner capability.

q: An organization runs agents in both prod and dev networks and must ensure production workspaces never execute on dev agents. How are agents grouped for this isolation?
options: Workspaces
Variable sets
Teams
Agent pools — named groups of agents; a workspace bound to a pool executes only on that pool's agents
explain: D is correct: agent pools partition the agent fleet, and workspaces bind to a pool. A is wrong: workspaces consume agents, they do not group them. B manages variables, not compute. C groups people and permissions, not agents.

q: An enterprise organizes 300 workspaces by business unit and wants to scope variable sets and team access to each unit's workspaces. What groups workspaces for this purpose?
options: Agent pools
A separate organization per business unit
Projects — the grouping construct for workspaces, used to organize them and scope variable sets and team permissions
Workspace tags
explain: C is correct: projects group workspaces for organization and for scoping variable sets and team permissions. A is wrong: agent pools group execution agents, not workspaces. B is overkill and misuses organizations. D is the trap: tags filter and label, but scoping is projects' job.

q: A run is blocked at the 'Policy Check' stage and cannot proceed to apply. What is being evaluated at this stage?
options: Whether the Terraform CLI version is current
Sentinel (or OPA) policies evaluated against the plan — a failing enforcement-level policy blocks the apply until the configuration is fixed
Whether all variable values are non-empty
The wording of the git commit message
explain: B is correct: the policy-check stage runs policy-as-code against the planned changes, and enforcement-level failures gate the apply. A is wrong: version checks happen earlier and do not block this way. C is wrong: variable presence is validated during plan. D is nonsense: commit messages are never policy inputs at this stage.

q: The team wants the #deploys Slack channel notified whenever a run fails in a production workspace. Where is this configured?
options: With a local-exec provisioner
HCP Terraform has no run notifications
Workspace Settings → Notifications — configure Slack, email, or webhook alerts for run events such as failures
With a Sentinel policy
explain: C is correct: workspace notification settings natively support Slack, email, and webhooks for run lifecycle events. A is the wrong tool: provisioners run commands during resource operations, they do not watch runs. B is false: notifications are a built-in feature. D is wrong: Sentinel enforces policy; it does not send chat alerts.

q: A workspace currently triggers runs on pushes to main, but the team now cuts releases from a release/2.0 branch and wants runs to follow it. How is this changed?
options: Workspaces automatically follow every branch
Delete the workspace and recreate it
The tracked branch cannot be changed after creation
Update the workspace's VCS Branch setting to the release branch — a workspace tracks a single branch for automatic runs
explain: D is correct: the workspace's version-control settings define which branch triggers runs, and it can be repointed. A is the misconception: automatic runs follow one configured branch, not all. B is unnecessary toil. C is false: the branch setting is editable.

q: An organization has 200 workspaces and an auditor needs to review all of them belonging to the payments team. What is the intended mechanism for finding them?
options: Workspace tags — tag workspaces (e.g. team:payments) and filter the workspace list by tag
Give every workspace the identical name
Tags change a workspace's execution mode
Workspace names cannot be searched or filtered
explain: A is correct: tags are the organization and filtering mechanism for workspaces at scale. B is impossible: workspace names are unique. C is wrong: tags do not affect execution. D is the misconception tags exist to solve.

q: A private registry module is backed by a version-control repository. The team just merged the code for v2.0.0. What publishes that version to the registry?
options: Uploading a zip archive in the HCP Terraform UI
Pushing a git tag such as v2.0.0 to the module repository — the registry publishes versions from VCS tags
Editing the version argument in consumers' module blocks
Versions are published automatically on every merge to the default branch
explain: B is correct: registry versions are cut from git tags on the module repo. A is wrong: the registry is VCS-backed, not zip-upload based. C confuses the consumer side (selecting a version) with publishing. D is the misconception: merges alone publish nothing — the tag is the release event.

q: A backend 'remote' block needs an organization and a hostname. A team on standard HCP Terraform (not Terraform Enterprise) asks what hostname to use. What is correct?
options: A custom hostname is always required
The remote backend does not need an organization
organization is required; hostname defaults to app.terraform.io and only needs setting for Terraform Enterprise with a custom hostname
The backend 'remote' block is deprecated
explain: C is correct: organization is mandatory, while hostname defaults to app.terraform.io — the SaaS address — and is only overridden for self-hosted Enterprise. A is wrong: no custom hostname is needed for SaaS. B is wrong: organization is required. D is false: the remote backend remains fully supported alongside the newer cloud block.

q: A workspace sets AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID as a Terraform variable, but provider authentication fails during runs. What is the misconfiguration?
options: HCP Terraform does not support AWS provider authentication
Credentials must be set as Environment variables, not Terraform variables — Terraform variables feed configuration; environment variables are exposed to the provider process
The variable needs the HCL checkbox enabled
A team token must be used instead of an access key
explain: B is correct: provider credentials belong in environment variables; Terraform variables become configuration values, which providers do not read for authentication. A is false: AWS auth works fine via environment variables. C is the trap: the HCL checkbox marks complex-typed Terraform variables — irrelevant to credential delivery. D confuses HCP API tokens with cloud provider credentials.
